lessons.title: Respiratory System, Its Properties and the Nose and Pharynx
lessons.notes_html:
Respiration is the exchange of respiratory gases and the release of energy from food. Breathing or ventilation is simply taking fresh air, with more O₂, into the lungs and removing air with more CO₂ out of the lungs. This lesson introduces the human respiratory system and its first parts, the nose and the pharynx.

14.1 Respiratory System of Man

External RespirationInternal Respiration
Exchange of respiratory gases (O₂ and CO₂) between the organism and its environment, and between the circulatory fluid and the external environmentA biochemical process within the cell that oxidises food molecules; exchange of gases between the cell and the circulatory fluid
No ATP or water is formedATP, CO₂ and water are produced
It is aerobicIt may be aerobic or anaerobic

14.1.1 Properties of Respiratory System

A respiratory surface shows three characteristics for ready exchange of gases through diffusion:

  • It should be large, moist and highly permeable, so respiratory gases can pass through it easily.
  • It should be a thin epithelium (1 mm or less) and possess a network of blood capillaries, which facilitates rapid transport and diffusion of gases between the surface and the blood.
  • A good ventilation mechanism should be present to maintain a steep diffusion gradient.

14.1.2 Components of Respiratory System

The respiratory system consists of the respiratory tract (the air passageway) and the respiratory organs, a pair of lungs. The upper respiratory tract includes the nostrils, nasal cavities and pharynx; the lower respiratory tract includes the larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. The air sac or alveolus is the functional unit of the lungs.

14.1.3 Nose

The nose is the only externally visible part of the respiratory system, made of bones, cartilages and fatty muscle tissue. Air enters through the external nostrils into the nasal cavities (nasal sacs), two vestibules separated by the nasal septum, and leaves by the internal nares into the pharynx.

  • The cavities contain a network of hair and are lined by mucus membranes that secrete mucus, along with cilia.
  • Hair, mucus and cilia trap dust and solid particles in the air; the cilia push them to the pharynx for removal. This is a defence mechanism.
  • The mucus also moistens the air and brings the temperature of inhaled air close to body temperature, about 30°C depending on the external temperature.

14.1.4 Pharynx

The pharynx is a muscular, mucus-secreting passage that connects the oral and nasal cavities to the oesophagus and the larynx, so it is part of both the respiratory and the digestive system. It has three sections: the nasopharynx, the oropharynx and the laryngopharynx. Air passes from the pharynx into the larynx, while food passes into the oesophagus.

Key Points

  • Breathing (ventilation) moves air in and out; internal respiration inside cells produces ATP, CO₂ and water.
  • A good respiratory surface is large, moist, permeable and thin, has many capillaries, and is well ventilated.
  • Upper tract: nostrils, nasal cavities and pharynx. Lower tract: larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.
  • The nose traps dust with hair, mucus and cilia, and moistens and warms the air.
  • The pharynx serves both respiration and digestion and has three sections.

lessons.title: Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi, Alveolar Ducts and Alveoli
lessons.notes_html:
From the pharynx, air passes through the larynx and the trachea into the bronchi, bronchioles and finally the alveoli, where gaseous exchange actually takes place.

14.1.5 Larynx

The larynx or voice box is made of cartilages and muscles and lies at the top of the trachea. Its opening, the glottis, is covered during swallowing by a flap, the epiglottis, which closes the passage to the lungs when food is coming and prevents food entering the windpipe. Inside the larynx, the vocal cords produce the voice.

14.1.6 Trachea and Bronchi

The trachea (windpipe) is a ciliated membranous tube about 10-12 cm long. It is supported by 15-22 C-shaped cartilaginous rings, which keep it open at all times. It runs ventral to the oesophagus up to the 5th thoracic vertebra, where it divides into two primary bronchi, one entering each lung.

  • Each bronchus redivides inside the lung into many bronchi made of plate-like cartilages.
  • The bronchi finally give rise to smaller membranous tubes, the bronchioles, less than 1 cm in diameter. Bronchioles lack cartilages and are made of ciliated cuboidal epithelium and a layer of circular smooth muscles.

14.1.7 Alveolar Ducts and Alveoli

The bronchioles divide and subdivide to form respiratory bronchioles, which eventually terminate into alveolar ducts. These ducts open into small collections of air sacs called alveoli, the actual sites of gaseous exchange.

  • Each lung possesses about 350 million alveoli, giving an enormous surface area for gaseous exchange. Note: the exercise in the book prints 35 million; the unit text figure of about 350 million is the one to learn.
  • Alveoli are made of simple squamous epithelium and have a rich network of capillaries, so gases diffuse rapidly between air and blood. The book prints the wall as 0.1 cm thick; that figure looks like a printing error, because the alveolar wall is in fact extremely thin, which is why diffusion is so rapid.
  • Alveoli contain collagen and elastin proteins, which allow them to expand and recoil easily during breathing.

Alveoli at the end of an alveolar duct, wrapped in capillaries: oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.

Key Points

  • The epiglottis covers the glottis during swallowing; the vocal cords in the larynx produce voice.
  • The trachea is 10-12 cm long with 15-22 C-shaped rings and divides at the 5th thoracic vertebra into two primary bronchi.
  • Bronchioles are under 1 cm wide and lack cartilage.
  • Alveolar ducts end in alveoli, about 350 million per lung, the real sites of gaseous exchange.
  • Collagen and elastin let alveoli expand and recoil during breathing.

lessons.title: The Lungs, Breathing Mechanism, Respiratory Volumes and Control of Breathing
lessons.notes_html:
The lungs are the respiratory organs of man and all terrestrial vertebrates. This lesson covers their structure, how breathing moves air in and out, the volumes of air they hold, and how breathing is controlled.

14.1.8 Respiratory Organs (Lungs)

There is a pair of lungs in the thoracic cavity, protected by the rib cage. Each lung is surrounded by a double-layered thin membrane, the pleura, and pleural fluid surrounds the lungs, reducing friction as they expand and contract. The right lung is larger and divided into lobes; the lungs are spongy and elastic because of their millions of alveoli.

14.1.9 Mechanism of Breathing (Ventilation)

Breathing takes place in two phases, driven by the ribs and the diaphragm, the muscular sheet below the lungs:

InspirationExpiration
Rib (intercostal) muscles contract; ribs move upward and outwardRib muscles relax; ribs move downward and inward
Diaphragm contracts and moves downward, becoming flatterDiaphragm relaxes and projects into the thoracic cavity, becoming dome-shaped
Chest cavity increases; its pressure drops below atmospheric pressureChest cavity decreases; pressure inside rises
Air rushes through the respiratory passage into the lungsThe elastic lungs contract and force the air out

Note: the unit Summary prints that intercostal muscles make the rib cage move downward and backward; that describes expiration, not inspiration, and contradicts the main text above, which should be followed.

When the diaphragm flattens the chest expands and air enters; when it domes up, air is forced out.

14.1.10 Lungs Respiratory Volumes and Capacities

  • Tidal volume — The amount of air moved in and out with each quiet breath, normally 500 ml.
  • Inspiratory reserve volume — The additional air, about 3000 to 4000 ml, that can be inspired by forced inspiration over and above the tidal volume.
  • Expiratory reserve volume — The extra air that can be expired by forced expiration after a normal expiration.
  • Residual volume — About 1200-1500 ml of air always remains in the lungs and never leaves them; this is the residual volume (about 1.5 litre).
  • Combinations of volumes give capacities, such as inspiratory capacity, functional residual capacity, vital capacity and total lung capacity, as shown in the book figure of respiratory volumes.

14.1.11 Controlling Centres of Breathing

Breathing is controlled both involuntarily and voluntarily. The medulla of the brain is the controlling centre for involuntary breathing; its lower portion acts as the inspiratory centre, while the upper and lateral portions act as expiratory centres. The normal breathing rate is 15-20 times per minute. The voluntary, conscious control centre is the cerebral cortex of the cerebrum, and the limbic system also acts as a respiratory centre during emotional acts.

Key Points

  • Each lung is covered by the double-layered pleura, with pleural fluid around it.
  • Inspiration: ribs up and out, diaphragm down, chest pressure falls, air rushes in. Expiration is the reverse.
  • Tidal volume is 500 ml; inspiratory reserve volume is 3000-4000 ml; residual volume is 1200-1500 ml.
  • The medulla controls involuntary breathing; the cerebral cortex controls voluntary breathing.
  • Normal breathing rate is 15-20 times per minute.

lessons.title: Respiratory Pigments and Transport of Oxygen
lessons.notes_html:
Respiratory gases, CO₂ and O₂, are transported to the various body regions by means of blood. Because oxygen is not very soluble in plasma, the blood uses special respiratory pigments to carry it.

14.2 Mechanism of Transport of Respiratory Gases

The blood carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs. In man the respiratory pigment is haemoglobin in the red blood cells, helped in the muscles by myoglobin.

14.2.1 Respiratory Pigments and Their Role

i) Haemoglobin is the most important respiratory pigment, present in many animals including man. It is a complex protein consisting of four polypeptide chains, 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains, having 574 amino acids. Each chain is associated with a haeme group, an iron-containing group consisting of porphin with a central atom of ferrous (iron) between four pyrrole rings.

  • Function of haemoglobin: this iron-containing protein in the red blood cells of vertebrates transports oxygen to the tissues. It increases the oxygen carrying capacity of the blood in humans to about 75 times.
  • Iron in haemoglobin combines loosely with oxygen in the RBCs of the pulmonary capillaries to form oxyhaemoglobin. This bright red blood circulates to the tissue cells, where oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen, because haemoglobin gives up its oxygen where the oxygen concentration is low; the blood then becomes purple red. The deoxygenated haemoglobin returns to the lungs to become oxyhaemoglobin again.
  • One haemoglobin molecule can carry four molecules of oxygen, one at each haeme group.

ii) Myoglobin is another respiratory pigment in man, present in the muscles of humans and other mammals, which is why meat is red. It is made of one iron-containing polypeptide chain of 154 amino acids and binds only one molecule of oxygen.

  • Function of myoglobin: it stores oxygen in the muscle and gives up oxygen when the partial pressure of oxygen is below 20 mm of Hg. It has a greater affinity for oxygen than haemoglobin.
HaemoglobinMyoglobin
In red blood cellsIn muscles
Four polypeptide chains, 574 amino acidsOne polypeptide chain, 154 amino acids
Carries four molecules of oxygenBinds one molecule of oxygen
Transports oxygen to the tissuesStores oxygen in muscle; releases it below 20 mm of Hg

14.2.2 Transport of Oxygen in Blood

About 97-98% of oxygen is carried by haemoglobin, while the remaining 2-3% is transported as dissolved oxygen in plasma. The reaction is: Hb (Haemoglobin) + 4O₂ → 4O₂Hb (oxyhaemoglobin). Note: the book prints the enzyme name carbonic anhydrase above this arrow; that enzyme belongs to CO₂ transport (next lesson), not to oxygen binding, which needs no enzyme.

The ability of haemoglobin to bind oxygen is called the oxygen carrying capacity of blood, and it is directly proportional to the partial pressure of O₂. The maximum O₂ carrying capacity of blood at sea level is 20 ml per 100 ml of blood (100% saturated). Haemoglobin loses oxygen when the partial pressure falls below 60 mm of Hg.

Key Points

  • Haemoglobin has 4 chains (2 alpha, 2 beta), 574 amino acids and 4 haeme groups, and carries 4 O₂ molecules.
  • Haemoglobin raises the oxygen carrying capacity of blood about 75 times.
  • Myoglobin, in muscle, has one chain of 154 amino acids, binds one O₂, and releases it below 20 mm of Hg.
  • 97-98% of O₂ travels as oxyhaemoglobin; 2-3% dissolves in plasma.
  • Maximum oxygen carrying capacity at sea level is 20 ml per 100 ml of blood.

lessons.title: Transport of Carbon Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
Compared with oxygen, CO₂ is more soluble and easily dissolves in the tissue fluid. CO₂ from the tissues passes into the blood plasma within the tissue capillaries, and is carried to the lungs in three ways.

14.2.3 Transport of Carbon Dioxide

  • i) As bicarbonate ions (about 70%)
  • ii) As carboxyhaemoglobin (about 23%)
  • iii) As dissolved CO₂ in plasma (about 7%) — the book also describes this same small share as carried with the help of plasma proteins, an inefficient way to carry CO₂. Learn the three shares as 70%, 23% and 7%.

i) As bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻): CO₂ released by oxidation in the tissues enters the blood plasma. In the blood, CO₂ combines with water inside the RBCs, in the presence of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, to form carbonic acid: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃. The carbonic acid splits quickly into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bicarbonate ions: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. All these reactions are reversible. The bicarbonates diffuse out of the red blood cells and are carried by the plasma, while the H⁺ is absorbed by the globin protein of haemoglobin. When the blood reaches the alveoli of the lung capillaries, the bicarbonate ions again combine with H⁺ to form carbonic acid, which splits into H₂O and CO₂; this CO₂ diffuses out of the capillaries into the alveoli and is expelled by expiration.

Role of hydrogen ions: the pH of blood may decrease due to H⁺ ions, but this does not occur, since haemoglobin acts as a buffer for hydrogen ions. Oxyhaemoglobin combines with hydrogen ions to become reduced into haemoglobin acid (HHb), and oxygen is released to the tissues: 4O₂Hb + H⁺ → HHb + 4O₂.

Hamburger phenomenon or chloride shift: this explains the maintenance of the balance of two ions, bicarbonate and chloride, moving in opposite directions through a special bicarbonate-chloride carrier protein in the plasma membrane of the RBC. When negatively charged bicarbonate ions diffuse out into the plasma, chloride ions diffuse into the RBCs to balance them. Inside the RBC the chloride combines with potassium (K⁺) to form potassium chloride (KCl), while in the plasma the bicarbonate combines with sodium (Na⁺) to form sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃). Thus the pH of blood is maintained at 7.4. The CO₂ concentration in arterial blood is 50 ml per 100 ml of blood, while venous blood contains 54 ml per 100 ml; only 4 ml of CO₂ is given off per 100 ml of blood as it passes through the lungs.

Inside the RBC, CO₂ forms bicarbonate, which leaves for the plasma while chloride enters in exchange — the chloride shift.

ii) As carboxyhaemoglobin: when the partial pressure of CO₂ is higher in the tissues than in the blood, CO₂ combines with the amino (globin) part of haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin (carbaminohaemoglobin), about 23% of the CO₂. In the lungs, where the partial pressure of CO₂ is less than in the blood, it breaks again and releases CO₂, which diffuses into the alveoli and is expelled.

iii) As plasma protein / dissolved CO₂: some CO₂, about 7%, is transported from tissue fluids to the lungs dissolved in plasma and with the help of plasma proteins, which is a rather inefficient way to carry CO₂.

Key Points

  • CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate ions about 70%, as carboxyhaemoglobin about 23%, and dissolved in plasma about 7%.
  • Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs forms carbonic acid, which splits into H⁺ and bicarbonate ions.
  • Haemoglobin buffers H⁺, forming haemoglobin acid (HHb) and releasing oxygen to the tissues.
  • The chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon) balances bicarbonate leaving the RBC with chloride entering, keeping blood pH at 7.4.
  • At the lungs all the reactions reverse and CO₂ is expired from the alveoli.

lessons.title: Upper Respiratory Tract Infections, Pneumonia and Lung Cancer
lessons.notes_html:
Many problems in the respiratory system can take place if the inner lining of the respiratory organs is exposed continuously to unhealthy air containing poisonous gases, such as smoke and other pollutants.

14.3 Respiratory Disorders

The book divides the common disorders into upper respiratory tract infections and lower respiratory tract infections.

14.3.1 Upper Respiratory Tract Infections

i) Sinusitis: the sinuses are holes in the skull between the facial bones, and inflammation in these holes is called sinusitis. There are four large sinuses: two maxillary, inside the cheek bones, and two frontal, above the eyes. The sinuses are lined with mucus-secreting membrane, which secretes antibody-rich mucus that helps to trap and prevent the entry of irritants. Sinusitis may be acute (symptoms last 2-8 weeks) or chronic (slowly progressing, symptoms last much longer).

  • Causes: atmospheric pollution, dust, smoke, cold and wet climate, excessive dryness, and bacterial or viral infections.
  • Symptoms: the inflamed, mucus-filled sinuses cause pain and pressure in the face and a blocked nose.
  • Treatment: antibiotics or sulfa drugs for bacterial infection; antiallergic drugs and decongestants; and steam inhalation, called nebulization.

ii) Otitis media: an inflammation of the middle ear in which the Eustachian tube (the tube between the middle ear and pharynx) fills with fluid and becomes closed. If the fluid does not clear up after three months or more, it becomes chronic otitis media.

  • Causes: infection, allergy, recurrent attacks of common cold, blockage of the Eustachian tube, nutritional deficiency, sinusitis and measles.
  • Symptoms: sudden and severe earache, deafness, fever, headache, a sense of fullness of the ear, tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear), fluid leaking from the ear, and difficulty in speaking and hearing. Sometimes the eardrum bursts, discharging pus and relieving pain.
  • Treatment: in most cases, around 80% of patients, the fluid clears within three to four days and the eardrum repairs itself; for complicated cases antibiotic therapy is prescribed, and painkillers may be given for pain and fever.

14.3.2 Lower Respiratory Tract Infections

i) Pneumonia: a serious disorder of the lower respiratory tract, characterised by inflammation of the alveolar wall and accumulation of fluid and pus in the alveolar sacs of one or both lungs.

  • Causes: mostly bacterial genera such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae and Mycoplasma; sometimes viral, fungal or protozoan infection.
  • Symptoms: chill, chattering teeth, shaking, chest pain, sweating due to high fever, increased pulse rate and breathing, and violent coughing (due to Mycoplasma). In viral and other forms: dry cough, headache, fever, muscle pain, bluish colour of lips, and red-brown rusty-coloured sputum.
  • Treatment: mostly antibiotic treatment is prescribed.

ii) Lung cancer: cancer is a malignant tumour which may develop due to uncontrolled cell division. Lung cancer is one of the most common cancers in the world.

  • Causes: smoking and inhalation of unhealthy air. The chances of lung cancer are ten times more in persons who smoke or live in crowded smoky areas; it is estimated that 90% of lung cancer is caused by smoking.
  • Symptoms: in the initial stages, thickening and callusing (hardening) of the cells lining the bronchi occur, and the cilia in the nasal passage are destroyed. The tumour of disordered cells spreads and penetrates other tissues, known as metastases. The tumours grow until the bronchus is blocked, cutting off the air supply to the lung; trapped secretions become infected, causing pneumonia or a lung abscess.
  • Treatment: removal of the tumour or the whole lung before secondary growth occurs; this operation is called pneumonectomy. Chemotherapy (chemical agents) and radiotherapy (ionizing radiation) may also treat or control the cancer.

Key Points

  • Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses; it is acute at 2-8 weeks and chronic when it lasts much longer.
  • Otitis media is inflammation of the middle ear with a fluid-filled, closed Eustachian tube.
  • Pneumonia inflames the alveolar walls and fills alveoli with fluid and pus; antibiotics are the main treatment.
  • Lung cancer is a malignant tumour; about 90% is caused by smoking.
  • Pneumonectomy removes the lung; chemotherapy and radiotherapy may treat cancer.

lessons.title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis, Emphysema, Effects of Smoking and Breathing in Special Conditions
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson completes the lower respiratory tract infections with tuberculosis and emphysema, then covers the effects of smoking and the book Science, Technology and Society (STS) notes on breathing.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis (TB)

TB is an infectious bacterial disease of the lower respiratory system, more common in poor people due to poor living conditions and malnutrition.

  • Cause: a Bacillus bacterium known as Mycobacterium tubercle. About 15% develop TB of the lymph nodes, joints and gastrointestinal tract. Malnutrition and poor living conditions facilitate the bacteria to grow.
  • Symptoms: the inside of the lungs is damaged; alveoli burst and are replaced by inelastic connective tissue. The cells of the lungs form a protective capsule around the bacteria, called a tubercle (a small rounded swelling). The patient has cough, fever, pale face and sweating at night; in severe form, chest pain and breathlessness may occur.
  • Treatment: the disease is curable with appropriate drug therapy taken regularly for 9 months, called Daily Observed Treatment Short Course (DOTS). Note: the book prints the drugs as antibodies; the therapy meant is antibiotic drug therapy. Vaccination is also available, and because TB is contagious, the patient should be kept in an isolated environment.

Emphysema

Emphysema is a lung disorder in which the air sacs (alveoli) degenerate and the elastic fibres present in them are destroyed. As a result, alveolar walls degenerate and small alveoli combine to form larger alveoli, giving fewer alveoli with increased volume and decreased surface area for complete gaseous exchange.

  • Causes: the root cause is long-term irritation of the lungs by cigarette smoke, polluted air or industrial dust, and exposure of the lungs to certain drugs, coal, etc. Substances in tobacco smoke weaken the walls of the alveoli.
  • Symptoms: increasing breathlessness and difficulty in walking; the lung loses elasticity, so exhaling becomes difficult and a lot of air remains in the lung during expiration; inflammation and narrowing of bronchioles; fatigue, coughing and cyanosis (blue skin).
  • Treatment: there is no cure for emphysema, but some care may be helpful: avoid smoking, treat all respiratory infections immediately, and use oxygen equipment and respiratory devices.

14.3.3 Effects of Smoking on Human Health

  • The book states that 87% of cigarette smokers also develop lung cancer. Smoking also causes cancer of the mouth, larynx and oesophagus, and diseases such as chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
  • Cigarette smoke contains chemicals which irritate the respiratory tract and lungs, resulting in early morning coughing and wheezing.
  • Smoking is an indirect cause of pneumonia, because cigarette smoke damages or destroys cilia, so microbes cannot be trapped and easily settle in the respiratory system.
  • In healthy people the lungs are light pink; in smokers, the lungs appear dark and mottled.

Breathing in Special Conditions (STS)

  • Artificial breathing apparatus: the aqua-lung or SCUBA apparatus (Self Contained Under Water Breathing Apparatus) is used under water and in areas with low oxygen, such as at high altitude, and by fire fighters. It contains compressed air, a mixture called nitrox, about 35% oxygen and 65% nitrogen.
  • Birds have the most efficient respiratory system: air flows one way through the lungs, blood flows opposite to the air in the parabronchi (counter-current exchange), and air sacs reach into all parts of the body and even some bones, so birds can fly at high altitudes of about 6000 metres or more.
  • Hiccups are a sharp respiratory sound produced by spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm while the glottis is closed. Sneezing is a deep inspiration followed by closure of the glottis; the forceful expiration then blasts air through the nasal cavity and clears the upper passages. Snoring is a rough, raspy noise made when a sleeping person inhales through mouth and nose, usually by vibration of the soft palate.
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning: gases from incomplete combustion produce CO and toxic fumes. From gas heaters left on overnight in closed rooms, CO binds to haemoglobin and prevents the uptake of oxygen by haemoglobin. Symptoms are nausea, vomiting, headache and mental status changes.

Key Points

  • Pulmonary TB is caused by Mycobacterium tubercle; it is treated by the 9-month DOTS drug course.
  • In emphysema, alveolar walls break down, surface area falls, and there is no cure, only care.
  • Smoking causes lung and other cancers, bronchitis and emphysema, and destroys cilia.
  • SCUBA uses nitrox, about 35% oxygen and 65% nitrogen; birds use one-way airflow and air sacs.
  • Carbon monoxide from gas heaters binds haemoglobin and stops oxygen uptake.

lessons.title: Homeostasis, Its Mechanism and Feedback
lessons.notes_html:
Homeostasis (homeo: similar, stasis: standing still) is the ability of an organism to maintain a relatively stable internal state that persists despite changes in the outside environment. The term was coined by the physiologist Walter Cannon in 1932 in his famous book Wisdom of the Body. The internal changeable factors of the body, such as body temperature, blood pressure and blood pH, are called variables, and the ideal or normal value of a variable is called its set point.

15.1 Homeostasis

The three components of homeostasis named in this unit are:

  • Osmoregulation — maintenance of water and dissolved solutes in a nearly constant state.
  • Excretion — removal of metabolic wastes from the body, especially nitrogenous wastes.
  • Thermoregulation — maintenance of a constant body temperature.

15.1.1 Mechanism of Homeostasis

Homeostasis is a self-regulating process by which an organism maintains stability while adjusting to changing external conditions. Every homeostatic system has three basic components, forming a biological control system:

  • Receptor — Detects the change in the internal environment. The change that excites the receptor is the stimulus. Information from the receptor travels by the afferent (incoming) pathway to the control centre.
  • Control centre (integrating centre) — Receives the information, compares the value of the variable with the set point and determines the appropriate response and course of action. Its information travels by the efferent (outgoing) pathway to the effector.
  • Effector — Gives the response which balances out the original stimulus and so maintains homeostasis.

Example: the maintenance of constant body temperature in man, i.e. 98.6F. When body temperature rises above this, we start sweating to cool ourselves so that the temperature is maintained.

The biological control system: stimulus, receptor, control centre and effector.

15.1.2 Concept of Feed Back Mechanism in Homeostasis

A feedback mechanism is a loop system wherein the system responds to a perturbation (change or disturbance). The response may be in the same direction (positive feedback) or in the opposite direction (negative feedback). In a biological sense, it is a process that tends to initiate or inhibit the production of any product (enzyme, hormone) in the body. It may be observed at the levels of cells, tissues and organs, and it regulates homeostasis to achieve a certain range of optimal conditions.

15.1.3 Negative Feedback Mechanism

Almost all homeostatic control mechanisms are negative feedback mechanisms. They change the variable back to its original state or ideal value, and thus create stability.

Example: control of blood glucose by insulin. When blood sugar (glucose) rises, receptors in the body sense the change and the control centre (pancreas) secretes insulin into the blood, effectively lowering the blood sugar level. Once the level reaches the homeostatic state, the pancreas stops releasing insulin. When the glucose level is low, glucagon is released from the pancreas; it stimulates the production of glucose in the liver, which increases the blood glucose level again.

15.1.4 Positive Feedback Mechanism

Positive feedback is exactly opposite to negative feedback: the output enhances the original stimulus. It is rare, takes place only in emergency situations, and creates instability.

Example: child birth. Contractions of the uterus send impulses to the pituitary gland. During labour, the hormone oxytocin is released from the pituitary gland and stimulates contractions of the uterus wall. The increase in contractions causes more oxytocin to be released, and the cycle goes on until the birth process is completed. Oxytocin is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland.

Key Points

  • Homeostasis is maintaining a relatively stable internal state despite outside changes; the term was coined by Walter Cannon (1932).
  • Variables are internal changeable factors; their normal value is the set point.
  • A control system has a receptor, a control centre and an effector.
  • Negative feedback reverses a deviation and creates stability, e.g. insulin and glucagon control of blood glucose.
  • Positive feedback enhances the stimulus, e.g. oxytocin in child birth.
  • Osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation are the components of homeostasis in this unit.

lessons.title: Osmoregulation and Osmoregulatory Adaptations in Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Osmoregulation is the process of maintaining water and solute concentration in the body at a constant or nearly constant state. It is important to maintain the mineral and water content of cells, and it also maintains the shape and size of cells, so it is an important mechanism for the homeostatic conditions of the body.

15.2 Osmoregulation

15.2.1 Osmoregulators and Osmoconformers

Osmoregulators are animals that maintain a constant internal osmotic environment in spite of changes in the external environment. They are hypotonic or hypertonic to their external environment and can live in almost all types of environments, i.e. fresh water, marine water and on land.

Osmoconformers are organisms whose body fluids are in osmotic balance with their environment. Their ionic composition may differ from that of the external environment, but their internal environment is isotonic to it. They can live only in the marine environment; generally, most marine invertebrates are osmoconformers.

OsmoregulatorsOsmoconformers
Maintain a constant internal osmotic state despite external changesInternal osmotic concentration changes with the surroundings
Hypotonic or hypertonic to the environmentIsotonic to the environment
Live in fresh water, marine water and on landLive only in the marine environment
Most vertebrates, including freshwater and marine bony fishesMost marine invertebrates

Problems Faced by Osmoregulators

  • In a hypotonic medium, endosmosis occurs, so they face excess of water and must eliminate the excess water.
  • In a hypertonic medium, exosmosis takes place, so they must continuously take in water.
  • Marine animals face excess of salts in the body, which come in along with water, so they have to get rid of the extra salts.

Note: in the book this Problems heading is printed without a number, between 15.2.1 and 15.2.3.

15.2.3 Osmoregulatory Adaptations in Animals

i) Fresh-water animals. Fresh water is hypotonic to the animals, so their main problem is excess of water:

  • They continuously excrete a large volume of dilute urine; their kidneys reabsorb the salts that are required in the body.
  • The book states that they remove extra salts in the form of ions to make the internal environment less hypertonic; the ion-removing cells are called ionocytes, located in amphibian skin and in the gills of fish. The book's figure also shows uptake of salt ions by the gills and gain of water and some ions in food.
  • Fresh-water protists possess a contractile vacuole to store and remove extra water.

ii) Marine animals. Marine water has a high salt concentration, so these animals face shortage of water and excess of salts:

  • Teleost (bony fish) continuously drink a large amount of water to compensate water loss, and excrete salt ions from the gills and in scanty urine.
  • Some marine fishes possess rectal glands in the rectum, which store and remove extra salts along with faeces.
  • Some marine fishes retain urea in the body to make the internal environment less hypotonic. To counteract the toxicity of urea they possess trimethylamineoxide (TMAO) in the blood. Urea and TMAO act as osmolytes — substances that contribute to the regulation of osmotic pressure in cells and tissues. Osmolytes are low molecular weight organic compounds, e.g. amino acids and urea.

iii) Terrestrial animals. Insects and most mammals are the successful groups of land animals; the threat of dehydration is their major problem, and adaptations that reduce water loss are the key to survival on land:

  • Insects have a waxy exoskeleton and excrete nitrogenous wastes in the form of uric acid; some are nocturnal and their eggs have an impermeable membrane to prevent water loss.
  • Terrestrial mammals usually have dead, keratinized, water-resisting cells in their skin; some are nocturnal, which reduces water loss by evaporation because of the lower temperature and higher humidity of night air.
  • The camel can store water and can survive even losing 25% of the water of its body.
  • Energy is utilized for osmoregulation activities, therefore these animals eat more food.

Note: the book prints, under mammals, anhydrobiosis (life without water) with the example Tradigrade — but as the book itself adds, the tardigrade is an invertebrate, not a mammal.

Key Points

  • Osmoregulation keeps water and solute concentration nearly constant and maintains cell shape and size.
  • Osmoregulators keep a constant internal osmotic state; osmoconformers stay isotonic with the sea.
  • Fresh-water animals excrete large volumes of dilute urine and reabsorb needed salts.
  • Marine bony fish drink sea water, lose water by osmosis, and remove salts through gills, urine and rectal glands; some retain urea with TMAO as osmolytes.
  • Land animals conserve water: waxy exoskeleton and uric acid in insects, keratinized skin in mammals; the camel survives losing 25% of its body water.

lessons.title: Excretion and the Relationship Between Excretory Products and Habitats
lessons.notes_html:
Excretion is a Latin word which means shifted out. It is the process by which animals remove metabolic wastes. Through excretion, organisms control osmotic pressure and maintain acid-base balance, so excretion promotes homeostasis.

15.3 Excretion

15.3.1 Relationship Between Excretory Products and Habitats

Most metabolic wastes must be dissolved in water to be excreted from the body, so the type and quantity of an animal's waste products mainly depend on the availability of water. The most significant excretory products are nitrogenous wastes, produced as a result of the breakdown of proteins and nucleic acids. The main nitrogenous excretory products are ammonia, urea and uric acid, which vary significantly in their toxicity and in the energy cost of producing them.

Ammonia

Animals that excrete ammonia as their chief nitrogenous waste need access to lots of water, because 1 gm of ammonia needs 500 ml of water for its elimination. Ammonia is the most toxic waste and cannot be stored in the body; it can only be tolerated at a very low concentration. Such a large amount of water is available only to fresh-water animals, so ammonia is the chief nitrogenous waste of fresh-water animals. Animals which excrete ammonia as their chief nitrogenous waste are called ammonotelic animals.

Urea

Most terrestrial animals and many marine species do not have access to sufficient water to excrete ammonia, so they convert ammonia into urea in their liver and excrete urea as their chief nitrogenous waste. The main advantage of urea is its low toxicity, and it needs less water: 1 g of urea requires only 50 ml of water for its removal. The main disadvantage is its energy cost — energy is consumed for the conversion of ammonia into urea. Animals which excrete urea as their main nitrogenous waste are called ureotelic.

Uric Acid

Insects, many reptiles and birds excrete uric acid as their chief nitrogenous waste. Uric acid is the least toxic and does not readily dissolve in water, so it can be excreted as a semisolid paste with very little loss of water: 1 gm of uric acid consumes only 1 ml of water for its excretion. It is a product of the metabolic breakdown of purine nucleotides, and it is even more energetically expensive than urea, requiring considerable ATPs for its synthesis from ammonia. Animals excreting uric acid as their primary nitrogenous waste are called uricotelics. In human adult males, deposition of uric acid crystals can cause gout, a painful joint inflammation.

Key Points

  • Excretion removes metabolic wastes, controls osmotic pressure and maintains acid-base balance.
  • The type of nitrogenous waste depends mainly on the availability of water.
  • Ammonia is most toxic and needs 500 ml water per gm — the waste of fresh-water, ammonotelic animals.
  • Urea is less toxic and needs 50 ml water per g — the waste of ureotelic land animals, made in the liver.
  • Uric acid is least toxic and needs only 1 ml water per gm, excreted as a semisolid paste by uricotelic insects, reptiles and birds.

lessons.title: Excretory System of Man, Kidney and Nephron
lessons.notes_html:
In man, the excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, each about 10 cm in length, and a pair of ureters for transporting urine. The two ureters drain into a common sac called the urinary bladder. During urination, urine is expelled from the bladder through a tube called the urethra, which empties to the outside near the vagina in females and through the penis in males. Sphincter muscles near the junction of the urethra and bladder regulate urination.

15.4 Excretory System of Man

15.4.1 Structure and Function of Kidney

The human kidney is a bean-shaped structure, reddish brown in colour, located in the lumbar region on both sides of the vertebral column. The left kidney is about 1.5–2 cm higher than the right kidney (the Summary's 1.5–20 cm is a printing error). Each kidney has an outer renal cortex and an inner renal medulla. The medulla contains cone-shaped structures called pyramids, whose pointed end is directed towards the hilus, the depressed area of the kidney in the middle. Both regions are supplied with blood by a renal artery and drained by a renal vein. Within the cortex and medulla lie tightly packed excretory tubules (nephrons) and associated blood vessels. The study of the structure, functions and diseases of the kidney is called nephrology.

The kidneys filter about 180-litre blood in 24 hours and only 1–1.5 litre urine is formed. In adults the kidneys form only 0.5% of body weight.

Nephron

The nephrons are the structural and functional units of the kidney; there are about 1 million nephrons in each kidney. Once a person reaches the age of 40, the number of functional nephrons starts falling at the rate of 1% a year. There are two types:

  • Cortical nephrons — Located in the cortex of the kidney; more in number, about 80–85% of the total nephrons. They have short loops of Henle.
  • Juxtamedullary nephrons — Their coiled part is located in the cortex while the long loop of Henle (the U-shaped part) is located in the medulla. They are essential for the production of hypertonic (concentrated) urine and are active when there is a shortage of water in the body.

Each nephron consists of a single long tubule as well as a ball of capillaries called the glomerulus. The blind end of the tubule forms a cup-shaped structure called Bowman's capsule, which surrounds the glomerulus. The part of the nephron behind Bowman's capsule is the renal tubule, which has three main parts:

  • Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) — Lies between Bowman's capsule and the loop of Henle.
  • Loop of Henle — A U-shaped structure with a descending limb and an ascending limb; it lies between the proximal and distal convoluted tubules.
  • Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) — Located between the loop of Henle and the collecting duct.

A collecting duct is a straight tubule which opens into the pelvis region of the kidney. A single collecting duct receives many nephrons, and many collecting ducts combine to form a large collecting duct.

A nephron: glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.

Blood Circulation in Nephron

Each nephron is supplied with blood by an afferent arteriole, which brings blood from the renal artery. The afferent arteriole gives a bunch of capillaries called the glomerulus. From the glomerulus, the efferent arteriole carries blood to the peritubular capillaries, which surround the nephron and extend downward to form the vasa recta at the base of the loop of Henle in the medulla region. The peritubular capillaries drain into renal venules, and the venules drain into the renal vein.

Function of Kidney

The kidney is a vital homeostatic organ. Its functions include production of hormones (e.g. renin, erythropoietin), regulation of fluid balance and control of blood pressure. However, the primary function of the kidney is to make urine and purify blood.

Key Points

  • The excretory system of man: a pair of kidneys (about 10 cm each), ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.
  • The kidney has an outer cortex and an inner medulla with pyramids; the left kidney is 1.5–2 cm higher than the right.
  • Kidneys filter about 180 litres in 24 hours and form only 1–1.5 litres of urine.
  • The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney — about 1 million per kidney.
  • Cortical nephrons are 80–85% with short loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and produce concentrated urine.
  • Blood route: renal artery, afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, renal venules, renal vein.

lessons.title: Urine Formation, Counter Current Mechanism and Hormonal Control of Kidney
lessons.notes_html:
The kidneys filter unwanted substances from the blood and produce urine. There are 3 main steps of urine formation: glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption and tubular secretion.

Urine Formation

i) Glomerular filtration (pressure filtration or ultra-filtration). Blood enters the afferent arteriole and flows into the glomerulus, where the filterable blood components, such as water and nitrogenous wastes, move towards the inside of the glomerulus, and the non-filterable components, such as cells and serum albumins, exit via the efferent arteriole. The filterable components accumulate to form the glomerular filtrate.

ii) Selective reabsorption (tubular reabsorption). Useful substances — water, ions, glucose, etc. — are reabsorbed into the peritubular capillaries from the entire length of the renal tubule and collecting duct. Most of the water is reabsorbed by osmosis. Some mineral salts and, in a normal individual, all of the glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed through the walls of the tubule into the surrounding blood capillaries. Selective reabsorption of solutes requires energy, so the process involved is active transport; only those substances which the body requires are reabsorbed readily. Excess water, mineral salts and nitrogenous waste products (e.g. urea) pass along the nephron and out through the collecting tubule into the renal pelvis as urine.

iii) Tubular secretion. In this final step, substances such as hydrogen ions, creatinine and drugs are removed from the blood through the network of peritubular capillaries into the renal tubule and collecting duct. The end product of all these processes is urine — essentially a collection of substances that have not been reabsorbed during glomerular filtration and tubular reabsorption.

The Mechanism of Formation of Concentrated Urine (Counter Current Mechanism)

The mechanism by which kidneys produce concentrated urine when there is a shortage of water in the body is called the counter current mechanism. It occurs in mammals and is an adaptation to conserve water:

  • Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are transported from the ascending limb of Henle's loop by the vasa recta; the ascending limb of the vasa recta, in turn, transports these ions to the interstitium (the tissue between the loop of Henle and the vasa recta).
  • Thus a concentration gradient of 300 mOsm in the cortex to 1200 mOsm in the inner medulla is created. (Book text prints mm; its figure labels mOsm.)
  • Urea contributes to this process by being transported from the descending limb of the loop of Henle to the interstitium.
  • As urine flows downwards in the collecting tubule, it encounters higher and higher concentrations of solutes in the interstitium, so it goes on losing water due to osmosis.
  • The antidiuretic hormone also plays a role in making concentrated urine by reabsorbing water from the kidneys.

The counter current gradient: 300 mOsm in the cortex rising to 1200 mOsm in the inner medulla; water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis.

The Functions of Kidneys as Both Excretion and Osmoregulation

  • The kidneys are excretory organs, removing mainly nitrogenous waste products (e.g. urea) and excess water and mineral salts in the form of urine.
  • By the selective reabsorption of useful substances along the nephron, the kidneys help to maintain the pH and composition of the blood plasma.
  • The kidneys regulate the salt and water balance of body fluid: when more water is present in the blood (increased liquid intake, increased tissue respiration or reduced sweating) they remove more water in urine; when liquid intake is reduced or sweat loss is excessive, they remove much less water, so more is reabsorbed to maintain the normal level.

Hormonal Control of Kidney Function

  • Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) — Secreted by the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland when there is a shortage of water in the blood; it helps in the reabsorption of water from the kidneys to the blood.
  • Aldosterone — Secreted from the cortical region of the adrenal gland; it helps in the reabsorption of sodium.
  • Insulin — Secreted by cells of the pancreas; the book lists it as helping to reabsorb glucose from the glomerular filtrate to the blood.

Table 15.1: Comparison Between Glomerular and Peritubular Capillaries

Glomerular CapillariesPeritubular Capillaries
Located in the mouth of the Bowman's capsuleLocated in the renal tubule of nephron
Has very low blood pressure (as printed)Have comparatively high pressure (as printed)
Impermeable to most substancesPermeable for most substances like glucose, mineral ions, etc.
Has a basement membraneHas no basement membrane

Note: the pressure row appears printed in reverse — the main text calls filtration pressure filtration, which needs high glomerular pressure.

Key Points

  • Urine formation has 3 steps: glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption and tubular secretion.
  • Filterable components (water, nitrogenous wastes) form the glomerular filtrate; cells and serum albumins do not filter.
  • All glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed; water is mostly absorbed by the proximal tubule.
  • The counter current mechanism concentrates urine when water is short, building a gradient from 300 mOsm (cortex) to 1200 mOsm (inner medulla).
  • ADH reabsorbs water, aldosterone reabsorbs sodium, and the book lists insulin for glucose reabsorption.
  • Glomerular capillaries lie in the mouth of Bowman's capsule; peritubular capillaries lie around the renal tubule.

lessons.title: Disorders of Urinary Tract: UTI, Kidney Stones, Kidney Failure, Dialysis and Transplant
lessons.notes_html:
The urinary tract includes kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra. Its disorders include urinary tract infections, kidney stones, kidney failure, bladder control problems and prostate problems. Some last only for a short time while others are long lasting. The branch of medical science which deals with urinary tract disorders and treatment is urology.

15.5 Disorders of Urinary Tract

15.5.1 Urinary Tract Infections (UTI)

Infections that affect any part of the urinary tract are called urinary tract infections (UTI). They are more virulent in females than males because of the shorter urethra in women, incomplete emptying of the bladder, and the large exposed surface area of the external genitalia. Ureters are less infected as compared to other parts of the urinary tract due to their acidic nature. Infection of the upper urinary tract is known as pyelonephritis (e.g. kidney infection); infection of the lower tract is cystitis (e.g. infection of the bladder).

The most common cause of infection is Escherichia coli; other bacteria, viruses and fungi may also cause UTI. Sexual contact with infected partners and unhygienic conditions are the major causes of UTI. Symptoms may include a burning feeling during urination, cloudy, dark or bloody urine or strange smelling urine, feeling tired, fever or chill. Treatment: antibiotics as prescribed, and drinking more water to flush out pathogens.

15.5.2 Kidney Stones (Nephrolithiasis)

The hard mineralized material that clings together and forms pebbles within the kidney or any other part of the urinary tract, like the ureter or bladder, is called a kidney stone. Stones are small, about 2–3 mm in diameter, and one to many in number; very small stones may pass out without symptoms. Symptoms may include pain while urinating, blood in urine, sharp pain in the back and lower abdomen, nausea and vomiting. Calcium stones are the most common type, usually made of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. Uric acid stones form when urine is often too acidic; uric acid can form a stone by itself or by mixing with calcium.

Treatment depends on the size, composition and location of the stone, traced by x-ray, CT scan, blood test and urine test. Small stones are usually treated with medicine, but large and complex stones usually need surgery or lithotripsy.

Lithotripsy is a medical procedure involving the physical destruction of hardened masses like kidney stones, bezoars or gallstones; the term is derived from Greek words meaning breaking (or pulverizing) stones. Its two types are:

  • Extracorporeal Shock Wave lithotripsy — Shock waves break the kidney stones into small pieces, which then pass through the urinary tract and out of the body. The treatment usually takes 45 minutes to one hour and may be done under general anaesthesia so the patient does not feel pain.
  • Laser lithotripsy — By ureteroscopy, in which a long tube-shaped tool is used to find, remove and break the stone; a laser breaks the stone into small pieces so they may pass through the urinary tract.

15.5.3 Kidney Failure

Kidney failure, also called end-stage renal disease (ESRD), is the last stage of chronic kidney disease: the kidneys are not working well enough for the survival of the patient without dialysis or a kidney transplant. Factors related to kidney failure include autoimmune diseases, kidney stones, diabetes, high blood pressure, use of drugs and bacterial infections. Diabetes is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (44%), followed by high blood pressure (28%). Symptoms include nausea and vomiting, muscle cramps, appetite loss, swelling in feet and ankles, too much urine and sleeplessness. Acute kidney failure is usually caused by injuries, vomiting, diarrhoea, water shortage from excessive sweating or diuresis, ureter blockage by a stone, and severe nephritis. The few options for kidney failure patients are the types of dialysis and kidney transplant.

15.5.4 Dialysis

Dialysis is the temporary treatment for kidney failure patients, in which toxins and wastes are removed from the body by artificial means, i.e. using dialyzing fluid. It is not a permanent cure for kidney disease.

  • Hemodialysis — The most common type. It uses an artificial kidney (hemodialyzer) to remove wastes, toxins and extra fluids from the blood. Blood passes through sterile tubing to a filter in the machine, via a gortex graft between an artery and a vein in the arm or leg, or a direct artery–vein connection (cimino fistula); a solution on the other side of the filter receives the wastes, and the cleaned blood returns to the patient.
  • Peritoneal dialysis — Uses the lining of the abdomen, the peritoneum, to filter blood. A catheter is placed near the navel a few weeks before treatment starts; the patient can do this dialysis himself. Dialysis solution (water with salt and other additives) is transferred from a bag into the peritoneal cavity, where it soaks up wastes and extra fluids; after a few hours the fluid, filled with waste, drains out into a separate bag and fresh fluid is entered. This process is called an exchange.

15.5.5 Kidney Transplant: Process and Problems

Kidney transplant is a surgical procedure of placing a healthy donor kidney into the belly of a chronic kidney failure patient. Transplantation is the preferred treatment over dialysis, as it improves and normalizes the life of the patient. The kidney may come from a deceased organ donor or from a living donor (living transplant); the living donor can live a healthy life with a single kidney. Before transplant, the tissue type of donor and recipient is matched. The operation takes 3–4 hours; usually one kidney is given, the affected kidney is left in place, and the new kidney is placed in the lower belly and attached to a large artery, starting to clean the blood as soon as it is connected. The first kidney transplant was done in Boston by Joseph E. Murray in 1954.

Problems: a kidney transplant is a major operation, with complications such as pain, delayed wound healing, bleeding and risk of infection. However, kidney rejection is the most serious problem. Medication like cyclosporine is given to suppress the immune system of the recipient to prevent rejection of the transplant kidney.

Key Points

  • UTI is most commonly caused by Escherichia coli; upper tract infection is pyelonephritis, lower tract infection is cystitis.
  • Kidney stones are hard pebbles about 2–3 mm; calcium stones are most common, uric acid stones form in acidic urine.
  • Lithotripsy breaks stones: extracorporeal shock wave (45 minutes to one hour) and laser lithotripsy by ureteroscopy.
  • Kidney failure (ESRD) needs dialysis or transplant; diabetes (44%) and high blood pressure (28%) are its leading causes.
  • Hemodialysis uses a hemodialyzer; peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum and peritoneal cavity in exchanges.
  • In transplant, rejection is the most serious problem and cyclosporine is given to prevent it.

lessons.title: Thermoregulation: Classification of Animals and Strategies in Man
lessons.notes_html:
Thermoregulation is the maintenance of internal body temperature at a nearly constant state so that the body can perform its metabolic activities at the optimum level. Any change in temperature will affect enzyme activity, and thus metabolic reactions will be disturbed.

15.6 Thermoregulation

15.6.1 Classification of Animals on the Basis of Temperature (Thermoregulation)

On the basis of temperature regulation, animals can be divided into two groups:

  • Poikilotherms — Animals not able to regulate their internal body temperature; they depend on an external source of heat (sunlight) to get themselves warm, and their body temperature changes with the external temperature. They have to hibernate in low temperature and aestivate (summer sleep) in high temperature. These include fish, amphibians and reptiles.
  • Homeotherms — Animals able to regulate their internal body temperature, not dependent on an external source of heat. They have a high metabolic rate and need more food to generate heat in their body. These include birds and mammals.

On the basis of heat production, animals can be divided into three categories:

  • Ectotherms — Generate metabolic heat at a low level due to a low metabolic rate, so they depend on an external source of heat for their survival. These include insects, fish, amphibians and reptiles.
  • Endotherms — Can generate enough heat to maintain their body temperature due to a high metabolic rate, and can survive in all sorts of habitats. These include birds and mammals. They generate their own body heat through heat production as a by-product of metabolism.
  • Heterotherms — Animals with a thermoregulatory strategy intermediate to ectotherms and endotherms: they produce heat in their body but also depend on an external source of heat. These include small mammals like the bat and small birds like the humming bird.
GroupMeaningExamples
PoikilothermsCannot regulate internal temperature; it changes with the environmentFish, amphibians, reptiles
HomeothermsRegulate internal temperature; high metabolic rateBirds, mammals
EctothermsLow metabolic heat; depend on external heatInsects, fish, amphibians, reptiles
EndothermsGenerate enough metabolic heat to maintain temperatureBirds, mammals
HeterothermsIntermediate: produce heat and also use external heatBat, humming bird

15.6.2 Thermoregulatory Strategies in Man

The body temperature of man is regulated and stabilized by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain basically concerned with homeostasis — it works as a complex homeostatic thermostat. In case of any variation in the set point, endocrine production initiates a control mechanism to increase or decrease energy production or dissipation, to return the temperature towards the set point.

During hot (hyperthermia) conditions — hyperthermia is increased body temperature:

  • Vasodilation, i.e. expansion of blood capillaries under the skin, so that more heat can be brought towards the skin for dissipation of heat.
  • Activation of sweat glands.
  • Relaxation of hair erector muscles.

During cold (hypothermia) conditions, to prevent heat loss and generate heat:

  • Inactivation of sweat glands.
  • Vasoconstriction.
  • Increase in metabolic activities.
  • Shivering may start.
  • Brown fats are consumed for more and rapid heat production.

Science, Technology and Society (STS)

Kidney donation: recipients of a living donor kidney usually live a longer, healthier life compared to those who receive a deceased donor kidney, and there can be benefit to the donor as well, such as saving the life of another person and a greater understanding of one's own health. Transplant centres: the book names Shifa International Hospital, the Kidney Transplant Program of Aga Khan University Hospital and Kidney Transplant Doctors Hospital and Medical Centre Lahore; the Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation (SIUT), established by Dr. Adeeb Rizvi in 1971, is the most prominent and pioneer institute in Pakistan, and in Balochistan the Balochistan Institute of Nephrology, Urology Quetta (BINUQ) is named.

Key Points

  • Thermoregulation keeps body temperature nearly constant so enzymes and metabolism work at their optimum.
  • Poikilotherms cannot regulate temperature (fish, amphibians, reptiles); homeotherms can (birds, mammals).
  • By heat production: ectotherms depend on external heat, endotherms generate enough metabolic heat, heterotherms (bat, humming bird) are intermediate.
  • In man the hypothalamus is the thermostat for body temperature.
  • In heat: vasodilation, sweating and relaxation of hair erector muscles lose heat.
  • In cold: vasoconstriction, stopped sweating, increased metabolism, shivering and brown fat use produce and conserve heat.

lessons.title: Bone: Structure, Bone Cells and Cartilage
lessons.notes_html:
Movement is a change in shape or position of body parts; in locomotion the whole organism moves from one place to another. In animals movement is provided by muscles, while support gives the body its proper shape and structure. Support is provided by hydrostatic skeletons, bones and cartilages. The skeletal tissues are bone and cartilage.

16.1 Human Skeleton

The human skeleton is the main supportive framework of the body. It mainly includes bones and cartilages, and muscles are attached to it for effective movement. Bone is a connective tissue impregnated with calcium salts. It is hard, provides support, protects internal organs and gives an environment for the production of blood cells. The protein component of skeletal tissue is collagen.

16.1.1 Structure of Bone

Bone tissue is of two types: compact (hard and dense) bone outside and cancellous (spongy) bone inside.

  • Compact bone, also called cortical bone, is hard white tissue surrounding all bones. Its fundamental units are osteons or Haversian systems: concentric layers called lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal containing blood and nerve supply. The central canal communicates with the perforating (Volkmann's) canal, which transmits vessels from the periosteum (dense vascular connective tissue enveloping the bone) into the endosteum (thin layer lining the medullary cavity).
  • Osteocytes lie in small cavities called lacunae between the lamellae. Canaliculi are microscopic channels that transport nutrients to the osteocytes and remove their wastes.
  • Spongy bone, also called cancellous or trabecular bone, is porous and highly vascular, mostly at the ends of long bones. Its lacunae lie in a lattice-like network of matrix spikes called trabeculae, with osteocytes irregularly placed within them. The spaces make it lighter and less dense than compact bone and contain red bone marrow, where blood cells are formed.

An osteon: concentric lamellae around a central canal carrying blood vessels and nerves.

Types of Bone Cells

Bone growth and repair are carried out by four types of cells:

  • Osteogenic cells — Undifferentiated stem cells in the cellular layer of endosteum and periosteum; they divide and develop into osteoblasts.
  • Osteoblasts — Bone-forming cells, mostly where bone growth occurs; they secrete collagen and the bone matrix and cause its mineralization.
  • Osteocytes — Mature bone cells entrapped in the matrix (osteoblasts surrounded by matrix become osteocytes); by secreting enzymes they maintain the mineral concentration of the matrix.
  • Osteoclasts — Large, multinucleated bone-breaking (bone-resorbing) cells at sites of old, injured bone, derived from monocytes and macrophages.

About 10% of bone is replaced every year, so we get a new skeleton about every ten years.

16.1.2 Cartilage

Cartilage is a connective tissue composed of cells called chondrocytes and fibres embedded in a firm, gel-like matrix. It is much more elastic than bone and is found at joints and between bones, e.g. at the elbow, knees and ankles. It has no blood vessels or lymphatics and no nerves, so it is insensitive; nutrition diffuses through the matrix. It is surrounded by a fibrous membrane, the perichondrium. When cartilage calcifies, the chondrocytes die and it is replaced by bone-like tissue.

BoneCartilage
Hard; cells are osteocytesSoft; cells are chondrocytes
Matrix inflexible, with calcium saltsMatrix flexible, calcium salts absent
Rich blood supply; vascular; bone marrow presentNo blood supply; non-vascular; bone marrow absent
Outer covering is periosteumOuter covering is perichondrium
Provides skeletal supportProvides flexibility

Key Points

  • Skeletal tissues are bone and cartilage; bone is impregnated with calcium salts and its protein is collagen.
  • Compact bone is built of osteons (lamellae around a central canal); spongy bone is built of trabeculae and holds red bone marrow.
  • Osteogenic cells divide, osteoblasts form bone, osteocytes maintain it and osteoclasts break it down.
  • Cartilage is made of chondrocytes in a gel-like matrix; it is avascular, without nerves, and covered by perichondrium.
  • Osteocytes lie in lacunae; canaliculi carry nutrients to them.

lessons.title: Functions of the Skeleton and the Axial Skeleton
lessons.notes_html:
The human skeleton is an endoskeleton: it lies inside the organism with muscles attached outside, and it is made of living tissues that grow with the organism.

16.1.3 Functions of Human Skeleton

  • It gives support to the body; without it the body would be flabby and shapeless.
  • It protects internal organs, e.g. the skull protects the brain and the rib cage protects the heart and lungs.
  • It provides a surface for the attachment of muscles, ligaments and tendons, and bones act as levers for movement; bones and joints work with muscles so we can walk and run.
  • It stores 97% of the body calcium and phosphorus (mineral storage).
  • Blood cells are made in red bone marrow, mostly present in the ribs and limb bones.

Divisions of Human Skeleton

The human skeleton of 206 bones is divided into the axial skeleton of 80 bones and the appendicular skeleton of 126 bones. The axial skeleton is mostly fused; the appendicular skeleton is unfused and consists of girdles and limbs. Hands and feet alone contain 106 bones: each hand has 27 bones and each foot 26 bones.

Axial Skeleton: Skull

The axial skeleton includes the skull (cranium and facial bones), hyoid bone, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The cranium is a bony cavity that contains and protects the brain. It has 8 bones, all flat and immobile: 4 unpaired — frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid — and 2 paired — parietal (left, right) and temporal (left, right).

There are 14 facial bones: 2 unpaired (mandible and vomer) and 6 paired (maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, inferior nasal conchae, lacrimal and palatine). They protect the sense organs of sight, smell and taste and provide a frame for muscle attachment. Note: the book says the cranium has "4 unpaired and 2 paired" bones — this means 4 unpaired bones plus 2 pairs, making 8 in total. The hyoid bone (lingual bone) gives attachment to the tongue and is unique because it does not articulate with any other bone.

Vertebral Column, Ribs and Sternum

  • The vertebral column supports body weight and maintains posture. Its regions are cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal; the coccyx is formed by the fusion of four posterior vertebrae in the pelvic region. Between vertebrae lie intervertebral discs: an outer strong ring, the annulus fibrosus, and a soft gelatinous inner portion, the nucleus pulposus.
  • Ribs are long, twisted flat bones forming the major part of the rib cage. True ribs (7 pairs, ribs 1–7) attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages; false ribs (3 pairs, ribs 8–10) attach to the cartilage of the rib above; floating ribs (2 pairs, ribs 11–12) have no anterior attachment.
  • The sternum (breast bone) lies in front of the chest, with the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

Key Points

  • The skeleton supports and protects the body, stores 97% of body calcium and phosphorus, and makes blood cells in red marrow.
  • Total 206 bones: axial skeleton 80 bones, appendicular skeleton 126 bones.
  • Cranium: 8 bones (frontal, parietal ×2, temporal ×2, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid). Facial bones: 14, of which mandible and vomer are unpaired.
  • The hyoid does not articulate with any other bone; the coccyx is four fused vertebrae.
  • Ribs: 7 pairs true, 3 pairs false, 2 pairs floating.

lessons.title: Appendicular Skeleton: Girdles and Limbs
lessons.notes_html:
Compared with the axial skeleton, the appendicular skeleton is unfused. It consists of the girdles and the limbs, 126 bones in all, and it is built for movement rather than protection.

Pectoral Girdle and Fore Limb

The pectoral (shoulder) girdle connects the fore limb to the trunk. It has two bones on each side: the clavicle (collar bone, from the Latin word clavicula) and the scapula (shoulder bone, a flat triangular bone; Latin scapul means shoulder blade). The lateral depression of the scapula, the glenoid cavity, receives the head of the humerus.

There are 30 bones in each fore limb:

  • Humerus (1) — Long bone of the upper arm; its head fits into the glenoid cavity at the shoulder and its lower end forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna.
  • Radius (1) and ulna (1) — Bones of the forearm.
  • Carpals (8) — Small bones of the wrist in two rows, giving the wrist flexibility.
  • Metacarpals (5) — Bones of the palm.
  • Phalanges (14) — Finger bones: three in each finger and two in the thumb.

Pelvic Girdle and Hind Limb

The pelvic girdle connects the hind limbs to the trunk and bears the weight of the upper body. Each hip bone is formed of ilium, ischium and pubis. Its deep socket, the acetabulum, provides the articular surface for the head of the femur.

There are 30 bones in each hind limb:

  • Femur (1) — Thigh bone, the longest bone; its head fits into the acetabulum.
  • Patella (1) — The knee cap, in front of the knee joint.
  • Tibia (1) and fibula (1) — Bones of the shank (lower leg).
  • Tarsals (7) — Larger, stronger bones of the ankle, including the calcaneus (heel bone) and talus; they bear body weight and give the foot strength and stability.
  • Metatarsals (5) and phalanges (14) — Bones of the foot and toes (three in each toe, two in the big toe).
CarpalsTarsals
8 bones of the wrist, in two rows7 bones of the ankle
Smaller, for flexibility of the wristLarger and stronger, for weight-bearing
Part of the hand (27 bones in each hand)Include calcaneus (heel) and talus; part of the foot (26 bones in each foot)

Key Points

  • The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) consists of girdles and limbs and is unfused, for movement.
  • Each fore limb has 30 bones: humerus 1, radius 1, ulna 1, carpals 8, metacarpals 5, phalanges 14.
  • Each hind limb has 30 bones: femur 1, patella 1, tibia 1, fibula 1, tarsals 7, metatarsals 5, phalanges 14.
  • The glenoid cavity of the scapula receives the humerus; the acetabulum of the hip bone receives the femur.
  • Carpals are 8 in the wrist; tarsals are 7 in the ankle.

lessons.title: Joints: Fibrous, Cartilaginous and Synovial
lessons.notes_html:
A joint is the attachment (place of meeting) between two bones, or between bone and cartilage, where movement takes place. Joints are classified by the tissue connecting the bones and by how much movement they allow.

Fibrous Joints

In fibrous joints the articular surfaces are connected by dense connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen. They are immovable joints because they allow no movement. Examples: the sutures between skull bones, the joint between a tooth and its socket, and the joint between the tibia and fibula.

Cartilaginous Joints

In cartilaginous joints the bones are connected by cartilage, so they are slightly movable and allow a little movement. Examples: hyaline cartilage in the costal cartilages attaching ribs to the sternum, and fibrocartilage in the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.

Synovial Joints

Synovial joints are the most mobile type. The articular surfaces are covered with hyaline cartilage, a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid (secreted by the synovial membrane) lies between them, and ligaments and a joint capsule hold the joint. Synovial fluid reduces friction and lubricates the surfaces. Ball and socket, hinge and pivot joints are all synovial joints.

Type of Synovial JointExample
Ball and socket jointHip and shoulder
Hinge jointElbow and knee
Pivot jointAtlas and axis (first two neck vertebrae)
Gliding jointBetween vertebrae
Ellipsoid (condyloid) jointSkull and 1st vertebra
Saddle jointCarpometacarpal joint of the thumb

A synovial joint: articular cartilage, a fluid-filled cavity and a joint capsule.

The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint of the human body. Ligaments join bone to bone inside and around joints, while tendons join muscle to bone.

Key Points

  • A joint is where two or more bones meet; movement takes place there.
  • Fibrous joints are immovable (skull sutures, tooth socket, tibia–fibula).
  • Cartilaginous joints are slightly movable (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, costal cartilages).
  • Synovial joints are freely movable, with synovial fluid reducing friction: hinge (elbow, knee), ball and socket (hip, shoulder), pivot (atlas–axis), gliding, ellipsoid and saddle.
  • The knee is the largest and most complex joint of the body.

lessons.title: Disorders of the Skeleton: Disc Slip, Spondylosis, Sciatica and Arthritis
lessons.notes_html:
Deformation of the skeleton may occur due to genetic diseases, hormonal problems and nutritional deficiencies. This lesson covers the disorders of the vertebral column and joints described in section 16.2.

16.2 Disorders of Skeleton

Disc Slip (Herniated Disc)

Each intervertebral disc has an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft gelatinous centre (nucleus pulposus). In a disc slip, the nucleus pulposus bulges or leaks out through a tear in the ring and may press on a spinal nerve, causing pain. It is a common cause of back pain and of sciatica.

Spondylosis

Spondylosis is the degenerative (wear-and-tear) disease of the vertebral column, mainly of the cervical and lumbar regions, in which the discs and joints of the spine wear out with age, making the neck or back stiff and painful.

Sciatica

Sciatica refers to back pain caused by a problem with the sciatic nerve, a large nerve that travels from the lower lumbar spine to the back of each leg. Any injury to the sciatic nerve causes pain in the lower back that travels to the hip, buttocks and leg. Common causes include a herniated (slip) disc, injury to the proximal sciatic nerve, spondylolisthesis (one vertebra slipping forward over another), muscle spasm in the back or buttocks, and improper injection into the buttocks. Pregnant women have a greater chance of a herniated disc and sciatica, and diabetes can also cause nerve damage. Recovery from sciatic injury is usually slow and incomplete.

Arthritis

Arthritis is the inflammation of a joint: the joints become swollen, stiffer and painful, the membrane lining the joint thickens, and fluid production decreases, which increases friction. Possible causes are infection or injury to the joints, abnormal metabolism and immune system dysfunction, and sometimes inheritance.

  • Osteoarthritis — The most common chronic arthritis, a degenerative joint disease in which the joint cartilage degenerates (wears away); it may also be caused by inheritance.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — Inflammation of the hand and wrist joints (including the finger joints), an immune-system disorder.
  • Gouty arthritis — Develops in people with a high level of uric acid in the blood, caused by deposition of needle-like crystals of uric acid in a joint, often the big toe.

Key Points

  • Skeletal deformities arise from genetic diseases, hormonal problems and nutritional deficiencies.
  • In disc slip the nucleus pulposus bulges out of the intervertebral disc and may press on a nerve.
  • Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve, from the lower back to the hip, buttock and leg; a slipped disc is a common cause.
  • Arthritis is inflammation of joints. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and most common; rheumatoid arthritis affects hand and wrist joints; gouty arthritis is due to uric acid crystals.
  • Spondylosis is age-related degeneration of the spine.

lessons.title: Fractures, Bone Healing and Joint Injuries
lessons.notes_html:
When there is a partial or complete break in the continuity of a bone, it is called a bone fracture. Fractures, dislocations and sprains are the common injuries of the skeleton, and each has its own first aid.

Types of Fractures

  • Simple (closed) fracture — The broken bones remain within the body, the skin remains intact and there is no damage to the surrounding tissues.
  • Compound (open) fracture — The broken bones penetrate the skin, or the force of injury breaks the skin, causing a risk of infection.
  • Complicated fracture — The broken bone damages the surrounding structures (organs), and there may be damage to arteries, veins and nerves; it heals more slowly.

Reduction and First Aid

Reduction is putting the broken fragments back into their normal position. In closed reduction the fragments are coaxed back by the physician's hands without surgical exposure; in open reduction surgery is performed by dissecting the tissues and the fragments are secured with pins or wires. After reduction the part is immobilized so healing can occur.

First aid for a fracture: do not move the injured part unnecessarily; immobilize it with a splint and support it in a comfortable position; apply cold to reduce swelling and pain; control any bleeding with a clean cloth and do not push back any bone that pierces the skin; keep the patient calm and still; and get medical help at once.

Healing of a Simple Fracture

Bone healing is a natural process that usually takes 8–12 weeks (longer for large weight-bearing bones, and slower in elderly people due to poor blood circulation), in four phases:

  • 1. Hematoma formation — Injured blood vessels bleed at the fracture site, the blood clots and forms a hematoma; bone cells deprived of nutrients begin to die, and the tissues swell and cause much pain.
  • 2. Soft callus formation — Within a few days capillaries grow into the hematoma and phagocytic cells clear the debris; fibroblasts produce collagen fibres connecting the ends of the broken bone while osteoblasts start forming spongy bone and some bone spicules appear. The soft callus lasts approximately 4–6 weeks.
  • 3. Hard (bony) callus formation — Osteoblasts and osteoclasts multiply rapidly, move inward and convert the soft callus into bony callus; woven bone is transformed into lamellar bone and a ring of new bone forms around the fracture, so the mended bone is slightly thicker there.
  • 4. Bone remodelling — The bony callus is remodelled by osteoblasts and osteoclasts; unwanted bits are broken down and reabsorbed, and the final mended bone is almost undetectable on X-ray. Remodelling may continue for months or even years.

Dislocation and Sprain

When the joint is moved away from its original position, it is called joint dislocation. A sprain is the stretching, tearing or twisting of ligaments.
