First aid for both is to rest and support the joint, apply cold to reduce swelling and pain, and seek medical help; a dislocated joint must be put back (reduced) by a trained person, not forced by untrained hands.

Key Points

  • A fracture is a partial or complete break in the continuity of a bone: simple (skin intact), compound (bone pierces skin, infection risk), complicated (organs, vessels or nerves damaged).
  • Reduction may be closed (by hand) or open (surgery with pins or wires).
  • Healing takes 8–12 weeks: hematoma, soft callus (4–6 weeks), hard callus, then remodelling.
  • Dislocation is displacement of a joint from its original position; a sprain is stretching, tearing or twisting of ligaments.
  • First aid: immobilize with a splint, apply cold, control bleeding, keep the patient still and get medical help.

lessons.title: Muscles and the Structure of Skeletal Muscle
lessons.notes_html:
The muscle is the contractile tissue found in animals, and its primary function is to produce movement. The study of muscle is called myology. A muscle is attached to bone by a connective tissue known as a tendon.

16.3 Muscles: Three Types

Skeletal MuscleCardiac MuscleSmooth Muscle
Attached to bones; striated; voluntaryOnly in the heart; striated; involuntary, controlled by the autonomic nervous systemIn walls of internal organs; non-striated; involuntary
Cells are long, cylindrical and multinucleated (polynucleated)Cells are uninucleated (single nucleus)Cells are spindle-shaped and uninucleated
Contracts quickly and strongly; fatiguesContracts rhythmically and does not fatigueContracts slowly and for long periods

Structure of Skeletal Muscle

Skeletal muscle is made of bundles (fascicles) of long, cylindrical, multinucleated muscle fibres (cells). Each fibre is covered by a membrane, the sarcolemma, whose infoldings form T-tubules, and it contains the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stores calcium ions. Inside the fibre are myofibrils divided into sarcomeres, the structural and functional units of muscle contraction, bounded by Z-lines.

  • Each sarcomere has thin actin filaments, about 7 nm in diameter, and thick myosin filaments, about 16 nm.
  • The regular overlap of these filaments gives the striated appearance: dark bands where thick and thin filaments overlap, and light bands.
  • The end of the muscle that remains fixed when the muscle contracts is the origin; the end attached to the movable bone is the insertion; the thick middle part is the belly.

A sarcomere between two Z-lines: thin actin filaments slide over thick myosin filaments during contraction.

Key Points

  • Muscle is contractile tissue; its study is myology, and it is attached to bone by tendons.
  • Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary and multinucleated; cardiac muscle is in the heart, involuntary and uninucleated; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.
  • The sarcomere, bounded by Z-lines, is the structural and functional unit of contraction.
  • Actin filaments are about 7 nm thick; myosin filaments about 16 nm. Calcium ions are required for contraction.
  • The sarcolemma's infoldings are T-tubules; the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca²⁺.

lessons.title: Sliding Filament Theory, Antagonistic Movement and Muscle Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Muscles can only pull, never push, so they are arranged in opposing pairs around joints. This lesson explains how a muscle contracts and what goes wrong in muscle disorders.

Sliding Filament Theory

The sliding filament theory explains muscle contraction. When a nerve impulse arrives, calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. They expose the binding sites on actin; the myosin heads attach to actin and, using energy from ATP, pull the thin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. The sarcomeres shorten, so the whole fibre — and the muscle — contracts, while the actual length of the actin and myosin filaments does not change: the actin filaments slide over the myosin filaments. When the impulse ends, calcium is pumped back and the muscle relaxes.

Antagonistic Movement

The opposite movement of flexor and extensor muscles is called antagonistic movement. Muscles work in opposing pairs: the muscle that is contracting is called the agonist, and the muscle that is relaxing is called the antagonist; for the reverse movement their roles swap. For example, at the elbow the biceps contracts to flex the arm while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to extend the arm while the biceps relaxes.

Movement of the Knee Joint

The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint of the body, a hinge-type synovial joint. The quadriceps (extensor) group on the front of the thigh contracts to extend (straighten) the knee while the hamstring (flexor) group at the back relaxes; the hamstrings contract to flex (bend) the knee while the quadriceps relax. Ligaments, the joint capsule and the patella (knee cap) stabilize the joint during this movement.

Muscle Disorders

  • Muscle fatigue — The reduced ability of a muscle to contract after prolonged or repeated activity, because ATP and glycogen are used up and lactic acid and other metabolites accumulate; the muscle feels weak and painful, and rest recovers it.
  • Cramp — A sudden, painful, involuntary contraction of a muscle or part of a muscle, usually brief, caused by overuse, dehydration or temporary electrolyte disturbance; it relaxes after a short time, often helped by stretching and rest.
  • Tetany — A disease appearing due to a low level of Ca²⁺ in the blood: the nerves become hyperexcitable and the muscles undergo sustained, involuntary contractions (spasms) that do not relax normally. Unlike a cramp, tetany is caused by a persistent low blood calcium level.

Key Points

  • In sliding filament theory, Ca²⁺ exposes actin binding sites and myosin heads pull actin to the centre; filament lengths do not change.
  • Antagonistic movement: when the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes, and vice versa.
  • At the knee, quadriceps extend and hamstrings flex, working antagonistically.
  • Fatigue follows prolonged activity and lactic acid accumulation; a cramp is a brief painful contraction.
  • Tetany is sustained spasm due to low Ca²⁺ in the blood.

lessons.title: Nervous Coordination, Receptors and Effectors
lessons.notes_html:
All animals respond to stimuli, that is, any internal or external change. The activities of different body parts in response to stimuli must be coordinated, and this coordination makes the integration of functions essential to animal behaviour possible. In humans and most animals there are two types of coordination: nervous coordination and endocrine coordination. This unit deals only with nervous coordination.

17.1 Nervous System of Man

The study of the nervous system is known as neurology. The working of different body parts in cooperation with each other and under the control of a coordinator (brain, spinal cord or ganglia) is called coordination. The system of the body that provides coordination through electric signals among different body parts during the response to a particular stimulus is called the nervous system. The most developed, advanced and evolved nervous system among all organisms is that of humans.

17.1.1 Steps Involved in Nervous Coordination

Nervous coordination involves highly specialized cells known as neurons, which are either connected together or linked via the centralized nervous system to form a network that is linked to the receptors and effectors. The nervous system in humans and higher animals consists of three basic elements:

  • Receptors — Cells, tissues or organs which receive stimuli and give information to sensory neurons.
  • The neuron — It has the capacity to generate and conduct impulses to the central nervous system, where processing and analysis of information takes place, and to pass responses to the effectors.
  • Effectors — Structures such as cells, tissues, muscles and glands which carry out action or make responses.

17.1.2 Receptors or Transducers

Receptors are organs, tissues, cells or nerve endings that detect changes (stimuli) in the external or internal environment of an animal. These stimuli are then transmitted to the brain or spinal cord through sensory neurons. Receptors act as transducers because they convert the energy of the stimulus into nerve impulses.

On the basis of stimuli, receptors are classified into five types:

  • Chemoreceptors — Detect the concentration of certain chemicals or ions, e.g. CO₂ level in the blood by the medulla of the brain and O₂ level by the carotid body. Chemoreceptors for blood glucose, amino acids and fatty acids are located in the hypothalamus of the brain; smell (olfaction) is in the nasal epithelium, taste (gustation) is found in the tongue, and osmoreceptors (which detect osmotic pressure of blood) are in the hypothalamus.
  • Mechanoreceptors — Detect stimuli of pressure, body position or acceleration. They include Meissner's corpuscles in the skin for touch, Pacinian's corpuscles also in the skin, baroreceptors in blood vessels for pressure, and stretch receptors in the ear for hearing and equilibrium.
  • Thermoreceptors — Mostly located in the skin to detect changes in temperature (cold and warmth).
  • Nociceptors — Pain receptors, widely distributed in the skin and other internal organs, which detect damage to body tissues.
  • Photoreceptors or electromagnetic receptors — Detect light stimuli, such as rods and cone cells in the retina of our eyes.

17.1.3 Processing / Analysis of Information

All types of sensory inputs from various receptors are conveyed to the coordinator, i.e. the brain and spinal cord, by sensory neurons. The information collected by them is processed and analysed for a suitable response by special types of neurons known as inter neurons, also called associated or relay neurons.

17.1.4 Effectors

Effectors respond to stimuli by impulses coming via motor neurons, such as muscles and glands. The glands secrete some types of chemicals, while muscles respond by contracting. The whole pathway can be summarized as: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Inter neuron (CNS) → Motor neuron → Effector → Response.

Key Points

  • Coordination is of two types: nervous coordination (by electric signals) and endocrine coordination; the study of the nervous system is neurology.
  • The three basic elements of nervous coordination are receptors, neurons (with the CNS as coordinator) and effectors.
  • Receptors are transducers: chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, nociceptors and photoreceptors.
  • Meissner's corpuscles detect touch, Pacinian's corpuscles detect pressure, and nociceptors detect pain.
  • Inter (associated or relay) neurons in the CNS process and analyse information; muscles and glands are the principal effectors.

lessons.title: Structure of a Neuron
lessons.notes_html:
Neurons are the chief structural and functional units of the nervous system. In addition to neurons, the nervous system contains neuroglial cells, which nourish the neurons and also protect them by the myelin sheath. The nervous system also contains about 50% neuroglial cells.

17.2 Neurons

A neuron generates and conducts nerve impulses. Its structure is specialized for receiving stimuli, conducting impulses and passing them on to the next neuron, muscle or gland.

17.2.1 Structure of Neuron

A typical neuron consists of three basic components, i.e. cell body, axon and dendrites.

  • Cell body — Also called soma, cyton or perikaryon. It contains the nucleus and various cellular organelles except centrioles. The neuron cell body contains a mass of granular cytoplasm enclosed by the cell membrane, and the nucleus is centrally placed. The cell body contains a group of ribosomes associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies known as Nissl's granules, which help in protein synthesis and in forming the acetylcholine-forming enzyme. These granules are absent in the axon and dendron.
  • Axon — A cytoplasmic process that conducts impulses away from the cell body. Each axon is a usually thick, long fibre (a few millimetres to more than a metre in length) with a constant diameter. The cytoplasm of the axon is called axoplasm and its cell membrane is called axolemma. Each axon terminates by branching to form small extensions with knob-like endings called presynaptic terminals. The fibres at the end of the axon are its terminal branches (telodendria).
  • Dendrites — Cytoplasmic extensions that carry impulses towards the cell body. If single, the fibre is called a dendron. They are thin, short and mostly branched, and the branches are gradually tapered from the base to their tips. The gap between the dendrites of one neuron and the axon terminals of another neuron is called a synapse.

The cell body of a neuron is surrounded by cytoplasmic fibres, which are of two main types, i.e. axon and dendrites. The neuroglia or glial cells nourish, protect and support the neurons. In the peripheral nervous system these cells are known as Schwann cells, which cover the axon by repeatedly wrapping around it. These cells are also covered by a fatty substance known as the myelin sheath, which acts as an insulator, so such axons are called myelinated fibres. The non-myelinated portion of the axon between two Schwann cells is called a node of Ranvier. The impulses jump from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier, which is known as saltatory conduction. The outer Schwann-cell membrane covering the nerve fibre is the neurilemma.

Note: On page 97 the book loosely calls the cell-body membrane the neurilemma. Strictly, as the book's own exercise answer confirms, the neurilemma is the outer membrane of the Schwann cell covering the nerve fibre (axon).

A typical neuron: dendrites carry impulses to the cell body, and the myelinated axon carries them away to the axon terminals.

Key Points

  • A neuron has three parts: cell body (soma or cyton), dendrites and axon.
  • Nissl's granules are groups of ribosomes with rough ER and Golgi bodies in the cell body; they help in protein synthesis and are absent in the axon and dendron.
  • Dendrites conduct impulses towards the cell body; the axon conducts them away from the cell body.
  • Axoplasm is the axon cytoplasm and axolemma is its membrane; the axon ends in telodendria with synaptic knobs.
  • Schwann cells form the insulating myelin sheath; the gaps between them are nodes of Ranvier, across which impulses jump in saltatory conduction.

lessons.title: Types of Neurons and the Reflex Arc
lessons.notes_html:
On the basis of function, neurons are of three types: sensory neurons, inter neurons and motor neurons. Together they form the pathway of every nervous response, best seen in the reflex arc.

17.2.2 Types of Neurons

  • Sensory neurons — Conduct impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. These are unipolar, because only one fibre originates from the cell body, which immediately gives rise to two branches, one towards the receptor and the other towards the central nervous system. Both fibres are structurally axon-like, except that their terminal portions differ: one behaves like dendrites and the other like an axon. The majority of sensory neurons are unipolar, but some are bipolar. The unipolar neurons are found especially in the dorsal root of the spinal cord, and their cell bodies lie outside the CNS, e.g. in dorsal root ganglia.
  • Associated or interneurons — Found only in the brain and spinal cord. They conduct impulses from sensory neurons to motor neurons and also convey messages between various parts of the CNS. Interneurons are mostly multipolar, because many fibres arise from the cell body. Their axon is thin and non-myelinated, while many dendrites carry impulses to the cell body.
  • Motor neurons — Conduct impulses from the CNS to effectors. These are multipolar neurons. Their cell body, which lies inside the CNS, contains many branched dendrites, and a single long axon runs towards the effector.

By structure, neurons are also described as multipolar (many fibres from the cell body), bipolar (two fibres) and unipolar (one fibre), as shown in the book's Fig. 17.2.

Myelinated and Non-Myelinated Neurons

Myelinated neurons (nerve fibres) are covered by a fatty layer known as the myelin sheath around the axon, whereas non-myelinated neurons do not have a myelin sheath (dendrites and cell bodies are non-myelinated). In myelinated neurons, conduction of impulses is faster than in non-myelinated neurons: the nerve impulse is 20 times faster in a myelinated neuron than in a non-myelinated neuron, because the impulse jumps from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier (saltatory impulse). Interneurons are non-myelinated, while motor and sensory neurons have myelinated portions. Myelinated fibres have larger and thicker axons, because the velocity of the impulse depends upon the diameter, length and myelin sheath.

Sensory NeuronMotor Neuron
Carries impulses from receptors to the CNSCarries impulses from the CNS to effectors
Cell body lies outside the CNS (e.g. dorsal root ganglion)Cell body lies inside the CNS
Usually unipolarMultipolar
Dendron connected to a receptorAxon ends at a muscle or gland

17.2.3 Reflex Action and Reflex Arc

Reflex actions or reflexes are involuntary, automatic, unconscious or immediate responses to external or internal environmental changes or stimuli. The pathway through which a reflex travels is called the reflex arc. The direction of a reflex action is from receptor to sensory neuron to CNS to inter neuron and then through the motor neuron to the effectors. Reflexes have no involvement of the conscious portion of the brain, therefore the response is quicker than the conscious pathway.

Example: If we unexpectedly touch a hot object or get a pin prick, our hand is rapidly removed from it. The receptors of the hand are activated by the heat of the object. This impulse is conveyed by the sensory neuron, leading to the spinal cord via the spinal nerve, then to the inter neuron, which lies entirely within the spinal cord. The inter neuron then passes this impulse to the motor neuron and then to the effectors, i.e. muscles, which causes them to contract.

The five fundamental parts of a reflex arc are: (1) receptor, (2) sensory neuron, (3) centre (inter neuron in the brain or spinal cord), (4) motor neuron and (5) effector. A reflex action is the response itself, while the reflex arc is the route the impulse travels.

The five parts of a reflex arc, in the order the impulse travels.

Key Points

  • Sensory neurons (mostly unipolar) carry impulses from receptors to the CNS; motor neurons (multipolar) carry them from the CNS to effectors; interneurons (multipolar) link the two inside the CNS.
  • Impulse conduction is about 20 times faster in myelinated than in non-myelinated neurons, by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
  • A reflex action is an immediate, involuntary and automatic response; the reflex arc is its pathway.
  • The five parts of a reflex arc are receptor, sensory neuron, centre, motor neuron and effector.
  • Reflexes do not involve the conscious part of the brain, so they are quicker than conscious responses and protect the body.

lessons.title: The Nerve Impulse and Resting Membrane Potential
lessons.notes_html:
A nerve impulse is the information about a stimulus that is transmitted from receptors to the CNS and from the CNS to the effectors. It is a wave of electrochemical change which runs along the length of the neuron, involving chemical reactions and movement of ions across the neurilemma.

17.3 Nerve Impulse

The measurement of the capacity to do electrical work is known as electric potential. It represents a type of stored energy produced during the separation of charge through a barrier; the charges are positive or negative, and the plasma membrane of the neuron acts as the separating barrier. An oscilloscope is an instrument with a screen which displays changes in the voltage on both sides of the plasma membrane of a neuron with time. The electric potential which exists across a cell membrane is known as membrane potential, which is either the resting membrane potential (RMP) or the action membrane potential (AMP). In humans, the normal speed of flow of impulse in a neuron is about 100–120 m/second. The refractory period lasts for about four milliseconds, so a neuron can conduct 250 impulses per second.

17.3.1 Resting Membrane Potential

A typical neuron at rest, or a non-conducting neuron, is said to be in the resting membrane potential state. In this case the neuron is more positive electrically outside than inside the plasma membrane, while the inside is more negative as compared to the outside. It measures about −70 millivolts (−0.07 volt). The non-conducting neuron is in a polarized state, and the RMP is maintained in an undisturbed membrane. If it is disturbed or stimulated by a sufficient stimulus, known as the threshold, then an action potential will occur.

Factors Involved in Resting Membrane Potential (RMP)

Sodium and potassium ions: Many kinds of ions are present inside and outside the plasma membrane of neurons, but the most important are sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions. Sodium ions are tenfold higher in concentration outside than inside the membrane, whereas potassium ions are thirty fold higher in concentration inside than outside the membrane. The membranes of all nerve cells possess sodium and potassium pumps, which transport these ions with the help of energy (ATP) against their concentration gradients: for every two potassium ions actively transported inside the membrane, three sodium ions are pumped out. Thus the inside becomes more negative (−70 mV) than the outside of the plasma membrane.

IonInside (mmol/L)Outside (mmol/L)
Sodium ions15145
Potassium ions1505
Negative ions15630

Table 17.1: Ionic concentration inside and outside a resting neuron.

Negative organic ions: Many types of large negative organic compounds are present on both sides of the plasma membrane of neurons. These organic ions include some proteins, amino acids, RNA, SO₄ and PO₄. These negative ions are much more concentrated inside the membrane than outside (outside, Cl⁻ ions are present), where they are only in negligible concentration. Thus the inside is more negative than the outside.

Channel proteins (gates): The plasma membrane is virtually impermeable to all ions except potassium ions. It is slightly permeable to potassium, so K⁺ leaks out of the neuron by diffusion. That is why the inside becomes more negative than the outside of the plasma membrane of the neuron.

Key Points

  • A nerve impulse is a wave of electrochemical change along the neuron; in humans it travels at about 100–120 m/second.
  • The resting membrane potential is about −70 mV (−0.07 volt), inside negative and outside positive: the polarized state.
  • Na⁺ is tenfold higher outside and K⁺ is thirty fold higher inside the resting neuron.
  • The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ pumped in.
  • Large negative organic ions trapped inside, and leakage of K⁺ out through channel proteins, keep the inside negative.
  • The refractory period is about 4 milliseconds, so a neuron can conduct about 250 impulses per second.

lessons.title: Action Potential and Saltatory Conduction
lessons.notes_html:
When a resting neuron receives a sufficient stimulus, its membrane potential reverses briefly and an impulse travels along the fibre. This lesson explains that reversal and how local circuits carry it forward, especially in myelinated axons.

17.3.2 Action Membrane Potential (AMP) (Depolarized State)

In the action or active membrane potential, the inside of the neuron becomes more positive and the outside becomes more negative. This is called the depolarized state, which happens when an appropriate stimulus is received and the positively charged sodium ions tend to move inside the neuron. The electrochemical change is so brief (about one millisecond) that only a portion of the neuron (i.e. one node of Ranvier to another node of Ranvier) is in the action membrane potential state, followed by recovery of the polarized state; thus impulses flow from one node of Ranvier to another.

The major factors involved in changing the resting membrane potential to the action membrane potential are:

  • Threshold stimulus — The capacity of a stimulus to bring an electrochemical charge on a neuron or to excite a given tissue. It is also known as the adequate stimulus (about −50 to −55 mV electric membrane potential). If a stimulus is not capable to excite, or is not appropriate, then it is called a sub-threshold or inadequate stimulus, and no action potential follows.
  • Influx of Na⁺ ions — When the threshold is reached, the membrane becomes more permeable to Na⁺ than to K⁺ due to the opening of Na⁺ gates. Thus an influx of Na⁺ ions by diffusion occurs, and the electric potential of the membrane changes from −70 mV towards zero and then reaches about 50 mV. This reversal of polarity across the two sides of the membrane is called depolarization. This state of electropositive inside and electronegative outside lasts for about one millisecond, till the Na⁺ gates are closed.
  • Repolarized state — After the peak of the action potential, called the spike potential, the permeability for Na⁺ decreases and the membrane now becomes more permeable for K⁺ by opening of K⁺ gates, so K⁺ rapidly diffuses out from the cytoplasm to the extracellular fluid. The sodium gate closes and the neuron gets its original polarity, i.e. it is repolarized (inside more electronegative and outside more electropositive). In fact, there is a slight overshoot into a more negative potential than the original resting potential, known as the hyperpolarized state, due to the slight delay in closing of all K⁺ gates compared with Na⁺ gates.
  • Refractory period (resting state) — After an action potential, the nerve fibre undergoes a period of recovery in which it regains the original ionic distribution and polarity, thus preparing itself for the next stimulation. The original ionic distribution is restored by the sodium–potassium exchange pump, which actively transports Na⁺ ions out and K⁺ ions into the neuron. This returns the membrane to its resting potential, i.e. from +50 mV to −70 mV.

In non-myelinated neuron fibres the impulse is continuous: K⁺ and Na⁺ ions can move across the membrane along the whole length of the neuron, so the action potential flows as a wave.

Note: The book's text gives the peak of the action potential as about 50 mV, while its Fig. 17.7 graph peaks at about +40 mV. Both describe the same spike; follow the text value of about +50 mV.

17.3.3 The Role of Local Circuits in Saltatory Conduction of Nerve Impulse

Saltatory conduction is the propagation of the action potential along a myelinated axon from node to node. The local circuits explain how the action potential (AP) is transmitted along the neuron. Basically, an action potential at a point in the axon develops a local circuit because the influx of sodium ions at that point makes that particular point positively charged. However, regions around that point are still negatively charged, because they are still in the resting potential state. The sodium ions at the point of the AP are then attracted to these negatively charged regions, hence setting up a local circuit at those regions. This circuit then opens the sodium channels at these points, sodium ions flow in, and the whole AP cycle continues; hence the AP moves along the axon.

Key Points

  • The threshold (adequate) stimulus is about −50 to −55 mV; a weaker, sub-threshold stimulus produces no action potential.
  • Depolarization: Na⁺ gates open, Na⁺ rushes in, and the potential rises from −70 mV to about +50 mV in about one millisecond.
  • Repolarization: Na⁺ gates close, K⁺ gates open and K⁺ diffuses out; a slight overshoot gives hyperpolarization.
  • During the refractory period the sodium–potassium pump restores the resting potential from +50 mV to −70 mV.
  • Local circuits between a depolarized point and the still-resting regions ahead move the action potential along the axon; in myelinated fibres this becomes saltatory conduction from node to node.

lessons.title: The Synapse and Synaptic Transmission
lessons.notes_html:
There is no cytoplasmic connection between successive neurons; however, impulses are transmitted from one neuron to the next, and this transmission occurs at a synapse.

17.4 Synapse

Synapses are microscopic gaps between successive neurons. These gaps are between the axon terminal of one neuron and the dendrites of another neuron. A single neuron may form synapses with many incoming fibres of different neurons. The gaps between successive neurons are cleave-shaped and are thus called the synaptic cleft. A neuron which carries information (impulse) towards a synaptic cleft is known as the transmitting neuron or presynaptic neuron, while a neuron which gets the impulse from the synaptic cleft is called the postsynaptic neuron or receiving neuron. The axon terminals of each presynaptic neuron have expanded endings called knobs, which contain many spherical sacs known as synaptic vesicles. Each vesicle contains as many as 10,000 molecules of a chemical messenger, the neurotransmitter substance. The dendrite of the postsynaptic neuron lacks these vesicles. The transfer of an impulse across the synapse is called synaptic transmission. There are about 100 known types of neurotransmitters.

There are two types of synapses: electrical synapses, which are rapid and whose synaptic cleft is only 0.2 nm thick, and chemical synapses, in which the gap is 20 nm and transfer of impulses occurs by neurotransmitters (chemicals).

Steps of Mechanism of Synaptic Transmission

  • Step 1 — When the action potential reaches the axon terminal, it is received by the synaptic knob. The calcium channels present in the presynaptic membrane open and calcium from the synaptic cleft transfers into the knob. Thus Ca⁺⁺ concentration increases, and the synaptic vesicles move towards the presynaptic membrane.
  • Step 2 — The vesicles containing neurotransmitter fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft.
  • Step 3 — The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptor molecules on the postsynaptic membrane.
  • Step 4 — The receptors of the postsynaptic membrane open some channels and allow sodium ions to diffuse across the postsynaptic membrane. As a result the postsynaptic membrane depolarizes (inside positive, outside negative) and an action potential is generated. Since this depolarization brings the membrane potential towards the threshold level, it is called the Excitatory Postsynaptic Potential (EPSP).
  • Step 5 — After the activation of the postsynaptic membrane, the neurotransmitters are immediately broken down by enzymes, like acetylcholinesterase for acetylcholine and monoamine oxidases for adrenaline, so the synapse resets for the next impulse.

A chemical synapse: vesicles in the presynaptic knob release neurotransmitter into the cleft, and it binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

17.4.1 Classification of Neurotransmitters

There are two major classes of neurotransmitters:

  • Excitatory neurotransmitters — These initiate nerve impulses and cause increased membrane permeability to sodium ions. They may be acetylcholine for the peripheral nervous system, and biogenic amines (derived from amino acids) for the central nervous system. Their types are epinephrine and norepinephrine, for heart beat rate during stress; serotonin and dopamine affect mood, sleep, attention and learning. All of these also function like hormones. Acetylcholine is the main transmitter for synapses that lie outside the CNS.
  • Inhibitory neurotransmitters — These decrease membrane permeability to Na⁺ ions, which results in raising the threshold of the stimulus, so the nerve impulse does not trigger, or lessens, in the adjoining neuron. Examples are the amino acid glycine and gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA), while the endorphins are peptides which decrease pain reception and act both as neurotransmitters and hormones.

Key Points

  • A synapse is a microscopic gap between two successive neurons; the cleave-shaped gap is the synaptic cleft (20 nm in chemical synapses, 0.2 nm in electrical synapses).
  • Synaptic knobs hold vesicles, each with up to 10,000 neurotransmitter molecules; about 100 types of neurotransmitters are known.
  • Transmission steps: action potential arrives, Ca⁺⁺ enters the knob, vesicles fuse and release transmitter, transmitter binds postsynaptic receptors, Na⁺ channels open and an EPSP is generated.
  • Transmitters are then broken down, e.g. acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase and adrenaline by monoamine oxidases.
  • Excitatory transmitters include acetylcholine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine; inhibitory ones include glycine, GABA and endorphins.

lessons.title: The Human Nervous System: Brain and Its Parts
lessons.notes_html:
Humans and most animals (except coelenterates and echinoderms, which possess a diffused nervous system) have a centralized nervous system. The human nervous system is the most advanced and also possesses some unique features, i.e. it enables us to convey our complex ideas, information and messages in the form of language, to make and use various tools, to preserve information (in written and video form), and it gives great learning and memory storage capacities.

17.5 Human Nervous System

The human nervous system consists of two primary divisions: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is the coordinating centre; the PNS (cranial nerves and spinal nerves) carries sensory (afferent) impulses in and motor (efferent) impulses out. Motor output works through the somatic nervous system (voluntary, to skeletal muscles) and the autonomic nervous system (involuntary, to cardiac muscles, smooth muscles and glands), which is divided into the sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight) and the parasympathetic nervous system (rest and digestion).

17.5.1 Architecture of Brain and Spinal Cord and Their Functions

The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord and acts as the coordinating centre; the brain lies in the skull and the spinal cord above (within) the vertebral column, i.e. in the midline of the body. The CNS is hollow and fluid filled. The brain has four cavities called ventricles, while the cavity of the spinal cord is known as the central canal. The fluid in these cavities, named cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (similar to blood plasma), acts as a cushion and bathes the neurons of the CNS.

Protection of the CNS: The brain is protected by the bony cranium of the skull, while the spinal cord is protected by the vertebrae of the vertebral column. Both brain and spinal cord are also covered by three membranes, collectively known as meninges (singular: meninx): the outer hard dura mater (next to the cranium), the inner pia mater (next to the brain and spinal cord) and the middle arachnoid mater. The cerebrospinal fluid is present between the pia mater and the arachnoid mater.

The brain of humans can be divided into the fore brain, mid brain and hind brain.

Fore brain has two subdivisions: the telencephalon (cerebrum) and the diencephalon (thalamus and limbic system).

  • Cerebrum — The cerebrum of humans is the largest among all other animals (more than half of the brain) and contains the highest number of neurons of any part of the brain. It is divided into two cerebral hemispheres, connected together by a band of axons known as the corpus callosum, which carries memory available on one side of the brain to the other side. The cerebrum contains four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. The left cerebral hemisphere controls the right side of the body, while the right cerebral hemisphere controls the left side of the body. Functionally, the cerebrum consists of the sensory area (receives impulses from receptors), the motor area (gives responses) and the associated area (interprets or analyses the incoming information). The cerebrum acts as the control centre for sight, smell, taste, speech and hearing. It also controls voluntary movements, thinking, learning, conscious sensations, judgment, reasoning, decision-making, dreams, emotional feeling, intelligence, analysis and interpretation of memory. The convolutions (grooves) on the outer cerebrum (cerebral cortex) are called gyri; deep grooves are called fissures and shallow grooves are called sulci. These grooves greatly increase the surface area of the cerebrum. According to Roger Sperry (printed as Roger Spray), the left cerebrum houses our language centre and logic and mathematical abilities, while the right hemisphere holds imagination, spatial perception, artistic and emotional abilities.
  • Thalamus — Lies below the cerebrum in the diencephalon. It acts as a relay centre and carries sensory impulses to the cerebrum and limbic system. The thalamus receives all sensory impulses (except the sense of smell).
  • Limbic system — Located in an arc just under the cerebrum. It consists of the hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus and some part of the cerebrum.
  • Hypothalamus — Located on the ventral side of the thalamus. It is both a nervous and an endocrine centre, i.e. a link between the nervous and endocrine systems. Its function is to maintain homeostasis, and it contains centres for regulating body temperature, water balance, menstrual cycle, blood pressure, sleep–wake cycle, hunger, sexual response and fight or flight.
  • Amygdalae — Two almond-shaped masses of neurons on either side of the thalamus. They produce sensations of pleasure and sexual arousal when stimulated, and punishment, love, hate, fear and rage.
  • Hippocampus — Consists of two horns that curve back from the amygdala and play an important role in the formation of long-term and short-term memory, thus it is required for learning.

Mid brain: In humans this portion of the brain is reduced. It contains an auditory relay centre and a centre that controls reflex movement of the eyes, and also contains an auditory reflex centre. The mid brain contains the reticular formation, which is a relay centre connecting the fore brain with the hind brain and is very important in screening the input information before it reaches higher brain centres.

Hind brain includes the pons, cerebellum and medulla.

  • Pons — A group of neurons located above the medulla; it acts as a bridge between the cerebellum, medulla and cerebrum. It is involved in the rate and pattern of breathing, sleep and wakefulness.
  • Cerebellum — The second largest part of the brain, bulb- or leaf-like in shape. It coordinates body movements and maintains body position, i.e. equilibrium. The cerebellum guides smooth and accurate motions and maintains body position. It is also involved in learning and memory storage for behaviour, and is best developed in birds, which engage in the complex activity of flight.
  • Medulla — The last part of the brain, but in evolutionary point of view it developed first. It controls several automatic functions, such as heart beat rate, blood pressure, breathing and swallowing.

The mid brain, together with the pons and medulla, is known as the brain stem, which supports life.

Ventricles of the brain: The human brain possesses four ventricles or cavities, which are filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The first and second ventricles are present between the limbic system and cerebrum and are known as lateral ventricles. Another ventricle is present between the limbic system and thalamus, called the third ventricle, while the fourth ventricle is present in the medulla. There is a tube between the third and fourth ventricle known as the iter or cerebral aqueduct, while an opening between the lateral ventricles and the third ventricle is called the interventricular foramen. The ventricles are lined by ependymal cells.

Key Points

  • The nervous system has two divisions: CNS (brain and spinal cord) and PNS (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • The CNS is protected by the skull and vertebral column and by three meninges: dura mater (outer), arachnoid mater (middle) and pia mater (inner); CSF cushions it and fills the four ventricles and the central canal.
  • The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, with two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum and four lobes; it is the seat of intelligence, memory, consciousness and voluntary control.
  • The thalamus is the relay centre for sensory impulses (except smell); the hypothalamus maintains homeostasis and links the nervous and endocrine systems.
  • The cerebellum is the second largest part and coordinates movement and balance; the medulla controls heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and swallowing.
  • Mid brain, pons and medulla together form the brain stem.

lessons.title: Spinal Cord and the Peripheral Nervous System
lessons.notes_html:
The medulla narrows down into the spinal cord, the second part of the CNS. Outside the CNS, the peripheral nervous system connects the CNS to every receptor and effector in the body.

17.5.2 Spinal Cord

The spinal cord is an elongated, hollow, fluid-filled and cylindrical structure. It extends from the foramen magnum (a hole in the bottom of the skull), lying in the neural canal of the vertebral column (up to the 3rd lumbar vertebra, as printed in the book). In a cross-section, the spinal cord exhibits inner butterfly-shaped grey matter and peripheral white matter. There is a tiny central canal in the centre of the grey matter, filled with CSF; around the central canal is a single layer of cells called the ependymal layer. The grey matter consists of the non-myelinated portion, i.e. mostly cell bodies of neurons, while white matter is composed of myelinated nerve fibres, i.e. mostly axons. The spinal cord controls reflexes below the neck region. It also conducts impulses to and from the different parts of the body and the brain, thus helping in the better function of the brain. Local anaesthesia is given at the fourth lumbar level, so as to protect the spinal cord.

17.5.3 Architecture of Human Brain Compared with Spinal Cord

Both the brain and spinal cord are made of white and grey matter. The difference is that in the brain, grey matter mostly lies outside (cerebral cortex) and white matter lies inside (cerebral medulla), while in the spinal cord grey matter lies inside, looking like a butterfly shape, and white matter lies outside.

Brain (Section)Spinal Cord (Section)
Grey matter outside: cerebral cortexGrey matter inside: butterfly or H-shaped
White matter inside: cerebral medullaWhite matter outside
Cavities are the four ventriclesCavity is the central canal

17.5.4 Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

The PNS includes all the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. A nerve is a collection of axons and dendrites. The cranial nerves arise directly from the brain; they may be sensory, motor or mixed: olfactory (smell), optic (sight), oculomotor, trochlear and abducens (eye movements), trigeminal (face sensation and chewing), facial (facial expression and taste), vestibulocochlear or auditory (hearing and balance), glossopharyngeal (tongue and throat), vagus (heart, lungs and gut), accessory (neck and shoulder muscles) and hypoglossal (tongue movements). The spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord and are all mixed nerves, each with a dorsal (sensory) root and a ventral (motor) root.

The PNS has two divisions:

  • Somatic nervous system — Carries sensory information from receptors to the CNS and motor orders from the CNS to the skeletal muscles, controlling voluntary actions.
  • Autonomic nervous system (ANS) — Controls involuntary organs (heart, gut and glands) through two opposing divisions. The sympathetic system arises from the thoracic and lumbar regions of the spinal cord; its preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long. It prepares the body for fight or flight: it increases heart rate, dilates the pupils and bronchi and inhibits digestion. The parasympathetic system arises from the brain and the sacral region; its preganglionic fibres are long and postganglionic fibres short. It restores rest-and-digest conditions: it slows the heart rate, constricts the pupils and stimulates digestion.
Sympathetic SystemParasympathetic System
Prepares the body for fight or flightRestores rest-and-digest conditions
Increases heart rate; dilates pupils and bronchi; inhibits digestionSlows heart rate; constricts pupils; stimulates digestion
Arises from thoracic and lumbar spinal cordArises from brain and sacral spinal cord
Preganglionic fibres short, postganglionic longPreganglionic fibres long, postganglionic short

Key Points

  • The spinal cord has inner butterfly-shaped grey matter (cell bodies) and outer white matter (myelinated axons), with a central canal of CSF lined by ependymal cells.
  • In the brain grey matter is outside and white matter inside; in the spinal cord this arrangement is reversed.
  • The PNS has 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
  • The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscles; the autonomic system controls involuntary organs.
  • Sympathetic action is fight or flight; parasympathetic action is rest and digest, and the two oppose each other.

lessons.title: Receptors for Smell, Taste, Touch and Pain
lessons.notes_html:
Section 17.1.2 classified receptors by stimulus. This lesson follows section 17.5.5 of the book and describes the structure and functioning of the receptors for smell, taste and touch and pain in detail.

17.5.5 Receptors

Olfactory receptors (smell): The olfactory receptors are chemoreceptors located in the olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity. They are stimulated by chemicals dissolved in the mucus (liquid) lining the nose. When stimulated, they send impulses through the olfactory nerve to the olfactory centre of the brain, where the sensation of smell is perceived. Smell is the one sense whose impulses do not pass through the thalamus relay.

Gustatory receptors (taste): The gustatory receptors are the taste receptors: chemoreceptors located in the taste buds on the tongue and in parts of the mouth and throat. They are stimulated by chemicals dissolved in saliva and produce the sensations of taste: sweet, sour, salty and bitter (and umami). The impulses travel through the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the gustatory centre of the brain, where taste is perceived. Both smell and taste receptors are chemoreceptors because they respond to chemical stimuli rather than to light, pressure or sound, and together they give the full flavour of food.

Receptors for touch and pressure: The receptors for touch and pressure are also called mechanoreceptors, as the book's Summary states. Meissner's corpuscles, lying close to the skin surface, respond to light touch. Pacinian's corpuscles, lying deeper in the skin, respond to pressure and vibration. Free nerve endings in the skin also respond to touch. When any of these is deformed by touch or pressure, it generates impulses that travel by sensory neurons to the sensory area of the cerebrum.

Receptors for pain: Nociceptors are the pain receptors. They are free nerve endings widely distributed in the skin and other internal organs, and they detect the stimulus of pain, i.e. damage to body tissues. Pain warns the body of injury and triggers protective reflexes, such as withdrawing the hand from a hot object.

Thermoreceptors in the skin detect changes of temperature, cold and warmth, completing the set of skin senses alongside touch, pressure and pain.

Key Points

  • Olfactory receptors are chemoreceptors in the nasal epithelium; they respond to chemicals dissolved in mucus and send impulses by the olfactory nerve.
  • Gustatory receptors are chemoreceptors in taste buds; they respond to chemicals dissolved in saliva and give sweet, sour, salty and bitter tastes.
  • Touch and pressure receptors are mechanoreceptors: Meissner's corpuscles for light touch and Pacinian's corpuscles for deep pressure.
  • Nociceptors are free nerve endings that detect pain and tissue damage; thermoreceptors detect temperature change.

lessons.title: Effects of Drugs on the Nervous System
lessons.notes_html:
Narcotic drugs are agents that interact with normal nervous activity. The use and abuse of drugs such as heroin, cannabis, nicotine, alcohol and inhalants damages the nervous system and general health, and their use is a major cause of addiction among young people.

17.6 Effects of Drugs on Nervous System

17.6.1 Heroin

Heroin is a powerful opioid narcotic drug made from morphine, obtained from the opium poppy. It is a depressant that produces euphoria, drowsiness and pain relief, but it is highly addictive: regular use causes tolerance and dependence, and an overdose depresses breathing and can be fatal. It is taken by injection, smoking or snorting and causes severe health and social harm.

17.6.2 Cannabis

Cannabis (marijuana, hashish) comes from the Cannabis plant and contains tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). It acts as a depressant and mild hallucinogen, distorting perception and impairing memory, concentration and coordination, and causing dependence with regular use.

17.6.3 Nicotine

Nicotine is an alkaloid derived from tobacco. It is a stimulant and highly addictive: it increases heart rate and blood pressure, constricts blood vessels and stimulates the nervous system. Smoking also damages the lungs and causes cancer and heart disease. Nicotine is one of the book's examples for both drug addiction and drug tolerance.

17.6.4 Alcohol

Alcohol is a depressant of the central nervous system. It slows reflexes and impairs judgment, coordination and consciousness, and long-term abuse damages the brain and liver. A dependent drinker who suddenly stops shows withdrawal symptoms, such as shaking, sweating, anxiety and, in severe cases, fits, because the nervous system has adapted to the drug.

17.6.5 Inhalants

Inhalants are volatile organic chemicals, commonly called glue sniffing, e.g. nail polish remover and glue, as the book's Summary states. Their vapours are inhaled and act quickly on the brain, causing intoxication, damage to the nervous system and, in some cases, sudden death.

17.6.6 Drug Addiction

Drug addiction is the compulsive need to keep taking a drug, with dependence of the nervous system on it. The terms drug addiction and drug tolerance are defined with reference to caffeine and nicotine: a person needs the regular dose to feel normal, and stopping the drug produces craving and withdrawal effects.

17.6.7 Drug Tolerance

Drug tolerance is the state in which the same dose of a drug produces less and less effect, so larger and larger doses are needed to get the original effect. Tolerance develops because the nervous system adapts to the drug, and it drives the user towards addiction and overdose.

17.6.8 Effects of Drugs on the CNS

Drug addiction and tolerance are directly associated with the functioning of the nervous system: drugs act at synapses by imitating, blocking or prolonging neurotransmitters, change mood, perception and consciousness, depress or stimulate the CNS, and damage neurons with long-term use. Depressants such as heroin and alcohol depress breathing centres in the medulla, which is why an overdose can stop breathing and kill.

DrugSource / TypeMain Effect
HeroinMorphine from opium poppy; opioid narcoticDepressant; euphoria and pain relief; highly addictive
CannabisCannabis plant (THC)Depressant and mild hallucinogen; impairs memory and coordination
NicotineTobacco alkaloidStimulant; raises heart rate and blood pressure; highly addictive
AlcoholDrinkCNS depressant; withdrawal symptoms on stopping
InhalantsGlue, nail polish remover (volatile chemicals)Rapid intoxication; damage to the nervous system

Key Points

  • Narcotic drugs are agents that interact with normal nervous activity, mostly at synapses.
  • Heroin is an opioid depressant made from morphine; cannabis contains THC; nicotine is a tobacco stimulant; alcohol is a CNS depressant; inhalants are volatile chemicals (glue sniffing).
  • Addiction is compulsive dependence on a drug; tolerance is needing ever larger doses for the same effect, as with caffeine and nicotine.
  • Stopping an addictive drug suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms, e.g. for alcohol.
  • Overdose of depressants can depress the breathing centre of the medulla and be fatal.

lessons.title: Disorders of the Nervous System and Diagnostic Tests
lessons.notes_html:
Nervous disorders are classified into five categories: vascular, infectious, structural, functional and degenerative. For each category the book describes the causes, symptoms and treatment of one example, and then explains the diagnostic tests used for nervous disorders.

17.7 Disorders of Nervous System and Diagnostic Tests

17.7.1 Vascular Disorders: Stroke

A stroke is a sudden loss of brain function caused by interruption of the blood supply to part of the brain, either by a clot blocking a blood vessel (ischaemic stroke) or by bleeding into the brain (haemorrhagic stroke). The affected brain cells are damaged, causing sudden weakness or paralysis (often on one side), loss of speech, vision problems and confusion. It is a medical emergency; treatment aims to restore blood flow or stop bleeding and then rehabilitate the patient.

17.7.2 Infectious Disorders: Meningitis

Meningitis is the inflammation of the meninges, the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, usually due to bacterial or viral infection. An infection of the central nervous system is called meningitis. Its symptoms are high fever, severe headache, stiff neck, vomiting and sensitivity to light. Bacterial meningitis needs urgent treatment with antibiotics and supportive care.

17.7.3 Structural Disorders: Brain Tumour

A brain tumour is an abnormal growth of cells in the brain. By pressing on or damaging brain tissue it causes headaches, fits, weakness and changes in senses or personality, depending on its position. Treatment is by surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, according to the type and site of the tumour.

Functional Disorders: Headache

A headache is the book's example of a functional disorder: the nervous system itself is not structurally damaged, but its working is disturbed, producing pain in the head. Rest, painkillers and removal of the trigger (such as stress or lack of sleep) are the usual treatment.

17.7.4 Degenerative Disorders: Alzheimer Disease

Alzheimer disease is a degenerative disorder in which brain neurons progressively die, causing loss of memory, confusion and changes in personality and behaviour, mostly in old age. There is no complete cure; medicines and care can only slow the symptoms and support the patient.

17.7.5 Diagnostic Tests

  • Electroencephalogram (EEG) — A record of the electrical activity of the brain, obtained by placing electrodes on the scalp, which detect the tiny voltage changes produced by brain neurons. The record shows rhythmic waves (alpha, beta, theta and delta waves) that change with sleep, wakefulness and disease. EEG is used to diagnose epilepsy (abnormal spike waves), sleep disorders, brain tumours and brain injuries, and to confirm brain death. It is painless, non-invasive and uses no radiation.
  • CT scan — Uses X-rays taken from many angles and combined by computer to give cross-sectional images of the brain. It is fast and good for bones, bleeding and emergencies.
  • MRI — Uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves, not ionizing X-rays, so it avoids radiation exposure. It gives much clearer images of soft tissues, brain, spinal cord and nerves, than CT, and can produce detailed images in several planes, revealing small tumours, strokes and demyelination that CT may miss. For soft-tissue nervous disorders, MRI is therefore a better diagnostic test than CT, while CT remains useful for fractures, bleeding and emergencies because it is faster and cheaper.

Key Points

  • Nervous disorders are classified as vascular (stroke), infectious (meningitis), structural (brain tumour), functional (headache) and degenerative (Alzheimer disease).
  • Stroke is caused by a blocked or burst brain blood vessel; meningitis is inflammation of the meninges by infection.
  • EEG records the electrical activity of the brain through scalp electrodes and diagnoses epilepsy and sleep disorders.
  • CT uses X-rays and is fast; MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, gives clearer soft-tissue images and uses no radiation.
  • For brain and spinal cord soft tissues, MRI is superior to CT; CT is better for bone, bleeding and emergencies.

lessons.title: Hormones as Chemical Messengers and Their Chemical Nature
lessons.notes_html:
The nervous system cannot reach every cell of the body, so another coordinating system is needed. The endocrine system fills this gap by chemical coordination. A hormone is a "chemical messenger", secreted by an endocrine gland. Traditionally, hormones are chemical products that travel within the bloodstream to all parts of the body, causing an effect on specific cells or target organs. They also affect exocrine glands or individual cells or tissues that secrete chemical substances.

18.1 Hormones- The Chemical Messengers

Glands that secrete hormones and pour them directly into the blood stream are called endocrine glands or ductless glands. Glands which secrete other substances such as digestive enzymes, milk, sweat and bile, and route their secretions to specific destinations by means of ducts, are called exocrine glands or ducted glands.

Path of Chemical Message (Hormone)

Hormones are "chemical messengers", secreted by cells that affect other cells. Hormones that travel within the blood stream and affect cells in another part of the body are known as endocrine hormones. Hormones that do not travel within the blood stream but only affect cells lying near the secretory cells are known as local hormones, e.g. serotonin, prostaglandin and gastrointestinal hormones.

Role of Hormones

Hormones are small soluble organic molecules which are effective in low concentration and act at a site where specific receptors are present. Therefore a hormone either increases, decreases or modifies the secretion of other glands. They also increase or decrease a body structure.

18.1.1 Chemical Nature of Hormones

Chemically, there are three basic types of hormones:

  • Steroid hormones.
  • Amino acids or their derivatives, proteins and glycoproteins.
  • A few belong to the fatty acids, e.g. prostaglandin.

Steroid hormones are derivatives of cholesterol and are secreted by the cortex of the adrenal gland (cortisol and aldosterone), testes (androgen), ovaries and placenta (estrogen and progesterone).

Amino acid derivatives are of two groups. Epinephrine and nor-epinephrine are secreted from the adrenal gland, and thyroxin and tri-iodothyronine (T₃), secreted by the thyroid glands. All these are derivatives of the amino acid tyrosine.

  • Polypeptide hormones are oxytocin, vasopressin, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, calcitonin, parathormone and melanocyte stimulating hormones. Oxytocin and antidiuretic hormones are peptides of only nine amino acids.
  • Proteinaceous hormones include somatotophic hormone (STH) and insulin.
  • Glycoprotein hormones are Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), Luteinizing Hormone (LH), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

Pheromones are hormone-like chemical messengers but removed outside the body. These are small, volatile chemicals that function in communication among animals and fungi. They act by influencing the physiology and behaviour of the receiving individuals.

Key Points

  • A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted by a ductless endocrine gland into the blood.
  • Endocrine hormones travel in blood to distant cells; local hormones act near the secretory cells.
  • Hormones are effective in low concentration and act only where specific receptors are present.
  • The three chemical types are steroids, amino acid derivatives / proteins and glycoproteins, and fatty-acid types such as prostaglandin.
  • Steroid hormones are cholesterol derivatives; thyroxin, T₃, epinephrine and nor-epinephrine are tyrosine derivatives.

lessons.title: Mode of Hormone Action: Fixed and Mobile Receptors
lessons.notes_html:
There are two modes of action of hormones. Which mode a hormone uses depends on its chemical nature: water-soluble hormones cannot cross the plasma membrane, while lipid-soluble hormones can.

18.1.2 Mode of Hormone Action

1. Fixed Membrane Receptor Mechanism

The peptide and protein hormones cannot pass through the cell's plasma membrane because they are water soluble. They attach with the receptors on the plasma membrane of the target cell and then start a series of steps in the cell. Adenylate cyclase is an enzyme of the plasma membrane, involved in ATP metabolism as a catalyst in the transformation of ATP into the second messenger, Cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP).

The hormone itself is the first messenger. The cAMP triggers various changes in the cell including activation of enzymes and gene activation. Another term used to describe this entire process is signal transduction (Fig. 18.1).

Fixed membrane receptor mechanism: a non-steroid hormone acts through cAMP, the second messenger.

2. Mobile Receptor Mechanism (Gene / Signal Modulation)

The steroid and amino acid derivative hormones can easily pass through the plasma membrane because both are lipid soluble. Their receptors are placed inside target cells, i.e. either in the cytoplasm or nucleus. Hormone and receptor together form a hormone-receptor complex, which then travels to the particular gene, acting as a transcription factor. The target gene is transcribed into messenger RNA, then it is translated into polypeptide (protein) in the cytoplasm. Thus the activities of target cells are modified by the altered gene expression (Fig. 18.2).

Fixed Membrane ReceptorMobile Receptor
Peptide and protein hormones, water-solubleSteroid and amino acid derivative hormones, lipid-soluble
Cannot pass through the plasma membranePass easily through the plasma membrane
Receptor is on the plasma membraneReceptor is inside the cell, in cytoplasm or nucleus
Acts through cAMP, the second messengerHormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor
Activates enzymes already present; signal transductionChanges gene expression and makes new protein

Key Points

  • Peptide and protein hormones are water-soluble and use fixed membrane receptors.
  • Adenylate cyclase converts ATP into cAMP, the second messenger; the hormone is the first messenger.
  • Steroid and amino acid derivative hormones are lipid-soluble and use mobile receptors inside the cell.
  • The hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, changing gene expression.
  • The whole fixed-receptor process is also called signal transduction.

lessons.title: Pituitary Gland and Its Anterior Hormones
lessons.notes_html:
The human endocrine system includes about 20 different endocrine glands, some of which are hypothalamus, pineal, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, adrenal, pancreatic islets and gonads (Fig. 18.3).

18.2 Endocrine Glands (System) of Human

18.2.1 Pituitary Gland

The pituitary gland is a small pea-sized gland, about 0.5 gram, lying in the brain. It is attached with the hypothalamus by a stalk known as the infundibulum, which is made of blood vessels and the nerve fibres of neurosecretory cells. The pituitary gland is divided into three lobes: the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis), posterior pituitary gland (neurohypophysis) and intermediate pituitary (median lobe) (Fig. 18.4).

Anterior Pituitary Gland

The anterior pituitary gland secretes six hormones, four of which are tropic hormones. Tropic hormones regulate the secretory action of other endocrine glands. Therefore the anterior pituitary gland is known as the master gland of the endocrine system. The tropic hormones are thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). The other two are primary hormones, growth hormone (GH) and prolactin (PRL), which directly affect body structure or an exocrine gland.

  • i) Growth Hormone (GH) or Somatotrophic Hormone (STH) — Its stimulating factor is somatotropin releasing factor (SRF or GHRF), secreted from the hypothalamus throughout life and inhibited by hypothalamic somatostatin. GH has a direct effect on growth of the body, skeleton and skeletal muscle. It stimulates cell growth and cell division and increases movement of amino acids to the cells, i.e. helps in protein synthesis. Over-secretion in early life is called gigantism: extraordinary elongation of bones and the person becomes giant. In adulthood, bones grow in thickness, thus enlargement of hand, feet, skull, nose and jaw bones occurs — acromegaly. Deficiency leads to pituitary dwarfism: development is much slower than normal, the individual has short stature, but brain development and Intelligence Quotient (IQ) are not affected.
  • ii) Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) — Controls the secretion and development of the thyroid gland. Its secretion depends on the level of thyroxin in the blood. The hypothalamus detects the level of thyroxin; if it is less, the hypothalamus secretes thyroid releasing factor (TRF) or thyrotropin, which stimulates the pituitary to release TSH. Low TSH may be harmful, heart disease and osteoporosis may occur, while high TSH in blood indicates hypothyroidism.
  • iii) Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) — Acts on the adrenal cortex and stimulates the secretion of corticosteroids. Its secretion is stimulated by adrenocorticotropic releasing factor (CRF) from the hypothalamus as a result of stress e.g. pain, cold, fear, stress, infection and pregnancy. Cushing disease is caused by a pituitary gland tumour that over-secretes ACTH, thus over-stimulating the adrenal cortex to secrete cortical production.
  • iv) Gonadotropins — Hormones that affect the gonads (testes / ovaries): FSH and LH.

Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH)

In human females, FSH targets the ovary and triggers the maturation of one egg (sometimes more than one egg) per month. In addition, it stimulates cells in the ovaries to secrete female sex hormones called estrogen. In males, FSH targets the testes and triggers the production of sperms. The secretion of FSH is stimulated by gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.

Luteinizing Hormone (LH)

Its secretion is also controlled by GnRH. In females a surge of LH near the middle of the menstrual cycle stimulates the release of an egg from the Graafian follicle of the ovary. LH also triggers the development of cells within the ruptured follicle to form a glandular structure called the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to prepare the uterus for the coming embryo. In the male, LH is also known as Interstitial Cell Stimulating Hormone (ICSH). It promotes production of the male sex hormone testosterone. Low secretion of both FSH and LH leads to delayed sexual maturation.

Prolactin Hormone (PRL)

It works in conjunction with estrogen, progesterone and other hormones. It causes enlargement of the mammary glands and prepares them for the production of milk (lactation) after birth. It stimulates mothers to care for their young ones. During the menstrual cycle, milk is not produced or secreted because the prolactin level in the blood is very low. Its secretion is inhibited by Prolactin Inhibiting Factor (PIF) from the hypothalamus.

Key Points

  • The pituitary is a pea-sized gland of about 0.5 gram, attached to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum, with anterior, posterior and median lobes.
  • The anterior pituitary secretes six hormones: four tropic (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) and two primary (GH, PRL); it is the master gland.
  • GH excess causes gigantism in early life and acromegaly in adults; GH deficiency causes pituitary dwarfism with normal IQ.
  • FSH matures the egg and estrogen in females and sperms in males; LH causes ovulation and corpus luteum in females and, as ICSH, testosterone in males.
  • Prolactin prepares the mammary glands for milk production and is inhibited by PIF.

lessons.title: Posterior and Median Pituitary, and the Hypothalamus
lessons.notes_html:
The posterior lobe does not make its own hormones — it stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus. The small median lobe makes one hormone of its own.

Posterior Pituitary Lobe (Gland)

The posterior lobe of the pituitary is non-glandular. It stores and releases two hormones that are produced by the hypothalamus: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) and Oxytocin. Lack of antidiuretic hormone causes diabetes insipidus: production of a large quantity of watery urine, and the person feels great thirst and is dehydrated.

  • i) Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) — It helps to regulate the volume of the blood by regulating the amount of water reabsorbed by the kidneys. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a low blood volume by detecting when the solute concentration of the blood is high; then the neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus make ADH, which is transported within the axon to the posterior pituitary, then released into the blood stream. ADH binds to target cells in the collecting ducts of the nephrons of the kidneys, increasing their permeability for water reabsorption, thus urine becomes concentrated. ADH also acts on the smooth muscles surrounding arterioles, an action that helps to raise the blood pressure. Alcohol suppresses ADH release, which is why excessive drinking leads to production of excessive quantities of urine and eventually to dehydration.
  • ii) Oxytocin — Also produced in the hypothalamus and transported within axons to the posterior pituitary for secretion. In women, it is secreted during the birth process, triggered by stretching of the cervix of the uterus at the beginning of birth; oxytocin binds to target cells of the uterus, increasing the contraction already taking place. It is also used artificially to induce labor. In lactating women, suckling causes the release of oxytocin, which targets muscle cells around the ducts of the mammary glands, thus promoting milk ejection. In the male, it helps to eject semen during copulation. Suckling also contracts the uterus to its normal size; over-secretion during child birth may cause rupture of the uterine wall, and under-secretion inhibits the normal labor process.

Median Lobe of Pituitary

It is smallest in humans, made of a thin layer of cells between the anterior and posterior pituitary gland. It secretes Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone (MSH). MSH releases due to the influence of external light, and more is secreted during pregnancy. It stimulates melanocytes in skin and hair to produce the brown pigment melanin, which darkens the skin. In Addison's disease, low cortisol removes feedback inhibition, so ACTH and MSH rise and the skin darkens.

18.2.2 Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus is a part of the forebrain, which is both nervous and endocrine. Thus it receives many sensory stimuli of the nervous system, which are converted into hormonal responses. It is the master control centre of the endocrine system because it monitors metabolites and hormonal level in the blood. It directly controls the pituitary gland. The hypothalamus has nerve cell clusters that produce and secrete many types of hormones. One of these centres produces releasing (tropic) and inhibiting hormones or factors — regulatory hormones, which regulate the synthesis and secretion of other endocrine glands. Another nerve cluster synthesizes antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin, then transports and stores them in the posterior pituitary gland (Table 18.1).

Hormone From HypothalamusAnterior Pituitary Response
Growth hormone releasing factor (GHRF)Secretion of growth hormone (GH)
SomatostatinInhibits growth hormone (GH)
Gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH)Secretion of FSH, LH and ICSH
Adrenocorticotropic releasing factor (CRF or ACRF)Secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
Prolactin inhibiting factor (PIF)Stops secretion of prolactin
Thyrotropin releasing factor (TRF)Secretion of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)
Secretes oxytocin and ADHStores these hormones in the posterior pituitary lobe

Key Points

  • The posterior pituitary is non-glandular: it stores and releases hypothalamic ADH and oxytocin.
  • ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, concentrates urine and raises blood pressure; its lack causes diabetes insipidus.
  • Oxytocin contracts the uterus in birth and ejects milk during suckling.
  • The median lobe secretes MSH, which stimulates melanin production in skin and hair.
  • The hypothalamus is both nervous and endocrine, the master control centre, acting through releasing and inhibiting factors.

lessons.title: Thyroid and Parathyroid Glands
lessons.notes_html:
Two glands in the neck control metabolism and blood calcium: the butterfly-shaped thyroid in front, and four tiny parathyroids embedded in its back surface.

18.2.3 Thyroid Gland

The thyroid gland is located at the base of the neck, attached to the trachea below the larynx. It is a bilobed, butterfly-shaped structure and both lobes are connected by a bridge of thyroid tissue known as the isthmus. The thyroid gland is made of spherical cells and secretes three types of hormones (Fig. 18.5):

  • Tri-iodothyronine or T3 — about 10%, but four times more potent than T4; it is more active in mammals.
  • Tetra-iodothyronine or T4 — about 90%, thus the major hormone, also called thyroxin.
  • Calcitonin hormone.

Both T3 and T4 have similar structure and function, but T3 has three iodine atoms while T4 has four iodine. The duration of action of T4 is four times more than T3. Their secretion is controlled by TSH from the anterior pituitary gland. T3 and T4 act on Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) by stimulating the breakdown of glucose, release of heat, generation of ATP and synthesis of cholesterol in the liver. Thyroxin, in conjunction with Growth Hormone (GH), acts on physical growth and mental development, and also promotes normal motility of the gastrointestinal tract. Thyroxin helps in metamorphosis of tadpole to adult frog; if its concentration is less, the tadpole does not metamorphose and instead remains a large size tadpole.

Effect of Over Secretion of T3 and T4 (Hyperthyroidism)

Excess secretion of thyroxin causes a condition known as Graves' disease. This disease causes exophthalmic goitre (bulging of the eye ball), a classical symptom of hyperthyroidism. If the patient's BMR increases, this can lead to cardiac failure, profuse perspiration and weight loss. It is an autoimmune disease: the blood serum of the patient has abnormal antibodies that mimic TSH and continuously stimulate thyroxin release.

Effect of Under Secretion (Hypothyroidism)

Less secretion of T3 and T4 (thyroxin) causes cretinism, goitre and myxoedema. Hypothyroidism may be due to absence of iodine, failure of the enzyme system involved in production of thyroid hormone, or lack of TSH.

  • Cretinism — In infants, less secretion of thyroxin causes the dwarf condition known as cretinism: stunted growth, mental retardation, coarse facial features, coarse scanty hair and retarded sexual development.
  • Myxoedema — (meaning mucous swelling) In adults, low secretion of thyroxin causes myxoedema: lower metabolic rate, thickness of skin of hands, brittleness of hair and nail, intolerance to cold, mental lethargy, weight gain, low pulse rate and low body temperature.
  • Goitre — Deficiency of iodine causes enlargement of the thyroid gland known as goitre. It is more common in mountainous areas where iodine is less in the soil or water, thus table salt with iodine is recommended. The thyroid gland works hard to produce a sufficient amount of thyroxin.

Note: the book's Summary wrongly says Graves' disease is caused by lower secretion of thyroxin. Follow the main text above: Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism — excess thyroxin. The book also loosely calls myxoedema "endemic or colloidal goitre"; keep myxoedema (adult hypothyroidism) and goitre (iodine-deficiency enlargement) as the separate conditions described here.

Calcitonin Hormone

The thyroid gland also secretes calcitonin, which plays an important role in controlling extra levels of calcium ions. If the calcium level rises in the blood, it promotes the deposition of calcium in bone, prevents reabsorption from nephrons of kidneys, and inhibits calcium absorption by the intestine. Over- and under-secretion of calcitonin disturb calcium metabolism, affecting skeletal muscle (weakened), the nervous system (impulses become irregular) and blood calcium composition, leading to massive kidney stone.

18.2.4 Parathyroid Glands

Parathyroid glands are very small glands embedded on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland. They are four in number and oval in shape. They secrete parathormone, which regulates the level of calcium and phosphorous in the blood and influences gene activation. A lower calcium level of blood stimulates the parathyroid directly to increase parathormone secretion. It absorbs calcium from intestine and kidney, while a high level suppresses its production (Fig. 18.6). Calcitonin is antagonistic to parathormone.

  • Deficiency of parathormone decreases blood calcium level, which results in excitability in nerves and muscles and convulsion. The nerves become very sensitive to stimuli; spasm and even death may occur in severe deficiency.
  • Over-secretion of parathormone causes increase of calcium level in the blood and low phosphate concentration. It causes weakness of skeleton similar to rickets, nerve and muscle do not respond well to stimuli, it increases reabsorption of Ca⁺⁺ by the kidneys and causes massive kidney stone formation. Both conditions may be fatal; removal of these glands causes death.

Key Points

  • The thyroid, at the base of the neck on the trachea, secretes T3 (about 10%, four times more potent), T4 / thyroxin (about 90%) and calcitonin.
  • T3 and T4 control BMR, growth and mental development, under TSH control.
  • Hyperthyroidism causes Graves' disease with exophthalmic goitre; hypothyroidism causes cretinism in infants and myxoedema in adults; iodine deficiency causes goitre.
  • Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; parathormone from the four parathyroids raises it — they are antagonistic.
  • Parathormone deficiency causes nerve excitability, spasm and convulsion; excess weakens the skeleton and forms kidney stones.

lessons.title: Pancreas: Insulin, Glucagon and Blood Glucose
lessons.notes_html:
The pancreas works both as an exocrine gland making digestive juice and as an endocrine gland controlling blood glucose.

18.2.5 Pancreas: (Islets of Langerhans)

The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine tissues. Exocrine tissues secrete pancreatic juices containing digestive enzymes; the pancreatic acinar cells are their functional units. The endocrine clusters of cells known as islets of Langerhans secrete two main types of hormones by two major types of cell: beta cells, about 60%, secrete insulin and alpha cells, about 25%, secrete glucagon; both hormones are protein in nature.
