The secretion of hormones is controlled by pituitary hormones STH and ACTH and responds directly to blood glucose level (Fig. 18.7). The islet figure also shows δ-cells (somatostatin), PP-cells (pancreatic polypeptide) and ε-cells (ghrelin).

Insulin

The beta cells secrete insulin, made of 51 amino acids. It is secreted when blood sugar level rises, such as after a meal.

  • It facilitates glucose transport across the plasma membrane.
  • It stimulates uptake of glucose by liver, muscles and adipose tissue (fat storing cells).
  • It promotes synthesis of proteins and fats by transferring glucose.
  • It inhibits gluconeogenesis (conversion of amino acids and fats into glucose), thus lowers blood glucose level.
  • It increases glycogenesis (insulin converts glucose into glycogen).

Glucagon

  • Alpha pancreatic cells secrete glucagon, made of 29 amino acids.
  • When blood glucose level decreases, glucagon converts glycogen, amino acids and fatty acids into glucose.
  • It is antagonistic to insulin.
  • The sympathetic nervous system stimulates its production.
  • It increases glycogen breakdown to glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the breakdown of protein, fats and lactic acids into glucose.

Note: the book prints "Glucogenesis" for the conversion of glycogen into glucose. The correct term, used in the solved exercises, is glycogenolysis — breakdown of glycogen.

Disorders Due to Insulin Deficiency

Deficiency of insulin may lead to a common metabolic disease called diabetes mellitus. It causes hyperglycaemia. Symptoms of hyperglycaemia: sugar is excreted in urine; frequent urine; abnormal thirst; rapid weight loss and weakness; drowsiness and fatigue; dehydration.

Disorders Due to Excess of Insulin

Excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia. Glucose utilization increases, in turn blood fat level gets high, which upsets nerve and muscle actions.

Other Types of Endocrine Cells in Pancreas

There are three other types of endocrine cells in the pancreas (about 15%) which secrete three types of hormones:

  • i) Somatostatin — It inhibits the release of gastrointestinal hormones.
  • ii) Pancreatic polypeptide — Self-regulates the pancreatic secretion activities and affects the hepatic glycogen level.
  • iii) Glycine acts as neurotransmitter — Its deficiency may lead to type-II diabetes; it increases insulin receptors in people without diabetes and is used as a supplement by type-II diabetes patients, as printed in the book.

Key Points

  • The pancreas is heterocrine: acinar cells make digestive enzymes; islets of Langerhans make hormones.
  • Beta cells (about 60%) secrete insulin (51 amino acids); alpha cells (about 25%) secrete glucagon (29 amino acids).
  • Insulin lowers blood glucose by uptake, glycogenesis and inhibiting gluconeogenesis; glucagon raises it — they are antagonistic.
  • Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus with hyperglycaemia; excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia.
  • Other islet products include somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide.

lessons.title: Adrenal Glands: Medulla and Cortex
lessons.notes_html:
Each kidney carries a small adrenal gland on its top. Its inner medulla handles emergencies, and its outer cortex makes steroid hormones needed all the time.

18.2.6 Adrenal Gland

Adrenal glands (ad: beside, renal: kidney) are located on the top of each kidney, thus two in number, each with two distinct regions. The adrenal cortex is the outer reddish brown portion. The adrenal medulla is the inner greyish portion. Both are under the control of the hypothalamus, which secretes ACTH releasing factor that stimulates the anterior pituitary, which in turn stimulates the adrenal cortex (Fig. 18.8).

Hormones of Adrenal Medulla

The adrenal medulla consists of modified ganglionic sympathetic neurons, which secrete two important hormones known as adrenaline (epinephrine) and nor-adrenaline (nor-epinephrine). Both prepare the body for stress and emergency situations, i.e. the sympathetic system. They stimulate liver cells to release glucose, thus making fuel for cellular energy.

  • Epinephrine dilates blood vessels in the brain, heart and skeletal muscles, thus increasing alertness to overcome stress, and heartbeat, breathing rate and metabolic rate increase.
  • Nor-epinephrine constricts blood vessels elsewhere, i.e. in the digestive system, and causes peripheral vasoconstriction. It also sustains blood pressure.

Disorders of medullary hormones: over-secretion may cause hypertension and aggressive behaviour during routine life, while under-secretion causes failure to combat stress situations. Epinephrine is sometimes given through injection as an emergency treatment in cardiac arrest (stopping of heart beat), anaphylactic shock and acute asthma.

Hormones of Adrenal Cortex

The adrenal cortex remains active all the time, especially after shock or stress situations and infections. It secretes two major groups (collectively called corticosteroids):

  • 1. Glucocorticoids — Regulate blood glucose level, e.g. cortisone.
  • 2. Mineralocorticoids — Regulate the level of minerals in the blood, e.g. aldosterone.

Cortisone: i) It is involved in glucose metabolism and is produced during anxiety, fever and disease. ii) It promotes the hydrolysis of muscle protein to amino acids, then amino acids to glucose. iii) It also helps to neutralize the inflammatory responses that lead to pain and swelling of joints in arthritis, etc. It favours metabolism of fatty acids rather than glucose, and is antagonistic to insulin.

Corticosterone is an example of both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid; it increases blood glucose level and regulates mineral ion balance.

Aldosterone promotes renal absorption of sodium and renal excretion of potassium, and maintains blood volume and blood pressure. The adrenal cortex mainly produces aldosterone. The adrenal cortex also produces a small amount of male sex hormones called androgen, in both male and female. Sometimes a tumour in the adrenal cortex of a female causes excess androgen production and thus development of certain male characteristics.

Disorders of Cortical Hormones

  • 1. Addison's disease — Occurs by lower secretion of corticosteroids, which leads to general metabolic disturbances, low blood sugar level, lethargy and weakness in muscle action, loss of salts, the skin has a bronze tone, and the patient cannot overcome stress conditions such as cold, heat and stress.
  • 2. Cushing's disease — Occurs due to over-production of cortisol; characterized by obesity (fat deposition on the back of neck), muscle wasting, hypertension and diabetes, and due to excess protein breakdown muscle and bones become weak.

Key Points

  • Adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys: outer cortex (reddish brown) and inner medulla (greyish).
  • The medulla secretes epinephrine and nor-epinephrine, preparing the body for stress and emergency.
  • The cortex secretes glucocorticoids (e.g. cortisone) for glucose regulation and mineralocorticoids (e.g. aldosterone) for mineral, blood volume and blood pressure regulation.
  • Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion by the kidney.
  • Low cortical hormones cause Addison's disease; excess cortisol causes Cushing's disease.

lessons.title: Gonads, Thymus, Pineal Gland and Artificial Steroids
lessons.notes_html:
The gonads make the sex hormones, the thymus trains immune cells, and the pineal gland keeps the daily rhythm. This lesson ends with the book's warning about artificial steroids in sports.

18.2.7 Gonads (Sex Organs)

The gonads (ovary and testes), besides gametogenesis, also secrete some important hormones.

Hormones of Ovary

The human female contains two ovaries in the abdominal cavities, which secrete two important female sex hormones, estrogen and progesterone.

1. Estrogen — There are three types of estrogen, almost similar in function (oestrone, oestriole and oestradiole). Estrogen is secreted from the ripening follicle (in some species from interstitial cells of ovaries) and placenta, under the influence of FSH from the anterior pituitary. These are steroid in nature. Functions:

  • At puberty it brings about secondary sexual characters (rounded appearance in females due to more fat deposition, large pelvic cavity and wide hips, enlargement of accessory sex organs such as vagina, uterus, oviduct, ovary and external reproductive organs) and high pitch of voice.
  • Conception and maintenance of pregnancy.
  • Help in formation and maturation of egg.
  • During the estrous (animals) and menstrual cycle (human) it exerts a positive feedback which results in a sharp rise in LH output by the pituitary.
  • Healing of the uterine wall after menstruation.
  • Prepares the uterine wall to secrete proteinaceous substance for the embryo.

Estrogen causes softness and smoothness of skin, therefore females possess softer skin than males. Disorders due to deficiency of estrogen: in young females it causes failure to mature sexually; in adults it causes sterility, while in old women after menopause its deficiency causes osteoporosis. Over-secretion may lead to development of fibroids (abnormal growth) in the uterus and polycystic ovary syndrome — numerous small collections of fluid known as follicles, which may disturb regular release of eggs, thus prolonged, frequent irregular menstrual periods and increased level of male sex hormones.

2. Progesterone — This hormone is produced by the ruptured follicle in response to LH from the anterior pituitary. The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. The placenta also secretes progesterone during pregnancy. Functions:

  • Prepares the uterus for implantation of the fertilized ovum.
  • Promotes the development of mammary glands during pregnancy.
  • Inhibits further secretion of FSH (to prevent any more follicles from ripening).
  • Further thickening and vascularization of the uterus wall.
  • Used in birth control pills (to prevent ovulation).
  • Regulates secretion of gonadotropin from the anterior pituitary.

Disorder due to under-secretion of progesterone: less secretion during the menstrual cycle decreases the chances of pregnancy and may cause early menstruation; it may lead to still birth or miscarriage.

Testes: (Male Sex Organs)

The testis, in the presence of FSH and ICSH, produces male sex hormones known as androgens, from its interstitial cells of Leydig. There are many types of androgen, the most important of which is testosterone. Functions:

  • In the fetus, androgen initiates the development of the sex organs.
  • At puberty it brings about secondary sexual characters (beard, moustaches, axillary and pubic hair, voice becomes low pitch, and spermatogenesis) and sex drive.
  • They increase secretion of sebaceous glands and sweat glands and increase subcutaneous fatty tissue.
  • Increase metabolic activities in general.
  • Inhibit formation of female genital organs in the fetus.
  • Increase Red Blood Cells (RBCs) production and thickness of bones.

Deficiency of androgens causes castration-like effects (i.e. secondary sexual characters do not appear in the male and the body looks like an immature female), thus causing male sterility.

18.2.8 Thymus Gland

This lobular endocrine gland is situated at the upper part of the chest behind the sternum. It consists of two lobes that join in front of the trachea. It is largest and more active in childhood. It is responsible for the development and differentiation of T-lymphocytes before they leave the thymus. The hormone of this gland is called thymosin or thymin.

18.2.9 Pineal Gland

It is a tiny cone-shaped body, located deep between the cerebral hemispheres of the brain. It produces the hormone melatonin. It is involved in a daily cycle called circadian rhythm (regulated by the eyes of mammals). In many mammals, it regulates the seasonal reproductive cycle, and the sleep and wake cycle in humans. It responds to external conditions of light and darkness as sensed through the eyes.

Role of Artificially Synthesized Steroids in Sports and Their Long-Term Effects

Steroids are artificial substances developed in order to do the job of testosterone. They can be classified as either anabolic or androgenic. Anabolic functions include those that promote formation of muscles, vertical growth and regulation of weight gain or loss. Androgenic refers to masculine attributes such as agility, strength and endurance. By the help of these drugs, sportsmen can become bigger, stronger, more agile, and hence more competitive. Artificial steroid use carries many severe health risks. Major medical problems associated with steroids include a weakened immune system, liver disease, kidney disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, increased risk for heart disease, blood clots, strokes, tissue damage and cancer.

Key Points

  • Ovaries secrete estrogen (from the ripening follicle, under FSH) and progesterone (from the corpus luteum, under LH); both are steroids.
  • Estrogen develops female secondary sexual characters; progesterone prepares the uterus for implantation and maintains pregnancy.
  • Testes secrete androgens, chiefly testosterone, from interstitial cells of Leydig, developing male characters and spermatogenesis.
  • The thymus (largest in childhood) secretes thymosin and develops T-lymphocytes; the pineal secretes melatonin for circadian rhythm.
  • Artificial anabolic / androgenic steroids build muscle and strength but cause liver and kidney disease, high blood pressure, heart disease, strokes and cancer.

lessons.title: Other Endocrine Tissues and Cells
lessons.notes_html:
Many hormones are also produced by organs or tissues whose function is not primarily endocrine; even neurons secrete hormones.

18.2.10 Other Endocrine Tissues / Cells

Hormones of Gut (Gastro-intestinal Tract)

  • i) Gastrin — Produced by the stomach wall, travels in the bloodstream but exerts its effect locally, stimulating the production of gastric juice (pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid). The secretion of gastrin depends on proteinaceous food in the stomach when it is partially digested.
  • ii) Secretin and Cholecytokinin (CCK) — These two hormones control pancreatic and liver secretion. Both are formed in the cells of the duodenal wall, in response to acidic chyme, fatty and proteinaceous food.

Placental Hormones

The placenta secretes hormones like progesterone, which maintains pregnancy. It also secretes estrogen, chorionic hormones, relaxin and chorionic gonadotrophin hormones. All of these facilitate pregnancy and birth.

Hormones Secreted from Kidneys

Kidneys produce erythropoietin, which increases red blood cell production. Stimuli such as bleeding or moving to high altitudes (where oxygen is scarcer) trigger release of this hormone. The kidney also secretes the hormone renin, which constricts arteries and monitors blood pressure, and takes corrective action if it drops. Calcitriol is also secreted from kidneys and acts on the cells of the intestine to promote the absorption of calcium from the diet.

Hormones of Liver

The liver secretes a group of hormone-like compounds called prostaglandins. These provide a protective response during infection. Somatomedins hormone is also secreted from the liver; it stimulates cell growth and development.

Hormones of Brain

Enkephalins and endorphins are two related hormones produced in the brain. Both bind to pain receptors and so block sensation. Enkephalins are found in the thalamus and some parts of the spinal cord, while endorphins are found in the pituitary gland, in other parts of the brain, or distributed throughout the nervous system.

Hormone of Heart

The heart secretes atrial natriuretic hormone, which increases sodium excretion and lowers blood pressure.

Adipose Tissues

Adipose tissue secretes a hormone leptin, which reduces appetite. Fig. 18.3 also lists resistin from adipose tissue, numerous hormones from the digestive tract, and ANP (atrial natriuretic peptides) from the heart.

Fig. 18.3 shows the same idea for the whole body: the heart gives atrial natriuretic peptides (ANP), the kidney gives renin, erythropoietin (EPO) and calcitriol, adipose tissue gives leptin and resistin, the digestive tract gives numerous hormones, the thymus gives thymosins, the pineal gives melatonin and the gonads give androgens, estrogens, progestins and inhibin — all from tissues whose main job is something else.

Key Points

  • Gut hormones: gastrin (stomach, gastric juice), secretin and CCK (duodenum, pancreatic and liver secretion).
  • The placenta secretes progesterone, estrogen, relaxin and chorionic gonadotrophin to facilitate pregnancy and birth.
  • Kidney hormones are erythropoietin (RBC production), renin (blood pressure) and calcitriol (calcium absorption).
  • The liver gives prostaglandins and somatomedins; the brain gives enkephalins and endorphins that block pain.
  • The heart secretes atrial natriuretic hormone and adipose tissue secretes leptin, which reduces appetite.

lessons.title: Feedback Mechanism and Nervous Versus Chemical Coordination
lessons.notes_html:
Hormones do not act unchecked. Their own products switch them on or off — this is feedback, the system that keeps homeostasis.

18.3 Feedback Mechanism (FBM)

It is a type of interaction in which the controlling mechanism is itself controlled by the products of the reactions it is controlling. Different hormones act as a system of check and balance for each other in order to keep homeostasis. In this case two opposing systems are required, i.e. if there is an excitatory system, there must be an inhibitory system.

18.3.1 Negative Feedback Mechanism

The type of FBM in which increase in production decreases the operation so as to stop the production of products. It stabilizes a system. Negative feedback is most common and self-limiting.

Example: If our blood glucose level becomes too high, then beta cells in the islets of Langerhans respond to secrete more insulin. The insulin lowers blood glucose by converting glucose into glycogen and making body cell membranes more permeable to glucose. Thus glucose is utilized by cells and surplus glucose is stored in the form of glycogen (Fig. 18.9). If the level of blood glucose gets too low, alpha cells in the islets of Langerhans secrete glucagon. It converts glycogen into glucose to raise and maintain blood glucose level. Thus the level of blood glucose is maintained by negative feedback mechanism.

Negative feedback: insulin lowers high blood glucose, glucagon raises low blood glucose, and the change switches the hormone off.

18.3.2 Positive Feedback Mechanism

The type of FBM in which increase in production of a substance increases the operation to produce more products. It speeds up the system rather than stopping it, e.g. oxytocin production during labor and suckling by the baby. It is rare, explosive and self-reinforcing (Fig. 18.10). In labour: nerve impulses from the cervix are transmitted to the brain, the brain stimulates the pituitary gland to secrete oxytocin, oxytocin is carried in the bloodstream to the uterus, oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions and pushes the baby towards the cervix, and the head of the baby pushes against the cervix — so the cycle repeats stronger until delivery. Positive feedback causes instability, so such responses are not homeostatic and are rare.

18.3.3 Similarities Between Nervous Coordination and Chemical Coordination

  • i) Both synthesize chemical messengers.
  • ii) Both release the chemical messengers in extracellular spaces of the body.
  • iii) Both help in coordination of the body.
  • iv) Both function in response to internal or external stimuli.
  • v) Both are homeostatic in function.
Nervous CoordinationChemical Coordination
Electrical and chemical transmissionChemical transmission (hormone) through blood system
Structural and functional units are the neuronsStructural and functional units are hormone-producing cells and neurosecretory cells
Chemicals act where they are producedHormones and neurohormones are poured into the blood, which affects the target cells
Rapid transmission and responseSlow transmission and relatively slow acting (adrenaline an exception)
Pathway is specific through nerve cells; response is very localized, e.g. one musclePathway is not specific (blood circulates whole body); target specific response may be very widespread, e.g. growth
Often short term changesOften long term changes
Neurohormones are broken down shortly after their releaseHormones remain active for much longer duration within the blood

Key Points

  • Feedback means the controlling mechanism is itself controlled by the products it controls; it keeps homeostasis.
  • Negative feedback: an increase in production decreases the operation — it stabilizes and is self-limiting, e.g. insulin and glucagon for blood glucose.
  • Positive feedback: an increase produces still more — it is rare, explosive and self-reinforcing, e.g. oxytocin in labour.
  • Nervous and chemical coordination both use chemical messengers, respond to stimuli and are homeostatic.
  • Nervous coordination is rapid, specific, localized and short term; chemical coordination is slow, widespread and long term.

lessons.title: Behaviour and Biological Rhythms
lessons.notes_html:
Behaviour is the sum of everything that animals do: all the actions and responses of an animal to stimuli. The scientific study of animal behaviour is called ethology, and a scientist who studies animal behaviour in natural conditions is called an ethologist. A stimulus is a form of energy that activates a specific type of sensory receptor and starts a behaviour.

19.1 Behaviour

Behaviour links the nervous system to the environment: a stimulus is detected by receptors, processed by the nervous system, and answered by effectors as an action. The book divides behaviour into two main types: innate behaviour, which is inborn, and learned behaviour, which is acquired through experience. Many behaviours repeat at regular intervals, and these are studied as biological rhythms.

19.1.1 Biological Rhythms

The behavioural activities of living organisms which take place at regular intervals are called biological rhythms or biorhythms. They are controlled by an internal biological clock even without environmental stimuli.

  • Internal rhythm (endogenous) — Controlled by an internal biological clock, e.g. body temperature regulation and the menstrual cycle. It continues even without external cues.
  • External rhythm (exogenous) — Controlled by synchronizing the internal cycle with the external environment, e.g. sleep, wakefulness and the day/night cycle. Exogenous stimuli are due to changes in the external stimuli, while endogenous rhythms are due to internal stimuli.

By their period, rhythms are of the following kinds:

  • Circadian rhythm — An endogenously generated rhythm with a 24-hour cycle, e.g. body temperature, sleep and wakefulness. It is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) in the hypothalamus.
  • Diurnal rhythm — A circadian rhythm synchronized with the day/night cycle. Animals active during the day are diurnal, those active at night are nocturnal, and those active in twilight (dawn and dusk, dim light) are crepuscular.
  • Ultradian rhythm — Much shorter than a circadian rhythm, e.g. the feeding cycle.
  • Infradian rhythm — A biological rhythm which is more than 24 hours. It can be monthly, e.g. the menstrual cycle in human females, or annual: the annual rhythm is less than or about 365 days, e.g. hibernation, reproduction in most animals and migration of birds.

Biological clock: The biological clock is an internal mechanism by which rhythmic phenomenon occurs and is maintained even without intervention of environmental stimuli. It is still not clear how the biological clock controls such rhythm.

Key Points

  • Behaviour is everything an animal does; its scientific study is ethology, and its student is an ethologist.
  • Biological rhythms are activities repeated at regular intervals, controlled by an internal biological clock.
  • Endogenous rhythms arise from internal stimuli; exogenous rhythms are synchronized with the external environment.
  • Circadian rhythms run on a 24-hour cycle under the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus; diurnal, nocturnal and crepuscular are its day/night forms.
  • Ultradian rhythms are shorter than 24 hours; infradian rhythms are longer, monthly (menstrual cycle) or annual, about 365 days (hibernation, migration).

lessons.title: Innate Behaviour: Orientation, Taxes and Tropisms
lessons.notes_html:
Innate behaviours are preprogrammed within the nervous system before birth and are demonstrated in a somewhat complete form the first time they are exhibited.

19.2 Innate Behaviour (Inborn or Instinct Behaviour)

For example, a newborn baby will turn to suckle when touched on the cheek near the mouth. The baby performs this without learning or altering its behaviour based on experience. Innate behaviours are important to the survival of an animal, because they help animals stay alive in certain situations and provide adaptive advantages that contribute to its fitness or ability to achieve reproductive success. Innate behaviour is especially beneficial for those animals which have a short life span and a weakly developed nervous system, so animals having a short life cycle depend on innate behaviour. All plants exhibit innate behaviour. The pathway of innate behaviour is simple and automatic, i.e. a highly developed nervous system is not involved.

19.2.1 Types of Innate Behaviour

Innate behaviour is genetically transmitted from parents to their offspring. There are two primary types of innate behaviours, i.e. orientation and non-orientation. The orientation behaviours are coordinated movements that occur in response to an external stimulus and are of two main types, i.e. taxis and tropism. In animals it is called taxis, whereas similar behaviour in plants is called tropism.

Taxes: Taxes (singular taxis) is a directional movement in which the whole animal either moves toward the stimulus or away from the stimulus, i.e. positive taxis or negative taxis respectively, e.g. in response to heat, chemicals (foods) and light. A good example is the unicellular protozoan Euglena, which shows positive movement towards dim light and negative movement to intense light. Thus Euglena during day time moves under the water where the intensity of light is less. The movement of Euglena towards dim light is therefore a positive taxis.

Tropism (means to turn): It is a directional growth movement in plants, i.e. towards or away from stimuli. Phototropism is movement towards or away from the stimulus of light: the shoot will grow towards light, while roots grow away from light. The root shows positive geotropism or gravitropism (towards soil and gravity), while the shoot is negatively geotropic and gravitropic. The roots also exhibit positive hydrotropism (towards water).

The non-orientation behaviour includes reflexes and instincts, both of which do not exhibit a particular movement in response to stimuli; they are covered in the next lesson.

Taxes in Euglena: it moves away from intense light (negative taxis) and towards dim light (positive taxis).

Key Points

  • Innate behaviour is inborn, genetically transmitted and shown in fairly complete form the first time; it is vital for short-lived animals with simple nervous systems.
  • Its two primary types are orientation and non-orientation behaviour.
  • Taxis is directional movement of the whole animal: positive towards and negative away from the stimulus, e.g. Euglena towards dim light.
  • Tropism is directional growth in plants: phototropism to light, positive geotropism in roots and negative geotropism in shoots, and positive hydrotropism towards water.

lessons.title: Reflexes and Instincts: Fixed Action Patterns
lessons.notes_html:
Non-orientation innate behaviours do not involve movement in a particular direction in response to a stimulus. The book describes two of them: reflexes and instincts.

19.2.2 Reflexes or Reflex Action (L. reflector, to bend back)

A reflex is an involuntary, automatic response to changes occurring inside or outside the body. The responses of reflexes may come from the unconscious portion of the brain, such as blinking of our eyes, but most responses come from the spinal cord, such as withdrawal of the hands when we touch a hot surface. The withdrawal of the hand on touching a hot object is the book's standard example of a reflex, carried out through the reflex arc described in Unit 17.

If a particle of food or a piece of hair enters your tracheal lining, it will initiate a coughing reflex, which cannot be suppressed. Most insects have simple startle reflexes triggered by small disturbances, as well as more comprehensive escape reflexes triggered by large disturbances. Innate behaviour or instinct is usually in the form of simple reflexes such as removing one hand from a hot stove, while the human suckling reflex is a good example of a complex unlearned behaviour.

19.2.3 Instincts (Fixed Action Patterns)

This type of innate behaviour is an unlearned, inherited fixed action pattern of responses or reactions to certain kinds of stimuli. It is performed without being based upon prior experience, i.e. in the absence of learning. In this genetically programmed, inflexible behaviour, the complete body of the animal is involved.

Each species displays its own characteristic instinctive behaviour. Some examples of instinctive behaviours are the migration of salmon fish, dances of bees, construction of hanging nests by birds, construction of intricate webs by spiders and mating behaviour of stickleback fish. These five examples are described in the next lesson.

Instincts are controlled by the brain and by hormones, which can function as a feedback system, as the book's Skill box shows for reproduction in ringdoves: gonadotropins stimulate the gonads of both males and females to produce steroids; courtship and nest building follow this increase in gonadal steroids; rising levels of female progesterone stimulate egg laying and incubation, at which stage gonadotropins decrease, as do female courtship displays, while males remain responsive to females; after approximately one week of incubation, levels of prolactin increase in both sexes, allowing both males and females to produce a milk-like substance, while gonadotropin and steroid levels decrease; when the eggs hatch and the chicks mature, prolactin levels decrease, gonadotropins increase, and the cycle begins again. From such examples we observe that hormones and the brain control instincts.

Key Points

  • A reflex is an involuntary, automatic response, mostly from the spinal cord (hand withdrawal) and sometimes from the unconscious brain (blinking, coughing).
  • Insects show startle reflexes to small disturbances and escape reflexes to large disturbances.
  • Instincts are unlearned, inherited fixed action patterns involving the whole body, performed without prior experience.
  • Examples of instinct: salmon migration, bee dances, hanging nests of birds, spider webs and stickleback mating behaviour.
  • Hormones and the brain control instincts, e.g. the gonadotropin, steroid, progesterone and prolactin feedback cycle in ringdoves.

lessons.title: Instinct in Action: Salmon, Weaver Birds, Bees, Spiders and Sticklebacks
lessons.notes_html:
The book gives five detailed examples of instinctive behaviour. Each is performed correctly the first time, without learning, by every member of the species.

Migration of Salmon

For spawning, the upriver male and female salmon fish migrate to the river. The female builds her nest and lays eggs, and the male then deposits his sperms over the eggs. The salmon die within a few days of spawning. After hatching, the young fishes for a few days remain in the river, then migrate to the ocean, where they spend their adult life (about 6 months to 7 years). When adult fishes reach their sexual maturity, the Pacific salmon may swim hundreds, even thousands of miles, to get back to the river where they hatched. During this journey most of the adult fishes die and only a few reach their breeding ground. The migration for spawning by salmon fish is an example of instinct behaviour.

Construction and Hanging Nest by Some Birds

A bird named Baya weaver (Genus Ploceus, about 100 species) constructs its nest during the breeding season. They nest in colonies of up to 20–30, close to the source of food, water and nesting material. These nests are made by the male and hang either between two twigs or a leaf. The female selects a nest, then the male and female are paired. The descendants of these birds exhibit this behaviour in each generation without learning, so it is also an example of instinct behaviour.

Dances of Bees

The dances of bees are also an example of instinct. When worker bees return to their hives, they do a dance called the waggle dance. They can do the waggle dance without learning, so it is an example of instinct behaviour. They dance to inform and tell other bees of the hive where the food is present. In the solved exercises, the round dance is added: it is performed when food is near the hive (within about 50–100 metres), the bee moving in circles to indicate food nearby but not its direction; in the waggle dance for farther food, the direction of the waggle run indicates the direction of food relative to the sun, and its duration indicates the distance.

Construction of Intricate Web by Spider

Many species of spiders have the instinct to construct intricate webs. Web spinning is stereotyped, hard-coded instinctive behaviour. Any member of a given species of spider will spin the same web, given the same environment, without ever having learned the shape of the web. The spider first lays a bridge thread, then builds a frame and radial threads, and finally a sticky spiral to catch prey; vibrations in the threads tell the spider where prey is caught.

Mating Behaviour of Stickleback Fish

There are about eight species of stickleback fishes, which belong to five genera. Their reproductive behaviour is highly rationalized (organized). They breed during spring, at which time the male becomes suffused with colour (red to yellow and orange to black, depending on species). The male fish builds a nest of plant materials glued together by thread-like mucus secretions from his kidneys. After building the nest, the male coaxes and drives a female into the nest to lay her eggs. He then follows her into the nest to fertilize the eggs. Each female may lay up to 200 eggs, and one or more than one female may be chosen by one male. When the nest is full, the male becomes the guard, i.e. he aggressively defends the eggs from intruders. The male also aerates the eggs with the help of his pectoral fins till hatching; thus parental care is given by the male fish. The whole sequence is a chain of fixed actions released by sign stimuli such as the male's coloured belly and the female's swollen belly.

Key Points

  • Salmon migrate from the ocean back to their home river to spawn, swimming hundreds to thousands of miles, and die after spawning.
  • The male Baya weaver builds the hanging nest by instinct; the female selects a nest, and colonies hold up to 20–30 nests.
  • Bees perform the waggle dance (and round dance for near food) without learning, to tell hive mates where food is.
  • Every spider of a species spins the same intricate web without ever learning its shape.
  • In sticklebacks the male builds the nest, the female lays up to 200 eggs, and the male fertilizes, guards and aerates them till hatching.

lessons.title: Learning Behaviour: Habituation, Imprinting and Conditioning
lessons.notes_html:
Learning behaviours are based on experience, and are not hereditary and inborn. Learning helps an animal change its behaviour to adapt to changes in environmental conditions. Learning is more prominent in those animals which have a comparatively long life and also have a well-developed nervous system.

19.3 Learning

Learning can be grouped into six categories, i.e. habituation, imprinting, classical conditioning, trial and error learning, latent learning and insight learning.

Instinctive BehaviourLearning Behaviour
Depends on the hereditary material the animal inherits; the animal may be born with the right responses built into the nervous systemDepends on environmental influence, but the ability to modify behaviour depends on the hereditary material
Experience has no obvious influence on this behaviourExperience has an obvious influence on this behaviour
Depends on selection during the history of the species; helps adaptability of the organism in the environmentDepends on selection during the lifetime of the individual; helps the organism adapt in the given environment
Advantageous for animals with short life spans and little or no parental care, e.g. honeybees inherit the tendency to fly towards flowers to seek nectar and pollenAdvantageous for animals with long life spans and parental care, e.g. conditioned reflex type I in dogs, which learn to salivate on the ringing of a bell alone
Evolves slowly in the speciesEvolves during the life cycle of the individual, though the ability to learn depends on its genetic basis

Table 19.1, corrected: in the book the two columns of this table are misprinted as External Respiration and Internal Respiration; they should read Instinctive Behaviour and Learning Behaviour, as the table's own title and contents show.

19.3.1 Habituation

In this type of learning, an animal learns by experience not to respond to a situation if the response has neither positive nor negative consequences. For example, pigeons and many other birds living in cities learn not to flee from people who pose no threat to them. This behaviour is adaptive and is reversible. Another example is feeling threatened by squirrels: when one in a group feels threatened, the other squirrels hear its signal and run to a protective area; if the signal comes from an individual who has caused many false alarms, the signal will be ignored. Habituation is the simplest form of learning: the animal learns to ignore a repeated, irrelevant stimulus, as when the marine snail Aplysia (sea hare) stops withdrawing its gill after repeated harmless touches.

19.3.2 Imprinting

Imprinting is a time-dependent form of learning. It involves exposure to sign stimuli, most often early in development, e.g. in response to a moving object and to certain sounds. Baby geese imprint on their mother and follow her during a short, sensitive period after hatching. They are neurally wired to learn crucial information and to identify the individual that would protect them in the months ahead; normally this individual is the mother or father. K. Lorenz explained imprinting: when incubator-hatched goslings (geese) spent their first few hours with Lorenz rather than with their parents, they imprinted on him and followed Lorenz from then on, and the goslings did not recognize their parents or other adult geese of their own species.

19.3.3 Difference Between Habituation and Imprinting

Habituation is reversible and imprinting is irreversible learned behaviour. Habituation is an example of simple learning behaviour, in which an animal gradually stops responding, or no longer reacts, to repeated stimuli. Imprinting, in contrast, is a specialized form of learning which occurs during a brief period in young animals after hatching or birth. They are able to learn from their parents, so animals' early experiences have a big effect on the way they behave as adults.

19.3.4 Classical Conditioning (Conditioned Reflex Type-I)

Ivan Pavlov's classical experiments with dogs are an example of classical conditioning. A dog will salivate just before eating. Pavlov's dogs were conditioned to salivate even in the absence of food: the dogs did so in response to the sound of a bell that was initially associated with the presentation of food. In this case, the animals learned to associate an automatic, unconditioned response with a novel stimulus that does not normally trigger the response. Solving a mathematical problem, by contrast, is an example of insight learning, not conditioning.

19.3.5 Instrumental Learning (Trial and Error or Operant Learning)

In this type of learning behaviour, an animal learns a response to a particular stimulus after many unsuccessful tries; it is also called conditional reflex type II. B. F. Skinner (USA psychologist) studied operant conditioning in rats by placing them in a specially designed box (also called the Skinner box) fitted with levers and experimental devices. The rats in the box ran feverishly this way and that, until one of them accidentally pressed a lever and a piece of food appeared. At first the rat would ignore the lever and continue to move here and there, but soon it learned that pressing the lever will give food to it. As the rat learns by chance, i.e. by trial, this type of learning has been named trial and error learning: responses followed by reward are repeated, while those followed by punishment are dropped.

Key Points

  • Learning is based on experience, is not inborn, and is most prominent in long-lived animals with well-developed nervous systems.
  • The six kinds of learning are habituation, imprinting, classical conditioning, trial and error, latent and insight learning.
  • Habituation is simple, reversible learning to ignore a repeated harmless stimulus (city pigeons; Aplysia).
  • Imprinting is time-dependent, irreversible learning in a short sensitive period after hatching or birth (Lorenz and the goslings).
  • Classical conditioning (Type-I) is Pavlov's dogs salivating to a bell; trial and error or operant conditioning (Type-II) is Skinner's rats pressing a lever in the Skinner box.

lessons.title: Latent Learning and Insight Learning
lessons.notes_html:
The last two categories of learning in the book do not depend on immediate reward or on repeated trials: in latent learning the animal learns without any reward or punishment, and in insight learning it solves a new problem correctly at the first attempt.

19.3.6 Latent Learning (Spatial Learning)

Latent learning is a type of behaviour in which an animal learns a response for a particular stimulus in its routine life without having any reward or punishment. However, sometimes, when the animal is particularly exposed to that stimulus, the animal suddenly responds to it by quickly recalling the previous experience, so latent learning is also called spatial learning: the animal forms a mental map of its surroundings.

An American physiologist, Lashley, used a maze. He put a rat in a maze and it wandered about and accidentally got food. Did the rat learn anything before getting food in the first experience? If we put the rat in the same maze again, it may directly reach the food without searching for food. That means when the rat was wandering, it did learn something without even the incentive of any reward. In the same way, rats learning a maze and bees learning the positions of landmarks use spatial learning to find food, shelter and home efficiently.

19.3.7 Insight Learning

Insight learning is a complex type of learning, because it requires that the animal must respond correctly in the first attempt to a particular situation it has never met before, unlike trial and error behaviour. Kohler, a German psychologist, performed many experiments on chimpanzees.

A chimpanzee is placed in a cage in which some bananas hang from the ceiling. The chimpanzee cannot reach the fruit, but the keeper has placed some boxes of different sizes in the cage. After a short period of head scratching, the chimpanzee moves the largest box, piles other smaller boxes over it, and climbs up to reach the bananas. Insight learning is the sudden understanding of a problem and its solution without trial and error; to solve a mathematical problem is an example of insight learning in humans. Insight needs intelligence and a developed brain, while habituation needs only a simple nervous system.

Key Points

  • Latent (spatial) learning occurs in routine life without reward or punishment and is revealed later, e.g. Lashley's rat directly reaching food in a maze it had only wandered through.
  • Insight learning is solving a new problem correctly at the first attempt, without trial and error.
  • Kohler's chimpanzees stacked boxes to reach hanging bananas: the classic insight experiment.
  • Insight learning requires a developed, intelligent brain; habituation is the simplest learning and needs only a simple nervous system.

lessons.title: Social Behaviour: Societies, Agonistic Behaviour and Altruism
lessons.notes_html:
Social behaviour (living in groups) is a set of interactions among individuals of the same species. It increases the efficiency and effectiveness of the species over the individuals of other species.

19.4 Social Behaviour

19.4.1 Animal Societies and Aggregation

A group of individuals of the same species who interact and influence each other's behaviour in different ways is called a social group or animal society; organisms living together in such organized groups are said to live in a society. The key characteristics of a well-organized society include cooperation and division of labour among animals of different sexes, age groups or castes. For example, in a pack of wolves or hives of bees, some individuals of the society are given the duties to find food, some to reproduce and rear, and some to defend. Aggregation, in contrast, is a group of animals that may be together but do not interact behaviourally, e.g. a group of buffaloes or zebras and huge flocks of birds.

19.4.2 Hostile and Helpful Intraspecific Interaction

Many species of insects (such as ants, bees and termites) and most vertebrates show a variety of hostile or friendly group behavioural activities associated with the number of individuals living together. A good example of hostile and helpful intraspecific interaction is seen among the worker bees. In the bee hives, the old and weak worker bees are killed by other worker bees (hostile interaction). Helpful interaction is observed among these bees as different bees have specific duties to perform over all functions of the hive: the collection and transformation of honey is done by the worker bees, and the queen lays eggs which are fertilized by drone bees.

19.4.3 Agonistic Behaviour (Gk. agon, struggle)

This type of social behaviour occurs in a competitive situation and includes a variety of threats or actual combat that settles disputes between individuals in a population. During these acts animals use enormous energy and cause injury to each other. Agonistic behaviour is displayed to maintain social order, such as territoriality and dominance hierarchy.

a) Territorial behaviour: The methods by which an animal or group of animals protects its territory from intrusions of other species (especially, as the solved exercises clarify, members of the same species). Territorial boundaries may be marked by sounds, such as bird songs, or by scent, such as pheromones secreted by the skin glands of many mammals. Pheromones are chemical messengers like hormones but which act outside the body of the secreting organism; a pheromone helps in searching for food and also affects many behavioural and sexual responses.

  • Mountain gorillas — Gorillas are highly social, relatively non-territorial, and live in groups called troops. The oldest and strongest adult male, called the Silverback, is usually the dominant one of the troop, and the silverback gorilla enjoys exclusive breeding rights with the females. Adolescent females are transferred to a different troop once they reach about 8 years of age. Adolescent males, on the other hand, usually remain in the troop until they can leave and establish a new troop on their own as the silverback gorilla. Although gorillas typically are not aggressive, they do exhibit territorial behaviour by standing upright on their two legs and pounding their chests in order to intimidate whatever threat they have been given; these gestures, however, are more for show and are not usually violent.
  • Gibbon monkeys — Gibbons defend their territories with vigorous visual and vocal displays. The voice of a mating pair can be heard up to one kilometre away. In most species males, and in some also females, sing solos that attract mates as well as advertise their territory. The song can be used to identify not only which species of gibbon is singing, but also the area it is from.

Note: The book first calls gorillas relatively non-territorial and then describes their chest-pounding territorial displays. Read together, gorillas defend the troop mainly by display rather than by holding a fixed, fought-over territory.

b) Dominance hierarchy: It is a social structure within a group of animals in which certain individuals are dominant over others. The dominant individual is able to claim access to better resources in the form of mates, shelter, food and other desirable commodities. Example: pecking order in chickens. The pecking order is literally determined by pecking (biting or striking something with the beak); when referring to this ordered social structure in chickens, and sometimes other bird species, it is called the pecking order. It is a natural process that chickens have to work out among themselves. This order of social dynamics determines the status of an individual bird of a flock and its role: the top bird pecks all others, the second pecks all but the top, and so on.

19.4.4 Altruism (Altruistic Behaviour)

Altruism means acting in the best interest of others rather than in one's own self-interest; some people believe altruism constitutes the essence of morality. In social insects, e.g. in honeybees (Apis), the female workers are sterile and never produce offspring; instead they spend their whole lives to look after their siblings (brothers and sisters), especially by helping their sister, the queen bee, to reproduce. Thus they are aiding in the production of new workers, drones and queens. Altruism is explained by kin selection: by helping relatives, the worker passes on shared genes.

The book's STS section adds why the marine snail Aplysia, given the common name of sea hare by the Ancient Greeks because of its supposed resemblance to the European hare, has proved very helpful in the study of neurobiology and behaviour: juvenile Aplysia has large brain cells (neurons), and the cell body of one neuron can measure up to 1 mm in diameter, which makes it relatively easy to study the physiology of these cells to find out how they accomplish learning. Its feeding behaviour has received attention from neurobiologists interested in operant conditioning. More broadly, behavioural neuroscience, also known as biopsychology or psychobiology, applies the principles of biology, in particular neurobiology, to the study of the physiological, genetic and developmental mechanisms of behaviour in humans and animals, investigating at the level of neurons, neurotransmitters and brain circuitry.

Key Points

  • A society is an organized group of the same species with cooperation and division of labour; an aggregation is a group together without behavioural interaction.
  • Agonistic behaviour is competitive threat or combat that maintains social order through territoriality and dominance hierarchy.
  • Territories are marked by song or by pheromones, hormone-like chemicals that act outside the body.
  • The dominant male gorilla is the Silverback; gorillas intimidate by standing upright and pounding their chests, and gibbon songs carry up to one kilometre.
  • Dominance hierarchy is shown by the pecking order in chickens; altruism is shown by sterile worker honeybees rearing their siblings and helping the queen reproduce.
  • Aplysia (sea hare), with neuron cell bodies up to 1 mm across, is a key animal for studying learning and memory.

lessons.title: Male Reproductive System and Its Hormonal Control
lessons.notes_html:
Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms give birth or give rise to new organisms, which may or may not be like their parents. It helps to continue their race, is seen in all organisms, and is important for survival and maintenance of the species — without it, life would come to an end.

20.1 Reproductive System of Human

The reproductive system of man is different from all other systems of the body in two ways:

  • It becomes functional at the age of puberty, while other systems are functional at birth or shortly after birth (in the exercise wording, it is non-functional at birth).
  • The other systems are almost similar in the two sexes, but the reproductive system is quite different in male and female humans.

20.1.1 Male Reproductive System

The male reproductive system performs the following main functions:

  • To produce, maintain and transport semen (sperms + fluids).
  • To discharge semen within the female reproductive tract during sexual intercourse.
  • To produce and secrete male sex hormones, responsible for maintaining the male reproductive system.

Unlike the female system, most of the male reproductive system is located outside the body, i.e. penis, scrotum and testicles (testes), while some parts, i.e. vas deferens and associated glands like seminal vesicles, prostate gland and Cowper's gland, are located inside the body.

Testes

The testes (singular testis) are the male gonads: oval-shaped organs about the size of large olive seeds, located outside the body in the scrotum. The scrotum is a large pouch-like sac of skin that hangs behind and below the penis; it acts as a climate control system for the testes, because for normal sperm development the testes must be at a temperature slightly cooler than body temperature. The testes are usually two in number. In the testes there are coiled masses of tubules called seminiferous tubules, in which sperms are produced. The testes also produce the male sex hormone testosterone by Leydig cells (interstitial cells). About 100 million sperms are released during intercourse; only one fertilizes the egg.

The human sperm: its head has a diameter of about 2.5 µm and contains a large nucleus with little cytoplasm and an acrosome; the nucleus carries a haploid set of chromosomes. The middle piece contains mitochondria, which provide energy for sperm activity, and the tail is a flagellum which enables the sperm to swim towards the egg.

A human sperm: head, middle piece and tail.

Accessory Ducts

  • Epididymis — A long coiled tube that rests on the back side of each testis. It stores and transports sperms, and here sperms also get mature. It is the first convoluted part of the vas deferens.
  • Vas deferens — A long muscular tube that travels from the epididymis into the pelvic cavity to just behind the bladder.
  • Ejaculatory ducts — The two vas deferens and two seminal vesicles join to form the ejaculatory duct; the ejaculatory ducts empty into the urethra.
  • Urethra — The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. In the male it has the additional function of ejaculating semen during sexual excitement, so the urethra is also called the urinogenital duct.

Copulatory Organ (Penis)

The penis is the male organ used in sexual intercourse. Its skin is loose and elastic to accommodate changes in size during an erection, and it consists mainly of tissues that can fill with blood to cause an erection. It delivers sperms into the female reproductive tract.

Accessory Glands

  • Seminal vesicles — Sac-like pouches attached to the vas deferens near the base of the bladder; they produce a sugar-rich fluid that provides sperms with a source of energy to help them move.
  • Prostate gland — A walnut-size structure located below the urinary bladder at both sides of the urethra; it contributes additional fluid to the ejaculate, to nourish and protect the sperms.
  • Bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands) — Pea-sized structures located on the side of the urethra, just below the prostate gland; they produce a clear, slippery fluid which serves to lubricate and neutralize any acidity in the urethra.

Hormonal Control of Male Reproductive Function

The primary hormones are follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH) and testosterone. FSH and LH are produced by the pituitary gland; their release is controlled by GnRH from the hypothalamus (book's figure). FSH is necessary for sperm production: it acts on the Sertoli cells for spermatogenesis. LH stimulates the production of testosterone by the Leydig cells, which is necessary to continue the process of spermatogenesis. Testosterone also helps in the development of male characteristics, including mass and strength, fat distribution, bone mass and sex drive. The inhibin hormone is produced by the Sertoli cells and controls spermatogenesis at a normal rate. Testosterone and inhibin act by negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.

Key Points

  • Reproduction continues the race; the reproductive system becomes functional at puberty and differs in male and female.
  • Most of the male system lies outside the body; the scrotum acts as climate control for the testes.
  • Sperms are produced in the seminiferous tubules, stored and matured in the epididymis, and carried by the vas deferens.
  • Seminal vesicles give a sugar-rich energy fluid, the prostate nourishes and protects sperms, and Cowper's glands lubricate and neutralize acidity.
  • FSH is necessary for sperm production; LH makes Leydig cells produce testosterone; inhibin from Sertoli cells controls the rate of spermatogenesis.

lessons.title: Female Reproductive System: Ovaries, Oviduct, Uterus and External Genitalia
lessons.notes_html:
The female reproductive system is more complex than the male reproductive system, because the male needs only to produce and deliver gametes, while the female system, besides producing gametes, also gestates, gives birth to and nourishes the new born. The female reproductive system is also under the influence of the menstrual cycle.

20.1.2 Female Reproductive System

The female reproductive system consists of: i) Ovaries, ii) Ducts, iii) External genitalia.

i) Ovaries

There is a pair of ovaries, which are oval-shaped and attached to the dorsal body wall just below the kidneys. Eggs or ova develop inside the ovaries of the mature female. There are approximately 400,000 potential (follicle) cells already present at birth (the book prints this as 4,000,00), only about 500 will ever become mature within the two ovaries, and they are released from puberty to menopause. Usually, only one egg is released every month, and the ovaries take turns, alternating to release an egg.

The egg is spherical in shape and about 120 µm in diameter, containing a large nucleus with a haploid number of chromosomes. The egg is the largest cell of the body; the book's extra information contrasts it with the sperm, the smallest human cell.

ii) Oviduct (Fallopian Tube or Uterine Tube)

The ovary releases the mature egg into the oviduct, which is a narrow muscular tube leading from the ovary to the uterus. The egg is fertilized in the oviduct. Fallopian tubes are about 12 cm long and as wide as a sewing needle.

Uterus

The uterus is a pear-shaped elastic sac about 7.5 cm long. It is the site for the development of the fetus. During pregnancy, the wall of the uterus consists of three layers:

  • Perimetrium — The outer layer.
  • Myometrium — The middle layer, thick and muscular.
  • Endometrium — The inner layer, a spongy lining of the uterus.

At the lower narrow end of the uterus is a circular ring of muscle known as the cervix. The uterus opens into the vagina through the cervix, and the cervix is the opening of the uterus. A female uterus is normally about 3 inches long and 2 inches wide, can expand up to 20 times during pregnancy, and contains one of the strongest muscles in the female body.

The female reproductive system: ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina.

iii) External Genitalia (Vagina)

Leading from the cervix to the outside is the birth canal or vagina. It is a thin-walled, 8–10 cm long tube. The opening of the vagina is the vulva. Semen is deposited in the vagina during intercourse. Note: the book heads this part External Genitalia (Vagina) — strictly, the vagina is the internal birth canal and the vulva is the external opening, as the book's own sentences show.

Key Points

  • The female system is more complex: it produces gametes, gestates, gives birth and nourishes the new born, and works under the menstrual cycle.
  • About 400,000 potential follicle cells are present at birth; only about 500 ever mature, usually one egg a month, alternately from the two ovaries.
  • The egg is spherical, about 120 µm in diameter, with a large nucleus and haploid chromosomes.
  • Fertilization occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
  • The uterus is a pear-shaped elastic sac about 7.5 cm long, with perimetrium, myometrium and endometrium; it opens into the vagina through the cervix.
  • The vagina is a thin-walled 8–10 cm birth canal; its opening is the vulva.

lessons.title: Female Reproductive Cycle, Hormonal Regulation and Gametogenesis
lessons.notes_html:
The female reproductive system is controlled by the follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), which are produced by the pituitary gland; their release is controlled by the hypothalamus. FSH stimulates the ovarian follicles to produce estrogen, which helps in the maturation of the egg, while LH stimulates the production of progesterone in the ovaries. Estrogen triggers the development of secondary sexual characteristics in the female. The pituitary gland also produces prolactin, which stimulates milk production, and oxytocin, which stimulates uterine contraction during child birth and milk let-down during sucking.

20.1.3 Female Reproductive Cycle and Its Hormonal Regulation

The start of the monthly discharge of blood, or menses, from the uterus via the vagina is the first sign of puberty in the female; this condition is called menstruation. The menstrual period usually lasts for five days, though it varies with the individual. The monthly cycle of events in the female reproductive organs is the menstrual cycle. The average menstrual cycle for an adult female is 28 days; cycles ranging from 21–33 days are not abnormal. Stress, illness and malnutrition may alter, make irregular or stop the cycle; a young girl may take about three years to become regular. Pregnancy is maintained by progesterone. The menstrual cycle has 4 phases:

Menstrual Phase

Menstruation is the elimination of the thickened lining of the uterus (endometrium) and blood from the body through the vagina. Menstrual fluid contains blood, cells from the lining of the uterus and mucus. The average length of this phase is 5 days.

Follicular Phase

The follicular phase starts on the stoppage of menstruation and ends with ovulation. The pituitary gland releases FSH, which stimulates the ovary to produce about 5–20 follicles; each follicle houses an immature egg. Usually only one follicle will mature into an egg while the others die. The growth of the follicles stimulates the lining of the uterus to thicken in preparation for possible pregnancy.

Ovulation Stage

Ovulation is the release of the mature egg from the surface of the ovary. It usually occurs in the middle of the cycle, about the 14th day. Rising estrogen from the developing follicle makes the hypothalamus release GnRH, which raises LH and FSH; within two days the high LH triggers ovulation — a decrease of FSH and increase of estrogen cause the pituitary to secrete LH. The egg is funnelled into the fallopian tube by waves of small hair-like projections. Its life span is only around 24 hours.

Luteal Phase

At ovulation the egg bursts out from its follicle, but the ruptured follicle stays on the surface of the ovary and, for the next two weeks or so, transforms into the corpus luteum. This structure starts releasing progesterone along with a small amount of estrogen; this combination of hormones maintains the thickened lining of the uterus. If a fertilized egg implants in the lining of the uterus, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is produced — the hormone that is detected in a urine test for pregnancy — and it maintains the corpus luteum. If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, usually during day 22 after menstruation; the drop in progesterone level causes the lining of the uterus to fall away, which is known as menstruation, and the cycle repeats.

The four phases of the menstrual cycle: menstrual, follicular, ovulation and luteal.

Extra Reading: Gametogenesis

The production of gametes is known as gametogenesis. It occurs in the gonads, starts at puberty, and has two types: spermatogenesis, the process of sperm formation in the male gonads (testes), and oogenesis, the process of ova (egg) formation in the female gonads (ovaries).

SpermatogenesisOogenesis
All four daughter cells of meiosis develop into mature gametesOnly one of the four cells gets mature
Starts at puberty and continues throughout lifeStarts at puberty but ceases at menopause
A continuous processHas long interruptions

Terms Used for Human Ovum

  • Zona pellucida — The thick transparent membrane surrounding a mammalian ovum before implantation.
  • Corona radiata — The many layers of follicle cells adhering to the oocyte, which supply vital proteins to the cell.
  • Corpus albicans — The regressed form of the corpus luteum.

Key Points

  • The average menstrual cycle is 28 days (21–33 days is not abnormal); the menstrual phase averages 5 days.
  • FSH stimulates 5–20 follicles and estrogen production; usually only one follicle matures.
  • Rising estrogen makes the hypothalamus release GnRH; the resulting high LH level triggers ovulation about day 14.
  • The corpus luteum releases progesterone, which maintains the uterus lining and pregnancy; hCG in urine is the pregnancy test.
  • Without pregnancy the corpus luteum degenerates about day 22, progesterone falls, and menstruation follows.
  • Gametogenesis: spermatogenesis is continuous for life and all four meiotic cells mature; oogenesis matures only one cell and ceases at menopause.

lessons.title: Disorders of the Reproductive System: Infertility, IVF and Miscarriage
lessons.notes_html:
A reproductive disorder is a disease or condition when there is a problem in the reproductive system of the male or female. The main disorders include abnormal puberty, infertility in male and female, and miscarriage in the female. Here infertility and miscarriage are discussed.

20.2 Disorders of Reproductive System

Infertility

In general, infertility is defined as not being able to get pregnant after one year (or longer) of unprotected sexual intercourse between partners. This infertility may be in the male or the female.

20.2.1 Causes of Male Infertility

  • Azoospermia — A condition in which there are no sperms in the semen when a man ejaculates, either because the man does not make sperms or because the sperms are blocked from entering the semen.
  • Oligospermia — Less amount of sperms is produced, due to increase in temperature of the testes, infections, etc.
  • Sperm deformities — A change in the shape or structure of sperms may also be a cause of male infertility.
  • Autoimmune disorder — The immune system starts fighting its own parts of the body; this autoimmunity may also attack sperms and cause infertility.

20.2.2 Causes of Female Infertility

The most common causes of female infertility include problems with ovulation, damage to the fallopian tube or uterus, or problems with the cervix. Age also contributes to infertility, because as a woman ages, her fertility naturally tends to decrease.

20.2.3 Treatment of Infertility

Some forms of infertility are treatable. Hormone therapy can sometimes increase sperm and egg production, and surgery can often correct ducts that formed improperly or are blocked. However, a commonly used technique to treat infertility is in vitro fertilization (IVF), commonly known as the test tube baby technique.

In Vitro Fertilization (IVF)

IVF means fertilization outside the female body in glassware. In this process, the egg and sperm of the couple are taken outside the body in a laboratory and fertilized in a test tube. The fertilized eggs are incubated until they have formed at least eight cells and are then transferred to the woman's uterus for implantation. If mature sperms are defective or low in number, a whole sperm or its nucleus is injected directly into the egg. The book's figure shows the steps: stimulation of the ovaries, egg retrieval, fertilization of eggs, embryo culture (day 0–5), embryo transfer (day 3–5), and a pregnancy test (hCG) 14 days after transfer. Although it is a costly procedure, IVF has enabled more than a million couples to conceive children.

20.2.4 Miscarriage

Miscarriage is a term used for a pregnancy that ends on its own, within the first 20 weeks of gestation. A pregnancy that ends before 37 weeks of gestation, resulting in a live born infant, is known as premature birth.

Causes of Miscarriage

There are many reasons why a miscarriage may happen, although the cause is often not identified. Most miscarriages happen when the unborn baby has fatal genetic problems, like abnormalities in chromosomal number and structure. Other causes include infection, medical conditions in the mother such as diabetes or thyroid disease, hormonal problems, immune system response, uterine abnormalities, and weakness in the cervix (cervical insufficiency).

Miscarriage Versus Abortion

MiscarriageAbortion
A natural, spontaneous termination of a pregnancyOccurs when a procedure is done with the purpose of ending a pregnancy
Unintentional — the pregnancy ends on its own, within the first 20 weeks of gestationWilful (deliberate) ending of pregnancy

Science, Technology and Society (STS): Ethics of Abortion

The book presents abortion as one of the most controversial issues associated with reproduction. The commonly raised ethical issues are: (i) it is considered as murder; (ii) it can increase sexual corruption. However, the book states abortion should be allowed when the mother's life is at risk, when there is a risk of injury or the mother's physical or mental health is at risk, and when prenatal testing predicts an abnormal or handicapped fetus.

Key Points

  • Infertility is not being able to get pregnant after one year or longer of unprotected intercourse.
  • Male causes: azoospermia (no sperms), oligospermia (few sperms), sperm deformities and autoimmune attack on sperms.
  • Female causes: ovulation problems, damage to fallopian tube or uterus, cervix problems, and age.
  • IVF fertilizes egg and sperm in glassware in a laboratory; embryos of at least eight cells are transferred to the uterus.
  • Miscarriage is the spontaneous end of pregnancy within the first 20 weeks, most often from fatal genetic problems of the unborn baby.
  • Miscarriage is natural and spontaneous; abortion is a deliberate procedure to end a pregnancy.

lessons.title: Sexually Transmitted Diseases: Gonorrhoea, Syphilis and AIDS
lessons.notes_html:
Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) are infections that are commonly spread by sexual activity. More than 30 different types of bacteria, viruses and parasites can be transmitted through sexual activity. Some examples are chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes and AIDS. Here only gonorrhoea, syphilis and AIDS are discussed.

20.3 Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)

Gonorrhoea

Gonorrhoea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. There is no blood test to diagnose gonorrhoea. In the male, typical symptoms are pain upon urination and a thick greenish yellow urethral discharge. If a baby is exposed during birth, an eye infection leading to blindness can result. Gonorrhoea can spread to internal parts of the body, causing heart damage or arthritis. It is transmitted through direct contact or sexual contact, and is treated using the antibiotics penicillin or tetracycline. Note: the book calls this bacterium gram positive; Neisseria gonorrhoeae is in fact a Gram-negative bacterium, so do not learn that point as printed.

Syphilis

Syphilis is caused by a spirochete bacterium, Treponema pallidum (printed in the book as palladium). It has three stages, typically separated by latent periods:

  • Primary stage — A hard chancre (an ulcerated sore with hard edges) appears.
  • Secondary stage — A rash appears all over the body.
  • Tertiary stage — Syphilis may affect the cardiovascular and nervous systems; it damages reproductive organs, eyes, bones, joints, the central nervous system, heart and skin.

Sexual contact is the major source of its dissemination. Syphilis is a very devastating disease, and control depends on prompt and adequate treatment of all cases with antibiotic therapy.

AIDS — A Worldwide Sexually Transmitted Disease

AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by a virus called HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus). HIV destroys the body immune system: it attacks a specific type of white blood cells called T-cells. HIV may transmit through blood transfusion, contaminated syringes and surgical instruments; however, the most prominent cause is sexual transmission. AIDS is a major global public health issue: there are approximately 38 million people living with HIV at the end of 2019, and over two thirds of all people with HIV infection live in the African region (26 million). HIV can be diagnosed through rapid diagnostic tests. However, still there is no cure for AIDS.

Measures That Can Help to Prevent Transmission of HIV

HIV is transmitted from one person to another by exchanging fluids of the body, so the following measures should be taken to prevent transmission, because prevention is so far the only cure for AIDS:

  • Follow the Islamic teaching and refrain from immoral sexual activities.
  • Avoid sharing instruments that are likely to break the skin and be contaminated with blood, e.g. razors and tooth brushes.
  • For acupuncture, ear piercing, nose piercing, etc., go to reliable operators and make sure the needles used are sterilized, or insist on using disposable instruments.
  • Blood of a donor must be screened before transfusion.
  • Use disposable syringes and sterilized operation tools for surgery.
  • Affected mothers must avoid breast feeding to their infants.
DiseaseCauseMain Features
GonorrhoeaBacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeaePain on urination and thick greenish yellow urethral discharge in males; eye infection and blindness in a baby exposed at birth; treated with penicillin or tetracycline
SyphilisSpirochete bacterium Treponema pallidumThree stages: hard chancre, rash all over the body, then damage to cardiovascular and nervous systems; treated with antibiotics
AIDSVirus HIVDestroys the immune system by attacking T-cells; about 38 million people living with HIV at the end of 2019; no cure

Key Points

  • STDs are infections commonly spread by sexual activity; more than 30 bacteria, viruses and parasites can be transmitted this way.
  • Gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) causes pain on urination and a thick greenish yellow discharge; it is treated with penicillin or tetracycline.
  • Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) has three stages: chancre, body rash, and cardiovascular and nervous damage.
  • AIDS is caused by HIV, which attacks T-cells and destroys the immune system; there is no cure.
  • About 38 million people were living with HIV at the end of 2019, 26 million of them in the African region.
  • Prevention of HIV: avoid immoral sexual activity and blood-contaminated instruments, screen donor blood, and use disposable syringes and sterilized tools.

lessons.title: Embryonic Development: Cleavage and Cleavage Patterns
lessons.notes_html:
What happens before birth is even more crucial than what happens after it: if an infant does not develop properly before birth, normal growth after birth becomes difficult and sometimes impossible. The embryo is the early stage of the young one up to the formation of organs, and the study of development from fertilized egg to formation of all major organs is called embryology.

21.1 Embryonic Development

Development begins with the formation of gametes (eggs and sperms) inside the reproductive organs of the parents. Fertilization, the second stage, starts when the plasma membrane of the sperm fuses with the plasma membrane of an egg and ends when the egg nucleus and sperm nucleus fuse, forming a zygote. After zygote formation, embryonic development has four stages: (i) cleavage, (ii) gastrulation, (iii) organogenesis and (iv) growth.

21.1.1 Cleavage

Cleavage is a programme of mitotic cell division that divides the volume of the zygote cytoplasm into a number of smaller, nucleated cells called blastomeres. In cleavage the number of cells increases but the size of the cells hardly increases, so the whole embryo stays about the same size as the zygote.

  • Morulation — After many cleavages the zygote is transformed into a solid, compact, mulberry-like ball of cells known as the morula (day 4 in humans).
  • Blastulation — Cleavage continues and the cells arrange themselves to form the blastula, a hollow ball of cells containing a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel. In mammals this stage is called the blastocyst: a hollow sphere of large, flattened cells, the trophoblast, with 20–30 small rounded cells, the inner cell mass, at one side (day 5).

21.1.2 Different Patterns of Cleavage Based on the Amount of Yolk

Yolk is a mixture of proteins, fats, phospholipids, calcium and some other minerals, and serves as food for the developing embryo. Eggs of most invertebrates and simple chordates are isolecithal: small amounts of yolk uniformly distributed. Eggs of higher chordates such as birds and reptiles are telolecithal: a large amount of yolk concentrated at one side, the vegetal pole; the opposite pole, where the embryo is placed, is the animal pole.

  • Holoblastic cleavage — The entire egg divides into daughter cells, e.g. in isolecithal eggs of bony fish and amphibians, and in mammals.
  • Meroblastic cleavage — Cell division occurs only in the blastodisc (the small disc of cytoplasm at the animal pole), e.g. eggs of reptiles, birds and some fish; also called discoidal or partial cleavage.
  • Radial cleavage occurs in most deuterostomes, the plane of division parallel to the vertical axis; spiral cleavage occurs in most protostomes, the divisions diagonal to the vertical axis. Some ecdysozoans (arthropods, nematodes) show radial or superficial (insects) cleavage, and tunicates and mammals have specialized patterns.

Key Points

  • Embryology is the study of development from fertilized egg to organ formation; stages after the zygote are cleavage, gastrulation, organogenesis and growth.
  • Cleavage produces blastomeres; cell number increases but cell size hardly increases, so the morula is the same size as the zygote.
  • The morula is a solid ball; the blastula (blastocyst in mammals) is a hollow ball with a blastocoel, trophoblast and inner cell mass.
  • Holoblastic cleavage divides the whole egg; meroblastic cleavage divides only the blastodisc of yolky (telolecithal) eggs.
  • Radial cleavage is found in deuterostomes; spiral cleavage in protostomes.

lessons.title: Gastrulation and the Three Germ Layers
lessons.notes_html:
