Gastrulation is the stage of major cellular reorganization in which the newly formed cells become arranged into two or three primary tissue layers, the germ layers, whose descendants will form all the tissues and organs of the adult.

21.1.3 Gastrulation

  • Ectoderm (outer layer) — The outermost layer, the one that forms first. It forms the integument (outer layer of skin, hair, nails, feathers and scales), the nervous system and parts of sense organs, and the inner layer of mouth, rectum, anus and teeth.
  • Mesoderm (middle layer) — It gives rise to the skeleton, muscles, blood and blood vessels, reproductive organs, connective tissues, excretory organs, lymphatic tissue and the innermost layer of the skin. The formation of mesoderm was a pivotal step in the evolution of nearly all large complex animals.
  • Endoderm (inner layer) — The innermost layer. It gives rise to the lining of the digestive tract, digestive organs and associated glands, the respiratory tract, lungs, urinary bladder and urethra.

In two-layered animals such as coelenterates, instead of mesoderm a jelly-like mesogloea is present between ectoderm and endoderm; it functions as a hydrostatic skeleton.

The gastrula: ectoderm outside, mesoderm in the middle and endoderm inside; every organ forms from these three layers.

Gastrulation in Human

In the human embryo gastrulation begins during the 3rd week of pregnancy. The trophoblast thickens at one point to form the inner cell mass, which after implantation breaks into two fluid-filled sacs separated by a double layer of cells, the embryonic disc. One sac is the amniotic sac (amnion), filled with amniotic fluid; the other is the yolk sac, which in humans contains no yolk because the embryo gets nutrients from the mother, first from the uterus lining and later by the placenta.

Gastrulation begins when a groove with raised edges, the primitive streak, appears on the dorsal surface of the embryonic disc and establishes the longitudinal axis of the embryo. At its cephalic end, closely packed cells from a local thickening form Hensen's node (printed "Hansen's node" in the exercise). The surface cells, the epiblast (upper layer), migrate and enter the primitive streak. The lower layer is the hypoblast, which is the future (presumptive) endoderm; the epiblast gives rise to ectoderm, and ectoderm cells migrating through the streak into the interior form the mesoderm. The cavity formed between the somatic and splanchnic layers of mesoderm is the coelom, and the primitive gut inside is the archenteron.

Key Points

  • Gastrulation arranges cells into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm; all adult tissues and organs come from these layers.
  • Ectoderm forms skin covering, nervous system and sense organs; mesoderm forms skeleton, muscles, blood, kidneys and gonads; endoderm lines the gut and respiratory tract and forms their glands.
  • In humans gastrulation starts in the 3rd week at the primitive streak, with Hensen's node at its cephalic end.
  • The epiblast is the upper layer of the blastoderm and the hypoblast the lower layer, mainly presumptive endoderm.
  • The blastocyst has an inner cell mass that forms the embryo and a trophoblast that gives rise to the placenta.

lessons.title: Neurulation, Neural Crest, Organogenesis and Growth
lessons.notes_html:
After gastrulation, the first major phase of organ formation is the building of the nervous system. The embryo at this stage is called the neurula.

21.1.4 Neurilation in Human Embryo

Neurulation begins during the fourth week of pregnancy. The mesodermal cells immediately beneath the early primitive streak aggregate to form a rod of mesodermal cells called the notochord, the first axial support of the embryo. The notochordal cells induce the overlying ectoderm to thicken, forming the neural plate. The central region of the neural plate pushes downward to form a depression, the neural groove, then the neural fold. The cells in the neural fold move to the upper margin and ultimately fuse to form the neural tube, which pinches off and becomes covered by surface ectoderm. At this point the embryo is designated as neurula.

The neural tube grows and differentiates into the brain and spinal cord. At the end of the fourth week the vesicles of fore, mid and hind brain are formed, while at the end of the eighth to ninth week all flexures are evident. Failure of the protective covering to close around the spinal cord leaves a gap and causes spina bifida, which can lead to permanent nerve damage and sometimes paralysis.

21.1.5 The Formation of Neural Crest and Its Derivatives

Many motor nerves arise from the developing brain and spinal cord, but the sensory nerves have a separate origin, the neural crest, developed in the region of the neural plate border. Neural crest cells migrate widely to the lateral side of the neural tube and give rise to the nerves and sympathetic ganglia. They also help in the formation of the cortical region of medulla, skull bone, teeth and many other parts. Therefore many embryologists consider the neural crest as the fourth germ layer.

21.1.6 Organogenesis

Organogenesis is the stage of development in which the formation of organs and organ systems takes place during embryonic development. The first major step in organogenesis is neurulation, the differentiation of ectoderm that produces the brain and spinal cord; all other organs then develop from the three germ layers.

21.1.7 Growth

Growth is the last step of development. It begins by the start of the third month (in the human embryo) and ends long after birth, and is characterized by increase in size and mass of the organism. From the third month till birth the human embryo is called the fetus, and the rest of the developmental period comprises only growth and maturation of organs and organ systems.

Key Points

  • Neurulation (4th week): notochord induces ectoderm to form neural plate, groove and folds, which fuse into the neural tube.
  • The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord; the embryo at this stage is the neurula.
  • Neural crest cells, from the neural plate border, form sensory nerves, sympathetic ganglia, parts of skull and teeth, and are called the fourth germ layer.
  • Organogenesis is the formation of organs and organ systems; neurulation is its first major step.
  • Growth begins at the start of the third month; from then until birth the embryo is called a fetus.

lessons.title: Control of Development: Nucleus, Cytoplasm and Embryonic Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Every body cell of a multicellular organism contains a complete set of chromosomes with all bodily genes, produced by mitosis of the zygote. Yet cells differentiate along different lines: studies confirm that the nucleus determines the characteristics of the individual, while the cytoplasm selectively turns some genes on and switches others off.

21.2 Control of Development

21.2.1 Role of Nucleus in Development

  • Dietrich (1891) took a sea urchin zygote after one division and separated the two daughter cells; each grew into a complete, normal larva. He concluded that both cells contained all the genetic information of the original zygote.
  • Spemann, experiment 1 — He divided a salamander zygote into two equal halves with a minute ligature of human hair; the nucleus was in one half only. Cleavage was completed in the nucleated half but the enucleated half did not divide. When the nucleated side reached the 16-cell stage, one cleavage nucleus crossed the narrow cytoplasmic bridge to the enucleated side, which immediately started dividing; both sides completed cleavage and formed two complete embryos.
  • Spemann, experiment 2 — He separated the two halves of an embryo, both containing nuclei; both developed into complete embryos. Even a single cell separated from a 16-cell embryo contains a complete set of genes and can form a complete embryo.
  • Sometimes the nucleated half developed into an abnormal ball of cells: development depends on the position of the grey crescent, the pigment-free area that appears at the time of fertilization. In the half lacking the grey crescent, no further development can take place.

Spemann's conclusions: (i) the nuclear information is the same in each daughter cell; (ii) the grey crescent area in the cytoplasm contains information essential for proper development. Differentiation is caused in two ways: (i) cytoplasmic segregation of determinants during cleavage, and (ii) induction or interaction with neighbouring cells.

Role of Cytoplasm in Development

Different cytoplasmic components contain different morphogenetic determinants responsible for cell differentiation. In the zygote of an ascidian (urochordate), four different colours of cytoplasm are segregated into different blastomeres: clear cytoplasm produces larval epidermis; yellow cytoplasm gives rise to muscle cells; grey vegetal cytoplasm gives rise to gut; grey equatorial cytoplasm produces notochord and neural tube.

Experiment on Acetabularia

Acetabularia is a unicellular alga with a foot, stalk and umbrella-shaped cap, and a single nucleus in the foot. A. mediterranea has a regular-shaped cap and A. crenulata an irregular-shaped cap. Hammerling showed that if the cap is removed a new one is regenerated. He cut off the nucleus-containing base (foot) of one species and grafted a similar piece containing the nucleus of the other species; the new regenerated cap had the characters of the species whose nucleus was grafted. So the nucleus, not the stalk cytoplasm, determined the structure of the cap: genes express according to the type of nucleus. Overall, both gene and cytoplasm play an important role: the nucleus contains all the genes, while the cytoplasm controls that genes transcribe at their proper time.

21.2.2 Differentiation and Embryonic Induction

The capacity of some cells to evoke a specific developmental response in others is called embryonic induction. Spemann removed a piece of ectoderm from a salamander embryo and grew it separately: the donor embryo formed a defective nervous system and the isolated piece formed no structure at all. When he separated the mesoderm underlying the ectoderm, no nervous system developed — proving that mesoderm stimulates ectodermal cells to form the nervous system.

Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold (1924) removed a piece of the dorsal lip of the blastopore from one salamander gastrula and transplanted it into a ventral or lateral position of another gastrula. It invaginated, developed a notochord and somites, and induced a second embryo with a neural tube and complete nervous system where the lip was placed. Only cells from the dorsal lip were capable of inducing a complete embryo; this area corresponds to the presumptive areas of notochord, somites and prechordal plate. Spemann designated the dorsal lip the primary organizer, and this was called primary induction. Many other cell types originate by later inductive interactions, called secondary induction, e.g. cells of the neural plate induce neural crest in the embryo.

Key Points

  • All cells carry the same nuclear information (Dietrich; Spemann's ligature experiments); even one cell of a 16-cell embryo can form a complete embryo.
  • The grey crescent of the cytoplasm holds information essential for proper development.
  • Acetabularia grafts (Hammerling) prove the nucleus determines characters such as cap shape.
  • Embryonic induction: one tissue evokes a specific response in another; the dorsal lip of the blastopore is the primary organizer (Spemann and Mangold, 1924).
  • Primary induction forms a secondary embryo; secondary induction covers later interactions such as neural plate inducing neural crest.

lessons.title: Human Development: Fertilization, Implantation and the First Trimester
lessons.notes_html:
Soon after syngamy, fertilization occurs and the one-celled zygote is formed. The zygote undergoes changes that lead to the formation of the embryo, the fetus and ultimately an adult.

21.3 Human Embryonic Development

Fertilization (conception) normally takes place in the proximal portion of the fallopian tube, and the zygote travels down towards the uterus. In the tube it undergoes cleavage, forming a blastocyst (a cluster of cells resembling a tiny raspberry) by the time it reaches the uterus: 2-cell stage on day 1, 4-cell on day 2, early morula on day 3, advanced morula on day 4, blastocyst on day 6, and implantation in the uterine wall on days 7–10.

Pregnancy is usually established when the blastocyst is implanted (embedded) into the endometrium of the uterus. The inner cells of the blastocyst become the embryo, while the outer cells become the membranes that protect and nourish it. After implantation the embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), the pregnancy hormone recorded in a pregnancy test, which retains the corpus luteum so progesterone secretion continues (FSH is inhibited) and the endometrium is maintained and developed. The outer protective membrane, the chorion, surrounds the embryo, develops villi (fibrous projections) and burrows into the endometrium; later the placenta begins to form and nourishes the fetus throughout pregnancy.

A normal human pregnancy or gestation lasts nine months: 280 days from the time of the last menstruation, or 266 days after fertilization. Note: the book's Summary prints "266 days after last menstrual period", which mixes the two figures — 280 days is counted from the last menstrual period and 266 days from fertilization. The gestation period is divided into three trimesters (three-month periods).

21.3.1 Development of Human Fetus in First Trimester

The first trimester begins from the last menstrual period (LMP) and consists of fertilization, blastocyst formation, implantation, development of extra-embryonic membranes, placental development and major events of organogenesis. At the end of the second week the blastocyst is implanted in the endometrium and covered by endometrial cells, so the embryo gets nourishment directly from the endometrium. The outer layer of the blastocyst, the trophoblast, with the endometrium slowly gives rise to the placenta.

Extra-Embryonic Membranes and Placenta

  • Amnion — The first protective coat, the embryo's personal pond, filled with (amniotic) fluid that gives a watery medium and protects the fetus from physical trauma. The fluid surrounding the embryo is the amniotic fluid.
  • Allantois — The second protective coat; it contributes to the circulatory system and its blood vessels become the umbilical cord vessels that transport blood to and from the placenta.
  • Chorion — The third protective coat; it covers all other membranes and becomes part of the placenta.
  • Yolk sac — Contains little or no yolk in humans; it is the first site of RBC formation and also becomes part of the umbilical cord.

The placenta is a disc-like structure that closely attaches the embryo, through the umbilical cord, to the mother's blood vascular system. It exchanges glucose, amino acids, salts, CO₂ and urea between mother and fetus and produces estrogen and progesterone to maintain pregnancy. It grows throughout pregnancy, but the mother's blood supply to it is completed by the end of the first trimester (about 12–13 weeks); the corpus luteum then slowly degenerates as HCG declines and the placenta takes over progesterone production. At the end of the first trimester the fetus is fully formed, weighing about one ounce and measuring an average 3 to 4 inches in length.

StageMajor Events of the First Trimester
By the end of 4 weeksAll major systems and organs begin to form; embryo looks like a tadpole; neural tube, digestive system, heart and circulatory system begin; beginnings of eyes and ears; tiny limb buds appear; heart is beating
By the end of 8 weeksBody systems continue to develop; embryo takes a human shape with a large head; mouth, tooth buds, eyes, nose and ears become distinct; arms and legs clearly visible; fingers and toes webbed but distinguishable; heartbeat can be heard with a fetal Doppler; bones begin to develop; embryo in constant motion, not yet felt by the mother
Weeks 9 to 12After 8 weeks the embryo is called a fetus; at 1 to 1½ inches all major organs are formed; external genital organs develop; finger and toe nails appear; eyelids form; fetal movement increases; arms and legs fully formed; voice box (larynx) begins to form

The fetus is most vulnerable during the first 12 weeks, when all major organs are forming and can be damaged by drugs, radiation, tobacco and toxic chemicals; even so, by the end of 12 weeks the fetus cannot survive independently.

Key Points

  • Fertilization occurs in the fallopian tube; implantation into the endometrium (days 7–10) establishes pregnancy.
  • HCG from the embryo retains the corpus luteum so progesterone maintains the endometrium.
  • Gestation is 280 days from the last menstrual period (266 days from fertilization), divided into three trimesters.
  • Extra-embryonic membranes are amnion, allantois, chorion and yolk sac; the placenta exchanges materials and makes estrogen and progesterone.
  • By 4 weeks the heart beats; by 8 weeks the embryo looks human; after 8 weeks it is called a fetus.

lessons.title: Second and Third Trimesters, Twins, Placenta and Umbilical Cord
lessons.notes_html:
After the first trimester, all major organs are already formed. The second and third trimesters are mainly periods of growth, maturation and preparation for birth.

Second Trimester

During the second trimester the fetus looks quite human and its sex becomes apparent and can be determined with the help of ultrasound. In girls the uterus and ovaries develop, while in males the testes begin to descend. The baby grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 metre long. The sensory organs are almost completely developed; the fetus can hear, and the eyelids and lashes are quite apparent. The heartbeat can be felt through a stethoscope. The head is about half of the overall body size. The mother can feel the movements of the fetus, and fingerprints begin to develop — fingerprints are unique to every individual; even identical twins have different fingerprints.

Third Trimester

The third trimester is a rapid growth period: body weight increases about 28 grams per day, i.e. it doubles several times. The eyes are open and subcutaneous fat begins to be deposited. At the end of this trimester the fetal head descends towards the cervix. After 9 months of pregnancy, at normal delivery, the baby might be about 18–20½ inches and weigh 6 to 9 pounds, or about 3400 grams. The lungs mature, the brain develops rapidly, and the fetus is fully formed and ready for birth.

21.3.2 Twins and Quadruplets

Two or more fetuses in one pregnancy are called multiple fetuses, either identical or non-identical (fraternal).

  • Identical twins or quadruplets come from a monozygote: a single ovum fertilized by one sperm. During the first, second or third cleavage the cells of the zygote separate and two, four or eight embryos are formed. All are of the same sex, blood type and most other features, though they do not always look exactly alike — fingerprints differ, and one may be right-handed while the other is left-handed. Identical twins mostly share the same placenta and chorion but usually grow in separate amniotic sacs.
  • Fraternal (non-identical) twins come from multiple fertilized eggs, i.e. they are dizygotic or multiple zygotic. They may be of the same sex or different sexes, their placenta and amniotic sacs are also separate, and they differ from each other in many features, sharing only about half their genes like ordinary siblings.

21.3.3 The Placenta and Umbilical Cord

The placenta was the source of nutrients and oxygen for the fetus and the site for removal of waste products from fetal circulation, because the fetal lungs were not functional as organs of gas exchange. The fetal body had two adaptations to limit blood flow to the lungs: the foramen ovale, a hole between the two atria, shunted most atrial blood directly into the left atrium, avoiding the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation; and the ductus arteriosus, a connection between the pulmonary artery and aorta, sent right ventricular blood into the aorta rather than through the lungs. At birth the foramen ovale is closed by two flaps of heart tissue that fold together and fuse; the ductus arteriosus is shut off by contraction of muscles in its walls, though complete closure may take several months, and the two umbilical arteries and one vein also close off.

The placenta consists of a fetal part (chorionic villi, which increase surface area for absorption) and a maternal part (projections from the endometrium). Its average weight is about 600 grams, 15–20 cm in diameter and 3 cm thick at the centre. The umbilical cord, also called the naval string, connects the embryo to the placenta. It normally contains one umbilical vein, which supplies oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta, and two umbilical arteries, which bring back deoxygenated, nutrient-depleted blood to the placenta; thus the fetal heart pumps only deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

21.3.4 Difference Between Gestation and Pregnancy

Gestation is the period of time between conception and parturition (birth), during which the young one grows and develops inside the mother's uterus. Gestational age is the common term used during pregnancy to describe how far along the pregnancy is; a normal pregnancy can range from 38 to 40 weeks, or 9 months.

Key Points

  • Second trimester: fetus looks human, sex can be determined by ultrasound, grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 m, heartbeat heard by stethoscope, mother feels movements.
  • Third trimester: rapid growth of about 28 g per day, fat deposited, head descends to the cervix; birth weight about 3400 g.
  • Identical twins are monozygotic (same sex, shared placenta and chorion); fraternal twins are dizygotic with separate placentae and sacs.
  • Foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the fetal lungs and close after birth.
  • The umbilical cord has two arteries and one vein; the placenta weighs about 600 g.

lessons.title: Birth, Premature Birth and Nursing
lessons.notes_html:
Birth is also called parturition or labour. Normally, towards the end of pregnancy the uterus becomes progressively more excitable and develops such strong rhythmical contractions that the baby is expelled.

21.4 Birth and Nursing

21.4.1 Role of Fetal and Maternal Hormones in Controlling Birth

For normal birth two things must happen: the muscles in the womb and abdominal wall have to contract, and the cervix needs to soften or increase in diameter. Estrogen and progesterone are secreted during pregnancy, but from the seventh month onward estrogen secretion becomes greater than progesterone secretion. Estrogen stimulates the myometrial cells of the uterus to form abundant oxytocin receptors; the myometrium becomes more irritable and weak, irregular uterine contractions begin — the Braxton Hicks contractions or false labour pains. False pains convert into real labour pains with the help of two other chemical signals:

  • Oxytocin — Secreted from the fetal pituitary gland (and the mother's posterior pituitary), it excites the uterus and causes contractions of the uterine myometrium.
  • Fetal ACTH — The fetal pituitary also secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal gland to release corticosteroids. These decrease progesterone production by the placenta and stimulate the fetal membranes to produce more prostaglandins, which increase the power of contraction.

These powerful contractions stimulate the mother's hypothalamus, which signals for oxytocin release by the mother's posterior pituitary gland. Thus true labour begins: a positive feedback mechanism releases more and more oxytocin, causing greater contractile force, and oxytocin is released in waves during labour. The process of labour has three steps: (1) cervix dilation — opening up and thinning of the cervix; (2) expulsion of the baby — strong continuous contractions force the fetus down and out of the uterus and vagina; (3) expulsion of the placenta soon after birth.

After delivery the umbilical cord is still attached to the baby. It is clamped artificially as early as 1 to 5 minutes after birth, and clamping is followed by cutting of the cord, which is painless due to the lack of any nerves. Following the birth, usually within 10–15 minutes, the placenta separates from the uterine wall and is expelled by uterine contractions through the birth canal; this expulsion is termed the afterbirth.

21.4.2 The Premature Birth

The book defines a premature (preterm) birth as birth at less than 27 weeks (6 months) of the gestational period, caused by many factors during the second and third trimesters: smoking and not getting good prenatal care; being overweight or underweight during pregnancy; high blood pressure, blood clotting disorders and diabetes mellitus; getting pregnant too soon after having a baby; and multiple births or a baby with certain defects. (Note: most medical sources call any birth before 37 weeks premature; 27 weeks is the book's figure.) The premature baby faces many complications: increased risk of infections, difficulty in maintaining body temperature, feeding problems and possible jaundice, breathing difficulty because the lungs are not fully developed, and long-term complications such as blindness and disturbance in hearing.

21.4.3 Colostrum, Lactation or Nursing

The secretion and yielding of milk by the mother after giving birth is called lactation. Initially the mammary glands produce a special yellow-coloured, lymph-like fluid known as colostrum, quite rich in antibodies (particularly IgA), with little fat and less lactose and globulin protein than milk. After 2 or 3 days, milk production begins by prolactin, secreted from the anterior pituitary under the influence of prolactin-releasing hormone; prolactin also prepares and enlarges the mammary glands for milk production and storage. Once the glands are filled with milk they synthesize the serotonin neurotransmitter, which slows down prolactin production. In the majority of cases, as soon as breast feeding stops, the mother's reproductive cycle begins again.

Role of oxytocin in the secretion of milk: sucking of the baby stimulates sensory receptors around the nipples; nerve impulses pass to the hypothalamus, which stimulates the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin. Oxytocin causes dilation of milk ducts within the mammary glands and thus promotes ejection (let-down) of milk. Nursing also helps the mother, because oxytocin causes uterine contraction — new mothers experience cramps in the uterus while nursing — returning the uterus to its pre-pregnant size.

Breast FeedingBottle-Feeding
Perfect balance of nutrients, high level of nutrientsNot efficiently utilized as breast milk; contents depend on proper preparation
Digested and absorbed easily, always at perfect temperatureSome babies have difficulty tolerating certain elements
Advantages: baby gets immunity; readily available at any time and place; creates affection of mother and child due to prolactin. Disadvantages: early breastfeeding may be uncomfortable; certain medication can interrupt itAdvantages: presence of mother is not necessary; but baby does not get immunity and there is no or less affection due to absence of prolactin. Disadvantages: preparation time varies and can be unhygienic; baby may not tolerate formula; bottles and mixing items must always be carried

Key Points

  • From the 7th month estrogen exceeds progesterone and induces oxytocin receptors; Braxton Hicks (false) pains become real pains.
  • Oxytocin and prostaglandins drive labour by positive feedback; labour has three steps: cervix dilation, expulsion of the baby, expulsion of the placenta (afterbirth, within 10–15 minutes).
  • The cord is clamped and cut 1 to 5 minutes after birth; cutting is painless as the cord has no nerves.
  • Colostrum is the first yellow fluid, rich in IgA antibodies; prolactin makes milk and oxytocin ejects it.
  • The book defines premature birth as before 27 weeks; its complications include infection, breathing difficulty and jaundice.

lessons.title: Disorders During Embryonic Development and Fetal Surgery
lessons.notes_html:
The fetus faces many disorders at birth, collectively known as embryonic development disorders or birth defects. The study of abnormal development is called teratology.

21.5 Disorders During Embryonic Development

21.5.1 Maternal Derived Abnormalities

These abnormalities are transmitted from mother to fetus during pregnancy or just after birth, such as rubella, neural tube defects, thyroid gland and limb development defects.

  • Rubella — Caused by the rubella virus and also called German measles. It is extremely dangerous if the mother is infected within the first twenty weeks of pregnancy: the baby may be born with Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS), comprising cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus), cerebral defects, ophthalmic defects (cataract) and deafness. It may also cause prematurity, low birth weight, anaemia and hepatitis.
  • Neural Tube Defects (NTDs) — Serious birth defects, from mild to severe impairment, due to abnormal closure of the neural fold, caused by incomplete development of the brain, spinal cord and meninges; the fetal spine fails to close properly during the early stages of pregnancy (spina bifida is one such defect).
  • Thyroid gland disorder — Congenital hypothyroidism of the newborn baby. The baby frequently has hyperbilirubinemia and delayed skeletal maturation, reflecting immaturity of liver and bone respectively, and is at risk of permanent mental retardation if thyroid hormone therapy is delayed or inadequate. Birth size, however, is normal.
  • Developmental (limb) defects — The upper and lower limbs have a large number of genetic and environment-derived abnormalities, some surgically repairable; partial or complete absence of limbs or digits is common.

21.5.2 Genetic Abnormalities Related to Spontaneous Abortions

Approximately 50% of first and second trimester miscarriages (spontaneous abortions) are due to a chromosome abnormality in the fetus. An extra chromosome (2n+1) or a missing chromosome (2n−1) can cause miscarriage, or lead to a child with learning difficulties, mental retardation and birth defects. These defects result from a mistake in cell division soon after conception — a random event that can occur in anyone's pregnancy. An inherited problem can also cause miscarriage: a parent may have a rearrangement (translocation) in which the chromosomes are structured differently. Another genetic cause is a change in a single gene or several genes on the chromosomes, causing specific genetic diseases or birth defects.

21.5.3 Fetal Surgery and Defected Fetal Development Problems

The surgery of the fetus within the maternal uterus to treat a prenatal defect is called fetal surgery. It helps correct detected fetal developmental problems before birth.

  • Open fetal surgery — The uterus is completely opened to operate on the fetus. It is done to treat or close neural tube defects and congenital diseases such as diaphragmatic hernia (an abnormal opening in the diaphragm, so organs move from the belly to the chest cavity near the lungs).
  • Minimally invasive foetoscopic surgery — Uses small incisions, guided by foetoscopy and sonography. It is used for fetal bladder outlet obstruction (blockage of the bladder), pulmonary/aortic valvuloplasty (widening of a stenotic aortic valve using a balloon catheter inside the valve) and atrial septostomy (a small hole created between the atria of the heart).

Key Points

  • Rubella (German measles) in the first 20 weeks can cause Congenital Rubella Syndrome: heart, brain, eye (cataract) defects and deafness.
  • Neural tube defects come from abnormal closure of the neural fold; congenital hypothyroidism risks mental retardation if treatment is delayed.
  • About 50% of early miscarriages are due to chromosome abnormalities (2n+1 or 2n−1), translocations or gene changes.
  • Fetal surgery treats defects before birth: open surgery for neural tube defects and diaphragmatic hernia; foetoscopic surgery for bladder obstruction, valvuloplasty and atrial septostomy.
  • Teratology is the study of abnormal development.

lessons.title: Postnatal Development and Ageing
lessons.notes_html:
Development does not stop at birth. After birth the body passes through five stages, grows at different rates in different parts, and finally undergoes the negative changes of ageing.

21.6 Postnatal Development

  • Neonatal — From birth to one month.
  • Infancy — From one month to two years of age.
  • Childhood — From the third year to 12–14 years.
  • Adolescence (puberty) — Begins at around 12 or 13 years of age till adulthood; puberty brings sexual maturity.
  • Adulthood (maturity) — Includes the years between 18 to 25 years of age.

The process of ageing is called senescence.

21.6.1 Allometric Growth

Allometric growth means differential growth, i.e. varying rates of growth for different parts of the body during development. The head of a human baby is larger than the rest of the body, while the tarsus of the foot, hands and legs grow more rapidly than the head. The reproductive organs grow more slowly than other organs till childhood. Some systems, like the lymphatic system, develop more rapidly in early age and decrease after puberty. The skull and brain reach their maximum size well before adulthood, i.e. about 90% of adult size soon after the age of 06 years.

21.7 Ageing

Ageing is the negative physiological changes in our body, the phenomenon of getting old. It is an inevitable process; it cannot be stopped or prevented, and it is a part of normal development. The study of ageing is called gerontology. Development continues throughout the stages of life, but after growth and differentiation cells begin to deteriorate. The average human life is between 70 to 80 years (maximum 110–115).

21.7.1 Genetic and Extrinsic Factors Responsible for Ageing

  • Genetic (intrinsic) factor — Ageing has a genetic basis. Human cells will divide less than 100 times outside the body because of telomeres: the specific nucleotide sequence at the end of each chromosome. Telomeres are at maximum length during the fetal stage and decrease after each mitosis; when they shorten to a critical length the cell can no longer divide, damaged tissues cannot regenerate, and we begin to wear out.
  • Extrinsic factors — Mostly poor health; osteoporosis and cardiovascular diseases are important factors. Osteoporosis is the progressive decline in bone density which results in bone fracture; its causes are menopause, cigarette smoking, heavy alcohol drinking and deficiency of Ca⁺ and vitamins. Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of ageing and death and can be prevented with a balanced diet including vegetables and fruits, and regular exercise.

21.7.2 Signs and Symptoms

Signs of ageing develop gradually, are very diverse, and differ widely between people; ageing cannot be diagnosed from isolated signs alone.

  • Primary ageing — An overall decrease in energy and vigour; changes in sleeping patterns; decreased memory; skin and hair changes such as wrinkles, brown (pigmented) spots on the skin, loss of skin elasticity and thinning hair; weakened muscles, so movement becomes slow; loss or decrease in vision and hearing; susceptibility to infection and stress; sexual dysfunction and urinary problems; changes in the menstrual cycle; abdominal obesity and inability to lose weight.
  • Secondary ageing — Results from diseases and poor health practices, e.g. no or less exercise, smoking, malnutrition, excess fat, exposure to ultraviolet light and other forms of self-damage. It is often preventable through lifestyle choice or modern medicines.

21.7.3 Cell Level Changes in Ageing

All cells change as they age: cells become larger and their capacity to divide and reproduce tends to decrease. Normal cells have built-in mechanisms to repair minor damage, but the ability to repair declines in ageing cells. DNA is damaged through the ageing process, and changes occur in the cellular membrane, in enzymes, in the transport of ions and nutrients, and in the nucleus, whose chromosomes undergo clumping, shrinkage and fragmentation. The numbers of mitochondria and lysosomes are reduced, causing cells to function less efficiently, and hormonal secretions decrease. Decreased metabolism has several effects: tolerance of cold is less, the tendency to gain weight increases, and there is decreased efficiency in the body's use of glucose. Waste pigments such as lipofuscin also accumulate in cells.

21.7.4 System Level Changes in Ageing

The gastro-intestinal tract mostly maintains its functional level well into old age, but taste is altered, stomach acidity decreases, blood flow to the liver decreases, and saliva secretion from the salivary glands becomes less than normal, affecting chewing, swallowing and the taste of food. Ageing is accompanied by a lower production of neurotransmitters, and only when the drop approaches 50% does dementia ensue (15% of old people have severe dementia). Due to malnutrition the heart becomes smaller than normal, while sometimes it becomes larger due to severe high blood pressure, or unchanged in size; fat accumulates in the heart muscle as total body fat increases. Infections occur more frequently in the elderly and are more often severe due to the low working of the immune system. Fertility in man gradually declines with age, while in women it ends with menopause.

Diseases of ageing and their treatment (STS): osteoarthritis — anti-inflammatory drugs and painkillers in the early stages, later a joint replacement may be necessary; osteoporosis — calcium intake as medicine or food, and hormone therapy (ERT) for most women after menopause; arteriosclerosis — lifestyle changes such as a healthy diet and exercising are often the best treatment, though medication or surgical procedures may also be recommended.

Key Points

  • Postnatal stages: neonatal (to 1 month), infancy (to 2 years), childhood (to 12–14 years), adolescence (from 12–13 years) and adulthood (18–25 years in the book).
  • Allometric growth is differential growth: the brain reaches about 90% of adult size soon after age 6, while reproductive organs grow slowly till childhood.
  • Ageing is the sum of negative physiological changes; its study is gerontology; average human life is 70–80 years.
  • Genetic ageing is linked to telomeres shortening at each mitosis; extrinsic ageing is driven by disease and lifestyle.
  • Primary ageing is inevitable (wrinkles, grey and thinning hair, weak senses); secondary ageing, from disease, disuse and abuse, is often preventable.

lessons.title: Mendel, Heredity and the Laws of Inheritance
lessons.notes_html:
Inheritance is the process by which genetic information is passed from parents to child, which is why members of the same family tend to have similar characteristics. We actually have two genomes: one copy from each parent. The passing of characters from parents to offspring is heredity. The differences shown by individuals of a species, and by offspring of the same parents, are variations; they may be harmful, useful or useless. The study of heredity and variations is called genetics.

22.1 Mendelian Inheritance

Mendelian inheritance refers to the patterns of inheritance characteristic of organisms which reproduce sexually. Gregor John Mendel, an Austrian monk, formulated fundamental principles of inheritance. Between 1856 and 1865 he cross-bred pea plants (Pisum sativum) with 7 pairs of contrasting characteristics, and explained his results with two laws of inheritance that introduced the idea of dominant and recessive genes. On the genetic level, all humans are more than 99% identical.

CharacterDominant FormRecessive FormF2 Generation Ratio
Flower colourPurple flowersWhite flowers3/4 : 1/4
Seed colourYellow seedsGreen seeds3/4 : 1/4
Seed shapeRound seedsWrinkled seeds3/4 : 1/4
Pod colourGreen podsYellow pods3/4 : 1/4
Pod shapeInflated podsConstricted pods3/4 : 1/4
Flower positionAxial flowersTerminal flowers3/4 : 1/4
Plant heightTall plantsDwarf plants3/4 : 1/4

22.1.1 Association of Inheritance with Laws of Mendel

Through his work on pea plants, Mendel discovered the fundamental laws of inheritance. He deduced that factors (genes) come in pairs and are inherited as distinct units, one from each parent. He tracked the segregation of parental genes and their appearance in the offspring as dominant and recessive traits, and he recognized the mathematical patterns of inheritance from one generation to the next. His two laws are:

  • The Law of Segregation — The two alleles of a single trait will separate randomly. Parental factors (genes) are randomly separated to the sex cells so that sex cells contain only one member of the factor (gene) pair. Offspring therefore inherits one allele from each parent when sex cells unite in fertilization.
  • The Law of Independent Assortment — The alleles of one gene separate independently of another allele. Genes for different traits are sorted separately from one another, so that the inheritance of one trait is not dependent on the inheritance of another.

Key Points

  • Inheritance passes genetic information from parents to offspring; heredity is the passing of characters, and differences are variations.
  • Mendel (1856 to 1865) cross-bred pea plants with 7 pairs of contrasting characters, each giving a 3:1 ratio in F2.
  • Law of segregation: the two alleles of a trait separate randomly, so each gamete receives only one.
  • Law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently of one another.
  • Factors (genes) come in pairs, one inherited from each parent, and appear in offspring as dominant and recessive traits.

lessons.title: The Monohybrid Cross: Law of Segregation in Action
lessons.notes_html:
A monohybrid cross follows the inheritance of a single trait. It is the cross Mendel used to demonstrate the law of segregation: a pair of alleles separates during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele, and the hidden recessive trait reappears in the F2 generation.

Inheritance of Single Trait (Monohybrid Cross)

A cross which involves only one pair of contrasting characters is called a monohybrid cross. Mendel crossed tall pea plants (about 2 meters high) with dwarf pea plants (about 20 to 50 cm). He used pure breeding varieties, that is, plants which when self-fertilized produced offspring that resembled their parents. He cross-pollinated tall plants with pollen from dwarf plants and vice versa. The resulting hybrid generation is called the first filial generation or F1 generation; in F1 all plants were tall. He then allowed the F1 plants to self-pollinate, producing the F2 (second filial) generation. In F2 he got 1064 plants: 787 were tall and 277 were dwarf, that is, in the ratio of about three tall to one dwarf (3:1). Mendel also made crosses using the 6 other contrasting characters and got almost similar results.

A monohybrid cross: segregation of T and t gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, and 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

Interpretation of the Results

  • In all his experiments one trait appeared in F1 while the other disappeared; the hidden character reappeared in F2 in about 1/4 of the total offspring. The character which appeared in F1 is called dominant, and the character which could not express itself in F1 is called recessive.
  • Hereditary characters are responsible for transmission of characteristics, and each characteristic is controlled by a pair of factors (genes), for example colour of flower, colour of seed, shape of seed and height of plant.
  • If the two factors differ, only the dominant one shows its effect: a plant with one factor for tallness and one for dwarfness shows only tallness. A dominant gene expresses itself even in the presence of its recessive allele; a recessive gene produces its phenotypic effect only in the presence of a similar allele.
  • The two factors in each pair separate or segregate during gamete formation and each gamete contains only one factor, so the gametes are always pure. A gamete of a Tt plant has either the tall factor or the dwarf factor, but not both.
  • The fusion of haploid gametes at fertilization restores the diploid condition in the zygote, and gametes unite at random so that a predictable ratio occurs among the offspring. Dominant does not mean healthier or more vigorous; both dominant and recessive alleles can be disease carriers.

Key Points

  • Inheritance passes genetic information from parents to offspring; heredity is the passing of characters, and differences are variations.
  • Mendel (1856 to 1865) cross-bred pea plants with 7 pairs of contrasting characters.
  • Law of segregation: the two alleles of a trait separate randomly, so each gamete receives only one.
  • Monohybrid cross TT x tt gives all tall F1, and F2 of 787 tall : 277 dwarf (about 3:1) out of 1064 plants.
  • The trait seen in F1 is dominant; the trait hidden in F1 and reappearing in 1/4 of F2 is recessive.
  • Gametes are always pure; fertilization restores the diploid condition.

lessons.title: Dihybrid Cross, Independent Assortment and Mathematical Probabilities
lessons.notes_html:
Mendel suggested his second law of inheritance by following two characters at the same time, such as seed colour and seed shape. From single character crosses, Mendel knew that the allele for yellow seed is dominant (Y) while the allele for green seed is recessive (y), and the allele for round seed is dominant (R) while the allele for wrinkled seed is recessive (r).

Inheritance of Two Traits (Dihybrid Crosses): Procedure and Observations

Mendel crossed a pure round-yellow seeded plant (RRYY) with a wrinkled green seeded plant (rryy) and got the F1 generation. In F1 he got all round-yellow seeded plants, but these plants were dihybrids, that is, RrYy. The key step was to see what happens when F1 plants self-pollinate and produce the F2 generation. If the hybrids transmitted their alleles in the same combinations in which they were inherited from the parents, the F1 hybrid would produce only two classes of gametes, RY and ry; this dependent assortment hypothesis predicts an F2 phenotype ratio of 3:1, just as in a monohybrid cross. The alternative hypothesis is that the two pairs of alleles segregate independently of each other, so the F1 plant produces 4 types of gametes in equal quantities, that is, RY, rY, Ry and ry. If sperms of the 4 classes fertilize eggs of the 4 classes, there will be 16 (4 x 4) equally probable ways in which the alleles can combine in F2, resulting in 4 phenotype categories with a ratio of 9:3:3:1. When Mendel did the experiment, his F2 results were close to the predicted 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio, supporting independent assortment.

F2 PhenotypeFractionRatio
Round, yellow9/169
Round, green3/163
Wrinkled, yellow3/163
Wrinkled, green1/161

Interpretation of the Results

Mendel tested all seven pairs of contrasting characters in various dihybrid combinations and always observed a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in F2. Looking only at pea colour in such a cross, there were 416 yellow and 140 green peas, a 2.97:1 ratio, or roughly 3:1, so the pea colour alleles segregated as if it were a monohybrid cross. The result of Mendel's dihybrid cross is the basis for the law of independent assortment: the alleles of two (or more) different genes get sorted into gametes independently of one another; the allele a gamete receives for one gene does not influence the allele received from another gene. The law of independent assortment can be determined by a dihybrid cross.

Limitations of the Law of Independent Assortment

  • This law applies only to those genes (allele pairs) located on different chromosomes (non-homologous chromosomes), or alternatively to genes that are very far apart on the same chromosome.
  • It fails for linked genes on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together unless crossing over separates them.
  • All the pea characters Mendel chose for analysis were controlled by genes on different chromosomes, which greatly simplified the interpretation of his multi-character crosses.

Usefulness and Scope of Independent Assortment in Variation

This law explains that desired characters of two parents can be expressed in a single offspring and undesired characters can be prevented from expression. Independent assortment also contributes to variation because it results in the shuffling of chromosomes into various gametes. Crossing over occurs when homologous chromosomes exchange genetic information, so chromosomes are formed that contain genes from both parents.

22.1.2 Inheritance and Mathematical Probabilities

Probability is the chance of occurrence of an event. Mendel's laws reflect the same rules of probability that apply to tossing coins, rolling dice and drawing cards from a deck. The probability scale ranges from 0 to 1: an event certain to occur has a probability of 1, and an event certain not to occur has a probability of 0. With a normal coin, the chance of tossing tails is 1/2 and the chance of tossing heads is 1/2. For every toss, the probability of a head is 1/2, and the outcome of any particular toss is unaffected by what happened on previous trials. Such phenomena are called independent events: each toss is independent of every other toss, and like two separate coin tosses, the alleles of one gene segregate into gametes independently of another gene's alleles (the law of independent assortment).

Product Rule

The product rule states that the probability of two or more independent events occurring together can be calculated by multiplying the individual probabilities. This rule is useful in genetics to predict frequencies of fertilization events. According to this rule, the probability of the round yellow phenotype in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross is equal to the product of the individual probabilities of round (3/4) and yellow (3/4) phenotypes, that is, P = 3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16.

Key Points

  • A dihybrid cross follows two characters at once: RRYY x rryy gives F1 all RrYy (round, yellow).
  • Independent assortment gives 4 gamete types (RY, rY, Ry, ry), 16 combinations and an F2 ratio of 9:3:3:1.
  • Each single character still segregates 3:1 in the dihybrid F2 (416 yellow : 140 green, roughly 3:1).
  • The law applies only to genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same chromosome; it fails for linked genes.
  • Probability ranges from 0 to 1; each fertilization is an independent event.
  • Product rule: multiply individual probabilities, for example 3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16 for round yellow.

lessons.title: Exceptions to Mendelian Inheritance: Incomplete Dominance, Co-dominance and Multiple Alleles
lessons.notes_html:
Today we know that there are many exceptions to Mendel's laws: not every gene has alleles that are strictly dominant or recessive. This does not mean Mendel was wrong; it means we know more today about genetics, diseases and inheritance than 150 years ago, when Mendel formulated his laws.

22.2.1 Incomplete Dominance

When two contrasting characters are crossed, and if in the F1 generation none of the characters is fully expressed, this phenomenon is called incomplete dominance. It was first described by Carl Correns. Example: when a red (RR) Japanese 4 o'clock flower plant (Mirabilis jalapa) is crossed with a white (WW) 4 o'clock flower plant, in the F1 generation the hybrid plants have pink (RW) flowers. This third, intermediate phenotype results from the flowers of heterozygotes having less red colour than the red homozygotes.

At first glance, incomplete dominance seems to support the blending hypothesis of inheritance, which would predict that red or white traits could never reappear among offspring from a pink hybrid. In fact, inbreeding F1 hybrids produces F2 offspring with a phenotypic ratio of one red to two pink to one white, that is, 1:2:1. Thus the genotype and phenotype ratios are the same (RR, 2RW, WW). The segregation of the red and white flower alleles in the gametes of the pink flowered plants confirms that the alleles for flower colour are heritable factors that maintain their identity in the hybrids; that is, inheritance is particulate. A genetic problem from the book: red x pink gives red and pink offspring in the ratio 2:2 (RR and RW).

22.2.2 Co-dominance

The dominance relation when two contrasting characters are crossed and in the F1 generation both of them fully express themselves is called co-dominance. For example, the human MN blood group is determined by co-dominant alleles for two specific molecules located on the surface of red blood cells, the M and N antigen molecules. A single gene locus, at which two allelic variations are possible, determines the phenotype of this blood group. Individuals homozygous for the M allele have red blood cells with only M molecules; individuals homozygous for the N allele have RBCs with only N molecules; but both M and N molecules are present on the red blood cells of individuals heterozygous for the M and N alleles (MN). The MN phenotype is not intermediate between the M and N phenotypes, which distinguishes co-dominance from incomplete dominance.

GenotypePhenotypeAntigen Present on RBC
L^M L^MMM
L^M L^NMNM and N
L^N L^NNN
Incomplete DominanceCo-dominance
An intermediate trait appearsHas independent effect; both traits appear simultaneously
Both alleles are expressed partiallyBoth alleles are equally conspicuous
None of the parental characteristics is expressed in the offspringBoth parental characteristics are expressed in the offspring

Multiple Alleles

Any one of a series of three or more alternative or allelic forms of a gene, only two of which can exist in any normal diploid individual, is known as a multiple allele. The ABO blood group is an example of multiple alleles, and it is also an example of an exception to Mendelian inheritance. The 4 blood groups A, B, AB and O are all determined by a single gene. Three alleles of this gene exist: I^A, I^B and i. I^A and I^B are dominant while i is recessive to both I^A and I^B. The term gene itself was coined by Johannsen, and an allele is an alternate (different) form of a gene.

Key Points

  • Exceptions to Mendel's laws do not disprove Mendel; they extend his laws.
  • Incomplete dominance: neither allele is fully expressed; the heterozygote is intermediate (red x white gives pink in the 4 o'clock plant).
  • Incomplete dominance gives an F2 ratio of 1:2:1, the same for genotype and phenotype, proving inheritance is particulate, not blending.
  • Co-dominance: both alleles express fully and independently, as in the MN blood group (M, MN, N).
  • Multiple alleles: three or more allelic forms of one gene exist in the population, but only two in any diploid individual; ABO blood groups are the example.

lessons.title: ABO Blood Group System, Antibodies and the Transfusion Principle
lessons.notes_html:
Although the ABO and Rh groups are most important for blood transfusions, there are 36 other known blood group systems that usually do not complicate transfusion; these are called rare types. Each blood group has a combination of sugars and proteins called antigens that are found on the surface of RBCs. There are about 600 antigens, so there is potential for a lot of variation between different people.

22.3.1 ABO Blood Group System

The ABO blood group is an example of multiple alleles, which is an exception to Mendelian inheritance. In 1900, Karl Landsteiner reported a series of tests which identified the ABO blood group system. The ABO blood group is also found in other primates like apes, chimpanzees and gorillas. Note: the book prints that Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in 1910; the prize for this discovery was actually awarded in 1930.

Antigens of ABO Blood Group

ABO antigens are glycolipid in nature, attached on the surface of red blood cells. These antigens stick out from the cell membrane and there are many antigen sites per red blood cell. Besides their presence on red blood cells, soluble antigens can be present in plasma, saliva and other secretions, and these antigens are also expressed on tissues other than red blood cells. There are two types of antigens, antigen A and antigen B. Their presence or absence makes 4 types of blood groups: blood group A when antigen A is present, blood group B when antigen B is present, blood group AB when both antigens A and B are present, and blood group O when both antigens A and B are absent.

Genetic Basis of ABO System

Blood groups are inherited from both parents. The ABO blood group is controlled by a single gene with three types of alleles, that is, I^A, I^B and i. The I stands for isoagglutinogen. I^A and I^B are both dominant alleles (and co-dominant with each other, as shown by blood group AB), while i is recessive. The gene is located on the long arm of chromosome number 9. Individuals with genotype I^A I^A or I^A i have type A blood group, and individuals with I^B I^B or I^B i have type B blood group. The genotype I^A I^B gives blood group AB, because both alleles are dominant and both types of protein, A and B, appear together on the surface of blood cells; this is another example of co-dominance. An individual having genotype ii has blood group O.

Blood GroupGenotypesAntigen on RBCAntibody in PlasmaCan Receive From
AI^A I^A, I^A iAAnti-BA or O
BI^B I^B, I^B iBAnti-AB or O
ABI^A I^BA and BNeitherA, B, AB or O (universal recipient)
OiiNeither A nor BBoth anti-A and anti-BO only (universal donor)

Antibodies of ABO Blood System

Two types of antibodies are present in blood plasma, and they occur together with the antigens in the opposite way: antigen A with antibody B, antigen B with antibody A, antigen AB with no antibodies, and no antigen with both antibodies A and B. There is an agglutination reaction between a similar antigen and antibody: antigen A agglutinates antibody A and antigen B agglutinates antibody B, causing clumping of red blood cells.

Transfusion Principle

Blood transfusion is the process of transferring blood into one's circulation intravenously. Transfusions are used for various medical conditions such as deficiency of blood, blood lost during pregnancy or any surgery, and blood cell diseases like thalassemia, sickle cell disease and leukaemia. Before transfusion, the blood groups of recipient and donor are tested. If transfusion is carried out between two incompatible blood groups, an antigen-antibody reaction will occur in the recipient and agglutination, that is, clumping of red blood cells, will occur. Therefore transfusions are carried out on the basis of the donor's antigens and the recipient's antibodies. A person with type A can receive blood from type A or O, because anti-B antibody means no blood carrying B antigen can be given; a person with type B can receive from B or O; a person with blood group AB can receive blood from all other types, A, B, AB and O; while a person with blood group O can only receive blood from its own type. Therefore blood group O is called the universal donor and blood group AB is called the universal recipient.

Science, Technology and Society (STS)

Blood donation is a service to suffering humanity: blood is the most precious gift anyone can give to another person, the gift of life, and one donation can save several lives if the blood is separated into components (RBC, platelets, plasma, WBC) used for patients with specific conditions. The STS section also explains why blood group O is more frequent in the human population: the recessive allele i is common because crosses between heterozygous I^A i x I^A i, I^B i x I^B i and I^A i x I^B i parents each produce 25% offspring of blood group O (ii), and O x O crosses give only O offspring.

Key Points

  • There are 36 other blood group systems (rare types) and about 600 RBC antigens in total.
  • Landsteiner identified the ABO system in 1900; its antigens are glycolipids on the RBC surface.
  • One gene on chromosome 9 has three alleles: I^A and I^B dominant and co-dominant with each other, i recessive; six genotypes give four phenotypes.
  • Plasma antibodies are opposite to the RBC antigens; a matching antigen and antibody cause agglutination.
  • Group O is the universal donor and group AB is the universal recipient.

lessons.title: Rh Blood Group System and Erythroblastosis Foetalis
lessons.notes_html:
The Rh blood group system is defined on the basis of the Rh factor present on the surface of red blood cells; the Rh factor is another blood group system. The ABO blood type is represented by a + or - sign: the +ve sign indicates the presence of Rh factor, while the -ve sign indicates the absence of Rh factor. Landsteiner discovered the Rh antigen from the blood of the Rhesus monkey.

Antigens of Rh Blood Group System and Genetic Basis

The Rh blood group system is encoded by three genes, C, D and E. These genes occupy two loci, that is, locus D and the C or E loci. Gene D is located on the D locus while the genes C or E are located on the other locus; however, the D locus has prime importance. The gene D has two alleles, D and d, and D is completely dominant over d. Therefore a person with DD or Dd is Rh +ve, and a person with genotype dd is Rh -ve. The O -ve blood type is the universal donor because it can donate blood to all blood groups, and AB +ve is the universal recipient because it can receive blood from all blood groups.

Anti-Rh Antibody and Transfusion Principle

The Rh antibody is not present naturally in the body; this antibody is produced in reaction to the Rh antigen. An Rh +ve donor is totally incompatible for an Rh -ve recipient. Sometimes an Rh -ve person receives Rh +ve antigen through a wrong Rh +ve blood transfusion; he starts producing anti-Rh antibodies against the Rh antigen and a reaction occurs. A donor who has never been exposed to Rh antigen can be transfused to an Rh +ve recipient.

How Rh incompatibility develops: sensitization in one pregnancy endangers the next Rh +ve baby.

22.4.1 Erythroblastosis Foetalis

Erythroblastosis foetalis, or haemolytic disease (haemo: blood, lytic: breakdown) of newborn babies, occurs when the baby's red blood cells break down at a fast rate. It develops in a foetus when anti-Rh antibodies produced by the mother pass through the placenta and start haemolysis. An erythroblast is a type of RBC which still retains a cell nucleus; it is the intermediate precursor of normal erythrocytes.

Problems and Complications in Foetus

  • Babies develop the symptoms of anaemia, with a pale and swollen body at birth, and an enlarged liver or spleen.
  • The anaemic foetus starts to release many immature erythroblasts into his blood system; therefore the disease is called erythroblastosis foetalis.
  • The anaemic foetus may lead to abortion or stillbirth. If the pregnancy continues, the liver and spleen produce and break down RBCs at a fast rate.
  • The breakdown of RBCs produces bilirubin. A high concentration of bilirubin in foetal blood damages the brain and turns the skin yellow; this condition is called jaundice.

Causes and Risk Factors

The most common cause of erythroblastosis foetalis is maternal foetal Rh incompatibility. Sometimes an Rh -ve woman marries an Rh +ve man and conceives a child with an Rh +ve blood group. If the man's genotype is DD, all offspring will have Dd genotype, that is, Rh +ve. If the man's genotype is Dd, half of the offspring will be Dd (Rh +ve) while half will have genotype dd (Rh -ve). The Rh -ve offspring will remain safe in the mother's body, but Rh +ve offspring will be at risk.

Prevention and Treatments

During a pregnant woman's first prenatal doctor's visit, she should be screened for blood and Rh type. If she has Rh-negative blood, the father's blood and Rh type should be tested; if the father has Rh-positive blood, an Rh-positive foetus may develop. In this case, Rh sensitization of the Rh-negative mother can be avoided by a simple therapy: she is given an injection of Rh antiserum (serum containing anti-Rh antibodies) during early pregnancy (1st trimester) and immediately after birth, within 72 hours of delivery. This causes any of the baby's red blood cells that may have crossed into the mother's blood to be destroyed before sensitizing the mother's immune system to produce maternal anti-Rh antibodies. The injected antiserum disappears before the next pregnancy, and this has to be done with each pregnancy, whether it ends in a delivery or an abortion.

Key Points

  • Rh +ve means the Rh factor (D antigen) is present on RBCs; Rh -ve means it is absent. DD and Dd are Rh +ve; dd is Rh -ve.
  • O -ve is the universal donor and AB +ve is the universal recipient when ABO and Rh are combined.
  • Anti-Rh antibody is not natural; it is made only after exposure to Rh antigen.
  • Erythroblastosis foetalis: maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and haemolyse the Rh +ve baby's RBCs.
  • Complications: anaemia, enlarged liver and spleen, jaundice from bilirubin, and possibly abortion or stillbirth.
  • Prevention: screen mother and father, and give Rh antiserum during pregnancy and within 72 hours after delivery.

lessons.title: Polygenic Inheritance: Wheat Grain Colour and Human Skin Colour
lessons.notes_html:
Polygenic inheritance, also known as quantitative inheritance, refers to a single inherited phenotypic trait that is controlled by two or more different genes. The traits determined by polygenic inheritance are not simply an effect of dominant or recessive traits and do not exhibit complete dominance; in fact, polygenic inheritance exhibits incomplete dominance, so the phenotype displayed in the offspring is a mixture of the phenotypes displayed by the parents. Each of the genes that contributes to a polygenic trait has an equal influence, and each of the alleles has an additive effect on the phenotype outcome. Polygenic inheritance should not be confused with the effects caused by multiple alleles: multiple alleles are several forms of one gene, while polygenic inheritance is one trait controlled by several genes.

22.5.1 Wheat Grain Colour (an Example of Polygenic Inheritance)

Nilsson-Ehle performed many crosses between varieties of wheat having red seeds and those having white seeds. The noteworthy feature of his experiment was the variation in the intensity of the red pigment in the wheat grains produced by F2 plants. There were many gradations from the deep red of one parent to the pure white of the other parent, so that the plants could be divided into 7 different colour classes in the ratio of 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1. Nilsson-Ehle could distinguish the red classes with varying intensities as follows: 1 deep red, 6 dark red, 15 reds, 20 medium red, 15 light red and 6 very light red. Only one of 64 plants produced completely white grain, and one other of 64 had red grains identical to the parents in the first cross. Note: the book lists six red shades; with the white class they make the seven classes of the 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 ratio.

Nilsson-Ehle postulated three pairs of genes controlling grain colour in wheat, with genes for red (ABC) dominant over genes for white (abc). It also appeared that all alleles contributed equally in the production or absence of red pigment. Each of the three gene pairs, when considered singly in crosses, segregated in the expected Mendelian fashion, producing F2 progeny of three red and one white. The parental cross is AABBCC (dark red) x aabbcc (white), giving F1 offspring AaBbCc with intermediate kernel colour; crossing the triple heterozygotes gives the range of colour variants in F2.

Contributing AllelesFraction of F2Colour Class
All contributing (6)1/64Deep red
5 contributing6/64Dark red
4 contributing15/64Red
3 contributing20/64Medium red
2 contributing15/64Light red
1 contributing6/64Very light red
All non-contributing (0)1/64White

22.5.2 Inheritance of Human Skin Colour

The pigment melanin is responsible for dark coloration in the skin, and there are at least three genes which control human skin colour. In a hypothetical example, the production of melanin is controlled by contributing alleles denoted A, B and C, resulting in dark skin colour, while light skin colour is produced by the non-contributing alleles a, b and c, so a whole spectrum of different skin colours can result in the offspring: AABBCC is very dark and aabbcc is very light, and the F1 (AaBbCc) is intermediate. In polygenic inheritance, alleles do not display dominance over others; rather, each contributing allele gives an additive effect rather than a masking effect, so the way the alleles interact is different from Mendelian genetics. In a cross between two parents heterozygous for each of the melanin producing genes, AaBbCc x AaBbCc, the additive effects and combinations of alleles result in all the possible genotypes and shades, from very light to very dark.

What is Pleiotropy?

Pleiotropy is the ability of a single gene to have multiple phenotypic effects; for example, sickle cell anaemia causes effects in multiple systems, only one of which is the actual sickle-celled condition. Pleiotropy is the opposite pattern to polygenic inheritance, where many genes affect one trait.

Key Points

  • Polygenic (quantitative) inheritance: one trait controlled by two or more genes, each allele having an equal, additive effect.
  • Wheat grain colour (Nilsson-Ehle): three gene pairs give 7 colour classes in F2 in the ratio 1:6:15:20:15:6:1; only 1/64 are white.
  • Each wheat gene pair alone segregates in Mendelian fashion, 3 red : 1 white.
  • Human skin colour is controlled by at least three genes acting on melanin; more contributing alleles mean darker skin.
  • Polygenic traits show continuous variation, not distinct classes.
  • Pleiotropy: one gene, many phenotypic effects, as in sickle cell anaemia.

lessons.title: Epistasis and Coat Colour in the Labrador Retriever
lessons.notes_html:
Epistasis is a word composed of Greek roots that means "standing upon". It is a form of interaction between non-allelic genes in which one combination of such genes has a dominant effect over other combinations. A gene is said to be epistatic when its presence suppresses the expression of a gene which is present on another locus of the same or another chromosome. The gene which is suppressed is known as the hypostatic gene.

22.5.3 Epistasis and How It Differs from Dominance

Epistasis is different from dominance, because dominance is the phenomenon in which the alleles of the same locus interact with each other to produce a phenotype, while epistasis is a type of interaction that occurs between alleles of different loci.

EpistasisDominance
This type of gene interaction involves two non-allelic pairs of genesOnly one pair of genes is involved, so there is no interaction between genes
One pair of genes masks the effect of another pair of genesAn allele masks the effect of another allele of the same gene pair
Expression of both the dominant and recessive alleles may be suppressed by the epistatic geneExpression of the recessive allele is masked by the dominant allele

Bombay Phenotype

The Bombay phenotype was discovered in 1952 in Bombay city of India. Individuals with the Bombay phenotype have the genes to make the ABO antigen at one locus but lack the gene that produces the H substance at another locus, so the ABO antigens cannot be expressed: an example of epistasis in humans. An individual with the Bombay phenotype can receive blood from another individual with blood group O but cannot donate blood.

Relationship of Epistasis with Polygenic Inheritance

Epistasis is a type of polygenic inheritance where the alleles at one gene locus can hide or prevent the expression of alleles at a second gene locus. Polygenic inheritance is not controlled by a single gene locus, but by the combined interaction of many gene loci; in epistasis, the interaction between genes is antagonistic, such that one gene masks or interferes with the expression of another.

An example of epistasis is pigmentation in mice. The agouti coat colour (AA) is dominant to solid coloured fur (aa). However, a separate gene (c) is necessary for pigment production: a mouse with a recessive (c) allele combination at this locus is unable to produce pigment and is albino, regardless of the allele present at locus A. Therefore the genotypes AAcc, Aacc and aacc all produce the same albino phenotype. In this case, the gene c is epistatic to the A gene.

Coat Colour in Labrador Retriever

The Labrador retriever is a highly popular type of dog found all over the world, trained for tasks such as screening and detection work for law enforcement agencies, and also used for hunting. There are three basic coat colours in the Labrador: black, yellow and chocolate. One gene locus affects coat colour by controlling how densely the pigment eumelanin is deposited in the fur: a dominant allele (B) produces the black coat, while the recessive allele (b) produces a brown (chocolate) coat colour. A second gene locus controls whether any eumelanin at all is deposited in the fur: dogs that are homozygous recessive at this locus (ee) will have yellow fur, no matter which alleles are at the first locus.

  • BB dogs are black; Bb dogs are also black but carry the chocolate gene, which can be passed to their offspring; bb genotype dogs have a chocolate brown coat.
  • A yellow Labrador is characterized by the recessive epistatic genotype (ee): any time the ee genotype is present, it masks the B coloration. For example, a BbEE dog has a black coat, but a Bbee dog has a yellow coat.
  • Black Labradors are dominant and therefore have the most genotype possibilities. Both yellow and chocolate Labradors are recessive, but because the ee genes of yellow Labradors mask both black and chocolate coloration, yellow Labradors are more common than chocolate Labradors.
  • In a dihybrid cross this recessive epistasis gives the modified ratio 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.

Duplicate Recessive Epistasis: Flower Colour in Sweet Pea

Complementary gene interaction involves the interaction of both genes: if any one locus has a homozygous recessive genotype, that is, AAbb or aaBB type combinations, it interferes with the dominant allele and hides the expression of purple colour, and the flowers will be white. In this case the epistatic alleles are recessive, and both types of recessive alleles cause the same epistatic effect, so this type of epistasis is called duplicate recessive epistasis. Bateson and Punnett crossed a white flower plant AAbb with another white flowered plant aaBB and got the F1 generation, in which all plants were purple flowered. They then self-crossed the F1 offspring and got the F2 generation, in which there were two types of plants, purple and white, in a 9:7 ratio. This result confirms duplicate recessive epistasis.

Continuous and Discontinuous Variation

Continuous variation is where there is a complete range of measurements from one extreme to another, for example height, weight and skin colour. Discontinuous variations are where individuals fall into distinct categories, for example pea plants with either purple flowers or white flowers, and tongue roller and non-roller in humans.

Key Points

  • Epistasis: a gene at one locus (epistatic) suppresses a gene at another locus (hypostatic); dominance acts between alleles of the same gene.
  • Bombay phenotype (1952): no H substance, so ABO antigens are not expressed, an epistatic effect in humans.
  • In mice, cc makes the animal albino whatever the A locus genotype; c is epistatic to A.
  • Labrador coat colour: B gives black, b gives chocolate, and ee (recessive epistatic) gives yellow by masking B; ratio 9:3:4.
  • Sweet pea duplicate recessive epistasis: white x white (AAbb x aaBB) gives all purple F1 and 9 purple : 7 white in F2.
  • Continuous variation (height, skin colour) grades between extremes; discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories.

lessons.title: Gene Linkage, Morgan's Experiments and Crossing Over
lessons.notes_html:
The term gene was introduced by Wilhelm Johannsson (Danish botanist and geneticist) in 1909. A gene is a small segment of DNA on a chromosome; it consists of a specific sequence of nucleotides which codes for a specific protein or polypeptide chain. The place on the chromosome where the gene resides is called the gene locus. Mendel did not know about genes; he used the term factor or element, which is now called a gene.

22.6.1 Gene Linkage

Genes that are located on the same chromosome are called linked genes. Alleles for these genes tend to segregate together during meiosis, unless they are separated by crossing over. Crossing over occurs when two homologous chromosomes exchange segments during meiosis. The closer together two genes are on a chromosome, the less likely their alleles will be separated by crossing over. Linkage explains why certain characteristics are frequently inherited together; for example, the genes for hair colour and eye colour are linked, so certain hair and eye colours tend to be inherited together, such as brown hair with blue eyes. If genes are linked on autosomes it is called autosomal linkage, and if genes are linked on sex chromosomes it is called sex linkage. Linked genes violate the law of independent assortment, because these genes are not free to participate in independent assortment.

Detection of Gene Linkage

A test cross is an ideal method to know whether the genes are linked or not. Any deviation from the ratio of offspring expected by the law of independent assortment is to be verified for linkage. In a test cross, one parent is homozygous recessive and the other parent of the original cross is heterozygous. All the offspring exhibit the possible combinations of traits in equal ratio if the alleles are not linked; any significant deviation from this indicates the possibility of linkage. Approaches to test crosses can include two-point test crosses for double heterozygotes and three-point test crosses for analysis with three genes. If all offspring in a test cross are parental types, it is called complete linkage, and if fewer recombinant and more parental types are produced, it is called incomplete or partial linkage. Gene linkage can only be detected accurately if the number of offspring is quite large, because probability determines the kinds of gametes and the chances of their fusion; the larger the number of offspring, the more accurate the detection.

Morgan's Experiment

Thomas Hunt Morgan (1866 to 1945) was an American geneticist and embryologist who performed several experiments on Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly). In one experiment he crossed long winged, broad abdomen flies with vestigial wing, narrow abdomen flies. Long wing and broad abdomen are dominant, while vestigial wing and narrow abdomen are recessive traits. The parental genotypes were WA/WA (long wing, broad abdomen) and wa/wa (vestigial wing, narrow abdomen), so in F1 all flies were long winged and broad abdomen (WA/wa). He then self-crossed two flies of the F1 generation. In F2 he obtained 3/4 of the offspring with long wings and broad abdomen and the remaining 1/4 with vestigial wings and narrow abdomen, with no recombinant types.

These results were unexpected and a violation of Mendel's law of independent assortment, that is, of the 9:3:3:1 ratio.
