Morgan concluded that the genes for long wings and broad abdomen are located on the same chromosome, so they could not assort independently during meiosis and were rather inherited together. In a second detection experiment, Morgan mated the dihybrid (GgWw, grey body, normal wing) with recessive parental type flies (ggww, black body, reduced wing). Independent assortment predicted a 1:1:1:1 result, 575 of each type, but the actual results were 965 grey normal and 944 black reduced (parental phenotypes) against only 206 grey reduced and 165 black normal (non-parental phenotypes): far more parental types and far fewer recombinant types, which is an indication of gene linkage.

Crossing Over

During the formation of gametes, the homologous pairs of chromosomes exchange their segments; this process is called crossing over. Crossing over results in a shifting of genetic material and is an important cause of genetic variation. It brings alleles together in new combinations; when these alleles distribute into gametes, a wide variety of gametes is produced, which is why siblings are not identical. Cross-over data may also be used to determine the location of a gene on a chromosome, that is, gene mapping. Crossing over takes place between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, at points visible as chiasmata.

Crossing OverLinkage
It leads to separation of linked genesIt keeps the genes together
It involves non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomesIt involves an individual chromosome
It increases variabilityIt reduces variability
It provides equal frequency of parental and recombinant types in test cross progenyIt provides higher frequency of parental types in test cross progeny

Key Points

  • The term gene was introduced by Wilhelm Johannsson in 1909; the place of a gene on a chromosome is its locus.
  • Linked genes lie on the same chromosome and are inherited together, violating independent assortment.
  • A test cross detects linkage: equal ratios mean no linkage; excess parental types mean linkage. Large numbers of offspring are needed.
  • Morgan's Drosophila cross gave only parental types in F2 (3/4 long broad : 1/4 vestigial narrow), not 9:3:3:1.
  • Morgan's test cross gave 965 and 944 parental types against 206 and 165 recombinants, instead of 575 each.
  • Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, creates new allele combinations and is used for gene mapping.

lessons.title: Sex Determination in Drosophila and Humans: XX-XY, XX-XO and ZZ-ZW Systems
lessons.notes_html:
In a hermaphrodite organism, having both male and female sex organs, the homologous pairs of chromosomes in body cells are similar. In a unisexual organism, where the sexes are separate, the chromosomes in male and female differ in one pair, which is associated with sex differentiation. These chromosomes are called sex chromosomes; all other chromosomes are autosomes. Not all organisms have sex chromosomes: wasps, bees and ants do not, and sex is determined by fertilization; a fertilized egg becomes female, and an unfertilized egg develops into a male.

22.7.1 Genetic Identification of Sex Phenotype

The differences between male and female phenotypes are generally because of their sex chromosomes. In bisexual (hermaphrodite) animals all pairs of chromosomes are similar, but in unisexual animals one pair is different in either the male or the female.

Sex Determination in Drosophila

Drosophila has four pairs of homologous chromosomes, of which one pair is the sex chromosomes, usually called X chromosomes. The female has two X chromosomes (genotype XX); the male has only one X, the other replaced by a hook-shaped Y chromosome (so the male is XY). The other three pairs are autosomes. The female produces one type of egg, each containing an X chromosome, while the male produces two types of sperms, one with X and the other with Y.

Sex Determination in Humans

In humans there are 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes. In the human male, the two sex chromosomes are quite different from each other: the male has an X chromosome and a much shorter Y chromosome. In the female, both sex chromosomes are similar in shape, that is, XX. So, like Drosophila, in humans the male determines the sex of the baby. A girl has inherited one X chromosome from her mother and one from her father; a boy baby has received an X chromosome from his mother and a Y chromosome from his father.

XX-XY sex determination: the sperm (X or Y) decides the sex of the baby.

22.7.2 Patterns of Sex Determination: Male Heterogamy

  • XY-XX type — The male possesses a single X chromosome with a Y chromosome, while the female possesses two X chromosomes. This type is found in humans, Drosophila and many other animals. The male produces two types of sperms, X and Y, while the female produces only X type eggs. If a male gamete with an X chromosome fuses with the egg, the baby will be a girl, and if a sperm with a Y chromosome fuses with the egg, the baby will be a boy. The ratio of male and female offspring will be 1:1, and it is the male which determines the sex of the baby.
  • XO-XX type — In bugs and grasshoppers, the male possesses an unpaired X chromosome, while the female possesses XX. Male gametes are of two types, one carrying X and the other without any sex chromosome, called a nullogamete, while the eggs are only one type. A sperm with X gives an XX zygote, a female; a sperm without X gives an XO zygote, a male. The ratio is equal, and the male again determines the sex.

Female Heterogamy: WZ-ZZ Type

In this case the female produces two types of gametes, W and Z, while the male produces only one type of gamete, Z, so in this type of sex determination the female determines the sex of the offspring. When a gamete of the male with a Z chromosome fuses with a Z female gamete, the zygote will be ZZ and develops into a male; if the male gamete fuses with a W type egg, the zygote will be WZ and develops into a female. The chances of male and female offspring are equal. This type of sex determination is found in birds and butterflies.

Comparison of Sex Determination in Drosophila and Human

In both Drosophila and humans there is male heterogamy, so the male determines the sex of the offspring. However, there are differences. In humans, male sex is determined by the SRY gene (sex determining region of Y chromosome) on the short arm of Y; it encodes a transcription factor which stimulates male development: testes develop, secrete anti-Mullerian hormone and destroy the female structures, while testosterone develops the male structures. Absence of this gene in the zygote develops a female. Absence of the entire Y in a human zygote gives a sterile female, Turner's syndrome (XO), but in Drosophila XO is a sterile male. XXY humans are sterile males, Klinefelter's syndrome, but XXY in Drosophila develops into a fertile female, because in Drosophila sex depends on the ratio of X chromosomes to autosomes. Therefore sex chromosomes in Drosophila have less influence than in humans.

Key Points

  • Sex chromosomes are the one pair that differs between male and female; all other chromosomes are autosomes.
  • Drosophila: 4 chromosome pairs, 3 autosome pairs and XX female / XY male. Humans: 23 pairs, 22 autosome pairs and XX female / XY male.
  • XX-XY type (male heterogamy): the male makes X and Y sperms and determines the sex; ratio 1:1.
  • XX-XO type (bugs, grasshoppers): the male makes X and nullo sperms; XO is male, XX is female.
  • ZZ-ZW type (female heterogamy, birds and butterflies): the female makes Z and W eggs and determines the sex.
  • Human sex depends on the SRY gene on Y; XO humans are sterile females (Turner's) and XXY humans are sterile males (Klinefelter's), while XO Drosophila are sterile males and XXY Drosophila are fertile females.

lessons.title: Sex Linkage in Drosophila and Humans: X-Linked and Y-Linked Inheritance
lessons.notes_html:
The sex chromosomes (X and Y) contain genes which are related to the sexual characters (traits) of male and female. However, besides controlling sexual traits, the sex chromosomes also contain other genes which are not concerned with sexual traits. This phenomenon is called sex linkage, for example the gene for blood clotting factor VIII, the gene for opsin pigment in the eye, and the gene for hairy pinna. An allele that is located only on the X chromosome (that is, on its non-homologous portion) is called X-linked. The allele that is located only on the non-homologous portion of the Y chromosome is called Y-linked, and such traits are called holandric traits. Alleles located on the homologous portion of the X and Y chromosomes are called XY-linked genes or pseudo-autosomal genes, because their pattern of inheritance is like that of autosomal genes.

22.8.1 Sex Linkage in Drosophila

T.H. Morgan (1910) for the first time discovered sex linkage in Drosophila. While experimenting, Morgan noted the sudden appearance of one white eyed male in a culture of normal red eyed Drosophila. This white eyed male was crossed with a red eyed female. The F1 flies were all red eyed, indicating that white eye colour is recessive to normal red eye colour. When these F1 flies were self-crossed freely, the red and white eyed flies appeared in the ratio 3:1 in the F2 generation, but the white eyed flies were all male. Among the red eyed flies, two thirds were female and one third were male: the females were all red eyed, whereas 50% of the males were white eyed and the remaining 50% of males were red eyed. When a reciprocal cross was performed between a white eyed female and a red eyed male, all females in the F1 generation were red eyed and all males were white eyed. When these F1 individuals were self-crossed, the female population in F2 consisted of 50% red eyed and 50% white eyed individuals, and the male population likewise consisted of 50% red eyed and 50% white eyed individuals. On the basis of these results, Morgan concluded that the white eye trait gene is located on the X chromosome, and this gene is recessive for eye colour.

22.8.2 Sex Linkage in Humans

There are many traits in humans which are linked with the sex chromosomes. Sex linked traits may be X-linked or Y-linked, and the X-linked traits may be recessive or dominant.

X-Linked Recessive Inheritance

X-linked recessive inheritance is due to a recessive allele on the X chromosome. These traits are more common in males than in females, because a female possessing one X-linked recessive allele is considered a carrier; a female can only be affected if she carries the allele on both of her X chromosomes. On the other hand, as a male has only one X chromosome, if a recessive allele is present on it, it will express itself. A father cannot donate an X-linked allele to his son, so the pattern of inheritance is from grandfather to daughter and then to grandson (criss-cross inheritance). Examples of X-linked recessive inheritance are haemophilia A and B, colour blindness and testicular feminization.

X-Linked Dominant Inheritance

X-linked dominant inheritance is due to a dominant allele present on the X chromosome, so this type of inheritance equally affects males and females. However, all female children of an affected father will be affected, but no male children of an affected father will be affected, because sons receive his Y chromosome. An affected mother may affect 100% of her children if the dominant allele is located on both of her X chromosomes, but if the dominant allele is located on only one X chromosome, the chances of affected children will be 50%. Examples of X-linked dominant inheritance are hypophosphatemia (rickets) and incontinentia pigmenti.

X-Linked RecessiveX-Linked Dominant
Recessive allele on X; males affected with one copy, females only with two copiesDominant allele on X; one copy affects both sexes
More common in males than females; females with one copy are carriersAffects males and females equally
Father cannot pass it to his son; pattern is grandfather to daughter to grandsonAll daughters of an affected father are affected; no sons are affected
Examples: haemophilia A and B, colour blindnessExamples: hypophosphatemia (rickets), incontinentia pigmenti

Y-Linked Inheritance

Y-linked inheritance is the inheritance of genes located on the Y chromosome. Since only males have a Y chromosome, Y-linked genes can only be transmitted from father to son, and Y-linked inheritance is also called holandric inheritance. The concepts of dominant and recessive do not apply to Y-linked traits, as only one allele is ever present in any one (male) individual, and Y-linked inheritance never occurs in females. Examples of Y-linked traits in males are hypertrichosis (growth of hair on the ear pinna, the hairy pinna), porcupine man (straight hair on the body) and webbing of toes. Two more genes located on the Y chromosome are the testis determining factor (TDF) and the minor histocompatibility gene (H-Y).

Key Points

  • Sex linkage: genes on the sex chromosomes control traits not concerned with sexual characters.
  • X-linked alleles are on the non-homologous part of X; Y-linked (holandric) alleles are on the non-homologous part of Y; XY-linked (pseudo-autosomal) alleles are on the homologous part.
  • Morgan (1910) discovered sex linkage in Drosophila: in F2 all white eyed flies were male, proving the white gene is recessive and on the X chromosome.
  • X-linked recessive traits are more common in males; a father cannot pass them to his son.
  • X-linked dominant traits affect both sexes; all daughters of an affected father are affected, but no sons.
  • Y-linked traits pass only from father to son and never appear in females, for example hairy pinna.

lessons.title: Sex-Linked Disorders in Humans and Sex Related Traits
lessons.notes_html:
Sex linked diseases are passed down in families through one of the X or Y chromosomes. This lesson covers the three disorders the book discusses in detail, haemophilia, colour blindness and muscular dystrophy, and then the sex related traits.

Genetics of Haemophilia

Haemophilia is a serious disease in which blood fails to clot after it starts flowing from an injury site. It is an X-linked recessive trait: its recessive allele is located on the X chromosome, written X^h, and its dominant allele, X^H, favours blood clotting. It is very rare in females, as a female requires the allele from both father and mother, and very few diseased males survive to marry and reproduce. A male can easily get this disease, as he only needs the recessive gene from his mother. Haemophilia is called the royal disease because the gene was passed from Queen Victoria, who became Queen of England in 1837, to the ruling families of Russia, Spain and Germany; her gene was caused by a spontaneous mutation.

There are three types of haemophilia, A, B and C. The alleles for haemophilia A and B are located on the X chromosome, so these two types are X-linked. The allele for haemophilia C is located on an autosome, so its chances are equal in males and females; however, haemophilia A and B are more common. Haemophilia A is caused by a missing blood clotting factor VIII and makes up about 80% of total haemophiliac patients. Haemophilia B is due to the absence of blood clotting factor IX and is about 20%. Haemophilia C is due to a missing blood clotting factor XI and is very rare (less than 1%). Note: the book's main text places the haemophilia C allele on an autosome, even though the unit's exercise treats haemophilia as X-linked; follow the main text for type C.

Haemophilia AHaemophilia BHaemophilia C
Most common typeSecond most common typeLeast common
Very severeModerateMild
Caused by missing blood clotting factor VIII (about 80%)Caused by missing blood clotting factor IX (about 20%)Caused by missing blood clotting factor XI (less than 1%)

Genetics of Colour Blindness

Colour blindness is not blindness at all, but a difficulty in distinguishing certain colours; it is a colour vision deficiency. It is X-linked recessive, therefore more common in males than in females. The retina has two types of photoreceptor cells: rod cells, which are more abundant but cannot perceive colour, and cone cells, which are responsible for colour vision. There are three types of cone cells, receiving red, green and blue colours through opsin proteins coded by different genes. The genes for red and green opsin are on the X chromosome, while the gene for blue opsin is on chromosome number 7, an autosome, so it is equally expressed in males and females. Colour blindness may be dichromacy or monochromacy.

  • Dichromacy — The patient can perceive two primary colours but is unable to perceive one primary colour. Its three sub-types are protanopia (red colour blindness), deuteranopia (green colour blindness) and tritanopia (blue colour blindness).
  • Monochromacy — A severe type of colour blindness, true colour blindness, in which the patient cannot distinguish any colours and sees only in shades of grey (black and white); usually a monochromate cannot perceive red and green colours. Its pattern of inheritance is the same as other X-linked recessive inheritance, like haemophilia.

Genetics of Muscular Dystrophy

Muscular dystrophy is a group of diseases that cause progressive weakness and loss of muscle mass. In muscular dystrophy, abnormal genes (mutations) interfere with the production of the protein dystrophin, needed to form healthy muscles. There are many different kinds of muscular dystrophy; the Duchenne type muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive trait, so it is more common in males than in females. Symptoms typically appear in early childhood: the patient feels trouble in running and jumping, difficulty in rising from a lying or sitting position, muscle pain and stiffness, and large calf muscles. Patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy hardly survive further and usually die before the age of twenty.

22.8.4 Sex Related Traits

Traits which are associated with males or females are called sex related traits. These traits may be sex linked or autosomal, and there are two types: sex limited traits and sex influenced traits.

  • Sex limited traits — Characters that are expressed physically in only one sex of a species. They are controlled by sex limited genes or autosomal genes. Although these genes are present in both sexes, they express only in one sex, while in the other sex they remain turned off. Examples are human breast development in females and beard development in males: a woman does not grow a beard herself, but she can pass the genes of a heavy beard to her son. Other examples from the exercise are milk production in female mammals and egg-laying in hens. These traits are primarily concerned with sexual dimorphism.
  • Sex influenced traits — Autosomal traits that are expressed based on the influence of the sex, in particular sex hormones, for example testosterone in males and estrogen in females. Examples are the amount of hair on the body, muscle mass and baldness. Baldness is more common in males than in females, because the allele of baldness becomes active at a high level of testosterone.

Key Points

  • Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive failure of blood clotting (X^h); it is the royal disease, spread from Queen Victoria.
  • Haemophilia A: factor VIII missing, about 80%, very severe. B: factor IX, about 20%. C: factor XI, less than 1%, and its allele is autosomal in the book's main text.
  • Colour blindness is an X-linked recessive colour vision deficiency of the cone opsins: protanopia red, deuteranopia green, tritanopia blue; monochromacy is total colour blindness.
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive; the dystrophin protein is faulty and patients usually die before the age of twenty.
  • Sex limited traits are expressed in one sex only though the genes are in both sexes (beard, breast development).
  • Sex influenced traits are autosomal traits whose expression depends on sex hormones, for example baldness and testosterone.

lessons.title: Chromosomal Theory, Chromosome Structure and Composition
lessons.notes_html:
The chromosomal theory of inheritance links Mendel's factors (genes) to the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis. A chromosome is a thread-like structure in the nucleus that carries the hereditary material and becomes clearly visible during cell division.

23.1 Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance

Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (1902) independently noted the parallel behaviour of genes and chromosomes and proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance. Its main points are:

  • Both genes and chromosomes occur in pairs in diploid cells and singly in gametes.
  • Members of a gene pair and homologous chromosomes segregate during meiosis into different gametes.
  • Different gene pairs and different chromosome pairs show independent assortment.
  • Genes are located on chromosomes, so chromosomes are the carriers of heredity.

23.1.1 Chromosomes

Chromosomes were first observed by Walther Fleming in 1882; the name chromosome was assigned by Waldeyer in 1888. A typical chromosome seen at metaphase has two sister chromatids joined at the centromere (primary constriction). The centromere divides the chromosome into a short arm (p arm) and a long arm (q arm) and is the site where spindle fibres attach through the kinetochore. The ends of the chromosome are called telomeres; they protect the ends. Some chromosomes also have a secondary constriction (nucleolar organizer) and a small terminal part called a satellite; such chromosomes are called SAT chromosomes.

On the basis of centromere position, chromosomes are of four types:

  • Metacentric — Centromere in the middle, arms equal, V-shaped.
  • Submetacentric — Centromere slightly off-centre, arms unequal, L-shaped.
  • Acrocentric — Centromere near one end, one arm very short, J-shaped.
  • Telocentric — Centromere at the very end, only one arm, rod-shaped.

Chromatin exists in two forms. Heterochromatin is densely packed, darkly staining, genetically inactive and replicates late; it is found mainly near centromeres and telomeres. Euchromatin is loosely packed, lightly staining, genetically active and replicates early; most transcription takes place in euchromatin.

Every species has a fixed chromosome number. The book gives, for example: human 46, frog 26, monkey 48, pea 14, maize 20 and chimpanzee 48. In humans, 44 chromosomes are autosomes and 2 are sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males). The morphological characteristics of the chromosomes of a species, arranged in order, are collectively called the karyotype.

23.1.2 Composition of Chromosomes

Human chromosomes are composed of DNA + RNA + protein. DNA is the genetic material. Histone proteins (H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) form octamers around which DNA winds (about 200 base pairs per nucleosome) to form the beads-on-a-string structure, coiled further into the 30 nm fibre and then the chromatid. Non-histone proteins maintain structure and control gene activity. A small amount of RNA is also present. DNA provides the information, while proteins package it and regulate its expression.

Key Points

  • Sutton and Boveri proposed the chromosomal theory: genes lie on chromosomes, which segregate and assort independently in meiosis.
  • A chromosome has two chromatids joined at the centromere, with p and q arms, telomeres and, in some, a satellite.
  • Types by centromere position: metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric and telocentric.
  • Heterochromatin is condensed and inactive; euchromatin is extended and active.
  • Human chromosomes are DNA + RNA + protein; the karyotype is the complete set of chromosome features.

lessons.title: DNA as Hereditary Material: Griffith, Avery and Hershey-Chase
lessons.notes_html:
For many years scientists debated whether DNA or protein was the hereditary material. Three classic experiments — by Griffith, by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty, and by Hershey and Chase — settled the question in favour of DNA.

23.2 DNA as Hereditary Material

DNA carries the instructions for all the proteins of the cell, is copied exactly at cell division, and is passed from parent to offspring. The experiments below proved this step by step.

23.2.1 Griffith Experiment

Frederick Griffith (1928) worked with two strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae:

  • S strain (smooth) — Has a capsule, is virulent and kills mice.
  • R strain (rough) — Has no capsule, is non-virulent and does not kill mice.

Heat-killed S bacteria alone did not kill mice. But a mixture of heat-killed S + live R bacteria killed the mice, and live S bacteria were recovered from them. Griffith concluded that a transforming principle from the dead S bacteria had transformed live R bacteria into virulent S bacteria. He did not identify what the transforming principle was.

23.2.2 Avery, MacLeod and McCarty Experiment

Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) repeated Griffith's work with purified extracts. They treated the extract of heat-killed S bacteria with different enzymes. Only the extract treated with DNase (the enzyme that destroys DNA) lost its transforming ability; extracts treated with proteases or RNase still transformed R bacteria. This identified the transforming principle as DNA.

23.2.3 Hershey-Chase Experiment

Hershey and Chase (1952) gave the final proof using bacteriophage T2, a virus that infects E. coli:

  • One batch of phages was grown in radioactive sulphur (35S), which labels protein coats (DNA has no sulphur).
  • Another batch was grown in radioactive phosphorus (32P), which labels DNA (protein has almost no phosphorus).

After the phages infected bacteria, the mixture was shaken in a blender to remove the phage coats and then centrifuged. Radioactive 32P (DNA) was found inside the bacterial cells, while 35S (protein) stayed outside in the coats. Since only DNA entered the bacteria and directed the production of new phages, Hershey and Chase proved that DNA — not protein — is the genetic material.

ExperimentFinding
Griffith (1928)A transforming principle from dead S bacteria changes live R bacteria into S bacteria
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944)The transforming principle is DNA; only DNase stops transformation
Hershey and Chase (1952)32P-labelled DNA enters bacteria; 35S-labelled protein stays outside — DNA is the hereditary material

Key Points

  • Griffith discovered transformation: dead S bacteria could change live R bacteria into virulent S bacteria.
  • Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed the transforming principle is DNA.
  • Hershey and Chase (1952), using T2 phage labelled with 35S and 32P, proved DNA is the genetic material.
  • Only DNA entered the bacterial cell and directed the making of new viruses.

lessons.title: DNA Replication Models and the Meselson-Stahl Experiment
lessons.notes_html:
DNA replication is the copying of DNA to make two identical DNA molecules before cell division. Three models were proposed for how the two strands of the double helix are copied.

23.3 DNA Replication

In the Watson and Crick double helix, the two strands are complementary (A pairs with T, G pairs with C) and run in opposite directions. When the strands separate, each can act as a template for a new complementary strand.

Three Models of Replication

  • Semi-conservative model — Each daughter double helix keeps one old (parental) strand and has one newly made strand. This is the correct model.
  • Conservative model — The original double helix stays fully intact and a completely new double helix is made: one daughter molecule is entirely old, the other entirely new.
  • Dispersive (dispersal) model — The parental DNA is broken into fragments, and each daughter molecule contains a mixture of old and new segments scattered along both strands.
ModelOld and New DNA in Daughter Molecules
Semi-conservativeEach molecule: one old strand + one new strand
ConservativeOne molecule all old, the other all new
DispersiveOld and new segments mixed in both strands

Meselson-Stahl Experiment

Meselson and Stahl (1958) tested the three models using E. coli grown in a medium containing heavy nitrogen (15N), so that all its DNA became heavy. The bacteria were then shifted to a medium with light nitrogen (14N) and DNA samples were taken after each generation and separated by density in a centrifuge:

  • Generation 0 — All DNA was heavy (one heavy band).
  • Generation 1 — All DNA was of intermediate (hybrid) density: each molecule had one heavy and one light strand. This ruled out the conservative model, which would have given separate heavy and light bands.
  • Generation 2 — Half the DNA was hybrid and half was light. This ruled out the dispersive model, which would have kept giving a single band of decreasing density.

The results exactly matched the semi-conservative model: each daughter DNA molecule conserves one parental strand and synthesizes one new strand.

The DNA double helix: complementary base pairing lets each old strand template a new strand.

Key Points

  • Three models were proposed: semi-conservative, conservative and dispersive.
  • Meselson and Stahl (1958) used 15N and 14N labelling in E. coli to test them.
  • After one generation all DNA was hybrid; after two generations half was hybrid and half light.
  • The experiment proved semi-conservative replication: one old strand + one new strand in each daughter molecule.

lessons.title: Mechanism of DNA Replication: Initiation, Elongation and Termination
lessons.notes_html:
Replication takes place at a Y-shaped replication fork and needs many enzymes. Synthesis of a new DNA strand always begins with an RNA primer, because DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a free 3'-OH end.

Initiation Phase

Replication starts at a specific site called the origin of replication. Helicase unwinds and separates the two strands, breaking the hydrogen bonds, and topoisomerase relieves the twisting strain ahead of the fork. Single-strand binding proteins keep the separated strands apart and protect them. The unwound region with two forks is called a replication bubble. The enzyme primase (a type of RNA polymerase) then synthesizes a short RNA primer (about 5-10 nucleotides) on each template strand, providing the free 3'-OH end needed to start synthesis.

Elongation Phase

DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction only, using complementary base pairing. Because the two template strands run in opposite directions, the two new strands are made differently:

  • Leading strand — Synthesized continuously in the 5' to 3' direction toward the replication fork; it needs only one RNA primer.
  • Lagging strand — Synthesized discontinuously, away from the fork, in short pieces called Okazaki fragments; each fragment needs its own RNA primer.
Leading StrandLagging Strand
Made continuously toward the forkMade in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork
Needs one RNA primerNeeds many RNA primers
No gaps to join at the endFragments joined by DNA ligase

Later, DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA, and DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, giving two complete daughter strands.

Termination Phase

Elongation continues until the replication forks meet or reach the ends of the molecule. The primers are removed, gaps are filled, nicks are sealed, and the two new double helices separate as two identical daughter DNA molecules, each with one old and one new strand.

Main Enzymes of Replication

  • Helicase — Unwinds the double helix.
  • Topoisomerase — Relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork.
  • Primase — Makes the RNA primer.
  • DNA polymerase III — Main enzyme adding nucleotides in elongation.
  • DNA polymerase I — Removes RNA primers and fills gaps.
  • Ligase — Joins Okazaki fragments and seals nicks.

A replication fork: the leading strand grows continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand grows in Okazaki fragments away from it.

Key Points

  • Helicase unwinds DNA, primase lays an RNA primer, and DNA polymerase III elongates in the 5' to 3' direction.
  • The leading strand is continuous toward the fork; the lagging strand is discontinuous in Okazaki fragments.
  • DNA polymerase I removes primers and fills gaps; ligase seals the nicks.
  • Each daughter molecule has one old strand and one new strand.

lessons.title: The Gene, Central Dogma and the Genetic Code
lessons.notes_html:
A gene is the unit of heredity: a length of DNA that codes for a functional product. Gene expression is the process by which the information in a gene is used to make that product, in two stages — transcription and translation.

23.4 Gene Expression

Every body cell has the same genome, yet cells differ because different genes are switched on in different cells. Gene expression produces either a polypeptide (protein) or a functional RNA molecule.

23.4.1 Molecular Concept of Gene

Molecularly, a gene is a specific sequence of nucleotides on DNA that codes for a functional product — a polypeptide or an RNA molecule (mRNA, tRNA or rRNA). The term gene was coined by Johannsen. A gene has a promoter region where RNA polymerase binds, a coding region, and a terminator region. In eukaryotes the coding region is split into exons (coding parts) and introns (non-coding parts, removed during processing). One gene generally codes for one polypeptide (one gene-one polypeptide hypothesis, an extension of Beadle and Tatum's one gene-one enzyme hypothesis). Genes lie at specific positions (loci) on chromosomes; alternate forms of a gene are called alleles.

23.4.2 Central Dogma

The central dogma of molecular biology, proposed by Francis Crick, states the normal flow of genetic information: DNA → RNA → Protein. DNA is first copied into RNA by transcription, and RNA is then decoded into protein by translation. DNA also copies itself by replication. (In some viruses, RNA can make DNA by reverse transcription — an exception to the simple one-way picture.)

23.4.3 Genetic Code

The genetic code is the set of rules by which the base sequence of mRNA is translated into amino acids. It is a triplet code: a sequence of three nucleotides on mRNA, called a codon, codes for one amino acid. There are 64 codons: 61 sense codons code for amino acids and 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) terminate translation. AUG is the initiation (start) codon and codes for methionine. Anticodons are the complementary triplets present on tRNA. In theory, 61 types of tRNA are needed, one for each sense codon.

Properties of the genetic code:

  • Universal — Almost the same in all organisms.
  • Specific — Each codon codes for a particular amino acid.
  • Degenerate — More than one codon can code the same amino acid; for example, both UUU and UUC code phenylalanine. Note: the exercise in the book prints “UVC”, which is a misprint for UUC.
  • Non-overlapping and commaless — Codons are read one after another, in order, without gaps or overlaps.
  • Triplet — Each codon has exactly three nucleotides.

Key Points

  • A gene is a DNA sequence coding for a polypeptide or a functional RNA; it has a promoter, coding region (exons and introns in eukaryotes) and terminator.
  • Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein, by transcription then translation.
  • The genetic code is a triplet code: 64 codons — 61 sense codons and 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG is the start codon.
  • The code is universal, specific, degenerate, non-overlapping and commaless.
  • Anticodons are found on tRNA; codons are found on mRNA.

lessons.title: Transcription and mRNA Processing
lessons.notes_html:
Transcription is the copying of one strand of DNA into a complementary RNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase. The copying of mRNA from DNA is called transcription. It takes place in the nucleus in eukaryotes.

23.4.4 Transcription

Only one strand of DNA is copied for a given gene. The strand that is transcribed is the template (antisense) strand; the other strand, with the same sequence as the RNA (except T in place of U), is the coding (sense) strand. Note: the unit Summary on page 289 swaps these two names — follow the definitions given here, which match the main text: mRNA is complementary to the template strand.

Transcription has three phases:

  • Initiation — RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region of the gene and unwinds a short length of DNA.
  • Elongation — RNA polymerase moves along the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction, building the RNA in the 5' to 3' direction by complementary base pairing (A pairs with U in RNA). Only one strand is transcribed.
  • Termination — When RNA polymerase reaches the terminator region, the RNA transcript and the enzyme are released and the DNA helix reforms.

Different RNA polymerases make different RNAs; in eukaryotes, RNA polymerase II makes pre-mRNA. The first product is primary mRNA (pre-mRNA), which is not yet functional and must be processed before it leaves the nucleus.

Post-Transcriptional Modification of mRNA

In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA is modified in the nucleus in three ways:

  • 5' capping — A modified guanine cap is added at the 5' end (when 20-30 nucleotides of pre-mRNA have been made). The cap protects the mRNA and helps the ribosome bind.
  • 3' polyadenylation — A tail of adenine nucleotides, the poly-A tail (AAAAAA...), is added at the 3' end, increasing the stability of the mRNA.
  • Splicing — Introns (non-coding regions) are removed and exons (coding regions) are joined together. This is done by the spliceosome, a large machine in the nucleus assembled from small nuclear RNAs (snRNA) and approximately 80 proteins; the spliced exon fragments are joined with the help of RNA ligase.

The removal of introns and maturation of primary mRNA into functional, mature mRNA is called RNA splicing. The mature mRNA, with a 5' cap, joined exons and a poly-A tail, then moves to the cytoplasm for translation. In alternative splicing, different combinations of exons can be joined, so one gene can produce different mRNA molecules — an important way of regulating gene expression in eukaryotes.

Three kinds of RNA are made by transcription: mRNA carries the code for a polypeptide, tRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome and bears the anticodon, and rRNA forms part of the ribosome itself. In prokaryotes there is no nucleus, so the mRNA needs no processing and can be translated at once; in eukaryotes the processing described above is essential before translation can begin.

Key Points

  • Transcription copies the template (antisense) strand of DNA into RNA by RNA polymerase: initiation at the promoter, elongation, then termination.
  • RNA is built 5' to 3'; in RNA, U pairs with A.
  • Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed by 5' capping, 3' poly-A tail addition and splicing.
  • The spliceosome (snRNA + about 80 proteins) removes introns and joins exons to form mature mRNA.

lessons.title: Translation: Protein Synthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Translation is the formation of protein with the help of RNA — the second stage of gene expression. The mRNA is decoded by the ribosome to produce a specific amino acid chain (polypeptide) that later folds into an active protein. In prokaryotic cells translation occurs freely in the cytoplasm, while in eukaryotic cells it occurs in the cytoplasm and on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER).

23.4.5 Translation (Protein Synthesis)

The process of translation is divided into four phases: activation, initiation, elongation and termination.

i) Activation. Each amino acid is attached to its specific tRNA by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme, using ATP. The charged tRNA (aminoacyl tRNA) carries the amino acid to the ribosome; the tRNA anticodon will pair with the matching mRNA codon.

ii) Initiation. The small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA at the start codon AUG. The initiator tRNA carrying formyl-methionine (fMet) in prokaryotes (methionine in eukaryotes), with anticodon UAC, binds at the P site. The large subunit then joins to form the complete ribosome, and initiation factors (IF1, IF2 and IF3) are released. The ribosome has three sites: E site (exit), P site (peptidyl) and A site (aminoacyl).

iii) Elongation. Ribosomal subunits move along the mRNA and amino acids brought by tRNAs are linked into a polypeptide chain. A tRNA with the anticodon matching the codon exposed at the A site binds there, helped by elongation factors. The large subunit, through the enzyme peptidyl synthetase (transferase), forms a peptide bond: the growing chain is transferred from the P-site tRNA onto the amino acid at the A site. The ribosome then translocates three nucleotides (one codon) along the mRNA in the 5' to 3' direction; the empty tRNA moves to the E site and leaves, the growing chain sits at the P site, and the next codon is exposed at the A site. The cycle repeats.

iv) Termination. Elongation continues until a chain-terminating non-sense (stop) codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) is exposed at the A site. Stop codons bind no tRNA; instead they are recognized by release factors (RF), which release the polypeptide from the last tRNA. The tRNA leaves the ribosome and the two ribosomal subunits separate from the mRNA.

Protein Synthesis in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes Compared

ProkaryotesEukaryotes
Ribosomes are 70S (30S + 50S)Ribosomes are 80S (40S + 60S)
Occurs in the cytosol; transcription and translation occur together, with no mRNA processingTranscription in the nucleus, mRNA processed (capping, polyadenylation, splicing), translation in cytosol and RER
Initiating amino acid is N-formyl methionineInitiating amino acid is methionine
mRNA is polycistronic (codes for many proteins)mRNA is monocistronic (codes for only one protein)
Fewer initiation factors; one release factor (as given in the book table)More initiation factors; two release factors (as given in the book table)
Genes lack intronsGenes contain introns removed by splicing

Key Points

  • Translation decodes mRNA on the ribosome into a polypeptide, in four phases: activation, initiation, elongation and termination.
  • Initiation starts at AUG with the initiator tRNA at the P site; the ribosome has E, P and A sites.
  • In elongation, peptide bonds form and the ribosome translocates one codon at a time in the 5' to 3' direction.
  • A stop codon at the A site binds a release factor and the finished polypeptide is released.
  • Prokaryotes use 70S ribosomes and formyl-methionine; eukaryotes use 80S ribosomes and methionine.

lessons.title: Regulation of Gene Expression and the Lac Operon
lessons.notes_html:
Regulation of gene expression means the control of the amount and timing of appearance of a gene product. The genes of body cells are turned on or off in response to signals from the external or internal environment.

23.5 Regulation of Gene Expression

The body of an adult human contains more than 37 trillion cells and about 200 types of cells. The genome of all cells is the same, but all genes do not express in every cell — only some genes are turned on in each cell. Cells with the same genome expressing different genes is called differential gene expression, and it produces the different cell types of the body. Morphogenesis is the shaping of an organism by differentiation of cells, tissues and organs according to the genetic blueprint and environmental conditions.

23.5.1 Importance of Regulation of Gene Expression

  • It is essential for both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, as it increases the adaptability and versatility of an organism.
  • It helps the cell fulfil its protein needs — producing only the proteins it needs, when it needs them — so energy and resources are saved.
  • It drives cellular differentiation, morphogenesis and physiology, and creates different types of body cells.
  • If regulation of gene expression is disturbed, serious diseases such as cancer may occur.

23.5.2 Methods of Gene Regulation

Regulation is either positive or negative:

  • Positive gene regulation — Expression of a gene is quantitatively increased by specific regulatory proteins called activator proteins.
  • Negative gene regulation — Expression of a gene is stopped (seized) by a specific regulatory protein called a repressor protein.

23.5.3 Lac Operon (An Example of Negative and Positive Control of Gene Expression)

In bacteria and viruses, a cluster of genes with related functions that are regulated as a unit is called an operon. An operon has: (1) structural genes, which direct the synthesis of enzymes with related functions; (2) a promoter, the starting point for transcription; and (3) an operator, which acts as an on/off switch, located within or overlapping the promoter and serving as a binding site related to RNA polymerase attachment.

Escherichia coli (E. coli) is the bacterium scientists study to learn about gene expression in prokaryotes. The lac operon controls the metabolism of the milk sugar lactose. It has three structural genes — lacZ, lacY and lacA — which direct the synthesis of beta-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase respectively. When lactose is absent, E. coli has very few of these enzymes; when the bacterium is fed lactose, it quickly manufactures them.

Mechanism of negative control: The lac operon is on (transcribed) until transcription is switched off. The off switch is the lac repressor, a protein produced by a regulatory gene (lacI) that fits into the operator region like a key fits into a lock, blocking the attachment of RNA polymerase to the promoter, so transcription cannot occur. When lactose is present, it (as allolactose, the inducer) binds to the repressor and changes its shape; the inactivated repressor can no longer bind the operator, and the cell produces the enzymes for lactose metabolism.

Mechanism of positive control: Some operons must be switched on by proteins called activators. Activators bind to a specific nucleotide sequence at or within the promoter and stimulate transcription. Operons regulated by both activators and repressors have both positive and negative control; regulatory sites code for activator proteins as well as repressor proteins.

23.5.4 Relationship of Gene Expression with Introns and Exons (in Eukaryotes)

In eukaryotes, primary mRNA is processed in the nucleus and mature mRNA is then exported to the cytoplasm, which provides many opportunities for regulating gene expression that are not available in prokaryotes. One example is regulation at the RNA processing level by alternative RNA splicing, in which different mRNA molecules are produced from the same primary transcript, depending on which RNA segments are treated as exons and which as introns. Cell-type-specific regulatory proteins control this intron-exon choice by binding to regulatory sequences within the primary transcript.

Key Points

  • Gene regulation controls the amount and timing of a gene product; it allows differentiation of about 200 cell types from one genome.
  • Positive regulation uses activator proteins; negative regulation uses repressor proteins.
  • The lac operon (lacZ, lacY, lacA) controls lactose metabolism in E. coli.
  • Without lactose, the repressor blocks the operator; with lactose, allolactose inactivates the repressor and the operon switches on.
  • In eukaryotes, alternative splicing regulates expression by producing different mRNAs from one primary transcript.

lessons.title: Mutation: Sources, Types and Changes in Chromosome Number
lessons.notes_html:
A mutation is an alteration in the genetic material (genome) of a cell of a living organism, or of a virus, that is more or less permanent and makes up a new allele in the population. It can be transmitted to the descendants of the cell or virus. Mutations range in size from a change in a single DNA nucleotide to a large segment of chromosome, a whole chromosome, or a complete set of chromosomes.

23.6 Mutation

Mutation-causing agents are called mutagens, and an organism with mutated genetic material is called a mutant. The formation (origin/creation) of mutation in DNA molecules is called mutagenesis.

23.6.1 Sources of Mutation

  • Physical mutagens — Electromagnetic radiation such as UV rays, gamma rays and X-rays, radioactivity and high temperature alternation. Ionizing radiations break DNA strands or form abnormal bonds between bases.
  • Chemical mutagens — Nitrosomethylurea, nitrous gas/acid, mustard gas, pesticides, food preservatives, acridine orange, colchicine, caffeine, nicotine, atomic oxygen particles and reactive radioactive isotopes. Most of these are used in modern industrial societies; they alter base structure or cause wrong base pairing.
  • Biological mutagens — Micro-organisms such as viruses and bacteria, transposons (jumping DNA), and errors that occur during meiosis or DNA replication.

23.6.2 Types of Mutation

Natural and induced mutation: Spontaneous (natural) mutation takes place naturally and automatically due to internal or external factors. Induced mutation is produced by external factors (mutagens), for example to establish new varieties of organisms.

Gene and chromosomal mutation (by site and extent):

  • Point mutation — Change of one or a few nucleotides in the DNA, due to spontaneous pairing errors: a purine replaced by a purine, a pyrimidine replaced by a pyrimidine, or a purine replaced by a pyrimidine and vice versa. (The book prints “pyridine” here; read pyrimidine.) A point mutation may leave the amino acid unchanged (still tyrosine — normal protein), create a stop codon (incomplete protein), or change the amino acid (for example to histidine — faulty protein). Examples: sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria. In alkaptonuria, a point mutation causes enzyme deficiency so homogentisic acid is not changed further and the urine becomes black on exposure to air.
  • Frame shift mutation — One or more nucleotides are either deleted or inserted in the DNA of a gene. This shifts the reading frame, results in a completely new sequence of codons and a non-functional protein, and is thus often fatal.
  • Chromosomal mutation (aberration) — Change in the structure or number of chromosomes. Structural changes occur during meiosis, when a chromosome breaks into pieces that later reunite in a changed pattern: deletion (deficiency) — loss of a segment of a chromosome or part of its genes; duplication — a part of a chromosome is repeated, so a segment is in excess; inversion — a part of a chromosome becomes inverted, identified by alteration of the genetic map; translocation — transfer of a segment of a chromosome to a non-homologous chromosome.

23.6.3 Change in Chromosome Numbers

Change in chromosome number occurs due to non-disjunction during meiosis (failure of chromosomes to separate). Change by addition or loss of one or more chromosomes is called aneuploidy: monosomy (2n − 1), e.g. Turner's syndrome; nullisomy (2n − 2), loss of a pair of chromosomes; trisomy (2n + 1), e.g. Klinefelter's syndrome and Down's syndrome; tetrasomy (2n + 2), addition of a pair of homologous chromosomes. Change in one or more complete haploid sets is called euploidy: monoploid (single set), triploid (3 sets), tetraploid (4 sets), pentaploid (5 sets). Euploidy is favourable in plants but rarely found in animals, because sex balance is important in animals and variation from the haploid number results in sterility.

23.6.4 Importance of Mutations

  • Harmful aspects — Mutations that decrease fitness can cause serious effects: cancer, developmental abnormalities such as cleft palate and microcephaly, Down's syndrome, Klinefelter's syndrome, Turner's syndrome, and hereditary disorders such as sickle cell anaemia and haemophilia.
  • Useful aspects — Sometimes a mutation increases fitness. Mutations are the raw material of evolution: less favourable mutations are removed from the gene pool by natural selection, while favourable ones accumulate and ultimately lead to the origin of new species. They are also used in breeding improved varieties.

Key Points

  • A mutation is a permanent change in genetic material that creates a new allele; its agents are mutagens.
  • Mutagens are physical (UV, X-rays, gamma rays), chemical (mustard gas, nitrous acid, colchicine and others) and biological (viruses, transposons, replication errors).
  • Gene mutations are point mutations and frame shift mutations; chromosomal structural changes are deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation.
  • Aneuploidy changes chromosome number by ones (monosomy, trisomy); euploidy changes whole sets and is common and useful in plants.
  • Most mutations are harmful, but favourable mutations drive evolution by natural selection.

lessons.title: Chromosomal Syndromes: Down, Klinefelter and Turner
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson describes the best-known human disorders caused by mutation: three chromosomal aberrations caused by non-disjunction, and two gene mutations caused by point mutation.

23.6.5 Chromosomal Mutation or Chromosomal Aberrations

i) Down's Syndrome. Also called mongolism. The affected person has an extra autosomal chromosome number 21 — trisomy (2n + 1) = 47 chromosomes. It was first described in 1866 by J. Langdon Down. Cause: non-disjunction of autosome 21 during gamete formation produces a gamete with 24 chromosomes; fertilization of such a gamete produces a child with 47 chromosomes. Symptoms: delayed maturation of the skeletal system, so the person is generally short with poor muscle tone; mental retardation, defective nervous and blood vascular systems; protruding tongue, flat nose, flat broad face, small ears, small mouth, short hands with short fingers, a gap between the large toe and second toe, rounded head, excessive skin at the nape of the neck and squint eyes. The book gives life expectancy as approximately 16 years; note that with modern medical care people with Down's syndrome now live much longer than this old figure. Treatment: there is no cure for a chromosomal disease, but Down's syndrome can be managed to some extent by regular medical check-up and screening, medications, surgery, counselling and support.

ii) Klinefelter's Syndrome. A sex-chromosome non-disjunction found only in males, described by Dr. Henry Klinefelter in 1942. If an XX gamete joins a Y gamete, the XXY zygote (44 + XXY = 47) develops into a sterile male who, in addition to male genitalia and male characteristics, also has some female characteristics such as breasts and a high-pitched voice; some have lower than average intelligence. It occurs in about 1/600 male births. Affected males are sterile because of small testes (no sperm production), with poorly developed male secondary sexual characters, wide hips like a female, a tendency to tallness, long legs, a short trunk and shoulders equal to hip size. Treatment: Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT) around puberty helps more normal male body development and a normal, confident life; treatment usually continues throughout life but does not cure infertility.

iii) Turner Syndrome. Found in females with a missing X chromosome: 2n − 1 (44 + XO) = 45 chromosomes. It was first described by Henry Turner in 1938. Cause: non-disjunction of the sex chromosome pair during paternal or maternal meiosis, so one X chromosome is absent. (The book also prints “44 + OY” — an OY zygote has no X chromosome and cannot survive; Turner syndrome is 45, XO only.) Most affected pregnancies are aborted; survivors have a female appearance with short stature, webbed neck, no ovaries and germ cells (infertility), a low hairline at the back of the neck, abnormal bone development (especially of the hands and elbows), a larger than usual number of moles on the skin, and oedema (extra fluid) in the hands and feet. Treatment: growth hormone treatment can improve growth and final adult height if started early in childhood; estrogen replacement treatment (ERT), often started at about age 12 or 13, helps develop the changes of puberty, including breast development and menstrual periods.

SyndromeKaryotypeCause
Down's syndrome47 (trisomy 21)Autosomal non-disjunction of chromosome 21
Klinefelter's syndrome47, XXYSex-chromosome non-disjunction; sterile male
Turner syndrome45, XOMissing X chromosome; female

Key Points

  • Down's syndrome: trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes), described by J. Langdon Down in 1866; flat broad face, protruding tongue, short stature and mental retardation.
  • Klinefelter's syndrome: 44 + XXY sterile males with some female characteristics; treated with testosterone replacement therapy.
  • Turner syndrome: 44 + XO (45 chromosomes) females with short stature, webbed neck and no ovaries; treated with growth hormone and estrogen replacement.

lessons.title: Gene Mutations: Sickle Cell Anaemia and Phenylketonuria
lessons.notes_html:
Gene mutations change one or a few nucleotides in a single gene. Two classic examples caused by point mutation are sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria; both are autosomal recessive disorders.

23.6.6 Gene Mutation

Sickle Cell Anaemia, also known as Haemoglobin SS disease (Hb SS), is an autosomal recessive trait caused by a point mutation — base substitution — in haemoglobin. The 6th amino acid, glutamic acid, in the beta chain of normal haemoglobin is replaced by valine (codon GAG changes to GUG). The abnormal haemoglobin is called HbS; it loses oxygen-binding capacity, and the red blood cells become crescent- or sickle-shaped and deliver less oxygen to the tissues. The disease is due to a homozygous recessive gene received from both parents. Symptoms: painful episodes called crises, lasting from hours to many days, with pain in the bones of the back, the long bones and the chest; in severe anaemia, fatigue, fever, paleness, jaundice, damage to various organs, rapid heart rate and shortness of breath. Sickled cells also block capillaries. Treatment: the goal is to manage and control symptoms and limit crises — blood transfusions (also given regularly to prevent stroke), medicines to relieve crises, plenty of fluids, folic acid supplements; bone marrow or stem cell transplants can cure the disease.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a rare point-mutation condition in which a baby is born unable to properly break down the amino acid phenylalanine. It is due to an autosomal recessive gene. In a healthy baby, phenylalanine is converted into tyrosine by the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase; the affected baby has a defective enzyme, so phenylalanine is converted into toxic phenylketones that accumulate and damage the central nervous system. Symptoms: lighter skin, hair and eyes, delayed mental and social skills, head size below normal, hyperactivity, jerking movements of arms/legs, mental retardation, seizures, skin rashes and tremors. Treatment: a diet extremely low in phenylalanine, particularly while the child is growing; products containing phenylalanine, such as milk and eggs, are avoided. A special infant formula called Lofenalac, extremely low in phenylalanine, is used as a protein source and can be used throughout life. Early detection and diet prevent mental retardation.

DNA in forensics (STS): almost every cell contains DNA; any two people share on average 99.9% of their DNA, so only 0.1% is unique — yet each human cell contains 3 billion DNA base pairs, of which 3 million differ, which is enough to identify a person. Forensic scientists scan 13 DNA regions (loci) that vary from person to person to make a DNA profile (DNA fingerprint), used to identify suspects, exonerate the wrongly accused, identify victims of crime and catastrophe, establish paternity and determine evolutionary relationships. Harmful mutations are removed from populations by natural selection, through premature death or reduced reproductive success.

Key Points

  • Sickle cell anaemia: point mutation replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of the beta chain, forming HbS and sickle-shaped RBCs.
  • PKU: defective phenylalanine hydroxylase lets phenylketones damage the brain; controlled by a low-phenylalanine diet (Lofenalac).
  • Forensic DNA profiling uses 13 variable loci; harmful mutations are removed by natural selection.

lessons.title: Special Creation and the Concept of Evolution
lessons.notes_html:
The central idea of biological evolution is that all life on Earth shares a common ancestor. Evolution can be defined as descent with modification, a phrase Darwin used: the many species of Earth are descendants of ancestral species that were different from present-day species. More narrowly, evolution is a change in the genetic composition of a population from generation to generation.

24.1 The Evolution of the Concept of Evolution

Understanding evolution is critical for understanding biology. Evolution is the only scientific explanation for the diversity of life, and it explains similarities among the vast variety of life. Two major and contradictory concepts of evolutionary thought are: a) Special Creation and b) the Theory of Evolution. Evolution rarely follows a straight line from species to species; it is more like a tree with many branches — some branches lead to new branches, while others become dead ends.

24.1.1 Concept of Special Creation

The belief that the origin and diversity of life result from a supernatural event at a particular time in the past, whereby each species was created separately (from the act of God), is called special creation. Its supporters are called creationists. This theory is supported by most of the world major religions and civilizations, and the concept is based on the references of Holy books. According to their interpretations, Allah has created everything in the universe in six days, and man was created on the sixth day.

  • Faith accepts things for which there is no evidence in the scientific sense, so logically there can be no intellectual conflict between the scientific and theological accounts of creation, since they are mutually exclusive realms of thoughts.
  • To the scientist, scientific truth is tentative, but to the believer, theological truth is absolute.
  • In the solved-exercise sense: special creation holds that species were created separately, perfectly adapted, in their present form, and have not changed since creation — a religious and philosophical idea, not a testable scientific theory.

24.1.2 Concept of Evolution

In biology, evolution is the change in the characteristics of a species over several generations, and the theory of evolution is based on the idea that all species are related and change over time. Its supporters are called evolutionists. According to their point of view, the universe and man did not always exist in their present form, but result from many changes from lower to higher order, and they reject the theory of special creation.

  • According to the book, life began on Earth about 3.5 billion years ago (the book attributes this to the big bang theory; strictly, the big bang concerns the origin of the universe, while 3.5 billion years is the book age for the first life).
  • The fossil record supports the hypothesis that life originated from a simple prokaryotic organism, and then eukaryotic organisms developed from this prokaryote about 1.9-2.1 billion years ago.
  • Present-day biodiversity is the result of these continuous evolutionary changes. The concept of evolution did not begin with Darwin and his book Origin of Species: evolutionary concepts were present at the time of Aristotle, about 384-322 BC.
Special CreationTheory of Evolution
Each species created separately by a supernatural actAll species are related and change over time
Species are in their present form since creationPresent forms arose by many changes from lower to higher order
Based on Holy books and faith; truth is absolute to the believerBased on evidence such as fossils; scientific truth is tentative
Supporters are creationistsSupporters are evolutionists

Key Points

  • Evolution is descent with modification: all life shares a common ancestor.
  • Special creation: each species was created separately, in six days in the book account, and is unchanged.
  • The theory of evolution: species are related, change over generations, and arose from lower to higher forms.
  • Life began about 3.5 billion years ago; eukaryotes developed from prokaryotes about 1.9-2.1 billion years ago.
  • Evolutionary ideas existed in the time of Aristotle, long before Darwin.

lessons.title: Evolution of Man in the Holy Quran and the Origin of Life
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson presents the book account of the process of the evolution of man in the Holy Quran, and then the origin of life according to the concept of evolution.

24.1.3 The Process of the Evolution of Man in the Holy Quran

The book states that the Quran supports that humans came from lower beings and that creation had a process involving diverse successive stages: Allah Almighty started the creation of life on Earth, and then left it to evolve as a result of learning from adaptation to various environments, with His intervention to make His creation better.

  • Surah Nisa, Verse 1: O mankind! Be careful of your duty to your Lord Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate and from them has spread a multitude of men and women. The book explains: the beginning of life was a single soul, then its mate came out of it; in biological terms the earliest life was single-celled organisms in water, which multiplied by splitting, and later reproduction by mating pairs replaced splitting or dividing.
  • Surah Sajda, Verse 7: Allah is He Who has made everything He created better, and He began the creation of the human being out of clay. The key word is began (bada-a): creation happened in a process that had a beginning, not just at once.
  • Surah Nooh, Verse 14: He has created you in diverse (and successive) stages. This may refer to the successive stages of a foetus in its mother womb, or to the successive stages of human evolution.
  • Surah Al-Hajar, Verse 28: We created the human being from stinking, smooth and wet clay. The book reads this as the environment where life started: swamps, where still water combined with earth soil creates stinking but smooth clay, easy to take different forms.
  • Surah Infitar, Verse 7: It is He Who created you, fashioned you perfectly, and made you with the right proportions (straightened you up, to walk in an upright position). The book links this to three stages: creation of a living cell (Khlaqa, created); change from unicellular prokaryote to multicellular eukaryote (sawwa, fashioned perfectly); and the human departure from the animal stage, walking upright (adala).
  • Surah Ankabut, Verse 20: Roam the earth and observe how the creation was initiated — a direct command to travel the earth and observe how creation was brought forth; the book notes that Darwin followed this unknowingly.

24.1.4 Origin of Life According to Concept of Evolution

The vent hypothesis suggests that life may have begun at submarine hydrothermal vents. The first sea hydrothermal vent was discovered in 1977 in the Pacific Ocean. The fossils found in these vents are about 3.5 billion years old and belong to a group of prokaryotes, the archaeobacteria (now called archea). The early atmosphere of Earth was oxygen-free, hot and ozone-less, so there was frequent exposure to ultraviolet radiation.

  • The primitive atmosphere had very few nutrients, and the first prokaryotes were absorptive heterotrophs. Later, chemoautotrophs evolved.
  • The photosynthetic organism evolved about 3.2 billion years ago. It used hydrogen sulphide as a source of hydrogen for sugar instead of water, producing sulphur (S) as a by-product; some prokaryotes still use hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) in this way.
  • Later, when cyanobacteria evolved, they started using H₂O as the source of hydrogen for carbohydrates and liberated O₂ as a by-product. This O₂ accumulated in the atmosphere, and slowly the ozone layer formed, acting as a filter for ultraviolet radiations from the sun.
  • When eukaryotic photosynthetic organisms evolved about 1.9-2.1 billion years ago, O₂ production increased many times, the ozone layer grew thicker and more protective for life on land, and biodiversity increased.

The theory of evolution states that species change over time, its primary mechanism is natural selection, and the fossil record, morphology, biogeography, comparative anatomy, embryology and molecular biology all provide evidence for evolution.

Key Points

  • The book reads the Quran verses as describing creation in successive stages, beginning from clay and a single soul.
  • The vent hypothesis places the beginning of life at submarine hydrothermal vents, discovered in 1977.
  • Vent fossils are about 3.5 billion years old, from prokaryotes (archaeobacteria, now archea).
  • First prokaryotes were absorptive heterotrophs; photosynthetic organisms evolved about 3.2 billion years ago using H₂S.
  • Cyanobacteria used water and released O₂, which built up the protective ozone layer.

lessons.title: Evidences of Evolution: Biogeography and Palaeontology
lessons.notes_html:
Evidence to support the theory of evolution is provided by many sources. This lesson covers the first two: biogeography and palaeontology.

24.2 Evidences of Evolution

The important evidences discussed in the book are evidence from biogeography, evidence from palaeontology, evidence from comparative anatomy, and evidence from molecular biology.

i) Evidence from Biogeography

The study of the geographical distribution of fossil and living organisms is called biogeography. A comparison of recently formed fossil types with living organisms in the same geographic area shows that new organisms arise in areas where similar forms already lived.

  • Armadillos appeared in North and South America, where glyptodonts lived in the past. The armadillo is the armoured mammal that lives only in America.
  • Modern kangaroos appeared only in Australia, where they evolved from extinct giant kangaroos.
  • Darwin found 13 species of finches in the Galapagos Islands, not found anywhere else in the world, as far as he knew. He concluded that the finches had evolved from a common ancestral group that probably reached the island many generations earlier; in the isolation of the Galapagos Islands, the original finches evolved into the 13 species.
  • Closely related species are usually found in close physical proximity to one another, and the fossils from these regions resemble modern organisms. This suggests that these species share a common lineage.
  • The age of the Earth, estimated from the age of meteorites, is 4569 million years (journal Nature, August 2005, as quoted in the book).

ii) Evidence from Palaeontology

The study of past life with the help of fossils is called palaeontology: the study of forms of life existing in prehistoric or geologic times, as represented by the fossils (Latin fosilium, something dug up) of plants, animals and other organisms.

  • Palaeontology supports evolution because it shows a descent of modern organisms from common ancestors. It indicates that fewer kinds of organisms existed in past eras, and organisms were probably less complex.
  • As palaeontologists descend deeper into layers of rock, the variety and complexity of fossils decrease. The fossils from the uppermost rock layers are most like current forms.
  • The oldest known fossils are of prokaryotes, so prokaryotes are considered the ancestors of all life forms on Earth.
  • The fossil record can trace the history of one organism. The fossil record of horses shows that the earliest horses had four toes; after a long time the number of toes reduced to three, and in modern horses the large central toe is present, ending in a hoof.

Evolution of the horse: Eohippus (50 million years ago) to modern Equus, with toes reducing to a single hoof.

Key Points

  • Biogeography studies the geographical distribution of fossils and living organisms.
  • Armadillos and glyptodonts in America, kangaroos in Australia and 13 Galapagos finch species support common descent.
  • Palaeontology studies past life from fossils; deeper rock layers hold simpler, less varied fossils.
  • The oldest fossils are prokaryotes, the ancestors of all life.
  • Horse fossils show toes reducing from four to three to one central toe ending in a hoof.

lessons.title: Evidences from Comparative Anatomy and Molecular Biology
lessons.notes_html:
Two further lines of evidence come from comparing body structures and from comparing the molecules shared by all living things.

iii) Evidence from Comparative Anatomy

Anatomy is the field of biological science concerned with the identification and description of the internal body structures of living things. The study of comparative anatomy predates the modern study of evolution: early scientists like Buffon and Lamarck used comparative anatomy to determine relationships between species, believing that organisms with similar structures originated from a common ancestor. Today, comparative anatomy can serve as the first line of reasoning in determining the relatedness of species, but it must be supported by evidence from other fields.

Homologous and Analogous Structures

Homologous StructuresAnalogous Structures
Similar in structure, but may or may not have the same functionsDifferent in structure, but similar in function
Forelimbs of mammals such as human, cat, whale and bat have the same basic pattern of bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) but different functionsWings of bats and birds look similar from outside and have the same function, but the wing evolved independently in the two groups; bird wings and insect wings are also analogous
Indicate a common ancestorDo not indicate common ancestry; they show adaptation to a similar way of life
Show divergent evolutionShow convergent evolution
  • Some snakes have hip bones, which show they once had four legs like lizards, their close cousins.
  • Inside some whales and dolphins are small limb bones, showing their back legs and that their ancestors walked on land; these occasionally reappear as tiny rear flippers.

Vestigial Structures in Man (STS)

Human vestigial organs are organs that have lost all or most of their original functions through evolution; there are about 90 such structures in our body. They are homologous remnants of organs functional in ancestors:

  • Vermiform appendix — a vestige of the cecum.
  • Coccyx or tailbone — the remnant of a lost tail.
  • Wisdom teeth — vestigial third molars that human ancestors used to grind down plant tissue.
  • Ear muscles — minimally developed and non-functional, though some people can move their ears.
  • Tonsils and the fifth toe are also listed by the book among these structures.

Evidence from Molecular Biology

Certain key molecules and biochemical mechanisms are shared by different organisms:

  • All organisms use DNA and RNA for their genetic code. The DNA in all organisms is composed of 4 types of nucleotides: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Thymine.
  • The ATP molecule is the common energy currency in all organisms.
  • The processes of photosynthesis, cellular respiration, transcription and translation are all identical or very similar in various types of organisms.
  • Cytochrome C is found in all organisms and performs the same function in all of them. This highly conserved protein is a key component of the electron transport chain (part of cellular respiration), and it also plays a role in programmed cell death.
  • These molecules would not make sense if each appeared independently in each species. The shared biochemical molecules and pathways provide strong evidence for common descent and evolution. The book also notes that humans share about 50% of their DNA with a banana and approximately 31% of their genes with yeast.

Radiometric Dating (STS)

Geologists and palaeontologists determine the actual ages of rocks and fossils by radiometric (radioactive) dating, based on radioactive isotopes. Living organisms have the same constant ratio of ¹⁴C, a radioactive isotope, to ¹²C, a stable isotope, as the atmosphere. When an organism dies, its ¹⁴C decays and the ratio drops. Each isotope has a fixed half-life: for ¹⁴C it is 5600 years. A fossil with half the atmospheric ¹⁴C to ¹²C ratio is about 5600 years old; one with one fourth the ratio is about 11,200 years old.

Key Points

  • Homologous structures: same structure, different function, common ancestor, divergent evolution.
  • Analogous structures: different structure, same function, no common ancestry, convergent evolution.
  • Vestigial organs, about 90 in man, include the appendix, coccyx and wisdom teeth.
  • All organisms share DNA, RNA, ATP and cytochrome C — strong evidence of common descent.
  • Radiometric dating uses half-life; ¹⁴C has a half-life of 5600 years.

lessons.title: Evolution of Eukaryotes from Prokaryotes
lessons.notes_html:
Fossil records indicate that eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes somewhere between 1.9 and 2.1 billion years ago (the unit Summary rounds this to about 2 billion years). Two hypotheses have been proposed to describe this evolution.

24.3 Evolution of Eukaryote from Prokaryotes

The two hypotheses are the membrane invagination hypothesis (theory) and the endosymbiotic hypothesis (theory). Together, the book figure shows both: infolding of the plasma membrane forming the nucleus and endomembrane system, and engulfing of prokaryotes forming mitochondria and plastids.

24.3.1 Membrane Invagination Theory

In the form used in the solved exercises, this theory proposes that the plasma membrane of an early prokaryotic cell folded inward (invaginated) to form the nuclear envelope, the endoplasmic reticulum and other internal membranes, enclosing the DNA in a nucleus. Continued membrane infolding created the endomembrane system. The book main text describes the related engulfing step under this heading: the host cell membrane infolded to surround invading prokaryotic cells and transport them into the cell; the membrane did not dissolve but remained intact, creating a second membrane around the promitochondria and prochloroplast. This is why, in modern eukaryotes, the inner membrane of mitochondria and chloroplasts is more similar to prokaryotes, while the outer membrane retains eukaryote characteristics. Note the overlap: invagination best explains the nucleus and endomembrane system; the engulfed bacteria themselves are explained by endosymbiosis, next.

From prokaryote to eukaryote: membrane infolding forms the nucleus and ER, and engulfed prokaryotes become mitochondria and plastids.

24.3.2 Endosymbiosis Theory

Research conducted by Lynn Margulis supports the hypothesis that two separate, mutually beneficial invasions of a prokaryote cell produced the modern-day mitochondria and chloroplasts as eukaryotic organelles.

  • Ancestral mitochondria were small heterotrophs capable of using oxygen to perform cellular respiration and thereby create useful energy. They became part of a large cell either by direct invasion as an internal parasite or as an indigestible food source.
  • Later, a second invasion brought ancestral chloroplasts, thought to be small photosynthetic cyanobacteria.
  • Supporting evidence: both mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own genes, circular DNA and RNA, and reproduce by binary fission independent of the host cell cycle. They therefore appear to be more similar to prokaryotes than to eukaryotes.
Membrane InvaginationEndosymbiosis
Plasma membrane folds inwardSeparate prokaryotes are engulfed and kept inside
