Explains the nucleus, nuclear envelope and endomembrane system (ER)Explains mitochondria and chloroplasts
Internal membranes come from the host cell own membraneSupported by Lynn Margulis; organelles keep circular DNA and divide by binary fission

Key Points

  • Eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes about 1.9-2.1 billion years ago.
  • Membrane invagination: infolding of the plasma membrane formed the nucleus and endomembrane system.
  • Endosymbiosis (Lynn Margulis): engulfed aerobic heterotrophs became mitochondria; engulfed cyanobacteria became chloroplasts.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and RNA and reproduce by binary fission.
  • The inner membranes of these organelles resemble prokaryotes; the outer membranes are eukaryotic in character.

lessons.title: Lamarckism: Theory, Examples and Drawbacks
lessons.notes_html:
Jean Baptiste de Lamarck (August 1, 1744 - December 28, 1829) was a French naturalist and an early proponent of the idea that evolution (descent with modification) occurred and proceeded in accordance with natural laws. He wrote the book Philosophie Zoologique (Zoological Philosophy) in 1809. Lamarck is remembered today mainly for his now rejected theory of heredity, the inheritance of acquired traits. Note: the book also calls him a well known toponymist (expert in the study of place names); that description does not fit his biological work and looks like a printing error, so it is not part of the theory to learn.

24.4 Lamarckism

Lamarck theory is called Lamarckism. It is usually known as the inheritance of acquired characters.

24.4.1 Lamarck Theory of Evolution

Lamarck theory involved two ideas:

  • i) Use and disuse: an organ which is used more and more by an organism becomes bigger and stronger, and one that is not used becomes weak and eventually disappears.
  • ii) Inheritance of acquired characters: any feature of an organism that is improved through use is passed to its offspring.

Examples to Support Lamarck Theory

  • Evolution of giraffe: according to Lamarck, the ancestors of the giraffe looked like horses, with a small neck and forelimbs, and lived where there was no surface vegetation. They had to stretch their neck and forelimbs to eat leaves from tall plants, so these parts became elongated, and this trait was transmitted in successive generations.
  • Extinction of limbs in snakes: snakes are believed to have evolved from lizard-like ancestors that had two pairs of limbs. Due to disuse of the limbs, the limbs became weaker and shorter and eventually disappeared.
  • Flightless birds: the ancestors of birds such as the ostrich were able to fly. Due to environmental changes they had a lot of food and were well protected; they did not use their wings, and as a result the wings became vestigial.

24.4.2 Drawbacks of Lamarckism

  • i) There is no experimental proof of his theory.
  • ii) New organs are not formed in organisms by requirement.
  • iii) It is not necessary that an acquired character transmits into a new generation; changes in body cells do not alter the germ cells.
  • The German biologist August Weisman, in the 1880s, disproved the inheritance theory experimentally: he removed the tails of 68 mice, repeatedly for many generations, and reported that no mice were born without a tail or even with a shorter tail. This rejects the theory of inheritance of acquired characters.
  • Lamarckism also gives no mechanism for the origin of new variations, which modern genetics attributes to mutation and recombination.

Key Points

  • Lamarck (1744-1829) presented his theory in Philosophie Zoologique (1809).
  • Use and disuse: used organs grow stronger; unused organs weaken and disappear.
  • Inheritance of acquired characters: improvements gained in life are passed to offspring.
  • Book examples: the giraffe neck, loss of limbs in snakes, and vestigial wings of flightless birds.
  • Drawbacks: no experimental proof, and Weisman mice (68 mice, tails cut for generations) were always born with tails.

lessons.title: Darwinism and Darwin Observations During His Voyage
lessons.notes_html:
Charles Darwin was born on February 12, 1809 in Shrewsbury, England, and died at Down House in Kent on April 19, 1882. He is known as the father of evolution. He was selected as naturalist on HMS Beagle, a British naval ship about to sail around the world to expand the navy knowledge of natural resources, and he wrote the book Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.

24.5 Darwinism

Darwinism is Darwin theory of evolution by natural selection, set out fully in 1859 in On the Origin of Species.

24.5.1 Darwin Observations During His Voyage

In 1831, when Darwin was just 22 years old, he set sail on a scientific expedition on HMS Beagle. As the naturalist, it was his job to observe and collect specimens of plants, animals, rocks and fossils wherever the expedition went ashore. During this long journey Darwin made key observations:

  • Darwin finches: one of the most famous species he observed were the finches of the Galapagos Islands. He found 13 different species of finches and noted that the main difference among the finches on each island was their beak shape. The finches on each island had beak shapes suited to the type of food available on that island — seeds, insects or cactus, in the solved-exercise summary. They had clearly descended from a common mainland ancestor.
  • Giant tortoise: Darwin also observed giant tortoises in the Galapagos Islands, which were named for their giant tortoises (about 4 feet, 475 pounds, average life span 100 years, feeding on plants, as the book notes). A tortoise on one island had a saddle-shaped shell, while those on another island had a dome-shaped shell. This observation made Darwin think about the origin of species.
  • Fossils of South America: in South America, Darwin found fossils that resembled modern animals; however, they had differences in size and adaptations (for example, giant extinct forms related to the living armadillo, the armoured mammal found only in America). It made him realise that living things had ancestors and that species change over time.

Summary of the observations: species are not fixed; they change over time, and related species share common ancestors. Fossils of extinct animals resembled living animals in the same region, suggesting descent with change, and the geographical distribution of organisms (biogeography) showed related species in nearby areas.

The book figure of Darwin finches names forms such as the large ground finch, medium and small ground finches, the cactus finch and large cactus finch, the sharp-beaked ground finch, the vegetarian finch, tree finches, the woodpecker finch, the mangrove finch, the warbler finch and the Cocos Island finch. The point of the figure is that one ancestral finch stock produced all these different beaks in isolation on the different islands.

Key Points

  • Darwin (born 1809) sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle in 1831, aged 22.
  • Galapagos finches: 13 species, differing mainly in beak shape, each suited to its island food.
  • Galapagos tortoises differed in shell shape from island to island: saddle-shaped versus dome-shaped.
  • South American fossils resembled living animals of the same region but differed in size and adaptations.
  • Conclusion: species change over time and related species share common ancestors.

lessons.title: Development of Darwin Theory and Natural Selection
lessons.notes_html:
Darwin presented his theory of natural selection in 1859 in his famous book Origin of Species, but he started his work in 1836 after returning from the 5-year trip of HMS Beagle, collecting data to support his idea. His theory was also inspired by other scientists of his time.

24.5.2 Development of the Theory of Evolution

  • Charles Lyell: a well-known English geologist who wrote Principles of Geology. Lyell argued that gradual geological processes have gradually shaped Earth surface. Darwin was impressed and took his book with him on the Beagle voyage.
  • James Hutton (1726-1797): a Scottish geologist, chemist and naturalist who gave the concept of uniformitarianism, which explains the features of Earth crust by means of natural processes over geological time. The book also credits him as the first person to propose a mechanism of natural selection for evolutionary change over time.
  • Thomas R. Malthus (1766-1834): an English economist who wrote an essay on population. He argued that human populations grow faster than the resources they depend on; when populations become too large, famine and disease break out, keeping populations in check by killing off the weakest members. Darwin read this and was influenced by it.
  • Alfred Russell Wallace (1823-1913): Wallace lived at about the same time as Darwin and also travelled to study nature. He developed basically the same theory of evolution while working in distant lands, and sent Darwin a paper explaining his evolutionary theory, which confirmed what Darwin already thought and motivated him to publish.

Why the theory was attributed to Darwin: although Wallace developed basically the same theory, and Hutton had proposed a mechanism earlier, Darwin came up with great supporting evidence from a wide variety of scientific disciplines, including palaeontology, geology, vestigial organs, biogeography and comparative anatomy, and he spent more than 30 years studying and observing nature before concluding his ideas. Both Darwin and Wallace papers were published in the Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnaean Society, but Darwin book presented the theory in full. The phrase survival of the fittest, associated with Darwin, was coined by biologist Herbert Spencer after reading Darwin work. By Darwin death in 1882, Origin of Species had been translated into 29 languages.

24.5.3 Darwin Theory of Natural Selection

According to this theory, the various types of plants, animals and other living things on Earth have their origin in other pre-existing types, and the distinguishable differences are due to modifications in successive generations. There are two main points: descent with modification and natural selection.

  • Descent with modification means passing on traits from parent organisms to their offspring. According to Darwin, all species descended from only a few life forms that had been modified over time; this forms the backbone of his theory.
  • Natural selection is the process in nature by which organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more than those less adapted to their environment.

The four observations about natural selection are:

  • a) Overproduction: each species has the capacity to produce more offspring than can possibly obtain food and survive. If all offspring remained alive and reproduced, they would overcrowd the Earth. Example from the book: if each breeding pair of elephants produces six offspring during its 90-year life span, in 750 years a single pair will give rise to a population of 19 million — yet elephants have not overrun the planet.
  • b) Struggle for existence: individuals increase enormously in number, but space and food remain almost constant, so there is active competition. The three-fold struggle is: 1. Intra-specific (among the same species), 2. Inter-specific (among different species living together), and 3. Environmental struggle (against various environmental conditions).
  • c) Variations: individuals in a population exhibit variation in their traits. Some traits improve the chances of survival and reproductive success, whereas others do not. Variation necessary for evolution by natural selection must be heritable.
  • d) Survival of the fittest: as a result of competition, the stronger variants survive while the weaker, less fit variants are rooted out; for example, in a flood only organisms that can swim or respire in water have a better chance to survive. Fittest means best fitted to the environment in reproductive success, not merely physical strength. Natural selection thus increases favourable alleles and decreases unfavourable alleles in the population, and over succeeding generations members become better adapted to local conditions, leading to the evolution of new species.

Key Points

  • Lyell (gradual geology), Hutton (uniformitarianism) and Malthus (population grows faster than resources) all influenced Darwin.
  • Wallace reached the same theory independently and his paper pushed Darwin to publish; the theory is attributed to Darwin because of his vast evidence and full book of 1859.
  • The two main points of Darwin theory are descent with modification and natural selection.
  • Natural selection rests on overproduction, struggle for existence, heritable variation, and survival of the fittest.
  • Elephant example: one pair could give 19 million descendants in 750 years, yet numbers stay in check.

lessons.title: Neo-Darwinism and the Hardy-Weinberg Theorem
lessons.notes_html:
Neo-Darwinism, also called the modern evolutionary synthesis or modern synthesis, generally denotes the integration of Charles Darwin theory of evolution by natural selection, Gregor Mendel theory of genetics as a basis of biological inheritance, and mathematical population genetics. It introduced the connection between the unit of evolution (the gene) and the mechanism of evolution (natural selection), and it has been one of the most significant overall developments in evolutionary biology since Darwin.

24.6 Neo-Darwinism

In neo-Darwinism, evolution is studied as changes in allele frequencies in a population gene pool. The Hardy-Weinberg theorem gives the baseline: a population that is not evolving.

24.6.1 Hardy-Weinberg Theorem

Godfrey Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg developed the relationship between the frequencies of alleles and genotypes in 1908. The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that both the ratios of genotypes and the frequency of alleles remain constant from generation to generation in a sexually reproducing population, provided other conditions are stable. Genetic equilibrium occurs when there is no evolution within the population and allele frequencies do not change.

Conditions and assumptions for stability:

  • 1. No mutation (change) in DNA sequence.
  • 2. No migration (moving into or out of a population).
  • 3. Random mating.
  • 4. No natural selection.
  • The solved exercises add the fifth standard condition: a large population, so there is no genetic drift. These conditions rarely occur in nature; if one or more does not hold, evolution can occur, allele frequencies keep changing, and populations are constantly evolving.

Factors That Change Allele Frequencies

  • a) Mutation: a change in the genome of an organism; the major source of variations and of material for natural selection.
  • b) Migration or gene flow: the movement of individuals from one population to another, which disturbs the gene pool. Note: the book swaps the two words here — correctly, leaving a population is emigration and entering a population is immigration; the book prints them the other way round.
  • c) Non-random mating: mating among a specific group of individuals in a large population; individuals mate more frequently with close individuals than with distant ones. It cannot develop new alleles, but it can increase homozygous genotypes.
  • d) Natural selection: populations vary in their individuals and their reproductive success. Individuals who leave more offspring pass on more of their alleles and dominate the population. Selection may also be artificial, when a breeder selects for desirable traits.

Hardy-Weinberg Equation

This mathematical equation calculates the genetic variation of a population at equilibrium. For a simple locus with two alleles, A and a: p is the frequency of the A (dominant) allele and q is the frequency of the a allele. The sum of allele frequencies must be 1, so p + q = 1, and the genotype frequencies are p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p² is homozygous dominant AA, 2pq is heterozygous Aa, and q² is homozygous recessive aa.

  • Book example: if there are 200 M alleles and 800 m alleles in the gene pool, then p = 0.2 and q = 0.8, and 0.2 + 0.8 = 1. Genotypes: MM = (0.2)² = 0.04, Mm = 2(0.2 x 0.8) = 0.32, mm = (0.8)² = 0.64, totalling 1 or 100%.
  • The equation is also used in public health to estimate the percentage of people carrying alleles for certain diseases. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is never achieved in nature, but it is very useful in studying populations: if observed genotype frequencies differ from those predicted, the population is evolving.
  • Book problem noted: grey body B is dominant to black body b, with 30% recessive alleles in a gene pool of 1000 individuals — students are asked to calculate the numbers of grey and black individuals using this equation.

Key Points

  • Neo-Darwinism (modern synthesis) joins Darwin natural selection with Mendel genetics and population genetics.
  • Hardy-Weinberg (1908): allele and genotype frequencies stay constant in a non-evolving population at genetic equilibrium.
  • Conditions: no mutation, no migration, random mating, no natural selection, and a large population.
  • Mutation, migration (gene flow), non-random mating and natural selection change allele frequencies.
  • Equation: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p is the dominant allele frequency.

lessons.title: Genetic Drift and Speciation
lessons.notes_html:
This final lesson covers genetic drift, change by chance, and speciation, the formation of new species — the most important outcome of reproductive isolation.

24.6.2 Genetic Drift

Genetic drift is a change in allele frequency in a population due to a random selection of certain genes — change by chance. Mostly, a mutation within the DNA can have no effect on the fitness of an organism; such changes can increase or decrease in a population simply due to chance (neutral selection). In the largest populations, the allele frequency of each gene stays relatively stable, because the genes do not affect fitness and there is no selection pressure for or against them. In the smallest populations, the frequencies can fluctuate greatly: some alleles become fixed in the population, while others disappear.

Types of genetic drift:

  • i) Bottleneck effect: a type of genetic drift in which a population size severely decreases due to a natural disaster such as disease, predation or competition. Book example: a population of 100 rabbits in a forest has many coat colours — black, brown, tan, white, grey and red — with the alleles equally distributed. A disease kills 98% of the rabbits; only red and grey rabbits are left, simply by chance, and the other alleles disappear. The rebuilt population has much less genetic variation. The solved exercises also give cheetahs and northern elephant seals as examples of low variation after bottlenecks.
  • ii) Founder effect: population size and genetic variability decrease when a few individuals in a population colonise a new location separate from the old population. Example: if only two birds of a species land on an island, their alleles alone account for the diversity present; those alleles dominate at first, mutations then arise and lead to new adaptations that stay with the founding population. With enough time, the two populations can diverge to a point where they can no longer interbreed. A recent-research model in the book predicts that speciation occurs more rapidly when natural selection acts on two large subpopulations than on many small subpopulations.

The bottleneck effect: a disaster leaves only a chance sample of the original gene pool.

24.6.3 Speciation

Speciation is an evolutionary process by which individuals within a population undergo change to such a degree that they become a new and distinct species. This most often occurs due to geographic isolation or reproductive isolation within the population. As species evolve and branch off, they can no longer interbreed with members of the original species. There are three types of natural speciation in the book; the other type is artificial speciation, when scientists create new species for experiments. Reproductive isolation — seasonal, behavioural, mechanical, gametic or hybrid sterility, in the solved summary — is the most important factor for speciation.

TypeHow It Happens
Allopatric (allo = other, patric = place)Caused by geographic isolation: a physical barrier gets between members of a population, from something as small as a fallen tree for small organisms to being split by oceans. Species occurring in different geographical areas are allopatric. Its special type is peripatric speciation, where very few individuals survive in the isolated population.
Parapatric (para = beside, patric = place)Two subpopulations evolve reproductive isolation while continuing to exchange genes; very rare. The populations are not separated by a physical barrier; isolation is temporal or behavioural. Example: plants on boundaries between very distinct climates may flower at different times and become unable to interbreed. Animal examples: mormyrid fish and tropical cave snail.
Sympatric (sym = same, patric = place)Individuals are not separated at all and all live in the same place. The cause is reproductive isolation, for example individuals coming into their mating seasons at different times, or preference to mate with a selected individual.

Key Points

  • Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance, strongest in small populations.
  • Bottleneck effect: a disaster drastically reduces a population and its variation (book example: 98% of 100 rabbits killed).
  • Founder effect: a few colonists start a new population with only their alleles.
  • Speciation forms a new species that can no longer interbreed with the original population.
  • Allopatric speciation needs a physical barrier; parapatric has no barrier, only adjacent different environments; sympatric occurs in the same place by reproductive isolation.

lessons.title: Biogeochemical Cycles, Reservoirs and the Water Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
Every organism must get nutrients for its survival. Elements such as carbon, nitrogen and water move again and again between living organisms and the non-living environment. This unit studies these cycles, the flow of energy, succession, populations, and how man affects his environment.

25.1 Biogeochemical Cycles

The flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment is known as a biogeochemical cycle. Chemicals absorbed or ingested by organisms are passed through the food chain and returned to the soil, air and water by processes such as respiration, excretion and decomposition. As an element moves through the cycle, it often forms compounds with other elements as a result of metabolic processes in living tissues or by natural reactions in the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water) or lithosphere (the outer rigid strong layer of the earth). The carbon (CO₂) cycle shown in the book links photosynthesis, animal and plant respiration, decay organisms, dead organisms and waste products, fossils and fossil fuels, ocean uptake and automobile and factory emissions.

25.1.1 Primary Reservoirs of Nutrients

Chemicals are sometimes held for long periods of time in one place. This place is called a reservoir, for example coal deposits that store carbon for a long period of time. When chemicals are held for only a short period of time, they are being held in exchange pools; examples of exchange pools include plants and animals. Plants and animals utilize carbon to produce carbohydrates, fats and proteins, which build their internal structure or give energy; they temporarily use carbon and release it back into the air or surrounding medium. Generally, reservoirs are abiotic factors. The period of time that a chemical is held in one place is called its residence time — the length of time a substance remains in the adsorbed, suspended or dissolved state. The book also notes that, according to the United Nations, two thirds of the world's population are projected to face water scarcity by 2025.

Water Cycle

There is as much water today as there was thousands of years ago, because of the water cycle. The ocean is the major source of water and contains about 97% of the total water. The water cycle is driven by solar energy, which evaporates water, and by gravity, which draws water back to earth in the form of precipitation — rain, snow, dew or hail. Water vapour cools and condenses into clouds; precipitation then falls on oceans and land, and the cycle repeats through evaporation, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, streamflow, infiltration and ground-water discharge.

Water in Environment

Water falling on land takes different paths. Some water is evaporated from the soil, lakes and streams, and a portion runs off the land back to the oceans. When rain water falls, some of it sinks or percolates into the ground and saturates the earth to a certain level. The top of the saturation zone is called the water table. Wherever the earth contains basins or channels, water appears to the level of the water table: water within basins is called lakes and ponds, and water within channels is called streams or rivers. Ground water is sometimes also located in underground layers called aquifers. An aquifer is an underground layer where the material contains water, and it supplies water for wells, springs, etc.

Water in Living Bodies

The bodies of living things contain roughly 70% water. Some water of the water cycle enters the living communities of ecosystems: it is absorbed by the roots of plants and much of it is evaporated back to the atmosphere from their leaves (transpiration). A small amount is combined with carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to produce high-energy molecules; eventually these are broken down during cellular respiration, releasing water back to the environment. Heterotrophs get water from their food or by drinking, and some of this water is released back to the environment by vaporization.

The water cycle: driven by solar energy and gravity — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and ground-water storage.

Key Points

  • A biogeochemical cycle is the flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment.
  • Reservoirs hold chemicals for long periods (e.g. coal deposits); exchange pools, such as plants and animals, hold them briefly; residence time is how long a chemical stays in one place.
  • The water cycle is driven by solar energy; oceans hold about 97% of all water.
  • The water table is the top of the saturated zone; aquifers are underground water-bearing layers that supply wells and springs.
  • Living bodies are about 70% water; plants return much absorbed water to the air by transpiration.

lessons.title: The Nitrogen Cycle: Fixation, Nitrification, Assimilation and Denitrification
lessons.notes_html:
Nitrogen is the necessary element of organic molecules such as amino acids, nucleic acids and proteins, yet most organisms cannot use nitrogen gas directly.

25.1.2 Nitrogen Cycle

The nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen between the earth and the atmosphere, through processes that convert nitrogen gas to organic substances and back again. It is a continuous cycle maintained by decomposers and other bacteria, explained in four reactions: decomposition, nitrogen fixation, assimilation and de-nitrification.

1. Decomposition

Decomposition is the breakdown of a complex substance into its components; decomposition of organic nitrogen compounds is the first source of soil nitrates. It occurs in two steps:

  • a) Ammonification — The nitrogenous wastes of animals and the nitrogenous compounds of dead organisms are decomposed by saprophytic soil bacteria and fungi to form simple substances like water, carbon dioxide, amino acids and energy. The amino acids are converted into ammonia or ammonium ions. Production of ammonia during decomposition by micro-organisms (ammonifying bacteria) is called ammonification.
  • b) Nitrification — Some ammonia escapes into the soil, but much of it and the ammonium ions are converted into nitrates by nitrifying bacteria, in two groups: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrites, and Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates. This process is called nitrification. It takes place only in well-aerated soils because the bacteria are aerobic in nature.

2. Nitrogen Fixation

Any process of combining atmospheric nitrogen with other elements, by chemical means or bacterial action, is called nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen gas (N₂) has a very strong triple bond (N≡N), so a large amount of energy is required to break it. It can be fixed in three ways:

  • a) Atmospheric fixation — Fixation that occurs spontaneously by lightning; a small amount (5-8%) is fixed in this way. Lightning allows nitrogen and oxygen to combine and produce various oxides of nitrogen, which are carried by rain into the soil, where plants can use them.
  • b) Industrial fixation — The synthesis of nitrogen-containing fertilizers is called industrial fixation. (Ammonia, at 46% nitrogen as the book notes, remains the most important fertilizer.)
  • c) Biological fixation — Nitrogen-fixing bacteria fix about 60% of nitrogen gas in the atmosphere. Reduction of nitrogen gas to ammonia is energy intensive: it requires 16 molecules of ATP and a complex set of enzymes: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Only a few bacteria can carry out this reaction. Fixed nitrogen is made available to plants by the death and lysis of free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria, e.g. Azotobacter (aerobic) and Clostridium (anaerobic), or from the symbiotic association of nitrogen-fixing bacteria with plants, e.g. Rhizobium.

3. Assimilation

The formation of organic nitrogen compounds like amino acids from inorganic nitrogen compounds in the environment is called nitrogen assimilation. Plants obtain nitrogen as ammonia and nitrates from the soil, whereas animals take their nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.

4. Denitrification

Denitrification is the process in which a nitrate becomes molecular nitrogen, by the action of de-nitrifying bacteria; for example, Pseudomonas reduces nitrates in the soil to the gaseous state: NO₃ (nitrate) → NO₂ (nitrite) → NO → N₂O → N₂ (nitrogen gas). It returns nitrogen to the atmosphere — the opposite of nitrification.

NitrificationDenitrification
Ammonia → nitrites → nitratesNitrates → nitrites → nitrogen gas
By Nitrosomonas and NitrobacterBy Pseudomonas
Adds usable nitrogen for plantsRemoves nitrogen from the soil to the air

The nitrogen cycle: fixation brings N₂ into ammonia, nitrification makes nitrates for plants, and denitrification returns N₂ to the air.

Key Points

  • The nitrogen cycle moves nitrogen between earth and atmosphere through decomposition, fixation, assimilation and denitrification.
  • Ammonification makes ammonia from dead matter; nitrification converts ammonia to nitrites (Nitrosomonas) and then nitrates (Nitrobacter).
  • Fixation is atmospheric (lightning, 5-8%), industrial (fertilizers) or biological (bacteria, about 60%, needing 16 ATP).
  • Plants assimilate ammonia and nitrates; animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
  • Denitrification by Pseudomonas converts nitrates back to nitrogen gas.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels and Productivity
lessons.notes_html:
Energy moves life. Species are classified into trophic levels on the basis of their main source of nutrition and energy, and the rate at which producers fix that energy is the productivity of the ecosystem.

25.2 The Flow of Energy in Ecosystem

The cycle of energy is based on the flow of energy through different trophic levels in an ecosystem.

25.2.1 Concept of Trophic Levels

In an ecosystem the organisms are arranged in different feeding groups, each known as a trophic level:

  • First trophic level (T1) — Primary producers (plants, algae and some bacteria), the autotrophs of the ecosystem, use solar energy to produce organic plant material through photosynthesis. Producers have 10,000 kcal in the book's energy-flow figure.
  • Second trophic level (T2) — Herbivores or primary consumers that eat producers (1,000 kcal in the figure; e.g. rabbit).
  • Third trophic level (T3) — Predators, the secondary consumers that eat herbivores (100 kcal; e.g. snake). If larger predators, i.e. tertiary consumers, are present, they represent still higher trophic levels.
  • Fourth trophic level (T4) — Organisms that feed at several trophic levels, predators (a carnivore eating another carnivore) and omnivores, are classified at the highest trophic level at which they feed (10 kcal; e.g. eagle as tertiary consumer).
  • Fifth trophic level (T5) — Decomposers, which include bacteria, fungi, molds and detritivores such as worms and insects, break down wastes and dead organisms and return nutrients to the soil.

Note on the book's figures: the text places decomposers at T5, while Figure 25.5 labels the top (apex predators) as T5 and shows producers as T1 with 100% energy, herbivores 10%, carnivores 1%, secondary carnivores 0.1% and apex predators 0.01%. Remember the main idea both figures share: energy falls sharply at each step, and decomposers in fact feed on dead matter from every trophic level.

25.2.2 Concept of Productivity

The ultimate source of energy for ecosystems is the sun (solar energy). Only 1% of solar energy is incorporated into the ecosystem. The total amount of solar energy fixed by the producers during photosynthesis is called gross primary productivity (GPP). The amount of energy that remains available for plant growth after subtracting the fraction that plants use for respiration is termed net primary productivity (NPP), or biomass: NPP = GPP − respiration.

Productivity in land ecosystems depends on temperature and moisture. It generally rises with temperature up to about 30°C, after which it declines, and it is positively correlated with moisture. On land, primary productivity is thus highest in warm, wet zones in the tropics, where tropical forest biomes are located. In contrast, desert shrub ecosystems have the lowest productivity because their climates are extremely hot and dry.

Productivity in aquatic ecosystems is controlled mainly by light and nutrients. In oceans, light penetrates only up to 500 m. Marine primary productivity is high near coastlines. Among aquatic ecosystems, algal beds and coral reefs have the highest net primary production, while the lowest rates occur in the open ocean due to a lack of nutrients in the illuminated surface layers.

Key Points

  • Trophic levels: T1 producers, T2 herbivores (primary consumers), T3 secondary consumers, T4 higher predators and omnivores, T5 decomposers in the book's text list.
  • Only 1% of solar energy is incorporated into the ecosystem.
  • Gross primary productivity is all energy fixed in photosynthesis; net primary productivity is what remains after respiration.
  • Land productivity rises with temperature to about 30°C and with moisture — highest in tropical forests, lowest in deserts.
  • In oceans, light reaches only 500 m; algal beds and coral reefs are the most productive aquatic ecosystems.

lessons.title: Energy Flow Between Trophic Levels and Ecological Pyramids
lessons.notes_html:
A lot of energy is lost to the environment as food is transferred from one trophic level to the next. This loss is shown graphically by ecological pyramids and explains why food chains are short.

25.2.3 Energy Flow between the Trophic Levels

Ecosystems are transformers of energy. On average, about 10% of net energy production at one trophic level is passed on to the next level — the 10% rule: when energy is passed in an ecosystem from one trophic level to the next, only 10% of the energy will be passed on. Factors that reduce the energy transferred between trophic levels include respiration, growth, reproduction, defecation, non-predatory death (organisms that die but are not eaten by consumers) and the nutritional quality of the material.

Significance of decomposers in energy flow: decomposers process large amounts of organic material and return nutrients to the ecosystem in inorganic form, which is then taken up again by primary producers. Energy is not recycled during decomposition; rather, it is released in the form of heat. The book notes that more than 100,000 different types of decomposers are estimated to exist.

Ecological Pyramids

The diagram that shows the relative amount of energy or matter or numbers of organisms within each trophic level in a food chain or food web is called a pyramid. Ecological pyramids are therefore the graphical representation of ecological data. There are three types:

Pyramid of energy. Energy is lost to the environment as food is transferred from one trophic level to the next, in the following ways: as heat during respiration at every trophic level; through undigested matter egested by consumers; and through excretory products, e.g. urea, from consumers. The total energy level decreases progressively along the food chain, so the pyramid of energy is always broad at the base and narrow towards the apex (producers 100%, primary consumers 10%, secondary consumers 1%, third-level consumers 0.1%, apex predators 0.01%). Normally about 90% of energy is lost at each transfer. This progressive loss explains why food chains are generally short: a shorter food chain means more energy is available to the final consumer, so more energy is available to man if he feeds directly on crop plants rather than eating cattle that feed on plants.

Pyramid of biomass. Biomass is the total mass of living matter in each trophic level at any one time. For the food chain considered in the book, the pyramid of biomass has a similar shape to the pyramid of numbers: the mass of all grasses together is larger than the biomass of the snakes, and three hundred snakes are heavier than the ten hawks.

Pyramid of numbers. Consider a simple food chain of grass, rabbits, snakes and hawks. Suppose there are 10 hawks in a habitat and each hawk needs to feed on one snake every day: in one month the 10 hawks will need 300 snakes, while 300 snakes will need 4,500 rabbits in one month. A rabbit feeds voraciously and may require 20 or more grass plants per day, so in one month there must be about 2,700,000 grass plants to keep the rabbits alive. The number of organisms at each trophic level can thus be used to construct a pyramid of numbers, which for this food chain is broad at the base and narrow towards the top.

PyramidWhat It ShowsShape
EnergyEnergy at each trophic levelAlways upright — about 90% lost at each transfer
BiomassTotal dry mass at each levelUsually upright; inverted in some aquatic ecosystems
NumberNumber of organisms at each levelUsually upright; inverted for a single large tree with many herbivores

Key Points

  • Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next (the 10% rule); about 90% is lost as heat, egestion and excretion.
  • Because energy is lost at each step, food chains are short — usually only 4-5 levels.
  • Decomposers return nutrients in inorganic form, but energy itself is released as heat and is not recycled.
  • An ecological pyramid shows energy, biomass or numbers at each trophic level; the pyramid of energy is always upright.
  • Book example: 2,700,000 grass plants support 4,500 rabbits, 300 snakes and 10 hawks.

lessons.title: Ecological Succession: Primary, Secondary, Hydrosere and Xerosere
lessons.notes_html:
Ecological succession is the gradual process by which an ecosystem changes and develops over time, as one community replaces another, until a stable climax community is reached.

25.3 Ecological Succession

Succession is the change in community structure of an ecosystem over a period of time. Bare or disturbed areas are colonized step by step, each stage making conditions suitable for the next.

Kinds of Ecological Succession on the Basis of Origin

1) Primary succession. It is the start of vegetation on a bare or newly exposed area, such as land exposed as a result of soil erosion or melting of glaciers. The newly exposed land surface is unsuitable for a large number of species; only a few species are capable of growing in such areas. The first entrants are known as pioneer species or primary invaders. Primary succession modifies the habitat as a reaction of the plants to the environment and results in the creation of conditions suitable for the growth of other species: bare rock → colonized by pioneer species (e.g. moss) → decomposition creates a layer of topsoil → grasses grow and displace the pioneers → more nutrients in the soil allow shrub growth → increased soil depth allows growth of trees.

2) Secondary succession. It takes place in areas where the established or normal succession is disturbed by factors such as fire and grazing. The degree of resemblance to the original succession depends upon the degree of damage caused by the factors: if the damage is slight, the secondary succession will soon become primary-like; in case of severe damage, the secondary succession may remain different. Because soil already exists, secondary succession is faster than primary succession. In the book's comparison: primary succession runs bare rock → pioneer species appear → grassy weeds take root → tree seedlings and shrubs appear; secondary succession runs weeds and wildflowers grow → pine seedlings and other plants begin growing → pine forest grows → pine-oak-hickory forest develops.

Primary SuccessionSecondary Succession
Starts on a bare area with no soilStarts where a community was disturbed but soil remains
Begins with pioneer speciesBegins with weeds and fast-growing plants
Slow — soil must first be formedFaster — soil is already present

Successions According to Habitats

  • a) Hydroseres — Succession initiated in open water where plants can grow; the pattern is almost similar in all aquatic habitats. Succession beginning in ponds, lakes, marshes or elsewhere in water is termed hydrarch, and its stages are called a hydrosere.
  • b) Mesoseres — Succession that starts in areas which possess sufficient moisture for vegetation to develop.
  • c) Xeroseres — Colonization of bare rock by plants is a very good example of xerosere succession. The rock surface is extremely xeric except for short periods of rain when moisture is available. Succession initiated on bare rocks, sand dunes and rocky slopes (dry areas) is termed xerarch, and its stages are called a xerosere.

Stages Involved in the Development of Xeroseres (Xerarch Succession)

  • i) Crustose lichen stage — The pioneer species are always lichens, e.g. Rinodina (book spelling Rindodina) and Lecidea, which flourish during short moist periods but can withstand long periods of drought. These pioneers cause the accumulation of some organic matter and dust, providing a base for higher lichens.
  • ii) Foliose lichen stage — The crustose lichens are gradually replaced by foliose lichens such as Parmelia, Umbilicaria and Dermatocarpon. Foliose lichens absorb more and lose less water; more organic matter accumulates and a base for the growth of mosses is provided.
  • iii) Moss stage — Xerophytic mosses like Polytrichum and Tortula occupy the soil formed by the lichens. The mosses absorb much more water and nutrients owing to their longer rhizoids and can withstand desiccation. Further accumulation of organic matter forms a thick layer of humus capable of supporting herbs and grasses.
  • iv) Herbaceous stage — Annual herbs invade the area for a few generations; their growth is poor at first. As the dead parts of these herbs decay and form humus which enriches the soil, biennial and perennial herbs appear. These plants reduce evaporation and increase the moisture of the soil, and gradually a soil layer a few inches thick and rich in organic contents is produced, which can support shrubs. The herbaceous stage is the fourth stage of xerosere.
  • v) Shrub stage — Shrubs then invade the soil formed by the previous inhabitants and overshadow the herbs. More organic matter accumulates, the soil becomes richer and its water-retaining capacity increases.
  • vi) Tree and climax stage (the book prints “Three and Climax stage”, meaning Tree and Climax stage) — Among the first invaders are xerophytic trees, widely spaced; the trees increase in number and become stronger and widespread as the soil becomes deeper. Mesophytic trees replace the xerophytic shrubs. The interaction between species and environment continues for generations, and the result is a climax forest with thick growth of mesophytic trees associated with characteristic under-shrubs and herbs.

Key Points

  • Ecological succession is the gradual change and development of an ecosystem over time, ending in a climax community.
  • Primary succession starts on bare ground with pioneer species; secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains, so it is faster.
  • By habitat: hydrosere begins in water, mesosere in sufficient moisture, xerosere in dry areas such as bare rock.
  • Xerosere stages in order: crustose lichen → foliose lichen → moss → herbaceous → shrub → tree and climax forest.

lessons.title: Population Dynamics and Population Control in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
A population is a group of individuals of a single species living in a specific area at a specific time. Population dynamics studies how and why population size changes.

25.4 Population Dynamics

Population dynamics is the branch of life sciences which deals with the study of long-term and short-term changes in size, age and composition of a population, and the biological and environmental processes influencing those changes. Population dynamics deals with the way populations are affected by birth and death rates and by immigration and emigration.

25.4.1 Characteristics of a Population

Members of a population rely on the same resources, are influenced by similar environmental factors, and have a high likelihood of interacting with and breeding with one another. The characteristics of a population are: growth, density, distribution, carrying capacity and viable size.

  • Growth — Increase in the number of individuals of a population is called population growth. If a few individuals enter an unoccupied area where there is enough food and predation and disease are not too severe, reproduction will occur and numbers will increase. At first there may be a lag phase as the individuals settle into their new environment. As reproduction gets underway, the population shows exponential growth: the population size doubles at regular intervals, and during the exponential phase the population is said to grow geometrically.
  • Density — Density is the number of individuals per unit area or volume, e.g. the number of apple trees per square kilometre in Ziarat, or the number of E. coli bacteria per millilitre in a test tube.
  • Distribution — The way a population is spatially distributed across an area, driven largely by food supply or other resources, is called distribution. Three patterns are found: clumped (individuals aggregate in patches), uniform (individuals are evenly spaced) and random distribution (unpredictable spacing among individuals).
  • Carrying capacity — There is a limit to the number of individuals that can occupy a habitat. The carrying capacity is defined as the maximum population size that a particular environment can support. Ecosystems cannot exceed their carrying capacity for a long period of time; otherwise species will deplete sources of food, water, etc.
  • Viable (minimum) size — The minimum population size needed for the survival of the species; below it, the population may die out.

Health Services through Various Programmes

The Department of Population Welfare is providing Family Planning and Reproductive Health Services. These include: (1) Family Welfare Centres, (2) Mobile Service Units and (3) Reproductive Health Services (RHS). These centres are run by various NGOs with the assistance of the Population Welfare Department.

Control of Population Growth in Pakistan

The Ministry of Population Welfare, Government of Pakistan is responsible for the control of population growth in Pakistan. The population welfare programme is an ongoing programme launched by the ministry since 1960. The first ever population policy in Pakistan was announced on 11th July, 2002. The policy is wide in scope: it states a commitment to reduce the incidence of unwanted fertility, promote the small family norm, make an investment in the youthful population and focus on male involvement. The overall vision is to achieve population stabilization at replacement level — a total fertility rate of 2.1 children per woman by 2020 (the book prints “2:1 child per woman”). It aims to increase awareness of the adverse consequences of rapid population growth at national, provincial, district and community level, promote family planning as an entitlement based on informed and voluntary choice, and attain a reduction in infertility. Rapid human population growth strains the carrying capacity of the Earth and increases consumption of resources, so controlling it protects future generations.

Key Points

  • Population dynamics studies long- and short-term changes in population size, age and composition, driven by births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
  • Characteristics of a population: growth, density, distribution, carrying capacity and viable size.
  • Growth begins with a lag phase, then becomes exponential (geometric) as numbers double at regular intervals.
  • Carrying capacity is the maximum population size a particular environment can support.
  • In Pakistan, the Population Welfare Department (programme since 1960; first population policy 11 July 2002) provides family planning through Family Welfare Centres, Mobile Service Units and RHS centres.

lessons.title: Human Impact: Nuclear Power, Carbon Dioxide and Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
Human activity has been affecting the environment for thousands of years. Population growth leads to loss of natural habitat, and activities such as the use of nuclear fuel, industrialization, urbanization and transportation directly cause deforestation, ozone layer depletion, water pollution, global warming, desertification and increased erosion of land.

25.5 Human Impacts on Environment

Deforestation causes loss of species of fauna and flora, and loss of oxygen production and carbon dioxide elimination. Man's impact is studied here under nuclear power, carbon dioxide and global warming, acid rain and ozone depletion.

25.5.1 Nuclear Power

Nuclear power is the use of a nuclear reaction that releases nuclear energy to generate heat. This heat is used in steam turbines to produce electricity in a nuclear power plant. The scarcity of fossil fuels, which are not available in all countries, is the reason for the development of nuclear power stations.

Advantages of nuclear power:

  • 15% of the world's electricity is provided by nuclear power.
  • Nuclear power costs about the same as coal, so it is not expensive to make electricity.
  • It does not produce smoke or carbon dioxide, so it does not contribute to the greenhouse effect.
  • It produces huge amounts of energy from small amounts of fuel, and produces small amounts of waste.
  • Nuclear power is a reliable and un-exhaustible source of energy (in the book's wording).

Disadvantages of using nuclear power:

  • It releases radioactive wastes into the environment, so disposal and safety are important.
  • It incurs a heavy initial cost to construct a power plant.
  • There are hazardous implications for human lives, and the technology can be misused, especially by terrorists; nuclear weapons can destroy humanity.

Chernobyl Nuclear Power Incidence. The Chernobyl disaster was a nuclear accident that occurred on 26 April, 1986 at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine. An explosion and fire released large quantities of radioactive contamination into the atmosphere, which spread over much of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) and Europe. Approximately over 500,000 workers were affected, apart from the 57 direct deaths in the accident itself. The United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation predicted in 2005 that up to 4,000 additional cancer deaths related to the accident would appear among the 600,000 persons receiving more significant exposures. (The book's side box also records the Japan earthquake of 11 March 2011, magnitude 9.00, which ruptured a 500 km fault zone off the northeast coast of Japan.)

25.5.2 Carbon Dioxide and Global Warming

Due to the burning of fossil fuel in motor vehicles and industrial processes, the amount of CO₂ is increased in the atmosphere. CO₂ absorbs high-energy radiations and thus results in an increase in atmospheric temperature. This rise in temperature is known as global warming. CO₂ is also injurious to human health, as it decreases the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.

Causes of increasing concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere: burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas for industry, driving transport, heating homes and generating electricity; the burning of wild forests; a marked increase in the CO₂ percentage since the industrial revolution; and eruption of volcanoes from time to time.

CO₂ concentration and global warming: the amount of CO₂ in the air is increasing day by day. It makes up about 0.04% of the air now, compared with 0.03% in the mid-twentieth century. It is very likely that raised atmospheric CO₂ levels are causing the average temperatures on Earth to increase — the process called global warming or the greenhouse effect: the Sun's radiation travels toward the Earth; some energy is reflected and the rest is absorbed by the Earth's surface; the Earth also emits heat back to space and some of it passes directly through the atmosphere, but greenhouse gases trap most of it, keeping the planet warm.

Long-term effects of global warming: CO₂ increase prevents reflection of infra-red radiation, which warms the Earth. A worst-case scenario suggests the warming would be great near the poles. The resulting melting of polar ice might raise sea level by an estimated 100 m, gradually flooding areas 150 km (or more) inland from the current coastline. A warming trend would also alter the geographical distribution of precipitation, making major agricultural areas drier. These figures are the book's worst-case estimates.

Key Points

  • Human activities — deforestation, industrialization, urbanization, transport and nuclear fuel use — drive habitat loss, pollution, global warming and desertification.
  • Nuclear power generates heat for steam turbines; it provides 15% of world electricity and no CO₂, but produces radioactive waste and carries accident and misuse risks.
  • The Chernobyl accident occurred on 26 April 1986 in Ukraine; 57 direct deaths and widespread radioactive contamination followed.
  • CO₂ has risen from 0.03% to about 0.04% of the air, mainly from burning fossil fuels, causing the greenhouse effect and global warming.

lessons.title: Acid Rain and Ozone Depletion
lessons.notes_html:
Two further results of human activity are acid rain, which damages soil, water, buildings and health, and ozone depletion, which removes Earth's shield against ultraviolet radiation.

25.5.3 Acid Rain

Acid rain, or acid deposition, is a broad term that includes any form of precipitation that contains acidic components such as sulphuric acid or nitric acid. The precipitation is not necessarily wet or liquid: the definition includes snow, fog and hail. The type of acid rain that contains water is called wet deposition, while acid rain that contains dust or gases is called dry deposition.

Causes of acid rain: acid rain may fall hundreds of miles away from the source of pollution. It is a natural phenomenon caused by chemicals emitted during volcanic eruptions and forest fires. However, the majority of acid rain is caused by human activity, such as the burning of coal by electricity generating plants, industrial boilers and large smelters that obtain metals from ores, which release sulphur dioxide (SO₂); in addition, nitrogen oxides (NOx) are emitted by automobiles. The causes of acid rain due to human activities are called anthropogenic sources. These gases react with water vapour in the atmosphere to form the acids.

Effects of acid rain:

  • It increases soil acidity.
  • It damages life in farms and forests.
  • It kills aquatic organisms and prevents their successful reproduction.
  • It increases the quantity of certain metals, such as aluminium, that may prove toxic to many organisms in the ecosystem.
  • It causes extensive damage to buildings and stone structures, known as stone cancer.
  • It adversely affects the nervous, respiratory and digestive systems of man.

25.5.4 Ozone Depletion

The ozone layer protects all life from the Sun's harmful radiations. The Earth's atmosphere is composed of several layers: the lower layer is the troposphere (10 km altitude) and the next layer is the stratosphere (10-50 km). The ozone layer is concentrated in 15-30 km above the Earth's surface in the stratosphere and contains O₃ molecules. Ozone is constantly being formed and broken down in the high atmosphere. Today there is widespread concern that the ozone layer is deteriorating due to the release of pollution containing the chemicals chlorine and fluorine.

Composition of the ozone layer: ozone is a bluish, explosive and highly poisonous gas. In the stratosphere, the normal concentration of ozone is about 0.1 part per million (ppm), compared with 0.02 ppm in the lower atmosphere. The ozone hole is not technically a hole where no ozone is present, but a region of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over the Antarctic that appears at the beginning of Southern Hemisphere spring (August-October). The average concentration of ozone in the atmosphere is about 300 Dobson Units; any area where the concentration drops below 220 Dobson Units is considered part of the ozone hole. In 1985 it was discovered that springtime levels of stratospheric ozone over Antarctica had declined by over 40% since 1977.

Formation of the ozone layer: ozone is formed in the atmosphere when ultraviolet radiation from the Sun splits one oxygen molecule into two oxygen atoms; the atomic oxygen then combines with another oxygen molecule to form ozone (O₃).

Causes of ozone layer depletion: in the stratosphere there is a group of commercially important compounds called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). They have been used as propellants in aerosol cans, as coolants (e.g. Freon) in air conditioners and refrigerators, as foam (e.g. Styrofoam) for insulation and packing, and as cleaners in the electronic industry. Ultraviolet radiation breaks CFCs and similar compounds into chlorine, fluorine and carbon. As CFCs rise to the atmosphere, the ultraviolet rays release chlorine. Under certain stratospheric conditions, chlorine and fluorine react with ozone, converting it into molecular oxygen (O₂) and atomic oxygen (O), so the ozone layer is thinned and the ozone hole develops over Antarctica.

Role of the ozone layer in protecting life on Earth: ozone molecules in the stratosphere absorb incoming solar ultraviolet radiations, protecting life on Earth from harmful UV rays.

Effects of ultraviolet radiation on human health: with depletion of the ozone layer, UV radiations reach the Earth's surface. Excessive exposure to UV radiation is linked to a number of human health problems, including sunburn, premature aging of skin, skin cancer and cataracts. Photosynthesis by phytoplankton is also affected and reduced by ultraviolet radiation, and increased UV harms crops, aquatic life and the immune system.

Key Points

  • Acid rain (acid deposition) contains sulphuric or nitric acid and falls as wet deposition (rain, snow, fog, hail) or dry deposition (dust, gases).
  • Most acid rain is anthropogenic: SO₂ from burning coal in power plants, boilers and smelters, and NOx from automobiles; it can fall hundreds of miles from the source.
  • Acid rain increases soil acidity, kills aquatic organisms, damages farms, forests and buildings (stone cancer) and harms human health.
  • The ozone layer (O₃) lies in the stratosphere, concentrated at 15-30 km, and absorbs harmful UV radiation.
  • CFCs release chlorine under UV radiation, which destroys ozone; the ozone hole forms over Antarctica, increasing skin cancer and cataracts.

lessons.title: Environmental Resources, Energy Sources and Protection of Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Wherever humans have gone, they have altered the environment according to their needs. The future of mankind depends on the protection and conservation of environmental resources.

25.6 Environmental Resources and their Depletion

Living organisms are important natural resources.

25.6.1 Kinds of Natural Resources

All resources of the environment can be divided into two groups: renewable and non-renewable resources.

  • Renewable resources — Un-exhaustible resources that replace themselves quickly enough to keep pace with consumption. Examples are air, water, land and wild life. Living organisms use these resources continuously, but they are constantly replaced by natural cycles, e.g. the water cycle, carbon cycle, oxygen cycle and nitrogen cycle.
  • Non-renewable resources — Resources formed at a rate much slower than their environmental consumption. They are exhaustible and cannot be replaced if destroyed. Examples are various metals, non-metallic minerals, coal, oil and natural gas.
Renewable ResourcesNon-Renewable Resources
Replace themselves quickly; un-exhaustibleForm much slower than they are used; exhaustible
Air, water, land, wild lifeMetals, minerals, coal, oil, natural gas
Replaced by natural cyclesCannot be replaced once destroyed

25.6.2 Conventional and Non-Conventional Energy Sources

Conventional energy sources are energy sources used for a long time: fossil fuels (coal, natural gas, oil), firewood, wood, peat and uranium. Fossil fuels provide 95% of the energy requirement and are non-renewable — they are the remains of plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. Humans prefer conventional sources because they are inexpensive and use established technologies that produce energy around the clock. Their disadvantages are a limited supply and that burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, etc.) and contributes to acid rain and pollution.

Non-conventional energy sources are continuously replenished by natural processes and are not commonly used. They include solar energy, hydro-electric energy (dams in rivers), wind, tidal and ocean wave energy, geothermal energy (heat from deep under the ground), ocean thermal power, biomass, bio-fuel (ethanol from plants) and bio-gas; they are also called renewable energy sources. They are abundant, pollution-free and eco-friendly, but can be inconsistent and costly to operate. In Pakistan, non-conventional sources are wind energy, hydroelectric power, solar energy and biogas.

Conventional SourcesNon-Conventional Sources
Used for a long time; inexpensive, established technologyNewer and less commonly used; continuously replenished
Fossil fuels, firewood, peat, uraniumSolar, wind, hydro-electric, tidal, geothermal, biomass, bio-gas
Limited supply; release greenhouse gasesAbundant and pollution-free, but inconsistent and costly to operate

Depletion of Resources

Resource depletion is the exhaustion of raw materials within a region; use of resources beyond their rate of replacement is considered resource depletion. Causes of resource depletion include over-consumption (excessive or unnecessary use of resources), non-equitable distribution of resources, overpopulation, slash-and-burn agricultural practices, technological and industrial development, erosion, irrigation, mining for oil and minerals, and pollution or contamination of resources.

25.6.3 Protection of Environmental Resources

Our health and well-being are closely linked to the quality of our air, water, soil and biological resources. We can protect them by reusing and recycling, educating the common masses, conserving resources, using renewable resources for energy, and planting trees.

Role of Government: the government controls and develops forests, dams, irrigation systems, power stations, roads, mines and industries. The Ministry of Environment plans and coordinates environment and forestry programmes: conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife, prevention and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas. Environmental impact is assessed before any project that can damage the environment. Earth Day on 22nd April and tree plantation week are observed every year to educate the people. The book's example is the Tsunami Billion Tree Scheme, launched in 2014 by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK), restoring 350,000 hectares of forests and degraded land.

Role of Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs): NGOs play a very important role in environmental protection and in creating mass awareness of problems caused by neglect and uncontrolled exploitation of natural resources; some work in awareness, others in research. Pakistan faces deforestation, air pollution, climate change, pesticide misuse and desertification, and the government alone cannot tackle these efficiently. Well-known organizations named in the unit include the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF).

Key Points

  • Renewable resources (air, water, land, wild life) replace themselves through natural cycles; non-renewable resources (coal, oil, gas, metals, minerals) form far slower than they are used.
  • Conventional energy sources have been used for a long time — fossil fuels provide 95% of energy needs; non-conventional sources (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass) are renewable and cleaner.
  • Resource depletion is caused by over-consumption, overpopulation, unequal distribution, slash-and-burn farming, industry, mining and pollution.
  • Protection needs reuse and recycling, conservation, tree planting, government action through the Ministry of Environment, and NGO awareness work (IUCN, WWF).

lessons.title: Cloning of Genes Through Recombinant DNA Technology
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology is any technique that uses living organisms to make products. It was used as far back as biblical times — yeast to bake bread, ferment wine and make cheese. In 1862, Louis Pasteur discovered that fermentation is caused by micro-organisms, not an inorganic chemical process. After Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900, geneticists made advances that led to the new era of DNA technology: genes can now be removed from one organism and inserted into another to produce insulin, growth hormone, drugs and vaccines, clean up pollutants, kill insect pests and increase soil fertility. This unit deals with genetic engineering — the manipulation or alteration of the genetic material of an organism.

26.1 Cloning of Genes

Cloning of genes produces many identical copies (clones) of a single gene. There are two ways of cloning a gene: recombinant DNA technology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Recombinant DNA technology is used when a very large quantity of a gene is required, while PCR is used to create an optimum number of copies in a test tube in the laboratory. Cloning is a technique for developing a large number of genes, identical cells, tissues or organisms.

26.1.1 Gene Cloning through Recombinant DNA Technology

Recombinant DNA technology, popularly called genetic engineering, is a series of procedures used to join together (recombine) two or more segments of DNA from different sources. The recombinant DNA (rDNA) is also called chimeric DNA. To produce recombinant DNA, these components are required:

  • The gene of interest (desired gene) to be cloned.
  • Molecular scissors (restriction endonuclease) to cut out the gene of interest.
  • A vector or molecular carrier to carry the gene of interest.
  • The enzyme ligase, which forms the phosphodiester linkage between two adjacent nucleotides.
  • An expression system (such as bacteria) in which the gene, along with the vector, is inserted to get a large number of desired genes or specific chemical products.

26.1.2 Role of Molecular Scissors and DNA Ligase

Molecular scissors are restriction endonucleases, natural enzymes of bacteria first isolated by Hamilton D. Smith (1970) at John Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, USA. He observed that the enzyme cuts viral DNA to prevent replication of viral DNA in bacteria. Different species of bacteria produce different restriction endonucleases, which cut DNA at a very specific sequence of four to eight nucleotides arranged symmetrically in reverse order. Such sequences are called palindromic sequences and their cutting points are restriction sites. Over 3,000 restriction enzymes have been studied in detail and more than 600 are available commercially (230 different DNA sequences); about twenty are frequently used in recombinant DNA technology. Restriction enzymes are named after their host of origin.

EcoRI (isolated from Escherichia coli) is the most commonly used restriction enzyme. It cuts double-stranded DNA so that single-stranded complementary ends are left, with (AATT) bases at the cleavage site of its palindromic sequence (GAATTC in the book's Fig. 26.1). These complementary ends are called sticky ends (a staggered cut) because they bind by complementary base pairing, so foreign DNA with the same palindromic sequence is easily inserted into vector DNA.

Gene of Interest

The desired gene can be acquired in three ways:

  • Isolated from the chromosomes by cutting at the flanking sites of the gene with restriction endonucleases (enzymes bacteria use for their own protection against viruses — they cut viral DNA but do not harm the bacterial chromosome).
  • Synthesized in the laboratory from mRNA using reverse transcriptase, naturally found in retroviruses; this DNA is called complementary DNA (cDNA).
  • If the gene is small, synthesized artificially by a machine called a DNA synthesizer, which creates DNA molecules of a desired nucleotide sequence.

Role of Molecular Carriers or Vectors

A vector acts as a vehicle for carrying foreign DNA into a host cell for multiplication. A common vector is a plasmid — a small extra-chromosomal circular DNA molecule in bacteria, containing genes for antibiotic resistance and fertility, etc. Commonly used vectors are plasmids, lambda phage DNA, yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs) and bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs).

DNA Ligase

DNA ligase acts as molecular glue: it seals the foreign pieces of DNA into the vector to form recombinant or chimeric DNA. The complementary ends of two DNA molecules are joined by hydrogen bonding, and ligase forms the phosphodiester linkage between adjacent nucleotides.

Key Points

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms to make products; genetic engineering alters genetic material.
  • Genes are cloned by recombinant DNA technology (large quantities) or PCR (copies in a test tube).
  • Restriction endonucleases are molecular scissors; Hamilton D. Smith first isolated them in 1970.
  • They cut at palindromic restriction sites of 4-8 nucleotides, leaving sticky ends; EcoRI is the commonest example.
  • A gene of interest is obtained by isolation, from mRNA as cDNA, or by a DNA synthesizer.
  • Vectors (plasmids, lambda phage, YACs, BACs) carry the gene; DNA ligase is the molecular glue that seals it in.

lessons.title: Expression of Recombinant DNA, Gene Delivery and Gene Validation
lessons.notes_html:
Once a gene of interest has been sealed into a vector, the recombinant DNA must enter a living system that will multiply it and express it as a product. This lesson completes section 26.1.2: the expression system, the cut-copy-paste steps for creating recombinant DNA, the techniques that deliver genes into cells, and how successful transformants are validated (selected).

Expression of Recombinant DNA / Expression System

The most suitable organism to multiply and express recombinant DNA is bacteria, because they have a short generation time and a simple genetic system. Bacterial cells easily take up recombinant plasmid, especially if treated with calcium chloride to make them more permeable. As the bacterium reproduces, each daughter bacterium contains the gene of interest, which expresses itself and makes a product, e.g. in Agrobacterium tumefaciens.

Steps for Creation of Recombinant DNA (Plasmid)

The simplified steps for creating a recombinant DNA and a transgenic species are cut, copy and paste:

  • 1. Cut: A gene of interest is removed from the cell of an organism using molecular scissors.
  • 2. Copy: Multiple copies are made (gene cloning), usually in bacteria (sometimes phage), e.g. Escherichia coli is the regulating system.
  • 3. Paste: The genes are inserted (pasted) into a bacterium, an egg cell or a plant cell of another species and (after fertilization in the case of an animal) become part of the newly formed transgenic organism's DNA.
  • 4. The transgenic organism develops into a mature organism with the new gene 'switched on' to function.

Transformation of Expressing System / Gene Delivery Techniques

  • Agrobacterium-mediated transformation — bacteria take up recombinant plasmid, especially after calcium chloride treatment makes them more permeable; as the cell reproduces, a bacterial clone forms and each new cell contains at least one plasmid.
  • Micro-injection — in animals, DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an egg, usually under an optical microscope, when creating transgenic species.
  • Electroporation — high-voltage electric shocks increase membrane permeability to introduce DNA into cells.
  • Biolistics — delivery of nucleic acid (recombinant genes) into plant cells by high-speed particle bombardment; DNA-coated metal particles are propelled by a gene gun.
  • Vectors — DNA may be carried by an adenovirus, a liposome or a bacterial plasmid into cells; it either enters directly into blood or may be delivered by aerosol (nasal or oral). Liposomes are minute spherical sacs of molecules enclosing a water droplet, carrying genes or drugs.

Gene Validation

For a bacterial clone: a particular antibiotic is added to the transformed clone; if the clone has resistance against the antibiotic, it remains alive and continues to grow. Important antibiotic markers are ampicillin (the book prints 'Ampiciline'), kanamycin (printed 'Kalamycine') and streptomycin, etc.

For animal and plant cells: a gene for a fluorescent protein from jellyfish is now used to determine whether an individual has successfully incorporated a transgenic gene. The fluorescent gene is used as a marker, attached to the gene of interest that will be inserted into the prospective transgenic organism, so the resulting offspring (cell) gives fluorescence under certain lighting conditions.

Key Points

  • Bacteria are the main expression system: short generation time, simple genetics, and calcium chloride makes them permeable to plasmids.
  • Creating recombinant DNA is cut (remove the gene), copy (clone it, usually in bacteria) and paste (insert it into another species).
  • Gene delivery methods: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, micro-injection, electroporation, biolistics and vectors such as adenovirus, liposomes or plasmids.
  • Bacterial transformants are validated with antibiotic markers such as ampicillin, kanamycin and streptomycin.
  • In animal and plant cells, a jellyfish fluorescent-protein gene attached to the gene of interest marks successful transformants by fluorescence.

lessons.title: Polymerase Chain Reaction: Components, Mechanism and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) can create millions of copies of a single gene or any specific small piece of DNA quickly in a test tube. It was originally invented by Kary Mullis in 1983; he received the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1993. PCR is based on the in vitro replication process and takes its name from the DNA replication enzyme in a cell; it is a chain reaction because polymerase carries out replication over and over again until there are millions of copies of the desired gene (DNA). The book notes that millions of copies of the gene of interest can be obtained after 30 cycles of PCR.

26.1.3 Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)

Components of PCR Technique

  • Template DNA or target DNA — the specific DNA to be copied, e.g. a useful gene, DNA of an infected organism, or DNA for fingerprinting.
  • Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) — four types of free nucleotides, dATP, dGTP, dTTP and dCTP, used as raw material for new DNA.
  • Primers — sequences of about 15-20 bases needed because DNA polymerase cannot start replication itself; they are complementary to the bases on either side of the target DNA. Primers are of two kinds: forward (sense) primers and reverse (antisense) primers.
  • Taq polymerase — a temperature-tolerant (thermostable) enzyme extracted from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which lives in hot springs; the book states it can withstand high temperature up to 115°C. PCR is done in an automatic PCR machine or thermocycler, which regulates temperature during the steps.

Mechanism of Polymerase Chain Reaction

Typically, PCR consists of a series of 20-40 repeated temperature and time change cycles, programmed in the thermocycler. Each cycle has three steps:

  • Denaturation (unwinding): The template is heated to 94-95°C for one minute (maximum up to five minutes). The double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) becomes single-stranded (ssDNA), and each strand acts as a template for in vitro DNA synthesis.
  • Primer annealing (hybridization): The forward and backward primers anneal to the single-stranded template DNA at complementary regions, usually at 54-55°C for approximately 1-2 minutes (temperature depends on primer length and sequence).
  • Extension or polymerization: Taq DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands at the 3' ends of the primers using dNTPs, standardized at 72°C and taking one minute. At the end of the first cycle, one target DNA molecule is converted into two daughter molecules; the number of DNA molecules doubles after each cycle, so amplification is exponential.

The Application of Polymerase Chain Reaction

  • To diagnose viral infections, genetic disorders and cancer; PCR is an efficient diagnostic technique for specific infectious agents e.g. HBV, HCV, HIV.
  • To identify criminals in forensic laboratories (DNA fingerprinting); suspect DNA and crime-scene DNA are analysed by PCR.
  • To determine the evolutionary history of human populations — DNA was sequenced from a 76,000-year-old mummified human brain and from a 17 to 20 million-year-old plant fossil after PCR amplification.
  • Detection of micro-organisms in food samples, water and the environment with species-specific primers.
  • Reactions for DNA sequencing; genome analysis and generating markers for genetic and physical maps; RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase-PCR) makes cDNA directly from purified mRNA.
  • Detection of genetic mutations responsible for genetic diseases and cancers, even in embryonic conditions and in sex cells (sperm and egg).

Key Points
