  • PCR makes millions of copies of a gene in a test tube; Kary Mullis invented it in 1983 (Nobel Prize 1993).
  • Components: template DNA, dNTPs (dATP, dGTP, dTTP, dCTP), primers of 15-20 bases, and Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus.
  • One cycle: denaturation at 94-95°C, annealing at 54-55°C, extension at 72°C; 20-40 cycles double the DNA each time.
  • Applications: diagnosis (HBV, HCV, HIV), forensics, evolutionary studies, detecting micro-organisms, sequencing and genome analysis.

lessons.title: Genomic Library, cDNA Library and Locating a Gene with a Probe
lessons.notes_html:
A cloned gene is most useful when it can be stored and found again. A genomic library stores the whole DNA of an organism as a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, and a labelled probe is then used to locate the one clone that carries the gene of interest.

26.1.4 Genomic Library

A genome is a full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual. A genomic library is a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, each clone containing a particular segment of DNA from the source cell. The collection of genomic libraries of different organisms is called a gene bank.

Making a Genomic Library

  • An organism's DNA is sliced into pieces by a molecular scissor (restriction enzyme).
  • The pieces are put into vectors (plasmids or viruses) cut with the same molecular scissor, and the vectors are taken up by host bacteria.
  • The ligase enzyme connects the DNA pieces, now called recombinant DNA.
  • The entire collection of these bacterial or bacteriophage clones contains all the genes of that organism.

Complementary DNA Library (cDNA Library)

The complementary DNA library is the collection of clones of DNA which are complementary copies of mature mRNA (devoid of introns) separated from a particular cell.

How Reverse Transcriptase Helps to Make a Mammalian Gene for Cloning

For a mammalian gene to be expressed in a bacterium, the gene must be accompanied by a proper regulatory region, and the DNA should not contain introns, because bacterial cells do not have the necessary enzymes to process or mature primary mRNA. The enzyme reverse transcriptase is used to make a DNA copy of all the mature mRNA molecules from a cell. This DNA is called complementary DNA (cDNA) and does not contain introns: the gene is transcribed to RNA, introns are removed and exons spliced together for mRNA, the mRNA is isolated and reverse transcriptase synthesizes a DNA strand, the mRNA is digested, and DNA polymerase synthesizes the second strand.

Locating a Gene of Interest with a Particular Probe

A particular probe is a single-stranded nucleotide sequence that will hybridize (pair) into a certain piece of DNA; it is used to search a genetic library for a certain gene. Location of the probe is possible because the probe carries either a radioactive isotope of phosphorus or a fluorescent dye. Steps:

  • Bacterial cells, each carrying a particular DNA fragment, are plated onto agar in a petri dish.
  • The probe is placed on these petri dishes; the probe is made of nine or more nucleotides.
  • The probe hybridizes (forms pairing) into the gene of interest.
  • The gene can be isolated from the fragment.
  • This particular fragment can be cloned further or even analysed for its particular DNA sequence.

Key Points

  • A genome is the full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual.
  • A genomic library is a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones covering all the genes of an organism; libraries of different organisms form a gene bank.
  • It is made by cutting DNA and vectors with the same restriction enzyme, joining with ligase, and taking the vectors up into host bacteria.
  • A cDNA library holds complementary copies of mature mRNA, without introns.
  • Reverse transcriptase makes intron-free cDNA from mature mRNA, so mammalian genes can be expressed in bacteria.
  • A labelled probe (radioactive phosphorus or fluorescent dye) hybridizes to and locates the gene of interest in the library.

lessons.title: DNA Sequencing and Gel Electrophoresis
lessons.notes_html:
DNA sequencing is the process of determining the order of the four chemical building blocks known as 'bases' that make up the DNA molecule. The sequence tells scientists the kind of genetic information carried in a particular segment. One of the important tools used in DNA sequencing techniques is gel electrophoresis.

26.2 DNA Sequencing

26.2.1 Gel Electrophoresis

This laboratory technique is used to separate fragments of DNA, RNA and proteins in an effort to identify their origin. Enzymes chop the long filaments of DNA into fragments of varying size. The fragments are placed into small wells (holes) in a gel made of agarose or polyacrylamide, aligned along one end. The gel is exposed to an electric current, positive on one side and negative on the other. DNA fragment travel is inversely proportional to its length: the biggest, heaviest fragments do not move easily, get stuck close to the wells, and the most (small, highly) charged particles pass through with less difficulty; intermediate particles are distributed in between. In the end, fragments of different sizes leave a banded pattern of DNA on the gel.

Agarose GelPolyacrylamide Gel
Used for relatively large DNA molecules (more than 50 nucleotides)Used for high resolution of short DNA fragments (less than 50 nucleotides)

Visualization of Fragments

To visualize DNA fragments, the gel is stained with DNA-binding fluorescent dyes and viewed under an ultraviolet transilluminator. DNA bands can also be transferred from the gel to a nitrocellulose membrane for autoradiography (X-ray imaging). Thick bands represent a high concentration of same-size fragments, while thin bands exhibit low concentration. If a particular sized fragment is to be used for further analysis, the piece of gel containing that band can be cut and its DNA purified again.

26.2.2 DNA Sequencing Techniques

In the late 1970s, methods were developed that allowed the nucleotide sequence of any purified DNA fragment to be determined simply and quickly. These methods are based upon three steps:

  • To generate pieces of DNA of different sizes, all starting from the same point and ending at a different point.
  • Separation of these different pieces of DNA on agarose gel.
  • Reading of the sequence from the gel.

Horizontal and Vertical Gel Electrophoresis

The book's Fig. 26.6 shows the apparatus in two forms. In horizontal gel electrophoresis, the gel lies flat in a tank of buffer solution, with slots for samples at one end, electrodes at the two ends, and the bands (visible after suitable treatment) moving across the gel in the direction of movement. In vertical gel electrophoresis, the gel stands upright in a plastic frame: sample wells and buffer are at the top, the stacking gel lies above the running gel, the cathode (−) is at the top and the anode (+) at the bottom, with buffer below. In both forms the separated fragments form bands whose position shows their size.

Key Points

  • DNA sequencing determines the order of the four bases in a DNA molecule.
  • Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA and protein fragments; fragment travel is inversely proportional to length.
  • Agarose is for large DNA (more than 50 nucleotides); polyacrylamide gives high resolution for short fragments (less than 50).
  • Bands are visualized with fluorescent dyes under UV, or by autoradiography; thick bands mean high concentration.
  • Sequencing methods rest on three steps: make different-sized pieces, separate them on a gel, and read the sequence.

lessons.title: Sanger-Coulson, Maxam-Gilbert and Automated DNA Sequencing
lessons.notes_html:
Three methods are generally used to generate DNA fragments of different sizes for sequencing: the Sanger-Coulson method, the Maxam-Gilbert method and automated DNA sequencing (next generation sequencing).

26.2.3 Methods of DNA Sequencing

i) Sanger-Coulson Method / Dideoxy Method

In this method, dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) are used to terminate DNA synthesis at different sites, so it is also called the dideoxy method. It was developed by Frederick Sanger along with Andrew Coulson in 1977; they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1980. It has become the standard because of its practicality and is similar to the natural process of DNA synthesis.

Procedure: Dideoxyribonucleotides are the same as deoxyribonucleotides except they contain a hydrogen group on the 3' carbon instead of a hydroxyl group (OH). When a dideoxyribonucleotide is integrated into a sequence, no phosphodiester bond can form with the next nucleotide, so the DNA chain is terminated. For sequencing, double-stranded DNA is denatured by heat into single strands; the template strand is tagged with a known sequence at its 3' end so a complementary primer can bind. The solution is divided into four tubes labelled 'G', 'A', 'T' and 'C': the 'G' tube gets all four dNTPs, ddGTP and DNA polymerase; the 'A' tube ddATP; the 'T' tube ddTTP; the 'C' tube ddCTP. Normal free A, T, G and C nucleotides and Taq polymerase are also present, and the tubes are placed in a PCR machine. Whenever a dideoxynucleotide is incorporated, a chain-terminating event occurs — e.g. in the ddTTP tube, only fragments terminating on 'T' are produced. All reactions start from the same nucleotide and end with a specific base, so bands of all different lengths are produced. The DNA is denatured again and the contents of each tube are run in separate lanes on a polyacrylamide gel; the gel is exposed to UV light or X-rays, depending on the labelling method, and the sequence is read.

ii) Maxam-Gilbert Method

This method was developed by Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert (1976-77). It is also known as the chemical cleavage method because it is based on chemical modification of DNA and subsequent cleavage at specific bases.

Procedure: The DNA to be sequenced must denature so the two strands separate; one strand is purified and divided into four samples (G, A+G, T+C and C). Each sample is treated with modified chemical reagents and cleavage reagents: the former chemically modify the nucleotides they are specific for, making them susceptible to cleavage, while the latter cut the DNA strand at specific points. For example, in the 'G' sample the fragment is cleaved from all points where G is present; in 'A+G' from A as well as G, and so on. The products are run through gel electrophoresis and the sequence is finally read from the autoradiograph of the gel pattern.

iii) Automated DNA Sequencing

Automatic sequencing machines have greatly improved the quality and speed of sequencing; the basic principle is the same as manual sequencing except for a few differences. There is no need for radiolabelling and autoradiography: fluorescently labelled ddNTPs make reading easy, convenient and automatic with UV laser detectors. Each of the four types of ddNTPs can be labelled with a specific dye, so a specific colour is attributed to a particular nucleotide or base. After electrophoresis, the computer reads the sequence: laser beams excite the fluorescent dyes, which emit specific spectral waves (coloured light) recorded by a photoelectric device; the data is fed to a computer, converted into the nucleotide sequence, and also represented as specific peaks indicating each nitrogen base.

Sanger-Coulson MethodMaxam-Gilbert Method
Enzymatic: DNA synthesis with ddNTPs terminates the chainChemical: bases are chemically modified, then the DNA is cleaved at those bases
Four tubes, each with one ddNTP (ddGTP, ddATP, ddTTP, ddCTP)Four samples: G, A+G, T+C, C
Developed by Sanger and Coulson, 1977Developed by Maxam and Gilbert, 1976-77

Key Points

  • Sanger-Coulson (1977, Nobel Prize 1980) uses ddNTPs, which lack the 3'-OH group, to terminate chains — the dideoxy method.
  • Four tubes (G, A, T, C), gel lanes and band order give the sequence in the Sanger method.
  • Maxam-Gilbert (1976-77) is the chemical cleavage method, with four samples: G, A+G, T+C and C.
  • Automated sequencing uses fluorescently labelled ddNTPs, UV laser detectors and a computer, with no radiolabelling or autoradiography.
  • In automated sequencing each base has its own dye colour and is shown as a peak.

lessons.title: DNA Analysis, DNA Fingerprinting and RFLPs
lessons.notes_html:
The process of matching an unknown sample of DNA with a known sample to see if they correspond is called DNA profiling. It is also called DNA fingerprinting because of its similarity to identifying fingerprints (the techniques are very different; it is also called DNA testing / DNA typing). If, after separation by gel electrophoresis, the band patterns of two samples are identical, both must have come from the same individual; if the pattern is similar, the two individuals are probably related. Forensic scientists use it to identify individuals by their nucleotide sequence. The first DNA fingerprint was made by Alec Jeffreys (the book prints 'Alec Jeffrey'), an English geneticist, in 1985.

26.3 DNA Analysis

26.3.1 Use / Applications / Purposes of DNA Analysis

  • DNA fingerprinting in paternity suits, when the identity of someone's biological father needs to be known for legal reasons, and establishment of paternity and other family relationships.
  • At a crime scene, forensic specialists collect samples such as blood or semen, which contain DNA.
  • To identify crime and catastrophe victims.
  • To match organ donors with recipients in transplant programs.
  • To detect bacteria and other micro-organisms that pollute water, air, food and soil.

26.3.2 Procedure / Mechanism of DNA Analysis

One of the most important methods is restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP), pronounced 'Riflips' — the different-sized fragments of DNA produced by a particular restriction enzyme. The book's extra information notes that humans share about 98% of their genes with chimpanzees, 92% with mice, 76% with zebrafish, 51% with fruit fly and 18% with E. coli bacteria.

1. Collection of DNA samples: A very small fraction of DNA is sufficient, because it can be copied several times with PCR. DNA can be collected even from a drop of blood, a cell of a single hair root, or a single sperm. DNA samples can also be collected from mummified organisms or fossils when evolutionary relationships are to be studied.

Placement of RFLPs: Every person has a unique set of RFLPs, because the restriction site of a particular enzyme is always different in number and distribution in all humans on earth except monozygotic twins. Humans have 99% similarity in the nucleotide sequence of their genomes; the 1% difference establishes the individuality of every person. Placement of RFLPs is the digestion of DNA samples by a particular restriction enzyme, producing a set of different-sized DNA fragments.

Separation of RFLPs: The DNA fragments are electrophoresed on agarose gel, and the mixture of RFLPs is loaded in polyacrylamide gel and run for electrophoresis. Fragments of various lengths move at different rates from the negative to the positive pole within the gel; when movement is stopped, the gel is treated further to observe the banding pattern.

Southern Blotting

This method was invented by British biologist Edwin Southern. A Southern blot is routinely used for detection of a specific DNA sequence in DNA samples. Southern blotting combines transfer of electrophoresis-separated DNA fragments to a filter membrane with subsequent fragment detection by probe hybridization: the double-stranded fragments separated by electrophoresis are denatured to single-stranded fragments, transferred from gel to membrane, covered with a radioactively labelled probe in single-strand form and incubated; excess probe is washed off.

Autoradiography

After hybridization, excess probes are washed from the membrane, and the pattern of hybridization is visualized on X-ray film by exposing the membrane to an X-ray source. This technique is known as autoradiography. The banding pattern originally obtained in the gel due to separation of RFLPs is now developed on an X-ray film.

Key Points

  • DNA profiling / fingerprinting matches an unknown DNA sample with a known one; identical band patterns mean the same individual.
  • First DNA fingerprint: Alec Jeffreys, 1985.
  • Uses: paternity, crime-scene evidence, identifying victims, organ-donor matching, and detecting polluting micro-organisms.
  • RFLPs are different-sized fragments from one restriction enzyme; they are unique to each person except monozygotic twins (99% of the human genome is shared, 1% differs).
  • Steps: collect DNA (even a drop of blood or one hair root), digest to RFLPs, separate by electrophoresis, Southern blotting, then autoradiography on X-ray film.

lessons.title: Genome Maps and the Human Genome Project
lessons.notes_html:
The gene is the basic unit of biological information; hereditary characteristics pass from parents to offspring through genes in their gametes. The collection of all the genes found in one complete set of chromosomes is called the genome. The haploid organism, or egg and sperm, has one copy of the genome, while a diploid organism (cell) contains two copies. The book compares the human genome to a book with 23 units (chromosomes), each with several thousand stories (genes), made of paragraphs called exons interrupted by introns, written in letters called bases — thymine, guanine, cytosine and adenine (TGCA).

26.4 Genome Maps

Genome Analyses

For the study of the genomes of various organisms, a new sub-branch of biotechnology has been created called genomics, which deals with exploration and analysis of the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome. The genome of Haemophilus influenzae was published in 1995. Frederick Sanger also sequenced the first bacteriophage genome.

Genome Maps

Genome analysis helps develop two broad categories of maps:

Genetic MapsPhysical Maps
Exhibit the sequence (order) of gene loci along the length of DNAPhysical mapping finds the order and physical distance between DNA base pairs by DNA markers

Physical mapping can determine the sequence of DNA base pairs with high accuracy.

Genetic Markers

Genetic maps have landmarks called genetic markers, which contain variable numbers of tandem repeats (short tandem repeats and single nucleotide polymorphism). Genetic markers are useful for generating genetic maps when there are occasional, predictable mutations during meiosis; over many generations these lead to a high degree of variability in the DNA content of the marker from individual to individual.

26.4.1 Human Genome Project (HGP)

In 1990, an international cooperative venture called the Human Genome Project (HGP) set out to sequence the complete human genome — a catalogue of the bases A, T, C and G in human DNA. The project was originally founded by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, which established the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI). Its first director was James D. Watson; later the institute was led by Dr Francis Collins (the book prints 'Collin'). The 'Wellcome Trust' of the UK became a major partner, with additional contributions from China, France, Japan, Germany and others. In 2003, the project announced it had succeeded: the human genome comprises 3.22 billion nucleotides and approximately 20,000 to 25,000 genes. Note: the unit's exercise rounds the genome size to 3 billion nucleotides.

26.4.2 Major Goals of Human Genome Project

  • To identify all the approximately 20,000 to 25,000 genes in the human genome.
  • To determine the sequences of the chemical base pairs that make up human DNA, about 3.22 billion.
  • To store this information in databases.
  • To improve tools for data analysis.
  • To transfer related technologies to the private sector, and address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) that may arise from the project.

Benefits of HGP — Molecular Medicine

  • Improved diagnosis of diseases.
  • Earlier detection of genetic predisposition to certain diseases.
  • Rational drug design.
  • Gene therapy and control systems for drugs.
  • Pharmacogenomics — the study of how genes affect a person's response to drugs.

Key Points

  • The genome is all the genes in one complete set of chromosomes; genomics studies complete genome sequences.
  • Genetic maps show the order of gene loci; physical maps show order and distance in base pairs using DNA markers.
  • Genetic markers include short tandem repeats and single nucleotide polymorphisms.
  • HGP (1990-2003), first directed by James D. Watson, sequenced the human genome: 3.22 billion nucleotides, about 20,000-25,000 genes.
  • HGP goals included identifying all genes, storing data, improving analysis tools, technology transfer and addressing ELSI.
  • Benefits lie in molecular medicine: better diagnosis, early detection, rational drug design, gene therapy and pharmacogenomics.

lessons.title: Tissue Culture and Plant Tissue Culture Methods
lessons.notes_html:
Tissue culture is the growth of a tissue in an artificial liquid culture medium. In 1902, the German botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt revealed that plant cells are totipotent — each cell has the full genetic potential of the organism, so a single cell could become a complete plant. In 1958, the British botanist F.C. Steward grew a complete carrot plant from a tiny piece of phloem, providing sugars, minerals and vitamins and adding coconut milk (later found to contain the plant hormone cytokinin). The cultured cells divided and produced a callus (an undifferentiated group of cells), which later differentiated into shoot and root and developed into complete plants.

26.5 Tissue Culture

The initial plant part used to develop tissue culture is known as an explant; it may be a single cell (protoplast), a piece of tissue, or a complete organ (seed, leaf or twig). On this basis, tissue culture is called cell culture or organ culture. Plantlets are the young plants developed during tissue culture, and micro-propagation is the production of a large number of plants from small plant material.

Somatic embryogenesis is an artificial process in which a plant or embryo is derived from a single somatic cell; somatic embryos form from ordinary plant tissue not normally involved in embryo development, and no endosperm or seed coat forms around a somatic embryo. Plants produced from tissue culture are genetically identical to the original plant, so they are called soma clones; however, genetic variation is sometimes observed among progeny of plants regenerated from somatic cells cultured in vitro — this is called soma clonal variation.

Cell CultureOrgan Culture
Cells are artificially grown under laboratory conditions (in vitro)Culture of isolated organs such as root, stem, anther, etc.; named after the organ used

26.5.1 Methods of Tissue Culture

Methods are based on the type of explant used: meristem, anther, ovary, embryo, callus and suspension culture, etc.

Meristem culture: Meristems are tissues of undifferentiated cells capable of rapid division; culture using meristems is meristem culture. With the correct proportions of auxins and cytokinin added to a liquid medium, many new shoots develop from a single shoot tip, and when these are removed more shoots form. Meristem culture has led to micro-propagation — the commercial production of thousands, even millions, of identical seedlings in limited space. Its advantage is that the plants are germ free (devoid of viruses), because meristems lack a vascular system, which is the main route for viruses travelling through the body. Note: the book mentions a 'single root tip' in one sentence and a 'single shoot tip' in the next; the shoots develop from the shoot tip.

Anther culture technique: Anthers are cultured in a medium containing vitamins and growth regulators; the haploid cells within the pollen grains divide, producing pro-embryos of as many as 20-40 cells. When the pollen grains rupture, haploid embryos are released. The experimenter can generate a haploid plant, or add a chemical agent to encourage chromosomal doubling; after doubling, the plants are diploid but homozygous for all their alleles. Anther culture is a direct way to produce plants that express recessive alleles.

Callus CultureCell Suspension Culture
Callus is formed by proliferation of the parent tissue; its cells are parenchymatous, amorphous and unorganized; culturing callus in an appropriate medium is callus culture, which can initiate cell suspensionsRapidly growing cultures are cut into small pieces and shaken in a liquid nutrient medium so single cells or small clumps break off and form a suspension; these cells produce the same chemicals as the entire plant

Cell suspension cultures of Cinchona ledgeriana produce quinine and those of Digitalis lanata produce digitoxin. Scientists imagine cell suspension cultures will be maintained in bioreactors to produce chemicals for drugs, cosmetics and agricultural chemicals.

Protoplast culture: A plant cell with its cell wall removed is a protoplast, commonly isolated from leaf mesophyll cells or cell suspensions. Protoplast culture can develop a whole plant by somatic embryogenesis (synthetic embryos from somatic cells); genetic variation can be induced in these embryos by chemical or physical mutagens — soma clonal variations. Protoplasts are also ideal targets for transformation.

Embryo culture: The culture of mature embryos; zygote or seed embryos are often used as explants, and the embryo develops properly when nourishing tissues (endosperms) were present in the seed during development.

Ovary culture: An in vitro technique in which an unpollinated flower is grown on a suitable nutrient medium to grow new haploid plants; this process of ovary culture is called gynogenesis, and the ovary can regenerate into a fully differentiated plant.

Key Points

  • Tissue culture grows tissue in an artificial medium; plant cells are totipotent (Haberlandt, 1902; Steward's carrot, 1958).
  • Explant is the starting plant part; callus is the undifferentiated cell mass; plantlets are the young plants produced.
  • Micro-propagation makes many plants from small material; tissue-culture plants are soma clones, and variation among them is soma clonal variation.
  • Meristem culture gives virus-free plants; anther culture gives haploid plants that can be doubled to homozygous diploids.
  • Callus culture grows an unorganized callus; suspension cultures of Cinchona make quinine and of Digitalis make digitoxin.
  • Other methods: protoplast culture, embryo culture, and ovary culture (gynogenesis) for haploid plants.

lessons.title: Animal Cell Culture: Techniques and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Animal cells can also be cultured in artificial media, but unlike plant and bacterial cells, these cells can grow only for a limited number of generations. Growth also depends on the source tissue: some cells cannot divide and grow, e.g. nerve cells and lens cells, while others can repeatedly divide and grow for a limited generation, e.g. fibroblasts. Cultured animal cells are used in recombinant DNA technology, industrial processes (vaccine, monoclonal antibody and drug production), genetic manipulation and cancer research, etc.

26.5.2 Methods of Animal Cell Culture

Techniques of Animal Cell Culture

Plastic containers are used to culture animal cells. A cell culture initiated by cells isolated from a tissue or an animal's organ is known as primary cell culture. If a primary culture is subcultured in fresh media, it establishes secondary cultures, called a secondary culture or cell line.

  • Organ culture — culture of native tissue that retains most of the in vivo histological features.
  • Histotypic culture — culture of cells for their reaggregation to form a tissue-like structure.
  • Organotypic culture — culture of different cell types to form a tissue or organ.

A special incubator is needed for animal cell culture, maintaining the level of carbon dioxide, oxygen, temperature and all other necessary substances. There are two patterns of animal cell growth:

Anchorage DependenceAnchorage Independence
An increase in proliferation seen when cells are allowed to attach to a solid surfaceA cell maintains its capacity to spread, divide and function despite the absence of a stable or inert surface to anchor with

Applications of Animal / Tissue Culture

  • Produce antiviral vaccines and pharmaceutical drugs using cell lines.
  • Amniocentesis — chromosomal analysis of the fetus for various diseases.
  • Produce monoclonal antibodies required from cell lines in culture.
  • Helpful to study the function of cell neurons.
  • Use of artificial skin.
  • Culture tumour cells, to know whether a tumour is benign or cancerous.
  • To know the effects of toxins and pollutants using cell lines.

Note: on one page the book prints 'monoclonal antibiotics' in a list of cultured-cell uses; from the rest of the unit (Sections 26.5.2 applications and 26.7.2) this is monoclonal antibodies.

The unit's summary restates the key definition: a cell culture which is initiated by the cells removed from an animal's organ is called a primary cell culture. The main limitation running through this section is lifespan — unlike bacteria, cultured animal cells divide only for a limited generation, and some, such as nerve and lens cells, do not divide at all, which limits how long a culture can be maintained and used.

Key Points

  • Animal cells grow only for limited generations; nerve and lens cells do not divide, fibroblasts divide for a limited generation.
  • Primary culture comes directly from tissue or organ; subculturing it gives secondary cultures or cell lines.
  • Organ culture retains in vivo features; histotypic culture reaggregates cells into tissue-like structures; organotypic culture combines different cell types.
  • Animal culture needs a special incubator controlling CO₂, oxygen and temperature; growth is anchorage dependent or independent.
  • Applications: vaccines and drugs, amniocentesis, monoclonal antibodies, neuron study, artificial skin, tumour study, and testing toxins and pollutants.

lessons.title: Transgenic Bacteria and Transgenic Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Modern genetic technology can modify the genomes of living organisms — this process is also called genetic engineering. A gene of one species can be modified, or transplanted from one species to another; organisms that have altered genomes are known as transgenic. Bacteria were the first transgenic organisms, produced in 1973, and many transgenic plants and animals have since been produced.

26.6 Transgenic Organisms (Bacteria, Plants and Animals)

26.6.1 Transgenic Bacteria

Herbert Boyer (1978), University of California, produced a transgenic bacterium (E. coli) by inserting the human insulin gene into it; the bacteria synthesized human insulin 'in vats'. Later, many other human genes and genes for medicines were inserted into their plasmids or directly into their chromosome to get desirable products. Note: the book dates the first transgenic organisms (bacteria) to 1973 on the previous page, and Boyer's insulin-producing E. coli to 1978.

  • Formation of ice crystals: Pseudomonas syringae, called ice-plus bacteria, have a surface ice-nucleation-active (INA) protein that promotes ice crystal formation. In the new ice-minus strain the gene encoding INA protein is removed, so plants sprayed with these bacteria are protected from cold stress.
  • Bioreactors: Recombinant DNA technology produces bacteria that reproduce in large vats called bioreactors; if the foreign gene is replicated and actively expressed, a large amount of protein product is obtained.
  • Biotechnology products: insulin, human growth hormone, clotting protein for haemophilia (haemophilia factor VII), hepatitis B vaccine, interferon (to treat viral infections) and tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to dissolve blood clots (used by heart patients).
  • Anti-insect toxin: Bacteria that normally colonize corn roots have been endowed with a gene (from another bacterium) coding for an insect toxin, which protects the roots from insects.
  • Cleaning up beaches after oil spills: Bacteria can be selected and genetically engineered to degrade particular substances, e.g. to clean up oil spills.
  • Importance in industry: Bacteria in biofilters prevent airborne chemical pollutants being vented into the air; transgenic bacteria remove sulphur from coal before burning and clean up toxic waste dumps — one strain was given 'suicide genes' that caused self-destruction when the job was completed.
  • Synthesis of organic chemicals: A bacterial strain especially good at producing phenylalanine (needed to make aspartame) was engineered; aspartame is the dipeptide sweetener called 'Nutra Sweet'.
  • Extraction of metals and bioleaching: Mining companies use bacteria to obtain copper, gold and uranium from low-grade ores; genetically engineered organisms with improved bioleaching capabilities are being tested.

Ecological Concerns Surrounding Transgenic Bacteria

Their use may create serious hazards: if cancer cell genes were transferred into micro-organisms, antibiotic resistance may develop in many bacteria, and some bacteria create pollution. Transgenic bacteria can disturb the natural environment if their numbers exceed limits.

26.6.2 Transgenic Plants

The first transgenic plants (tobacco plants) were made and cultivated in France and the USA in 1986, with herbicide-resistant genes inserted. The aim is to produce a new trait that does not occur naturally in the species, so the plants can overcome environmental problems and grow more successfully. In gene transformation methods, the cell wall is removed and the cells are called protoplasts.

Electroporation method: Protoplasts are treated with an electric current while suspended in a liquid containing foreign DNA; the current makes tiny self-sealing holes in the plasma membrane through which the foreign gene enters the cytoplasm and then the nucleus; the transgenic protoplast develops into a complete plant.

Agrobacterium-mediated transformation: Foreign DNA is inserted into the tumour-inducing plasmid (Ti plasmid) of Agrobacterium tumefaciens — called the natural genetic engineering of plants. These bacteria naturally insert their T-DNA (Transfer DNA) into the plant genome at a wound site; T-DNA contains genes for auxin production, so infected plant cells divide and redivide to produce a tumour called a gall (crown gall disease). The gene of choice is cloned in the T-DNA region in place of unwanted sequences; when the transgenic bacteria infect plants, the gene enters the host nucleus and the transformed cells are regenerated into whole plants.

Particle gun: In 1987, John C. Sanford and Theodore M. Klein of Cornell University constructed the particle gun, which bombards a callus with DNA-coated microscopic metal (gold or tungsten); genetically altered somatic embryos then develop into adult plants. Many plants, including corn and wheat varieties, have been engineered by this method.

Advantages of Transgenic Plants

  • Resistance to pests: Foreign genes in cotton, corn and potato make their cells produce toxin against insects.
  • Resistance to herbicide: Transgenic soybeans are resistant to herbicides; some corn and cotton plants are also herbicide resistant.
  • Increase in protein, oil and starch contents: Improvements for protein or starch content and modified oil or amino acid composition, e.g. soybean, potato, canola, maize, golden rice.
  • Transgenic wheat and rice versions are being developed to meet increasing demand.
  • Green Revolution: World grain harvests have continued to rise since the 1960s, when special high-yield hybrid plants were developed.

Key Points

  • Transgenic organisms carry altered genomes; bacteria were the first, in 1973, and Boyer's insulin E. coli followed in 1978 (book).
  • Transgenic bacteria make insulin, growth hormone, factor VII, hepatitis B vaccine, interferon and tPA, and serve in bioreactors, oil-spill cleanup, biofilters, metal extraction and bioleaching.
  • Ice-minus Pseudomonas syringae (INA gene removed) protects plants from cold stress.
  • Ecological concerns: cancer genes or antibiotic resistance spreading, pollution, and disturbing nature if numbers exceed limits.
  • First transgenic plants: tobacco, France and USA, 1986, herbicide resistant.
  • Plant transformation methods: electroporation, Agrobacterium Ti plasmid / T-DNA, and the particle gun (Sanford and Klein, 1987).

lessons.title: Transgenic Animals and Genetically Engineered Farm Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Animals that have been genetically altered (carry foreign genes) using genetic engineering techniques are known as transgenic animals. The book gives three methods of developing them, and then shows how genetic engineering improves farm animals and turns some of them into living producers of human medicines.

26.6.3 Transgenic Animals

  • i) By micro-injection: A foreign gene is inserted into the eggs of animals through micro-injection; the fertilized egg is then transferred into the oviduct of a female to implant. The book's figure (Fig. 26.16) shows the human growth hormone gene micro-injected so that a transgenic goat produces human growth hormone in its milk. Note: the book names 'Dolly sheep' as the example here, but Dolly was a clone produced by nuclear transfer, not a transgenic animal made by micro-injection — use the book's transgenic goat figure as the example of this method.
  • ii) Vortex mixing: The egg is placed in an agitator with DNA and silicon-carbide needles; the needles make tiny holes through which the DNA can enter. When these eggs are fertilized, the resulting offspring are transgenic animals.
  • iii) Retrovirus-mediated gene transfer: Retroviruses are commonly used as vectors to transfer genetic material into the cells of a blastocyst under in vitro conditions; the blastocyst is then implanted into the womb of the female animal, and the resulting offspring is a transgenic animal.

Extra information from the book: Alpha-1-Antitrypsin (AAT), produced in the liver, protects the lungs from infections; its deficiency causes respiratory diseases.

26.6.4 Importance of Genetically Engineered Farm Animals

Genetic engineering has been used to produce bovine growth hormone, inserted into animals' eggs to produce large-size animals, e.g. larger fishes, cows, pigs and sheep. Genetically engineered fishes are kept in ponds that offer no escape to the wild, because there is much concern that they will upset or destroy the natural ecosystem.

Transgenic animals are also used to produce pharmaceuticals (drugs for the treatment of cystic fibrosis, cancer and blood disease); such transgenic animals are called transpharmer animals. The genes coding for therapeutically and diagnostically useful proteins are incorporated into the animal's DNA and the proteins appear in the animal's milk, e.g. Antithrombin III (hAT), which prevents blood clots and is used for blood clotting problems during surgery, and production of human growth hormone in mice, which excrete it in their urine. Human Lactoferrin (HLF) is a protein that helps protect the body from infections and strengthens the immune system; it is found in human tears and lung secretions, and is now produced by transpharmer animals. The use of a transgenic animal to produce pharmaceuticals is called gene pharming.

Key Points

  • Transgenic animals carry foreign genes; they are made by micro-injection, vortex mixing with silicon-carbide needles, or retrovirus-mediated transfer into a blastocyst.
  • Bovine growth hormone produces larger fishes, cows, pigs and sheep; engineered fish are kept in escape-proof ponds to protect wild ecosystems.
  • Transgenic animals that produce pharmaceuticals are called transpharmer animals (gene pharming).
  • Products appear in milk, e.g. Antithrombin III (hAT); human growth hormone is produced in mice and excreted in urine.
  • Human Lactoferrin (HLF) protects against infection and strengthens the immune system.

lessons.title: Biotechnology and Healthcare: Vaccines and Disease Diagnosis
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology has made a great difference to healthcare: its techniques and tools create new learning about the human and other organisms' bodies, and it has enabled researchers to develop products that fulfil our needs — safer vaccines and medicines.

26.7 Biotechnology and Healthcare

26.7.1 Development of Vaccine in Biotechnology

There are three different ways used in the development of vaccines:

  • Separation of a pure antigen using a specific monoclonal antibody, used for developing a vaccine against a pathogen.
  • Synthesis of an antigen with the help of a cloned gene or from cDNA.
  • Synthesis of peptides to be used as vaccines (the protein region of a pathogen for an immunogenic response).

26.7.2 Role of Biotechnology in Diagnosis of Diseases

Several human diseases can be diagnosed using biotechnology products such as monoclonal antibodies and DNA/RNA probes.

Monoclonal Antibodies

The response of the immune system to any antigen, even the simplest, is polyclonal; monoclonal antibodies (mAB) are a group of identical antibodies, because they are made by identical immune cells which are all clones of a unique parent cell. Monoclonal antibodies that specifically bind to a substance can serve to detect or purify that substance; they can diagnose a wide variety of illnesses and detect the presence of drugs, viral and bacterial products, and other unusual or abnormal substances in the blood. They are typically made by fusing myeloma cells (cancerous B-lymphocytes) with spleen cells from a mouse immunized with the desired antigen — a technique called somatic cell hybridization.

DNA/RNA Probes

A probe is a fluorescent or radioactive labelled piece of DNA or RNA of variable length (usually 100-1000 bases long), complementary to the sequence in the target DNA. Probes are widely used in diagnosis of many microbial diseases. Some specific DNA/RNA probes are useful to detect prenatal diseases, e.g. Short Tandem Repeats (STR).

Diagnosis of Diseases Caused by Protozoa and Helminths

Monoclonal antibodies and DNA probes are very sensitive tools to diagnose diseases caused by protozoa and helminths. Monoclonal antibodies can be used through serological tests which take only minutes, compared with conventional methods which require some weeks, as bacteria and viruses have to be cultured, e.g. in herpes virus. DNA probes are more sensitive than monoclonal antibodies and the process takes hours instead of weeks. Ready-made DNA probes for herpes virus and other human, animal and plant viruses are being prepared, and probes are available for a number of human parasites from the protozoa and helminths, e.g. polio, hepatitis, etc.

Key Points

  • Vaccines are developed by separating a pure antigen with a monoclonal antibody, synthesizing an antigen from a cloned gene or cDNA, or synthesizing peptides.
  • Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies from clones of one parent cell, made by somatic cell hybridization (myeloma cells fused with immunized mouse spleen cells).
  • DNA/RNA probes are labelled DNA or RNA pieces, usually 100-1000 bases long, complementary to target DNA.
  • Probes and monoclonal antibodies diagnose diseases in minutes to hours instead of weeks, e.g. herpes, polio and hepatitis, and detect prenatal diseases such as STR.

lessons.title: Gene Therapy and Cystic Fibrosis
lessons.notes_html:
Gene therapy is a technique to replace defective genes (by normal genes) responsible for disease development. This lesson covers the approaches and mechanism of gene therapy in section 26.7.3, and then the book's worked example in 26.7.4: cystic fibrosis and its treatment by gene therapy.

26.7.3 Gene Therapy

There are many approaches for correcting defective genes:

  • A normal gene may be inserted into a non-specific location within the genome to replace a non-functional gene — this approach is most common.
  • An abnormal gene could be swapped for a normal gene through homologous recombination.
  • The abnormal gene could be repaired through selective reverse mutation, which returns the gene to its normal function.
  • The regulation (the degree to which a gene is turned on or off) of a particular gene could be altered.

Mechanism of Gene Therapy

The technique is done either in vivo or ex vivo. In in vivo therapy the gene is delivered directly into the body; in ex vivo therapy cells are treated outside the body and the transgenic cells are again implanted into the body. Note: the book's text also writes 'in vitro' for the outside-the-body route and says the cells are re-implanted 'in both cases' — re-implanting treated cells is the ex vivo route. A 'normal gene' is inserted into the genome to replace an 'abnormal, disease-causing gene'. A carrier molecule called a vector must deliver the therapeutic gene to the patient's target cells. The virus is the most common vector: viruses have evolved a way of encapsulating and delivering their genes to human cells in a pathogenic manner, so scientists manipulate the virus genome to remove disease-causing genes and insert therapeutic genes. A non-viral approach uses a liposome — an artificial lipid sphere with an aqueous core carrying the therapeutic DNA, capable of passing the DNA through the target cell membrane.

26.7.4 Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an inherited disease that affects the mucus and sweat glands. A person with severe symptoms can have serious lung and digestive problems, while a person with a mild form shows symptoms after adolescence. In a normal person the mucus is watery, keeping the linings of certain organs moist and preventing them from drying out or getting infected. The cause of CF is a defect in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene, which encodes a protein by which the movement of salt and water in and out of cells is controlled. In a CF patient the gene does not work properly, so cells lining the passageways of the lungs, oviduct, pancreas and other organs produce abnormally thick, sticky mucus. This thick mucus causes obstruction to airways, ducts and glands due to deposition of mucus — the characteristic sign and symptom of cystic fibrosis.

Gene Therapy of Cystic Fibrosis

The cystic fibrosis genes were identified in 1989 and named CFTR. Gene therapy creates a healthy version of the flawed CFTR gene and infuses it into the affected patients: the normal human gene is cloned in a bacterium, inserted into a harmless virus (the book prints AVV), and the virus is dripped into the lungs through a thin tube inserted in the nose. The virus enters the lung cell nucleus and inserts the normal gene into the lung cell DNA, so the cells now with normal genes function normally.

Key Points

  • Gene therapy replaces defective genes with normal genes; approaches include inserting a normal gene, swapping by homologous recombination, repair by reverse mutation, and altering gene regulation.
  • Delivery is in vivo (directly into the body) or ex vivo (cells corrected outside and re-implanted), usually using a virus vector, or a liposome as a non-viral route.
  • Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease of mucus and sweat glands caused by a defective CFTR gene controlling salt and water movement.
  • In CF, thick sticky mucus obstructs airways, ducts and glands of the lungs, oviduct, pancreas and other organs.
  • CF gene therapy: the CFTR gene (identified in 1989) is delivered by a harmless virus (AVV in the book) dripped into the lungs through the nose.

lessons.title: Scope and Importance of Biotechnology: Biochips, Biofertilizers, Nanotechnology and Ethics
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology emerged as a new discipline during the 1970s. It is not a pure science, but an integration of biological science with technology that created a revolution in human life. It has been broadly defined as 'the development and utilization of biological processes, forms and systems for obtaining maximum benefits to humans and other forms of life', and as 'the science of applied biological processes'.

26.8 Scope and Importance of Biotechnology

Biochips and Biological Computers

Biochips are the result of a combination of the microchip business with biotechnology, and in the future biological computers may be developed. Biochips reveal the complex biochemical processes occurring inside cells, with the larger goal of understanding and treating human diseases. Through microminiaturization, biotechnologists pack their traditionally bulky sensing tools into smaller and smaller spaces, onto biochips — essentially miniaturized laboratories that can perform hundreds or thousands of simultaneous biochemical reactions. Biochips enable researchers to quickly screen large numbers of biological analytes for purposes from disease diagnosis to detection of bioterrorism agents. The book's colour terms: Blue biotechnology is the biotechnology of water and bodies of water, Red biotechnology is medical biotechnology, and Green biotechnology is plant biotechnology.

Biofertilizers

The use of microbial inoculants as a source of biofertilizers (nutrient inputs of biological origin for plant growth) has become a hope for most countries, economically and environmentally. Biologically fixed nitrogen can supply an adequate amount of nitrogen to plants and other nutrients to some extent. It is a non-hazardous way of fertilizing fields, and biologically fixed nitrogen consumes about 25 percent to 30 percent less energy than is normally done by the chemical process.

Nanotechnology

Nanotechnology gives the capability to engineer the tiniest objects, at the molecular level; it includes the study and manipulation of materials between 1 and 100 nanometres. Nanotechnologists impart their expertise in developing nanoparticles that can be used for efficient drug delivery at target cells and in the diagnosis of disease.

Scope of Biotechnology

Biotechnology is the fastest growing field in research and development, called the technology of the future (technology of tomorrow). Students of biotechnology can have scope in: communications/media; computer science (database development, bioinformatics, website development); pharmaceutical companies (drug development); genetic engineering (bioprocess chambers, instrumentation, fermentation technology); research (cancer, genetically linked diseases, AIDS); diagnostic laboratories; waste management and pollution control; medicine (medical genetics, genetic counselling, gene therapy, gene testing); bio power plants (corn, sugarcane, bamboo); bio-processing industry (enzyme, paper, protein engineering, food processing); agriculture and animal husbandry; the legal field (intellectual property rights, patents, genetic and paternity testing); the military (pathogen identification, protection against chemical and biological warfare, risk assessment); and crime and law (DNA fingerprinting in forensic science makes a data bank of criminals, so culprits are caught faster).

Social / Ethical Implications of Using Biotechnology

Alongside benefits in healthcare, agriculture, food production, industrial enzymes and environmental management, advancement has raised concerns and controversies (e.g. from Non-Governmental Organizations, NGOs). ELSI is the short form for the ethical, legal and social implications of biotechnology.

Concerns about Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs)

There are concerns regarding the biosafety, ethics and issues related to the release of GMOs in the environment; many countries and NGOs have opposed their release. The United Nations built an informal working group on biosafety, which in 1991 prepared the 'voluntary code of conduct for the release of organisms into the environment'. Main safety areas: to dispose of spent microbial biomass and purify effluents from biotechnological processes; the toxicity or allergy associated with microbial production; to deal with the increase in antibiotic-resistant pathogenic micro-organisms; to evaluate the pathogenicity of genetically engineered micro-organisms for humans, plants and animals; to prevent contamination, infection or mutation of the processed strains; and to evaluate the interaction of genetically engineered microbes with the natural environment.

Biological Warfare

Most countries of the world are signatories to the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 — a voluntary pledge by a nation 'never to produce microbial or other biological agents or toxins, whatever may be their method of production, for use in wars'. However, many people have expressed concern about the possible use of genetic manipulations for military purposes in the near future.

Intellectual Property

Intellectual Property includes patents, trade secrets, copyrights and trademarks. Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) is a collective term for the different types of legal rights granted by each country; these rights prohibit others from making, copying, using or selling the proprietary subject matter. In biotechnology, intellectual property covers the processes and products resulting from genetic engineering techniques using restriction enzymes to create recombinant DNA. Crop varieties are protected through Plant Breeder's Rights (PBRs), which ensure the plant breeder who developed a variety gets the exclusive rights for marketing it.

Key Points

  • Biotechnology (emerged in the 1970s) integrates biological science with technology for maximum benefit to humans and other life.
  • Biochips are miniaturized laboratories performing hundreds or thousands of reactions at once, used from disease diagnosis to bioterrorism detection.
  • Biofertilizers use microbial inoculants and biologically fixed nitrogen — non-hazardous, and using 25-30% less energy than the chemical process.
  • Nanotechnology manipulates materials between 1 and 100 nanometres; nanoparticles serve in targeted drug delivery and diagnosis.
  • Scope spans pharmaceuticals, bioinformatics, research, diagnostics, waste management, medicine, agriculture, law, the military and forensics.
  • Ethical issues (ELSI) cover GMO biosafety, biological warfare (Convention of 1972) and Intellectual Property Rights, including Plant Breeder's Rights.

lessons.title: Integrated Disease Management and Vaccination
lessons.notes_html:
The aim of this unit is to establish the proper importance of learning biology for human benefit. Biology has a strong influence in health and diseases. Health is defined as a state when an individual is free from illness and injury. Biology has an impact in diagnosing, treating and preventing diseases, gives awareness about causative agents (pathogens) for diseases and symptoms caused by them, and has contributed in enhancement of food production. Knowledge of biology is helpful in using microbes for human welfare, and biological control against pests and insects has greatly contributed in saving crops. Animal and plant breeds have been improved by techniques of genetics and biotechnology.

27.1 Integrated Disease Management and Vaccination

There are several methods of disease control that have been developed and are being used.

27.1.1 Integrated Disease Management

Integrated disease management is a struggle of combating fatal and other common diseases by using a range of measures to prevent and manage diseases by involving the whole society. All the effective measures necessary to get rid of a particular disease are taken. Its cycle (Fig. 27.1) is: Prevent, Detect, Inform, Respond, with Facilitate at the centre.

Objective

Integrated disease management aims to improve and maintain quality of life. It is concerned with improving health in populations and reduction of future complications associated with those diseases. By integrated disease management we can make our society healthy and progressive.

Procedure

The initial step in integrated disease management is to involve the community by creating awareness among them about a particular disease. This awareness can be created through social and electronic media, magazines or newspapers. Discussion programs among various colleges can be arranged in order to share information regarding disease. Certain causes of disease spread, effective remedies and precautions should be communicated to the whole community. Every possible method is used to prevent and cure disease such as vaccination, drug treatment and other therapies. Paramedics, doctors, Basic Health Unit, District and Provincial Level Hospitals, Provincial and Federal Health Authorities are all part of integrated disease management. The World Health Organization (WHO) is a global body to assist the governments and societies in promoting health and imparting health education.

27.1.2 Vaccination

The introduction of an antigenic substance (vaccine) in the body to produce active immunity against a specific disease is called vaccination.

A vaccine is a biological preparation; it contains a pathogen in killed or attenuated (weakened) form which can develop immunity but is not able to cause disease. A vaccine may also contain components of a pathogen such as its proteins or toxins. Vaccines artificially activate the immune system to produce antibodies against the antigen present in the vaccine, so that in future if one gets infected by such a pathogen, the body has the potential to form accurate antibodies to destroy that particular antigen. Vaccination provides a lasting effect; it usually takes several weeks to develop immunity.

In the last 70 years vaccines have helped to eradicate infectious diseases like small pox. WHO estimates that 2 to 3 million deaths are prevented every year through immunization against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and measles.

Importance of Vaccination

Vaccination is the most effective way used to boost the immune system and prevent serious life threatening diseases that were once common worldwide, i.e. polio, mumps, measles and tetanus. Vaccination is largely responsible for eradication of small pox worldwide. There can be mild side effects after vaccination such as low grade fever, nausea, fatigue, pain or redness on that area and chills (Fig. 27.2, vaccines for 14 deadly diseases).

Key Points

  • Health is freedom from illness and injury; biology helps diagnose, treat and prevent diseases.
  • Integrated disease management combats diseases using a range of measures involving the whole society, aiming to improve and maintain quality of life.
  • Its procedure starts with community awareness through media, then uses vaccination, drugs and therapies through health units, hospitals and authorities, assisted by WHO.
  • Vaccination introduces an antigenic substance to produce active immunity; a vaccine contains a pathogen in killed or attenuated form, or its proteins or toxins.
  • Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent polio, mumps, measles and tetanus, and eradicated small pox.

lessons.title: Vaccines Against Polio, Measles, Hepatitis and Tetanus, and the Vaccination Schedule
lessons.notes_html:
It is always better to prevent a disease than to treat it after it occurs, i.e. prevention is better than cure. Diseases that used to be common around the world can now be prevented by vaccines.

27.1.3 Role of Vaccines in Preventing Diseases

Viral DiseaseVaccine
Hepatitis AHep-A vaccine protects against hepatitis A
Hepatitis BHep-B vaccine protects against hepatitis B
FluFlu vaccine protects against influenza
Measles, Mumps and RubellaMMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps and Rubella
PolioOPV and IPV vaccine protect against polio

i) Vaccination Against Polio

Poliomyelitis is a disabling disease caused by polio virus that results in muscle weakness and paralysis. Two types of polio vaccines are used: (1) an inactivated polio virus (IPV) given by injection and (2) weakened polio virus (OPV) given by oral route. WHO recommends OPV vaccine at birth followed by a primary series of 3 OPV and at least one IPV dose starting at 6 weeks of age, with a minimum of 4 weeks between OPV doses. These vaccines have eliminated polio from most of the world. Vaccination is the best way to prevent polio.

ii) Vaccination Against Measles and Mumps

Measles and mumps are caused by different viruses but share unique symptoms. There is a common vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella called the MMR vaccine. MMR vaccine is administered via the subcutaneous route, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months of age and the second dose at 4-6 years of age. The maximum age for MMR vaccine administration is 12 years.

iii) Vaccination Against Hepatitis

Hepatitis is an inflammatory condition of the liver, commonly caused by viral infections of the liver that are classified as hepatitis A, B, C, D and E. Vaccine is available only for hepatitis A and B.

iv) Vaccination Against Tetanus (Lockjaw)

Tetanus, also called lockjaw, is a serious infection caused by a bacterium Clostridium tetani. This bacterium produces a toxin that affects the brain, leading to stiffness in the muscles. Tetanus is prevented by tetanus vaccine, also known as tetanus toxoid, an inactivated vaccine. During childhood five doses are recommended. Additionally, one dose every ten years is recommended. Td-vaccination is the best way to prevent a tetanus infection.

Vaccines cause herd immunity: if the majority of people in a community have been vaccinated against a disease, an unvaccinated person is less likely to get sick because others are less likely to get sick and spread disease.

Key Points

  • Prevention is better than cure; vaccines have prevented countless cases of disease.
  • Polio: OPV (oral, weakened) and IPV (injected, inactivated); WHO schedule starts at birth / 6 weeks.
  • Measles and mumps are caused by different viruses but share unique symptoms; the MMR vaccine is given subcutaneously at 12-15 months and 4-6 years.
  • Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver; vaccines exist only for hepatitis A and B.
  • Tetanus (lockjaw) is caused by Clostridium tetani; tetanus toxoid, five doses in childhood and one dose every ten years.
  • Vaccination also gives herd immunity, protecting unvaccinated people.

lessons.title: Animal Husbandry and Livestock in the National Economy
lessons.notes_html:
Good animal care is both a farming skill and a major part of Pakistan's economy.

27.2 Animal Husbandry

Animal husbandry is the branch of agriculture which deals with the practice of breeding, farming, management and care of livestock like cattle, sheep, horses, cow and chickens for advantages. In animal husbandry, genetic qualities and behaviours considered to be advantageous to humans are further developed. Animals are raised for meat, milk, eggs, fibre, leather and other products like vaccines and antiserum for medical use. Cattle and sheep are improved to yield more meat, milk and wool by agriculturalists.

Animal husbandry includes proper feeding, watering and cleaning the living area of animals. The breeding of farm animals is managed by farmers with a view to encouraging traits considered as desirable, including fast growth rates, low feed consumption, higher yields and better quality fibres. Selective breeding has been responsible for large increases in productivity. Good husbandry, proper feeding and maintaining hygiene contribute to animal health, which brings economic benefits. When animals become sick they are treated by veterinary medicines by the farmer and veterinarian.

Role of Livestock in National Economy

Livestock are the domesticated animals reared commercially for sale on a farm or agricultural business. It is an inclusive general word, which includes animals like cattle, sheep, goats and birds etc. Livestock animals give us food like meat, eggs and milk. Horses, donkeys and mules are also part of livestock.

The livestock plays an important role in the economy of Pakistan. About 30-40% of income in our country comes from livestock. The livestock sector contributes 50% of the agriculture value added products and 11% to national gross domestic product (GDP). 8% of total exports are derived from livestock and their products.

Pakistan is luckily having some best dairy breeds like Nili, Ravi and Kundi buffaloes and Red Sindhi and Sahiwal cattle (Table 27.3) (Fig. 27.3).

Key Points

  • Animal husbandry is the breeding, farming, management and care of livestock for meat, milk, eggs, fibre, leather, vaccines and antiserum.
  • It includes proper feeding, watering, cleaning, selective breeding and veterinary treatment.
  • Livestock are domesticated animals reared commercially; about 30-40% of income in our country comes from livestock.
  • Livestock contributes 50% of agriculture value added, 11% of GDP and 8% of total exports, as printed in the main text.
  • Best dairy breeds: Nili-Ravi buffalo (1500-2300 L) and Holstein-Friesian cow (12,700 L per lactation cycle).

lessons.title: Plant Breeding: Selection, Hybridization, Acclimatization and Backcross
lessons.notes_html:
Crop and fruit yields are enhanced by improving the plants themselves — plant breeding.

27.3 Latest Techniques Applied to Enhance Crop and Fruit Yields

27.3.1 Plant Breeding

Plant breeding is the application of genetic principles to produce plants that are more useful to humans. Genetic potential of crops is improved through plant breeding. Plant breeding was initiated by Mendel when he crossed different varieties of pea plants. There are various plant breeding techniques used for changing the traits of plants to improve quality and quantity of crops.

i) Selection

One of the ancient and major techniques of plant breeding is selection. In this method plants with desirable characteristics are selected and used for further breeding and cultivation. Selection is a method used for crop improvement.

ii) Hybridization

It is the frequently used method of plant breeding in which desired traits found in different plants are brought together into a plant via cross pollination. The individual produced as a result of a cross between two genetically different parents is called a hybrid. Hybridization does not change gene contents of organisms but it produces new combinations of genes. The main objective of hybridization is to create genetic variation. Segregation and recombination produce many new gene combinations in the second generation. Improved or increased function of any biological quality in a hybrid than both of its parents refers to heterosis or hybrid vigour. Heterosis is used to increase yields, uniformity and vigour. Hybrid breeding methods are used in maize, sorghum, rice, sugar beet, onion, spinach, sunflower and broccoli.

Hybridization brings desired traits from two parents together; a backcross crosses the hybrid back with one of its parents.

Acclimatization

This is the process in which plants are introduced to a new environment where plants adjust to gradual changes of climatic conditions in their new environment, i.e. change in temperature, humidity, photoperiod and pH. In acclimatization, the introduction of genotypes from the place where it is grown to an entirely new area takes place. Acclimatization is different from adaptation: acclimatization is a short term response to the change in the environment, while adaptation is a long term response to the change in environment and occurs over several generations. Moreover, acclimatization does not bring genetic change and is reversible, while adaptation brings genetic changes and is irreversible.

AcclimatizationAdaptation
Short term responseLong term response, over several generations
No genetic change; reversibleBrings genetic changes; irreversible

Backcross

A backcross is formed when a hybrid is crossed with one of its parents, to introduce a specific trait such as disease resistance. Backcross breeding is an effective method to transfer one or a few genes controlling a specific trait from one line into a second breeding line. Backcross is significant in horticulture and animal breeding to produce desired characters in species.

Key Points

  • Plant breeding applies genetic principles to produce plants more useful to humans; it began with Mendel's pea crosses.
  • Selection: plants with desirable characteristics are selected for further breeding and cultivation.
  • Hybridization crosses two genetically different parents; it makes new gene combinations, and heterosis (hybrid vigour) increases yield, uniformity and vigour.
  • Acclimatization is a short term, reversible adjustment to a new environment with no genetic change; adaptation is long term and genetic.
  • A backcross crosses a hybrid with one of its parents to transfer a specific trait such as disease resistance.

lessons.title: Home Gardening
lessons.notes_html:
A home garden brings food, health and beauty to the house itself.

27.4 Home Gardening

A home garden is a plot of ground usually inside or near a house where ornamental flowers, fruits, vegetables and herbs are cultivated. It is a delightful and fertile region of the house. It is a place for people to live, children to play, and it also produces a variety of foods and other things for use in home and to enhance income. A well-developed home garden is a complete farming system (Fig. 27.4).

Importance

A home garden creates a healthy atmosphere in the house. It provides instant access to fresh products; one can save time and money on buying products from the market. Organic fruits and vegetables can be grown at home by skipping the chemical fertilizers and pesticides. The flavour and quality of freshly picked produce from a home garden is superior to store-bought produce with unknown chemicals. Garden plots often reduce soil erosion by holding soil in place. Ornamental plants add beauty to the garden.

The solved exercises add that a home garden also gives physical exercise and recreation, improves air quality, and teaches children about plants and nature, while reducing dependence on market produce and pesticides.

Key Points

  • A home garden is a plot inside or near a house for ornamental flowers, fruits, vegetables and herbs; a well-developed one is a complete farming system.
  • It creates a healthy environment in the house and gives instant access to fresh products, saving time and money.
  • Organic fruits and vegetables can be grown without chemical fertilizers and pesticides, with better flavour and quality.
  • Garden plots reduce soil erosion, and ornamental plants add beauty.
  • Seasonal examples: spinach and cabbage in winter, mangoes and okra in spring and summer, apples and grapes in fall.

lessons.title: Microbes in Household Food and Industrial Production
lessons.notes_html:
Not all microbes cause disease. Living organisms that are not visible to the naked eye are called microbes or microorganisms. Microbes exist everywhere in air, soil, water, the human body and inside plants and animals. Microbes are essential components of life on earth and can be beneficial to humans in several ways. Not all microbes are pathogenic. There are more microbes in the human body than the number of cells in our body; their number is estimated to be in trillions.

Numbering note: the unit opener lists this section as 27.5 Role of Microbes in Human Welfare, but the main text prints it as 27.4, with sub-sections 27.4.1 to 27.4.4. The sub-section numbers below follow the main text.

27.4.1 Role of Microbes in Household Food Processing

Microbes are useful in household food processing in a number of ways. Microbes convert food items to other varieties. By the action of Lactobacillus bacteria, yogurt can be produced from milk. Dough used to make bread is fermented using baker's yeast. Other food items produced with the help of microbes are cheese, wine, soya sauce, etc. The yeast used to make bread is also used to ferment malted cereals and fruit juices to make beverages, i.e. beer, whiskey, wine, brandy, etc. Casein is the milk protein.

27.4.2 Role of Microbes in Industrial Production

Industries use microbes to make products that are valuable to humans. Microbes produce chemicals (antibiotics) that can kill or stop the growth of disease causing organisms. Detergents used to remove oily stains contain enzymes such as lipases derived from microbes. Further, microbes help to produce bioactive molecules like Cyclosporine-A, used to suppress the immune system during organ transplant. Microbes can also be used to produce certain non-microbial products such as the diabetes medication insulin. They produce chemicals like ethanol, which is used as fuel, solvent and for various other purposes. Biofertilizers consist of living microbes that are added to soil to increase fertility.

Key Points

  • Microbes are organisms not visible to the naked eye; they are everywhere and not all are pathogenic.
  • In food, Lactobacillus makes yogurt from milk and baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments dough for bread and beverages such as beer, whiskey, wine and brandy.
  • Cheese, soya sauce and vinegar are also microbial food products, as shown in Table 27.6.
  • In industry, microbes make antibiotics, lipase detergents, Cyclosporine-A, insulin and ethanol.
  • Biofertilizers consist of living microbes added to soil to increase fertility.

lessons.title: Microbes in Sewage Treatment and Energy Production
lessons.notes_html:
Sewage and energy are the other two big welfare roles of microbes in this unit: microbes clean the waste water humans produce every day, and they can generate electricity and renewable fuels.

27.4.3 Role of Microbes in Sewage Treatment

Sewage generated by humans daily is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) to make it less harmful before releasing it into natural water bodies. The main component of sewage is organic matter, but there are other substances such as oil, heavy metals, nitrogen and phosphorous compounds (from detergents and artificial fertilizers). Microbes use the organic material in sewage as their source of carbohydrate for respiration. Treatment of sewage by microbes involves three steps:

  • i) Primary Treatment — Filtration to remove large objects, which usually go to a landfill site or incinerator. The remaining material is then allowed to settle so that much of solid material drops to the bottom of the tank. Sedimentation removes soil and small pebbles. The solid material that settles is primary sludge, while the supernatant forms the effluent, which is then passed through secondary treatment.
  • ii) Secondary Treatment — Treatment of waste water, subsequent to removal of suspended solids, by microorganisms such as algae, fungi or bacteria under aerobic or anaerobic conditions, during which organic matter in waste water is oxidized, is termed biological treatment or secondary treatment. In aerobic conditions the organic contaminants are converted to CO₂, water and other products. In anaerobic conditions the organic contaminants are converted to a biofuel gas comprising CO₂, methane or other products.
  • iii) Tertiary Treatment — The final cleaning process that improves waste water quality before it is discharged. The treatment removes remaining inorganic compounds such as nitrogen and phosphorus (Fig. 27.5).

The three steps of sewage treatment.

27.4.4 Role of Microbes in Energy Production

Microbes have tremendous potential to produce energy. A microbial fuel cell is capable of generating electricity directly from a large variety of organic and inorganic compounds using microbes as catalyst. Conventionally, fuel cells convert chemical energy to electrical energy by consumption of fuel at the anode and an oxidant at the cathode. The electrons and protons released travel through an external circuit producing electricity. Microbes can be used to convert sunlight, CO₂ and nitrogen into renewable fuel sources. Production of biodiesel from microalgae and production of hydrogen gas (H₂) by bacteria are other examples of microorganisms in energy generation.

The Extra Reading adds: SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) viruses, thought to spread from animal sources (perhaps bats), affected 26 countries with more than 8000 infected cases reported in 2003 (SARS CoV-1). The recent Coronavirus was first identified in December 2019, named COVID-19, and in March 2020 the virus was named SARS-CoV-2; it is a +ve strand RNA enveloped virus, 65-125 nm in diameter, roughly spherical. An epidemic is rapid spread of disease to a large number of people in a given population within a short period of time; a pandemic is an epidemic occurring worldwide or over a very wide area, crossing international boundaries and usually affecting a large number of people. The book's COVID-19 case and death figures are those reported at the time of writing.

Key Points

  • Sewage treatment has three steps: primary (filtration and sedimentation), secondary (microbes oxidize organic matter) and tertiary (removes nitrogen and phosphorus).
  • The main component of sewage is organic matter, which microbes use as their source of carbohydrate for respiration.
  • In aerobic secondary treatment organic contaminants become CO₂, water and other products; in anaerobic conditions they become a biofuel gas of CO₂, methane or other products.
  • Microbes produce energy in microbial fuel cells, using microbes as catalyst, with fuel consumed at the anode and an oxidant at the cathode.
  • Other microbial energy examples are biodiesel from microalgae and hydrogen gas (H₂) by bacteria.
